    Leaving Religion Without Founding Another?

    A debate from Plato to the present: critiques of religion, sciences of the religious, and spiritualities without God

    Prologuethere is no such thing as “atheism”

    The history of the critique of religion is readily told as a relay race. Lucretius supposedly passed the baton to Spinoza, Spinoza to the Enlightenment, the Enlightenment to Feuerbach, Feuerbach to Marx, Marx to Nietzsche, Nietzsche to Freud, and so on down to our contemporaries, each adding an argument to the pile until the pile finally crushed God. This story is false, and not only because it simplifies. It is false because the authors it lines up do not criticize the same thing, do not aim at the same goal, and above all criticize one another with more violence than they bring against the theologians. It is false, too, because it forgets that the harshest critique of religion has often been waged from within faith: by Pascal against the God of the philosophers, by Kierkegaard against Christendom, by Barth against religion itself, by Simone Weil against the consoling God. And it is false, finally, because it assumes that we know what the thing is that we are leaving.

    It also begins too late and looks too narrowly. Our question was born neither with the Moderns nor with Christianity. Plato was the first to raise it, the other way round: he sought to found by reason a religion of the city, and in the same stroke he invented the prison for the impious. Aristotle made the god an object of science and noted that myths serve the laws. It was in medieval Judaism and Islam, with Maimonides in Cairo and Averroes in Córdoba, that philosophy first asked whether one can think God without representing him, and reserve for the learned a truth that the Law gives to others in images. They have their place here, as do the classical thinkers who built the God of the philosophers, Montaigne, Descartes and Leibniz, and Rousseau, who drew a civil religion from it. The essay remains centred on Christian and post-Christian Europe, and this must be said frankly: the “exit from religion” described by Weber and Gauchet is first of all a Christian story, and Jewish and Muslim societies have known other paths, which this essay touches on only in passing, through Averroes, Maimonides, Arkoun and Bidar. But Christianity did not forge the weapons of its own critique alone, and to forget this would be to perpetuate the relay fable. The essay finally widens the question beyond any particular religion: wonder at the fact that there is something, from Plato to Wittgenstein, is perhaps the barest form of spirituality, and it will have its own debate.

    Two further questions run through the essay. Where does Christianity come from, since nearly all the critiques examined here are critiques of it? Part Two follows its birth between Athens and Jerusalem and examines, without indulgence, the thesis that Jesus never existed. Why do people believe? Part Nine asks anthropologists, psychologists, sociologists and the cognitive sciences what the religious disposition owes to fear, to desire, to society, to death and to the very structure of the mind.

    Eight regimes of critique

    At least eight regimes of critique must be distinguished; they cannot be added together, and they will serve as the essay's map.

    In the first, religion is an error: a false representation to be corrected, or translated into its truth. This is the regime of Epicurus and Lucretius, for whom the gods exist but take no care of us; of Spinoza, for whom God exists but is not what the vulgar believe; of Hume and d'Holbach, who explain belief by ignorance of causes; and finally of Feuerbach, for whom God is man misrecognized. In the second, religion is a symptom: not first of all a false thesis, but the expression of a world that needs it, and which must be changed in order to abolish it. This is the regime of Marx. In the third, religion is a value, or rather a way of evaluating, whose genealogy one traces, and which survives belief in God in morality, in science, in grammar itself. This is the regime of Nietzsche. In the fourth, the Christian religion and Western philosophy are caught together in a single history, that of metaphysics, and the “death of God” is not the victory of one over the other but their common completion. This is the regime of Heidegger, which Pascal had foreseen and which Marion turns around.

    The next four regimes were born later. The fifth makes religion an illusion in the technical sense: not just any error, but a belief commanded by a desire, the desire for a protecting father. This is the regime of Freud. The sixth makes religion a social function: the sacred is the form in which a society represents its own strength to itself, and no society does without it. This is the regime of Durkheim and, through the sociology of rationalization, of Weber. The seventh raises the question of secularization: are the modern categories, the State, history, progress, theological categories in disguise, or new answers to inherited questions? This is the debate of Schmitt, Löwith, Blumenberg, Gauchet, Taylor and Habermas. The eighth shifts the whole terrain: it no longer asks whether dogmas are true, it starts from experience: intuition and feeling of the universe in Schleiermacher, individual experience in James, the numinous in Otto, mysticism in Bergson, inner experience in Bataille. It is this regime that forces us to widen the question of religion into that of spirituality.

    Other authors create no new regime, but show that several are older than one thinks. Social function begins with Plato, who makes theology a law of the city, and with Aristotle, who writes that myths were added to persuade the multitude; Averroes gives its learned version, Montaigne its descriptive version, Rousseau its republican version, Girard its darkest, since he has the sacred arise from the sacrifice of a victim, which bears directly on this essay's criterion. Onto-theology takes as its target the god of Aristotle, Descartes and Leibniz. The negative theology of Plotinus and Maimonides anticipates the regime of experience, to which Wittgenstein, Levinas and Jaspers give its twentieth-century forms. Ricoeur gathers under the name of the school of suspicion Marx's symptom, Nietzsche's genealogy and Freud's illusion, and asks what one can still believe after them. Finally, the cognitive science of Boyer explains why religious beliefs are so easy to think, without saying anything about their truth.

    These regimes do not complement one another, they accuse one another, and the accusation is almost always the same: you think you have left religion, but you are still in it. Stirner hurls it at Feuerbach, Marx at Stirner, Nietzsche at all the “atheists” of his century, Heidegger at Nietzsche, Camus at Marx, and, according to a reported phrase, Onfray at Comte-Sponville. It gives the essay its guiding question: can one leave religion without founding another?

    Religion and spirituality: two words, two etymologies

    Background: The religion of the Greek city: sacrifices, festivals, oracles, impiety trials

    We still need to know what it is we are leaving. The Latin word religio received two competing etymologies in Antiquity, and their conflict is no grammarians' quarrel: it sets two conceptions of the thing against each other.

    The first is Cicero's, in the De natura deorum (On the Nature of the Gods, 45 BCE). There the Stoic Balbus distinguishes the superstitious from the religious. The superstitious are those who spent whole days praying and sacrificing so that their children might survive them, superstites; the religious are those “qui autem omnia quae ad cultum deorum pertinerent diligenter retractarent et tamquam relegerent”, who carefully went back over and, as it were, reread everything that pertained to the worship of the gods, whence their name, “ex relegendo” (II, 72). Ciceronian religio is a scruple, an attentiveness, a rereading: a way of doing things exactly. Civic and ritual, it presupposes neither dogma, nor inner faith, nor a personal relation to a god.

    The second etymology is Christian. Lactantius (c. 250-c. 325), tutor to Constantine's son, gives it in the Divinae institutiones (Divine Institutes, c. 303-311), expressly refuting Cicero: “hoc uinculo pietatis obstricti deo et religati sumus: unde ipsa religio nomen accepit, non ut Cicero interpretatus est a relegendo”, it is by this bond of piety that we are bound and tied to God, and it is from this that religion took its name, not from relegere as Cicero interpreted it (IV, 28, 3). He adds, not without irony: if the religious took their name from attentive rereading, those who pray several times a day ought to lose their title, since they reread far more (IV, 28, 10). With religare, religion becomes a bond, a personal obligation towards a single God. It is this bond that the moderns will seek to undo; and that is why the question “can one leave religion?” is first of all a Christian question.

    Two modern definitions reproduce the same opposition twenty centuries apart. Émile Durkheim, in 1912, defines religion as a collective fact: “Une religion est un système solidaire de croyances et de pratiques relatives à des choses sacrées, c'est-à-dire séparées, interdites, croyances et pratiques qui unissent en une même communauté morale, appelée Église, tous ceux qui y adhèrent”, a religion is a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, that is to say, things set apart and forbidden, beliefs and practices which unite into one single moral community, called a Church, all those who adhere to them (The Elementary Forms of Religious Life, book I, ch. 1). William James, ten years earlier, defines it as an individual fact: “the feelings, acts, and experiences of individual men in their solitude, so far as they apprehend themselves to stand in relation to whatever they may consider the divine” (The Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902, lecture II). James specifies that he takes this definition “arbitrarily”. Durkheim is on the side of Cicero and the Church, James on the side of the solitary mystic.

    The word “spirituality” has lodged itself in the gap between these two definitions. In contemporary usage, it designates what remains of James's definition once Durkheim's has been removed: an experience without a Church, a relation to the absolute without dogma or obligatory community. But it has a more precise philosophical history, which Pierre Hadot and Michel Foucault have reconstructed. For Foucault, in the lecture of 6 January 1982 at the Collège de France, spirituality is “la recherche, la pratique, l'expérience par lesquelles le sujet opère sur lui-même les transformations nécessaires pour avoir accès à la vérité”, the search, practice and experience through which the subject carries out on itself the transformations necessary to have access to the truth (The Hermeneutics of the Subject, published in 2001, p. 16). Spirituality, in this sense, is a work of the subject upon itself; the Stoics and the Epicureans had one, so did Spinoza, and perhaps Nietzsche.

    Hence a distinction that will run through the essay. Religion, in the strong sense, involves an external absolute to which the individual is bound and subjected, dogmas that state its nature, and a community that keeps its worship. Spirituality, in Foucault's sense, involves only an exercise through which the subject transforms itself. One can have the one without the other: a religion of pure observance without inner life, such as the one Cicero describes and which Kant will call Afterdienst; or a spirituality without God, such as that of the Epicureans, of Spinoza or of Comte-Sponville.

    Thesis

    My thesis is twofold. On the one hand, every “exit” from religion examined here has reinstalled an absolute in the place of God: the city of civil religion in Rousseau, Man in Feuerbach and Comte, the Self in Stirner, emancipated Humanity in Marx, Society in Durkheim, Reason in Freud, History in the revolutionaries whom Camus indicts, Being in Heidegger, Civilization in Onfray. On the other hand, and this is the paradox, those who escape the trap are those who keep something of the religious knowingly: first Spinoza, who retains the name of God; then the Nietzsche of § 344 of The Gay Science, who admits that his own fire still comes from the Christian blaze.

    Widening the question to spirituality makes it possible to state this more precisely, and this is the hypothesis I shall put to the test. What distinguishes a successful exit from a refoundation is perhaps not the presence of God, but that of an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded, and the critique of which becomes sacrilege; self-offering freely consented to does not fall under it. The criterion admits of degrees: refoundation in the strict sense installs an absolute that demands, as in Plato, Rousseau or Comte; soft refoundation is content with the need to consecrate without demanding anything, the need for which Engels will reproach Feuerbach and which we shall find again in Ferry. A spirituality of exercise, which transforms the subject without subjecting it to anything external, would be the only exit that does not refound. It has two serious adversaries. Durkheim, for whom no society can live without the sacred, and who would make every private spirituality a religion unaware of itself. And Blumenberg, for whom the question itself is badly posed, since it presupposes that whatever occupies the place of God is a god. They will have to be given their strongest form.

    Dostoevsky occupies a place apart here. He does not argue, he embodies; and the figure he invents, the Grand Inquisitor, shows what becomes of a religion from which God has been removed. It will serve as a touchstone down to our contemporaries, among whom we shall find again, with Michel Onfray, the temptation to keep the Church while losing God. Voltaire, a century before Dostoevsky, had in fact written the Inquisitor's programme in a single alexandrine: “Si Dieu n'existait pas, il faudrait l'inventer”, if God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him.

    Top of the part

    Part Onethe Ancients and the monotheisms before reason7 authors

    Background: Greek myths: sources, gods and divine generations · Platonism and Neoplatonism: from the Academy to the Renaissance · Islam: birth, expansion and thought, from Muhammad to Averroes · Exodus: Moses, the departure from Egypt, Sinai and the Law · Medieval Christendom: from the fall of Rome to the stake · From the Judges to the Kings: Samuel, Saul, David and Goliath, Solomon and the Temple · The short books: Ruth, Esther, Jonah, Tobit, Judith, Lamentations, Ezra and Nehemiah

    The critique of religion, which is usually made to begin with Spinoza or the Enlightenment, has an ancient and medieval prehistory, which supplied it with its most durable arguments and its most radical gestures. Plato and Aristotle wanted a rational theology, which Plato armed with a penal law. The Epicureans invented the idea that religion is an error that causes suffering. Plotinus showed that one could seek union with the principle without temple or priest. Averroes and Maimonides, the one a Muslim, the other a Jew, asked what becomes of the revealed Law when a philosopher reads it. Eckhart, finally, carried the critique of the image of God into the heart of Christian mysticism. All of them already raise our question: some leave religion without leaving the gods, others criticize the representation of God in the name of God himself.

    Plato428/427-348/347 BCEthe first theology, and the first prison for the impious

    Background: Greek myths: sources, gods and divine generations · Platonism and Neoplatonism: from the Academy to the Renaissance · Plato's philosophy: Forms, soul, city, the Good · The religion of the Greek city: sacrifices, festivals, oracles, impiety trials · The philosophers against the myths: from Xenophanes to allegory · Plato's myths: Er, Gyges, the noble lie, the androgyne · Rousseau's thought: state of nature, social contract, general will, Emile · The thought of Iris Murdoch: the novels, the Good, attention

    We must begin with Plato, and not only for reasons of chronology. It was he who invented the word theology in the sense in which we understand it, speech about the gods subjected to rules (the term θεολογία, theologia, appears in Book II of the Republic, when Socrates lays down the “τύποι περὶ θεολογίας”, the models to which the poets' stories about the gods must conform, 379a); it was he who gave the first philosophical demonstration of the existence of the gods; and it was he, finally, who wrote the first penal law against unbelief. The three gestures are linked, and they are linked in Book X of the Laws (Νόμοι, Nomoi), his last work, unfinished at his death and published, according to tradition, by his disciple Philip of Opus. Anyone who wants to know what it means to “found a religion” through philosophy must read these thirty pages: they are the original of which almost all later refoundations are copies.

    The book opens on a problem of criminal law. The Athenian, who leads the dialogue with the Cretan Clinias and the Lacedaemonian Megillus, has finished legislating on acts of violence and comes to outrages against the gods. Before fixing the penalties, he makes a diagnosis that is the founding text of every typology of unbelief: “θεοὺς ἡγούμενος εἶναι κατὰ νόμους οὐδεὶς πώποτε οὔτε ἔργον ἀσεβὲς ἠργάσατο ἑκὼν οὔτε λόγον ἀφῆκεν ἄνομον, ἀλλὰ ἓν δή τι τῶν τριῶν πάσχων, ἢ τοῦτο, ὅπερ εἶπον, οὐχ ἡγούμενος, ἢ τὸ δεύτερον ὄντας οὐ φροντίζειν ἀνθρώπων, ἢ τρίτον εὐπαραμυθήτους εἶναι θυσίαις τε καὶ εὐχαῖς παραγομένους”, no one who believes, as the laws prescribe, that the gods exist has ever willingly committed an impious act or let slip a lawless word; rather, one of three things has befallen him: either he does not believe that they exist, or, secondly, he believes that they exist but take no care of men, or, thirdly, that they are easily appeased, won over by sacrifices and prayers (885b). Three impieties, then: atheism properly so called, indifferent deism, and what might be called mercantile religion, the kind that thinks it can buy the gods.

    This table already contains half of the essay. The first impiety is the one Plato attributes to the “learned men” of his time, natural philosophers and sophists, who explain the world by nature and chance and make the gods conventions of the law (889e-890a): it is, twenty-three centuries before d'Holbach, the regime of error. The second is the position that Epicurus will maintain a generation later: gods who exist but concern themselves with nothing. The third, finally, is the target of the whole moral critique of religion, from Spinoza to the Enlightenment and Kant. Plato therefore fights on two fronts. Against the unbeliever, he defends the existence and the providence of the gods; against the devout, their incorruptibility. His religion is at once an apologetics and a critique of popular religion, and that is what makes it formidable: it has already absorbed the objection.

    Then comes the proof, the first in history to present itself as a demonstration. It starts not, as Aristotle's will, from the motion of the heavens, but from the soul. Every communicated motion presupposes a first motion that is not communicated; this first motion is “τὴν δυναμένην αὐτὴν αὑτὴν κινεῖν κίνησιν”, the motion capable of moving itself (896a). Now this self-moving motion is the very definition of the soul; Cousin translates: “Une substance qui a la faculté de se mouvoir elle-même”, a substance that has the faculty of moving itself. The soul is therefore prior to the body, and the good souls that move the stars are gods. The Athenian concludes with a rhetorical question in which one recognizes the formula that tradition attributed to Thales: “ἔσθʼ ὅστις ταῦτα ὁμολογῶν ὑπομενεῖ μὴ θεῶν εἶναι πλήρη πάντα;”, is there anyone who, granting this, will bear to deny that all things are full of gods? (899b). I leave aside the worth of the argument, which modern criticism, from Hume to Kant, has taken apart thoroughly enough; what matters to me is its status: for the first time, belief in the gods is no longer handed down by the poets and the ancestors but demonstrated by a philosopher, and, once demonstrated, it can be required.

    After the proof comes the law, and it is terrible. Plato provides for three prisons in his city; one of them, near the place where the nocturnal council meets, bears the name “σωφρονιστήριον”, sôphronistêrion, the house where one is made wise (908a). The impious man in good faith, the one who has gone astray through want of judgement and not through vice, will spend at least five years there, with no visitors other than the members of the nocturnal council, who will come to converse with him “ἐπὶ νουθετήσει τε καὶ τῇ τῆς ψυχῆς σωτηρίᾳ”, for admonition and for the salvation of his soul; on his release, if he seems to have grown wise, he will live among the wise; if not, should he be convicted a second time, “θανάτῳ ζημιούσθω”, let him be punished with death (909a). Those who join impiety to trickery, the charlatans who claim to summon the dead and to sway the gods, will be shut up for life in the prison in the wilderness, and their corpse will be cast beyond the borders, unburied; any free man who buried it could be prosecuted for impiety (909c). To cut the root of the evil, a last law forbids private worship: “Ἱερὰ μηδὲ εἷς ἐν ἰδίαις οἰκίαις ἐκτήσθω”, let no one possess a shrine in his private house; whoever wishes to sacrifice will go to the public temples, into the hands of the priests (909d).

    I have proposed that a religious refoundation be recognized by the presence of an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded. Book X of the Laws is the pure case of it, and a philosophical case: it is not priests persecuting philosophers, it is a philosopher who founds a state religion, who demonstrates its articles, and who entrusts to a council of the wise the task of re-educating, and then of killing, those who do not adhere to it. Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor, who wants the happiness of men and to that end takes from them the freedom to believe, has his ancestor here; and one understands why Karl Popper, in 1945, made Plato the first enemy of the “open society” (I summarize the general thesis of The Open Society and Its Enemies, vol. I, without citing a page). Yet Plato must be given his best form. The sôphronistêrion is a compulsory school, not a place of torture; the impious man in good faith is treated there as sick in soul, not as a criminal; and the religion imposed on him is not that of the poets, whom Plato despises, but a purified theology in which the gods are good, do not lie, and cannot be bought. The violence of the law serves a religion more moral than the one it replaces. That is the argument of all later refoundations, and what makes them dangerous: Rousseau's civil religion, Comte's cult of Humanity, the education of the new man by the party, all plead that they are replacing a superstition with a truth.

    There is, however, another Plato, who nourished the critique of religion rather than state religion: the Plato of the Euthyphro, an early dialogue in which Socrates, a few days before his trial for impiety, questions a soothsayer very sure of his own piety. His question has become philosophy's most durable weapon against revealed morality: “ἆρα τὸ ὅσιον ὅτι ὅσιόν ἐστιν φιλεῖται ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν, ἢ ὅτι φιλεῖται ὅσιόν ἐστιν;”, is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or is it pious because it is loved by the gods? (10a). If the pious is pious because the gods love it, morality is merely the arbitrariness of a sovereign will; if they love it because it is pious, piety has its reason in itself, and the gods are merely the witnesses of an order they did not make. The dilemma does not deny the gods, it makes them useless for grounding the good. We shall meet it again, without Plato's name, in the quarrel that closes Part Four: Bayle maintaining that a society of atheists can have morals, Kant making religion the recognition of our duties as if they were divine commands, Dostoevsky putting into Ivan's mouth the claim that there is no virtue without immortality. It is a constructed confrontation, since none of them replies expressly to the Euthyphro; but all of them inhabit the question that Socrates opened.

    Between the Socrates of the Euthyphro and the Athenian of the Laws there is thus a tension that Plato did not resolve, and which I take to be the very tension of this essay: on one side, the philosopher who questions religion to the point of dissolving it into morality; on the other, the legislator who protects religion to the point of imprisoning those who question it. The trial of Socrates, accused of not recognizing the gods of the city (Apology, 24b-c, which I paraphrase), is the one that the law of the Laws makes possible: Plato watched his master die for impiety and wrote, forty years later, a law against impiety. One could not say more brutally that the exit from religion, when philosophy leads it, can end in a religion more demanding than the one it was leaving.

    There remains a third Plato, the Plato of the cave, whom the widening to spirituality obliges us to take seriously. In Book VII of the Republic, education is not the filling of an empty soul, it is a conversion of the gaze: just as an eye could turn towards the light only together with the whole body, one must, says Socrates, turn the whole soul, “σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ἐκ τοῦ γιγνομένου περιακτέον εἶναι”, it must be turned round, with the whole soul, away from what comes to be (518c), and the art of education is “τῆς περιαγωγῆς”, the art of this turning round (518d). The περιαγωγή, periagôgê, is the first philosophical name for what Foucault will call spirituality: a transformation of the subject necessary for access to the truth. And the goal of the conversion, the Good, is placed by Plato beyond all that is: it is not an essence, but “ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας”, beyond essence, which it surpasses in dignity and in power (VI, 509b). This Good beyond being has neither temple, nor priest, nor penal law. Plotinus will make it the One, Dionysius and Maimonides the God of whom nothing can be affirmed, Levinas the Other who escapes ontology.

    Plato thus holds both branches of our alternative: the civil religion demonstrated and imposed, with its nocturnal council and its prison for the impious; the spirituality of conversion, which subjects the soul to nothing external but turns it towards a Good it does not possess. The history that follows could be read as the struggle of these two Platos. Lucretius rises up against the first; the Neoplatonists develop the second; and Christianity, which inherits both, will make the Euthyphro a theological question (does God will the good because he is good?) and the Laws an institution.

    In literature Aristophanes, The Clouds (423 BCE) ; Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, Citadelle (1948)

    In The Clouds, the peasant Strepsiades comes to Socrates to learn the art of not paying his debts, and discovers that the master has replaced Zeus with the Vortex: “J'ignorais et que Zeus n'existât pas et que le Tourbillon régnât aujourd'hui à sa place”, I did not know that Zeus did not exist and that the Vortex now reigned in his place. When his son, trained in the same school, proves to him that a son has the right to beat his father, he changes his mind, “Insensé que j'étais. J'ai pris ce vase d'argile pour un dieu”, fool that I was, I took this earthen pot for a god, and sets fire to the thinkery: “Fais ton œuvre, ô torche ! jette une vive flamme !”, do your work, O torch, throw out a bright flame!

    Why here: twenty-four years before the trial of 399, the comedy shows the city burning the impious man, and doing so in the name of the fathers and the gods. Laws X will turn this reflex into an institution, with the sôphronistêrion and death for the reoffender; Aristophanes makes it laughable, and Plato, in the Apology, counts the play among the causes of Socrates' death. The legislator of the Laws is a Strepsiades who has learned to demonstrate.

    Citadelle, Saint-Exupéry's posthumous book, gives voice to a Berber chieftain who builds his empire by imposing rites, ceremonies and constraints, because, he says in substance, it is constraint that founds meaning and man left to himself comes apart. It is the legislator of the Laws without the demonstrated theology: the city that manufactures a sacred for itself in order to hold together.

    Sources: Aristophanes, The Clouds, French trans. Eugène Talbot (423 BCE) ; Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, Citadelle (posthumous, 1948).

    Portrait: D'après Silanion, photo Marie-Lan Nguyen, CC BY 2.5

    Aristotle384-322 BCEa god who thinks only himself

    Background: Greek myths: sources, gods and divine generations · Aristotle's philosophy: act and potency, causes, the unmoved mover, virtue, contemplation · The philosophers against the myths: from Xenophanes to allegory · Metaphysics and the proofs of the existence of God: from Anselm to Kant

    Aristotle wrote no law against the impious, and tradition even relates that he had to leave Athens in 323 under threat of a trial for impiety, after the death of Alexander (I report a late biographical tradition, whose details are uncertain). He nonetheless supplied Western theology with its most durable concept and, without meaning to, supplied its critique with its two strongest arguments: the idea of a god indifferent to human beings, and the idea that religious myths were invented in order to govern.

    The first is contained in Book Λ (XII) of the Metaphysics (τὰ μετὰ τὰ φυσικά, ta meta ta phusika), a brief, dense treatise, probably independent of the rest of the collection, which tradition traces back to the editor Andronicus of Rhodes (1st century BCE), though the origin of the title is not certain. The eternal motion of the heavens requires a first mover that is not itself moved, otherwise one would go on to infinity. Now what moves without being moved is the object of desire: “κινεῖ δὴ ὡς ἐρώμενον, κινούμενα δὲ τἆλλα κινεῖ”, it moves, then, as that which is loved, while the other things move by being moved (Λ 7, 1072b3). The world hangs upon it, “ἐκ τοιαύτης ἄρα ἀρχῆς ἤρτηται ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ φύσις”, it is on such a principle, then, that the heavens and nature depend (1072b13-14); but it does nothing for the world. It does not create it, since the world is eternal; it does not govern it, since it does not act; it attracts it, as the beloved attracts the lover, without knowing it.

    What, then, does it do? It thinks, and, being what is best, it can think only what is best, that is to say itself. Chapter 9 draws the conclusion with admirable dryness: to think anything other than itself would be a fall, for “μὴ ὁρᾶν ἔνια κρεῖττον ἢ ὁρᾶν”, it is better not to see some things than to see them; therefore “αὑτὸν ἄρα νοεῖ, εἴπερ ἐστὶ τὸ κράτιστον, καὶ ἔστιν ἡ νόησις νοήσεως νόησις”, it is itself, then, that it thinks, if indeed it is the most excellent of things, and its thinking is a thinking of thinking (Λ 9, 1074b32-35). Aristotle's god knows neither Socrates, nor the city, nor the prayers addressed to it; it can neither reward nor punish. It is, in the formula that comes earlier, “ζῷον ἀΐδιον ἄριστον”, an eternal and most excellent living being (1072b29), whose life is the activity of the intellect, and this life we share only “μικρὸν χρόνον”, for a short time (1072b15).

    Hence the paradox. By the table of the Laws, Aristotle falls under the second impiety, that of gods who take no care of human beings; Plato's Athenian would have sent him to the sôphronistêrion. Yet this indifferent god became, through Averroes, Maimonides and Thomas Aquinas, the God of the philosophers of the three monotheisms: the first mover of the Thomist “five ways” is a direct reprise of it. Everything Aristotle denied it had to be added: creation, knowledge of particulars, providence; and the tension between the Aristotelian god and the biblical God has never ceased to work on theology. I hold that Pascal was right in substance (Part Three): Aristotle's god is an object of contemplation, not of religion, and one does not pray to the thinking of thinking. But that is precisely what makes it an ancestor of the spiritualities without God: an absolute that demands nothing.

    Aristotle is not entirely consistent on this point, and this must be said so as not to modernize him. In the Nicomachean Ethics, he writes that the man who lives according to the intellect is “θεοφιλέστατος”, the most loved by the gods, and he immediately adds a conditional: “εἰ γάρ τις ἐπιμέλεια τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ὑπὸ θεῶν γίνεται, ὥσπερ δοκεῖ”, for if the gods take some care of human affairs, as people think (X, 8, 1179a22-24). The “as people think”, ὥσπερ δοκεῖ, marks a calculated prudence: Aristotle does not deny popular providence, he lodges it in opinion without integrating it into his theology.

    The second argument is more discreet, and more important. In chapter 8 of the same Book Λ, after calculating the number of the celestial movers, Aristotle makes a remark worthy of a historian of religions before the term existed: the ancients, he says, handed down in the form of myth that the stars are gods and that the divine encompasses the whole of nature; and he goes on: “τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ μυθικῶς ἤδη προσῆκται πρὸς τὴν πειθὼ τῶν πολλῶν καὶ πρὸς τὴν εἰς τοὺς νόμους καὶ τὸ συμφέρον χρῆσιν”, the rest has since been added in mythical form, to persuade the many and for its usefulness with a view to the laws and the common interest (1074b3-5). Gods in human form, genealogies, metamorphoses into animals: all this is superadded. Only the kernel, the idea that the first substances are divine, deserves to be said “θείως”, divinely, and it is a relic of a lost wisdom that the revolutions of the arts have several times destroyed and recovered.

    These three lines reach far. They contain the thesis of religion as social function, which Durkheim will systematize in 1912, and that of religion as a political instrument, which the libertines and the anonymous author of the Treatise of the Three Impostors will harden into the accusation of fraud. But in a subtler form than in his heirs: Aristotle does not say that the legislators lied, he says that myth was added to a truth, to make it effective among those who cannot contemplate it. Popular religion is a useful translation of a philosophical truth. Averroes in The Decisive Treatise, Spinoza in making Scripture a pedagogy of obedience, Hegel in making religion the truth in the form of representation, will give successive versions of it. It is a lineage, not a series of attested responses; but it is clear enough for me to hold Aristotle, and not Lucretius, to be the true ancestor of the “elitist” reading of religion, which does not deny its content but relegates its form.

    To him, finally, we owe the expression that will occupy Heidegger. In Book E of the Metaphysics, he classifies the theoretical sciences: “ὥστε τρεῖς ἂν εἶεν φιλοσοφίαι θεωρητικαί, μαθηματική, φυσική, θεολογική”, so there would be three theoretical philosophies, mathematics, physics, theology (E 1, 1026a18-19). First philosophy is thus at once the science of being qua being and the science of the highest being, the divine. It is this double vocation, ontology and theology fused, that Heidegger will call the onto-theo-logical constitution of metaphysics, and that he will make the common source of Western philosophy and of the Christian God of the theologians (we shall meet it again in Part Ten). If Heidegger is right, philosophy cannot lead the critique of religion, since it is already, and has been ever since Aristotle, a theology. This is the most radical of the accusations in this essay, you think you have left religion, but you are still in it, addressed not to this or that author but to metaphysics as a whole; it has its origin in an adjective of Aristotle's.

    There remains a spiritual Aristotle, an unexpected one. In Book X of the Nicomachean Ethics, the happiest life is the contemplative life, and Aristotle describes it in terms that border on mysticism: such a life “κρείττων ἢ κατʼ ἄνθρωπον”, would be higher than the human level, for it is not insofar as he is a man that one will live it, “ἀλλʼ ᾗ θεῖόν τι ἐν αὐτῷ ὑπάρχει”, but insofar as there is something divine in him; and we must not listen to those who advise man to think human thoughts and the mortal to think mortal thoughts, but must on the contrary, “ἐφʼ ὅσον ἐνδέχεται ἀθανατίζειν”, as far as is possible, make ourselves immortal (X, 7, 1177b26-33). The verb ἀθανατίζειν, athanatizein, is one of the most astonishing in the Greek philosophical language. It promises no survival; it designates a way of living, here and now, at the height of what does not die, without worship, without prayer, without community, through the sole exercise of the intellect.

    Aristotle's best lesson perhaps lies there. He supplied the religion of the philosophers with its god and its critique with its sociological suspicion; but above all he showed that one could have a relation to the divine that is neither a belief, nor an obedience, nor a hope. The god who thinks only himself demands no sacrifice, since he does not know that we exist; the man who makes himself immortal by thinking submits to nothing, he rises. It is, in a form that is still theological, the spirituality of exercise which I have hypothesized to be the only exit that does not refound. Spinoza, who did not like Aristotle, will give its version without transcendence with the intellectual love of God, and the eternity that he says is felt and experienced (Part Three) is very close to the Aristotelian ἀθανατίζειν.

    In literature Dante, Divina Commedia (1321)

    In the fourth canto of the Inferno, in Limbo where the righteous who did not know Christ dwell, Dante glimpses “'l maestro di color che sanno / seder tra filosofica famiglia”, the master of those who know, seated among his philosophic family, whom all look upon and honour. In the last canto of the Paradiso, the final vision addresses the eternal light “che sola in te sidi, / sola t'intendi, e da te intelletta / e intendente te ami e arridi”, you who alone abide in yourself, alone understand yourself, and, understood by yourself and understanding yourself, love yourself and smile upon yourself; and the poem ends on “l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle”, the love that moves the sun and the other stars.

    Why here: the two cantos give the Christian destiny of Aristotle's god. Line 124 is the νόησις νοήσεως in the vernacular, a thinking that thinks only itself; line 145 is the mover of Metaphysics Λ 7, which moves “as that which is loved”. Dante adds what Aristotle denied them, a smile turned towards the creature. And the philosopher who supplied this god remains in Limbo: honoured, cited, excluded from salvation by the very religion he equipped. The essay says the same thing in prose when it makes Λ 9 the God of the philosophers of the three monotheisms.

    Sources: Dante, Inferno IV, 131-133 ; Paradiso XXXIII, 124-126 and 145 (1321).

    Portrait: D'après Lysippe, photo Jastrow, Public domain

    Epicurus and Lucretius341-270 BCE; c. 98-c. 55 BCEterror and peace

    Background: The philosophy of Epicurus: atoms, canonic, pleasure and the remedy for fears · Lucretius and the De rerum natura: nature explained against religion · The Hellenistic schools: Stoicism, Epicureanism, Scepticism, wisdom as a way of life · The philosophers against the myths: from Xenophanes to allegory · D'Holbach: materialism, the Système de la nature, the militant atheism of the Enlightenment · Sisyphus and the underworld: Hades, Tantalus, the Danaids · The Trojan War: Iphigenia at Aulis, the wrath of Achilles, Priam

    Let us first correct an image: Epicurus is not an atheist. The Letter to Menoeceus, preserved by Diogenes Laertius in Book X of the Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, affirms the existence of the gods and even makes it the first article of wisdom. In Octave Hamelin's translation (1910): “Commence par te persuader qu'un dieu est un animal immortel et bienheureux, te conformant en cela à l'anticipation du dieu qui est gravée en toi”, begin by persuading yourself that a god is an immortal and blessed living being, in keeping with the common notion of god engraved in you; then: “Car les dieux existent, attendu que nous connaissons leur existence par une intuition évidente. Mais, quant à leur nature, ils ne sont pas tels que la foule le croit”, for the gods exist, since our knowledge of them is a matter of clear vision; but as to their nature, they are not such as the many believe. The Epicurean critique bears not on the existence of the gods, but on their character. The gods of the crowd grow angry, reward, punish, demand sacrifices; those of Epicurus, perfectly happy, concern themselves with nothing, for any care would disturb their blessedness.

    Hence the sentence that overturns the very notion of impiety: “Et celui-là n'est pas impie qui nie les dieux de la foule, c'est celui qui attribue aux dieux ce que leur prêtent les opinions de la foule”, the impious man is not the one who denies the gods of the many, but the one who attaches to the gods what the opinions of the many ascribe to them. The impious man is no longer the unbeliever, but the devout man who forms an unworthy idea of God. This reversal Spinoza will take up, and Simone Weil will push it to its limit in speaking of a purifying atheism. Religious error, for Epicurus, is first of all a lapse of metaphysical taste: we lend the gods our passions.

    This error is serious because it causes suffering. Epicurean philosophy is a therapeutics, and the religion of the crowd is, along with the fear of death, one of the two great causes of the soul's disturbance. Against the latter, the Letter gives the famous formula: “Prends l'habitude de penser que la mort n'est rien relativement à nous”, accustom yourself to thinking that death is nothing to us. The two fears are linked, for one fears the gods for what they will do with us after death: remove the one, and the other falls.

    Lucretius gives this therapeutics its epic form and its violence. The De rerum natura (On the Nature of Things), a didactic poem in six books whose date of composition is uncertain and whose author is almost unknown, opens with a eulogy of Epicurus that is a battle painting. Human life lay on the ground, shamefully, “humana ante oculos foede cum vita iaceret / in terris oppressa gravi sub religione”, crushed beneath the weight of religion (I, 62-63); and it was a Greek, a mortal, who first dared to raise his eyes against it, “primum Graius homo mortalis tollere contra / est oculos ausus” (I, 66-67). The victory is total and it has a precise meaning: “quare religio pedibus subiecta vicissim / opteritur, nos exaequat victoria caelo”, therefore religion in its turn is cast beneath our feet and trampled, and the victory makes us equal to heaven (I, 78-79).

    This last line announces our whole problem. Victory over religion makes us equal to heaven. Lucretius does not say merely that man is liberated, but that he takes the place of the gods, or at least rises to their height. The end of the Letter to Menoeceus promises it to the disciple: “vivras comme un dieu parmi les hommes”, you will live like a god among men. The exit from religion is accomplished as a divinization of man. Feuerbach, nineteen centuries later, will say nothing else, and Stirner will reproach him for it.

    Then comes the example, the most famous passage of the poem. So that no one should think that philosophy leads to impiety, Lucretius recalls that it is religion that has given birth to crimes, “religio peperit scelerosa atque impia facta” (I, 83), and he tells of the sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis: the girl led to the altar not for her wedding but to be slaughtered by her father, so that the Greek fleet might obtain a favourable wind. The account closes on the line that the whole libertine tradition engraved on the pediment of its books: “tantum religio potuit suadere malorum”, so great the evils religion could prompt (I, 101).

    The word religio in Lucretius does not have its Christian sense. It designates the scrupulous fear of the gods, the feeling of being bound by sacred obligations, and it is this feeling, more than any dogmas, that Lucretius combats. His critique belongs entirely to the regime of error: the fear of the gods comes from ignorance of natural causes, and atomist physics, by explaining lightning, earthquakes and disease, dispels the terror. But it already contains a spiritual dimension that the moderns will forget: knowledge of nature is not an end in itself, it is an exercise that procures ataraxia, the absence of disturbance.

    Michel Onfray will claim Epicurus and Lucretius as his ancestors. That is half right. He inherits from them the regime of error and the hatred of priests, not their piety: Epicurus and Lucretius, who mock the religion of the crowd, keep gods, and these gods are a model of life. The Epicureans leave religion without leaving the divine: it is the first form, and perhaps the wisest, of my paradox.

    In literature Horace, Odes (23 BCE) ; Giacomo Leopardi, La ginestra (1836) ; Marguerite Yourcenar, Memoirs of Hadrian (1951)

    Horace's ode I, 34 opens with the confession of a disciple of Epicurus: “Parcus deorum cultor et infrequens, / insanientis dum sapientiae / consultus erro”, a sparing and infrequent worshipper of the gods, while I strayed, versed in a wisdom that was folly; then a clap of thunder from a clear sky, “per purum tonantis”, brings him back to the gods, for Jupiter has driven his chariot without the help of a cloud, which the Epicurean physics of lightning does not foresee.

    Why here: the poem shows, from within and with irony, the fragility of the regime of error. Lucretius explains lightning to dispel fear; an unexplained bolt is enough for fear to make a god again. Hume will make a law of it: flux and reflux.

    Eighteen centuries later, Leopardi, who had read Lucretius, writes La ginestra at the foot of Vesuvius: the broom that grows on the lava asks nothing of heaven, does not think itself the centre of the world, and bends without pride beneath the flow that will destroy it; the poem mocks the centuries that paint on these slopes “dell'umana gente / "le magnifiche sorti e progressive"”, the magnificent and progressive destinies of the human race, and says, before the human anthill crushed by the lava, “Non so se il riso o la pietà prevale”, I do not know whether laughter or pity prevails; the broom will bow “sotto il fascio mortal non renitente / il tuo capo innocente”, unresisting beneath the mortal burden, its innocent head, “ma non piegato insino allora indarno / codardamente supplicando innanzi / al futuro oppressor”, but not having bowed it until then in vain, cravenly pleading before its future oppressor. It is Lucretius' ataraxia without his happy gods, and without the hope that knowledge will heal. Yourcenar, finally, lends her Hadrian the position of the Epicurean emperor who maintains the cults of the Empire without believing in them and composes his Animula vagula blandula in the face of death: religion kept as a form, the divine kept as a question.

    Sources: Horace, Odes I, 34 (23 BCE) ; Giacomo Leopardi, “La ginestra, o il fiore del deserto”, Canti XXXIV (1836) ; Marguerite Yourcenar, Memoirs of Hadrian (1951).

    Plotinus205-270a mysticism without a Church

    Background: Platonism and Neoplatonism: from the Academy to the Renaissance · The philosophy of Plotinus: the hypostases, procession and conversion · From Constantine to Theodosius: Christianity as the religion of the Empire · Porphyry: the editor of Plotinus and the critic of the Christians · The mysteries and Orphism: Eleusis, Orpheus, Cybele, Isis, Mithras · The thought of Pierre Hadot: ancient philosophy as a way of life

    Plotinus is one of the few Ancients in this story who neither fought nor founded any religion, and that is precisely why he must appear here. Born in Egypt, a pupil of Ammonius Saccas in Alexandria, he taught in Rome from 244 onwards and did not begin to write until he was fifty. After his death his fifty-four treatises were arranged by his disciple Porphyry into six groups of nine, the Enneads (Ἐννεάδες, the “nines”), in a thematic order that is not the order of composition; Porphyry added a Life of Plotinus, which is our main source. The Plotinus of this Life “paraissait honteux d'avoir un corps”, seemed ashamed of having a body, refused to let anyone paint his portrait, and never spoke of his family or his homeland (Life, 1, trans. Bouillet). He was a teacher, not a founder; and yet he described with precision an experience of the absolute that owes nothing to a revelation, a Church or a cult.

    The starting point is Platonic. Of the Good of the Republic, beyond essence, Plotinus makes the principle of everything, the One (τὸ ἕν, to hen), and he draws every consequence from the formula. If the One is beyond essence, it is also beyond thought: “ὅτι ἐπέκεινα οὐσίας, ἐπέκεινα καὶ ἐνεργείας καὶ ἐπέκεινα νοῦ καὶ νοήσεως”, because it is beyond essence, it is also beyond activity, beyond intellect and thought (I 7, 1). The distance from Aristotle is great: his first principle was a thought thinking itself; that of Plotinus is above thought, and does not even think itself: one treatise goes so far as to say that it is not absurd that it should not know itself (V 6, 6). Between the One and us come, in descending order, the Intellect (νοῦς, nous), which is Aristotelian thought demoted to second place, then the World Soul; everything proceeds from the One by superabundance, without decision or creation, as light proceeds from the sun.

    But Neoplatonism is less a cosmology than a path of return. The soul that has scattered itself among bodies must climb back to its source, and the method of this ascent is a stripping away. At the end of treatise V 3, having shown that the One can be neither spoken nor thought, Plotinus asks how it can be seen, and answers with two words, perhaps the most famous in the whole of Western mysticism: “Πῶς ἂν οὖν τοῦτο γένοιτο; Ἄφελε πάντα”, how then could this come about? Take away everything (V 3, 17). One is not united with the absolute by adding a belief, a rite or a body of knowledge, but by removing everything that is not it.

    The experience itself is described at the end of treatise VI 9, On the Good or the One, which Porphyry placed at the end of the whole work as its crowning. The one who has seen, says Plotinus, cannot say that he has seen, for there were no longer two, the seer and the seen: “ἐπεὶ τοίνυν δύο οὐκ ἦν, ἀλλʼ ἓν ἦν αὐτὸς ὁ ἰδὼν πρὸς τὸ ἑωραμένον, ὡς ἂν μὴ ἑωραμένον, ἀλλʼ ἡνωμένον”, since there were not two, but the one who saw was one with what was seen, as though he had not seen it but been united with it (VI 9, 11). Plotinus compares it to the mysteries, whose secret may not be divulged to the uninitiated: not because that would be sacrilege, but because the thing cannot be divulged. And the treatise, and so the Enneads, ends on the formula that sums everything up: the life of the gods and of godlike men is “ἀπαλλαγὴ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν τῆιδε, βίος ἀνήδονος τῶν τῆιδε, φυγὴ μόνου πρὸς μόνον”, release from the other things of this world, a life that takes no pleasure in the things of this world, flight of the alone to the alone (VI 9, 11). Bouillet's translation adds “Dieu” and “l'âme”, God and the soul, which the Greek does not name: a small example of the way the Christian tradition read Plotinus.

    What is striking is the complete absence of religious apparatus in this experience. No revelation: the One does not speak, does not manifest itself in history, chooses no people. No grace: it is the soul that strips itself bare, through philosophy and virtue. No Church: the flight is “of the alone to the alone”. No cult, or rather a sovereign contempt for cult: Porphyry reports that Amelius, a disciple punctilious in sacrificing, wanted to take Plotinus to the festival of the new moon, and that Plotinus replied: “C'est à ces dieux de venir me chercher, et non pas à moi d'aller les trouver”, it is for those gods to come to me, not for me to go to them (Life, 10, trans. Bouillet); Porphyry admits that the disciples, not understanding this pride, did not dare to question him. All of this is nonetheless religious in James's sense: a solitary experience of what the subject holds to be divine. Porphyry gives the count with an archivist's precision: during the six years he lived with him, Plotinus “eut quatre fois le bonheur de toucher à ce but, non par simple puissance, mais par un acte réel et ineffable”, four times had the happiness of reaching this goal, not merely in potency but by a real and ineffable act, and Porphyry himself only once, at the age of sixty-eight (Life, 23, trans. Bouillet). The last words of the dying Plotinus, according to the same Life, were: “je m'efforce de réunir ce qu'il y a de divin en nous à ce qu'il y a de divin dans l'univers”, I am striving to unite what is divine in us with what is divine in the universe (Life, 2, trans. Bouillet).

    It will be objected that this mysticism did not leave religion, since it had never entered it in the Christian sense; and that Plotinus is a pious pagan, who believed in the gods, in daemons, in providence. This is true, and it is what makes him precious: he shows that an experience of the absolute can exist without any of the structures that modern critique will attack. The sacrifice criterion does not apply to him. The One demands nothing: it is what the soul turns towards of its own accord when it ceases to scatter itself. It is he, far more than Epicurus, who is the distant ancestor of the spiritualities without God of the last part. And it is no accident that Pierre Hadot, before writing on the spiritual exercises of antiquity, devoted his first book of his own to Plotinus, Plotin ou la simplicité du regard (1963): he saw in him the model of an inner transformation that dispenses with every institution.

    Plotinus had two posterities, which fought each other. The first is pagan and polemical. Porphyry, his editor, wrote a treatise Against the Christians in fifteen books, condemned to the flames by the Christian emperors and known to us only in fragments; and Plotinus himself composed a treatise against the Gnostics (II 9), which Porphyry entitles Against the Gnostics, in which he reproaches these sects of Christian origin for despising the world and its creator. Neoplatonism was thus, in the third century, the last great philosophy to oppose rising Christianity, and Julian the Apostate would try, in the following century, to make it the theology of a restored paganism: a refoundation, this time, in the strict sense.

    The second, Christian, proved the more lasting. Augustine relates in the Confessions how, in Milan, he was supplied by a man “immanissimo typho turgidum”, swollen with monstrous pride, with “quosdam platonicorum libros ex graeca lingua in latinam versos”, certain books of the Platonists translated from Greek into Latin, and that he read in them, not in those words but in substance, that “in the beginning was the Word”; but that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, “non ibi legi”, I did not read that there (Confessions, VII, 9, 13-14). Augustine's sentence draws the frontier between Plotinian spirituality and the Christian religion: everything is there, except the incarnation, that is, except history, the Church and the salvation of a God made man. The “books of the Platonists” had been translated by Marius Victorinus, as Augustine himself says (Confessions, VIII, 2, 3); that they were treatises of Plotinus, of Porphyry or of both is the common opinion of historians, and the detail remains disputed. Through Augustine, then through Pseudo-Dionysius, Neoplatonic negative theology would pass into Christianity, and it is this that we shall find again, transformed, in Maimonides and in Eckhart, whose God beyond God owes as much to Plotinus as to the Gospels.

    I therefore hold, against a widespread opinion, that Plotinus is not a precursor of Christianity, but the accomplished example of a spirituality that might never have become a religion. Christianity absorbed him by adding to him what Augustine “did not read there”; late paganism wanted to make him a state religion. Plotinus wanted neither. Take away everything: the formula holds for Churches too.

    Before the Rhineland mystic, a detour by way of Córdoba and Cairo is necessary, and it is not an ecumenical courtesy. Our question presupposes an older one: can one think God as a philosopher within a religion of revealed Law, without betraying either the Law or philosophy? It was first posed, and more radically than in Latin Christianity, in Islam and in the Arabic-speaking Judaism of the twelfth century, by judges and court physicians who read Aristotle in the text handed down by the translators of Baghdad and had to account for their philosophy before jurists. It is largely through Averroes's commentaries that scholasticism read Aristotle. Averroes and Maimonides, born twelve years apart in the same city, do not leave religion, but they invent the two instruments that every later exit will need: the interpretation that separates the apparent meaning from the true meaning, and the division of human beings into those who can hear the second and those who must keep to the first.

    In literature John of the Cross, Noche oscura (c. 1578) ; Rumi, Mathnawi (13th century)

    The poem of the Dark Night (Noche oscura) tells in eight stanzas of the soul's going out from the sleeping house, with no other light than the one that burns in the heart, until union: “¡Oh noche que juntaste / Amado con amada, / amada en el Amado transformada!”, O night that joined the Beloved with the beloved, the beloved transformed into the Beloved; then the forgetting of everything: “Quedéme y olvidéme,[…] cesó todo y dejéme”.

    Why here: this is Plotinus's “flight of the alone to the alone”, almost word for word, but with what Plotinus does not have and the poem cannot do without: a Beloved who waits, that is, a revelation. The same experience, described in the same terms of stripping away, is spirituality in the one and religion in the other; the difference is not in the experience, it is in what one takes to be its object.

    Rumi's Mathnawi opens with the lament of the reed flute, cut from the reed bed, every note of which tells of separation and of the longing to return to the origin. The flute preaches nothing, legislates nothing: it remembers. It is, within Islam, the exact figure of the spirituality without a Church that Plotinus embodies within paganism, and one of the rare places where Sufism and Neoplatonism answer each other almost without intermediary.

    Sources: John of the Cross, Noche oscura, stanzas 5 and 8 (c. 1578) ; Rumi, Mathnawi, prologue (13th century).

    Averroes1126-1198the Law commands philosophy

    Background: Islam: birth, expansion and thought, from Muhammad to Averroes · The philosophy of Averroes: the Commentator, the intellect, the reply to al-Ghazali, Latin Averroism · The thought of Maimonides: the Guide for the Perplexed, the Mishneh Torah, prophecy · Plato's myths: Er, Gyges, the noble lie, the androgyne · Scholasticism and the condemnations: faith and reason in the medieval university · The thought of Mohammed Arkoun: the critique of Islamic reason, the unthought, applied Islamology · How the Bible has been read: allegory, the four senses, historical criticism

    Abū l-Walīd Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Rushd, whom the Latins would call Averroes and, more simply, “the Commentator”, was a judge before he was a philosopher, or rather he never ceased to be both. Grandson of a chief qadi of Córdoba, himself qadi in Seville and then in Córdoba, physician to the Almohad caliph in Marrakesh, he commented on almost the whole of Aristotle at the sovereign's request, before falling into disgrace in 1195, being exiled to Lucena and seeing his books burned, then being recalled shortly before his death. The text that concerns us, a short one, is entitled Faṣl al-maqāl, the “decisive discourse”, or more exactly the examination that settles the question of the relation between the religious Law and philosophy, and it dates from around 1179. Léon Gauthier translated it under the title Accord de la religion et de la philosophie (Algiers, 1905; the title page of the digitized copy bears 1906).

    The form of the text is already a thesis: Averroes poses the question not as a philosopher but as a jurist, in the categories of Islamic law, which classify every action as obligatory, recommended, permitted, reprehensible or forbidden. The task, he writes, is to “examiner, au point de vue de la spéculation religieuse, si l'étude de la philosophie et des sciences logiques est permise ou défendue par la Loi religieuse, ou bien prescrite par elle soit à titre méritoire soit à titre obligatoire”, to examine, from the standpoint of religious inquiry, whether the study of philosophy and the logical sciences is permitted or forbidden by the religious Law, or else prescribed by it, either as meritorious or as obligatory. The answer is the strongest possible: philosophy is a duty. If philosophy is nothing but the study of the universe insofar as it makes its Maker known, and if the Law invites us to consider the universe, then philosophy is “de par la Loi religieuse, ou bien obligatoire ou bien méritoire”, by virtue of the religious Law, either obligatory or meritorious. Averroes quotes the Qur'an: “Draw a lesson [from this], O you who are endowed with understanding!” (sura LIX, 2), and reads in it a formal injunction to reason. Since the most perfect form of reasoning is demonstration (burhān) in the sense of the Posterior Analytics, the Law itself commands the study of Aristotle's logic.

    The gesture is striking: philosophy has no need to leave religion, since religion orders it to exist. But it comes at a price, stated in the most famous sentence of the treatise: “la vérité ne saurait être contraire à la vérité : elle s'accorde avec elle et témoigne en sa faveur”, truth cannot be contrary to truth: it agrees with it and bears witness in its favour. If demonstration arrives at a knowledge that the apparent meaning (ẓāhir) of the revealed text contradicts, the text must be interpreted, that is, led back to its inner meaning (bāṭin) by taʾwīl, the interpretation that brings the word back to what it truly signifies. Demonstration never bends; the text does.

    Then arises the question of the addressee: if the Qur'an has an apparent meaning and a true meaning, to whom should the second be told? Averroes answers with an anthropology of assent, which human beings do not give in the same way: some through demonstration, others through dialectical arguments, most through oratorical, that is, rhetorical, arguments. Hence the division: “Les gens [se divisent] donc, au point de vue de la Loi religieuse, en trois classes”, people are therefore divided, from the standpoint of the religious Law, into three classes: those who are “hommes de démonstration en aucune façon”, in no way people of demonstration, who “constituent la grande masse”, make up the great mass; the dialecticians; and “les hommes de démonstration par nature et par art, je veux dire l'art de la philosophie”, the people of demonstration by nature and by art, I mean the art of philosophy. The consequence is a rule of silence: the duty of the common people is to take the symbols “dans leur sens extérieur”, in their outward sense, and “il n'est pas permis qu'ils connaissent, en aucune façon, cette interprétation”, it is not permitted that they should know this interpretation in any way; more than that, “les interprétations vraies ne doivent pas être traitées dans les livres destinés au vulgaire, à plus forte raison les fausses”, true interpretations must not be treated in books intended for the common people, still less false ones. Averroes traces the sects of Islam back to this fault: the community split because interpretations were set out openly before the people.

    This rule is aimed at a named adversary, al-Ghazālī (1058-1111), who, in the Tahāfut al-falāsifa, which Gauthier proposes to render as L'Effondrement des falāsifa (The Collapse of the falāsifa) rather than La Destruction des philosophes (The Destruction of the Philosophers), had declared al-Fārābī and Avicenna unbelievers on three points: the eternity of the world, the claim that God does not know particular things, and the interpretation of the resurrection of bodies. Averroes recalls this in the Faṣl and answers as a jurist: the charge of unbelief for having broken the consensus is only “hypothétique”, hypothetical, since no unanimous consensus can be established on questions that the ancients themselves reserved for “hommes d'une science profonde”, people of profound learning. The philosophical answer would come in the Tahāfut al-tahāfut, the “Collapse of the Collapse”, which turns the title of Ghazālī's book against him. This is an attested response: the first debate on the right to philosophize within a revealed religion sets two Muslims against each other, one of whom had been dead for nearly seventy years when the other replied to him.

    Let us correct here a stubborn legend, which distorts everything that follows: Averroes never taught the “double truth”, the idea that a proposition could be true in philosophy and false in religion. He teaches the opposite: a single truth, two modes of access, a single arbiter, demonstration. The formula of the “double truth” comes from elsewhere: in 1277 the bishop of Paris, Étienne Tempier, condemning two hundred and nineteen propositions taught in the faculty of arts, reproaches certain masters in his prologue for saying things that are true according to philosophy but not according to the Catholic faith, as though there were two contrary truths. Historians still debate whether a single one of the “Latin Averroists” targeted, Siger of Brabant or Boethius of Dacia, ever upheld the thesis in that form; what is certain is that Averroes did not uphold it and that the label is polemical. Renan devoted his first major book, Averroès et l'averroïsme (1852), to this posterity, and it was he who made Ibn Rushd the patron saint of freethinkers. The Commentator deserved both better and less: he was not a freethinker, but a judge who thought freely.

    Where should he be placed among our eight regimes? Not in the regime of error: religion is not false, it tells the truth in symbols. Nor outside critique, for the doctrine of the three classes is already, in theological form, a theory of the social function of religion. The Law is a medicine for the many: Averroes compares the lawgiver to the skilful physician who gives everyone precepts of health to which each can assent, because “il ne lui est pas possible de les rendre tous médecins”, it is not possible for him to make them all physicians; and whoever divulges the interpretations to the people resembles the man who would ruin the patients' confidence in the physician's prescriptions without being able to give them an understanding of them. Plato had wanted the city to impose a salutary theology; Aristotle had acknowledged, as we have seen, that the myths had been added to persuade the multitude. Averroes gives this tradition a more elegant form: for him, the religion of the people is not a useful lie, but the truth itself, clothed for those who cannot see it naked. He ends on an image that says everything: philosophy is “la compagne de la religion et sa sœur de lait”, the companion of religion and its foster sister, and harm that comes from a friend is more painful than harm that comes from an enemy.

    The confrontation that follows is constructed. Spinoza did not, to my knowledge, discuss the Faṣl, which did not circulate in Latin. But when he attacks the method of Maimonides, which on this point is the same, he is aiming at the Averroist arrangement: if Scripture can be understood only in the light of demonstration, then the common people, who do not know what a demonstration is, “ne pourrait connaître l'Écriture sainte que sur l'autorité et le témoignage des philosophes”, could know Holy Scripture only on the authority and testimony of the philosophers, and one would have invented “une autorité fort nouvelle dans l'Église, une nouvelle espèce de prêtres et de pontifes”, a quite new authority in the Church, a new kind of priests and pontiffs (Theological-Political Treatise, ch. VII, trans. Saisset). The objection goes deep: the Averroist division does not lead out of religion, it installs at its summit a caste that knows what the text means and hides it. Averroes, at least, believes that the Law is true; but the structure will outlive the faith that justified it.

    My judgement is therefore twofold. Averroes does not leave religion and founds nothing: he divides. He demands no sacrifice of the philosopher, who enjoys the truth without guilt since the Law itself commands it of him. But he demands of the people a sacrifice he does not name, that of access to the truth. By the criterion, he installs no new absolute; he ranks access to the old one. It is the most stable solution the question has ever received, and so it will return under every regime, in Spinoza himself, in Comte, in Renan, and even in the Straussian theory of esoteric writing.

    In literature Jorge Luis Borges, “La busca de Averroes” (1947) ; Umberto Eco, Il nome della rosa (1980)

    In Borges's story, collected in El Aleph (The Aleph), Averroes, in Córdoba, is commenting on Aristotle's Poetics and stumbles over two words whose meaning he cannot find in any library of Islam, “tragedy” and “comedy”. Beneath his window, children are playing at being the muezzin and the faithful; in the evening, a traveller describes a ceremony he saw in Canton, where masked men acted out a story on a platform. Averroes recognizes nothing in it and concludes that tragedy is panegyric and comedy satire; Borges confesses on the last page that in recounting this failure he has lived his own, that of imagining a man from a few lines of Renan.

    Why here: the tale states the limit of the Averroist gesture. The commentator who makes the Law compatible with Aristotle can read in Aristotle only what his city allows him to recognize; the division between apparent meaning and inner meaning presupposes a reader who already knows what the text must mean. Renan had made Averroes a freethinker; Borges, starting from Renan, gives him back to his world.

    In The Name of the Rose, old Jorge of Burgos poisons the pages of the second book of the Poetics, the one that deals with comedy, so that laughter will not undo the fear of God among the simple. It is the Averroist prohibition of interpretations for the common people, turned into a crime: the truth reserved for some, and the sacrifice of access to the truth demanded of the others.

    Sources: Jorge Luis Borges, “La busca de Averroes”, El Aleph (1949; story of 1947) ; Umberto Eco, Il nome della rosa (1980).
