    Maimonides1138-1204of God, we know only what he is not

    Background: Judaism: from the Second Temple to emancipation · Islam: birth, expansion and thought, from Muhammad to Averroes · The philosophy of Averroes: the Commentator, the intellect, the reply to al-Ghazali, Latin Averroism · The thought of Maimonides: the Guide for the Perplexed, the Mishneh Torah, prophecy · The patriarchs: Abraham, the sacrifice of Isaac, Jacob · Exodus: Moses, the departure from Egypt, Sinai and the Law · Scholasticism and the condemnations: faith and reason in the medieval university · Sacrifice in the Bible: from Abel's altar to self-offering · The God of the Bible: his names, his images and the formation of monotheism

    Moses ben Maimon was also born in Cordoba. His family fled after the Almohad conquest of 1148, wandered through Andalusia and Morocco, then settled in Egypt, at Fustat, where Maimonides became head of the Jewish community and physician at the court of Saladin. We owe him the greatest code of Jewish law, the Mishneh Torah, written in Hebrew, and the greatest book of Jewish philosophy of the Middle Ages, written around 1190 in Arabic set down in Hebrew characters: Dalālat al-ḥāʾirīn, which the Hebrew translators rendered as Moreh nevukhim, the Latins as Dux neutrorum or Dux perplexorum, and Salomon Munk, in the standard French translation (1856-1866), as Le Guide des égarés, the guide of those who have gone astray. Munk notes that the translation closest to the literal sense would be Guide des perplexes, guide of the perplexed, but that it would have “l'inconvénient de paraître prétentieuse”, the drawback of seeming pretentious.

    The introduction defines its addressee with a precision that speaks volumes. The book aims “de donner l'éveil à l'homme religieux chez lequel la vérité de notre Loi est établie dans l'âme et devenue un objet de croyance, qui est parfait dans sa religion et dans ses mœurs, qui a étudié les sciences des philosophes”, to awaken the religious man in whose soul the truth of our Law is established and has become an object of belief, who is perfect in his religion and his morals, who has studied the sciences of the philosophers, but who is “embarrassé par le sens extérieur (littéral) de la Loi”, troubled by the external (literal) sense of the Law, so that he “reste dans l'agitation et dans le trouble”, remains in agitation and confusion (Introduction, trans. Munk). The perplexed man is neither the unbeliever nor the simple, but the cultivated believer who has read Aristotle and can no longer read the Bible to the letter. Maimonides does not invite him to choose: he teaches him to read.

    The first lesson concerns names. The Bible speaks of a God who sees, who hears, who comes down, who sits, who has a hand and a face. A large part of the first part of the Guide is a lexicon of these terms, showing for each that it is a homonym, and that taken in its proper sense it would make God a body. Yet God's incorporeality is demonstrated, and it governs the reading. Maimonides says so with a frankness that Spinoza will copy out in order to combat it: if he rejects the eternity of the world, it is not because of the verses on creation, for “de même que nous avons expliqué ces endroits de l'Écriture de façon à éloigner de la nature de Dieu toute matérialité, nous aurions également trouvé moyen d'interpréter les passages sur la création dans un sens favorable à l'éternité du monde”, just as we have explained those places in Scripture so as to remove all materiality from the nature of God, we would likewise have found a way to interpret the passages on creation in a sense favourable to the eternity of the world; it is only that the eternity of the world “n'est établie par aucune démonstration”, is established by no demonstration (Guide, II, 25, quoted in the Theological-Political Treatise, ch. VII, trans. Saisset). The revealed text yields before demonstration, not before mere probability. Creation is therefore upheld, but for want of a proof to the contrary, and Maimonides leaves open, in the eyes of an attentive reader, a question that faith believed closed.

    The second lesson goes further and founds a tradition. If no name fits God in its proper sense, nothing positive can be said of him. “Nous ne saisissons de lui autre chose, si ce n'est qu'il est, mais non pas ce qu'il est”, we grasp nothing of him except that he is, but not what he is (I, 58). The only legitimate attributes are negative: to say that God is living is to say that he is not dead; powerful, that he is not powerless. Knowledge of God advances by subtraction: “à mesure que tu augmentes les négations à l'égard de Dieu, tu t'approches de la perception”, as you multiply the negations concerning God, you draw nearer to apprehension (I, 59). The end of this path is silence. Maimonides finds it in Psalm 65, 2, lekha dumiyya tehilla, which he reads thus: “pour toi le silence est la louange”, for you, silence is praise (I, 59). For, he adds, “quoi que ce soit que nous disions dans le but d'exalter et de glorifier (Dieu), nous y trouverons quelque chose d'offensant à l'égard de Dieu”, whatever we say with the aim of exalting and glorifying (God), we shall find in it something offensive towards God.

    This negative theology joins the critique of religion: from within faith, it destroys all the representations of God that popular faith sustains: the God who grows angry, who rewards, who hears prayers in the way a king hears a petition. Eckhart received it; he quotes “Rabbi Moyses” abundantly in his Latin commentaries, and the debt is well enough established for a recent study to bear precisely that title, “Verba sunt Rabbi Moysis”. When Eckhart prays God to rid him of God, he carries into prayer the negation that Maimonides had carried into silence.

    It also has a modern adversary. Feuerbach, in Das Wesen des Christenthums, attacks the theology that denies God every positive predicate. A God of whom every determination is denied, he says, has an existence “ohne Existenz”, an existence without existence, indistinguishable from nothingness; and the negation of the positive predicates of the divine essence is nothing other, in his view, than “ein subtiler, verschlagner Atheismus”, a subtle and cunning atheism, which keeps the appearance of religion and is not recognized as negation (1841, Introduction, ch. 2, p. 21-22 of the first edition). Feuerbach does not name Maimonides in this passage, so the confrontation is constructed; it is the best objection that can be made to the Guide. For Feuerbach, religion lives on predicates: to remove them all is to leave it without daring to say so. For Maimonides, true religion begins when they are removed; to keep them is idolatry. I believe Feuerbach is right about the ordinary believer, who does not pray to a God of whom he knows nothing, and Maimonides about the philosopher, who cannot worship a God he understands. This disagreement runs through the whole essay: it sets those for whom religion is a representation against those for whom it is the surpassing of all representation.

    The third lesson, the most surprising, makes Maimonides, in my view, one of the first theorists of the historical function of rites. In the third part of the Guide, he undertakes to give the reasons for the commandments, the ṭaʿamei ha-mitzvot, and comes up against the sacrifices, which occupy an immense place in the Torah and for which no philosophical reason accounts. His answer is historical: God proceeded with the Hebrews as nature proceeds with the infant, by degrees: “comme il est impossible de passer subitement d'un extrême à l'autre, l'homme, selon sa nature, ne saurait quitter brusquement toutes ses habitudes”, since it is impossible to pass suddenly from one extreme to the other, man, by his nature, cannot abruptly abandon all his habits (III, 32). Now the universal worship of the time consisted in offering animals in the temples of idols. To forbid all worship of that kind would have been as inconceivable as a prophet coming today to say that God forbids prayer and fasting. “C'est pourquoi Dieu laissa subsister ces différentes espèces de cultes ; mais, au lieu d'être rendues à des objets créés et à des choses imaginaires, sans réalité, il les a transférées à son nom”, that is why God allowed these various kinds of worship to remain; but instead of their being rendered to created objects and to imaginary things without reality, he transferred them to his name (III, 32). The sacrifices are not willed for their own sake; they are a detour, like the detour through the desert that God has the people take on leaving Egypt so as not to expose them to war (Ex 13, 17-18), an example Maimonides himself invokes.

    Let us weigh this thesis. It says that part of the revealed Law is explained by the historical conditions of its revelation and by the psychology of a people, that it is a pedagogical concession and not an eternal truth: a functional and historical explanation of worship, given from within faith by the greatest rabbi of his century. Hume, Durkheim and Weber will say in other ways what rites do to human beings; Maimonides had said it by referring it to the wisdom of God. The step separating his explanation from an explanation without God is a short one: it is enough to remove the divine “ruse” and keep the history. Maimonides does not take it, but he showed where it lay.

    There remains the question of writing. The Guide itself announces that it contradicts itself, and that it does so on purpose. Among the seven causes of contradiction it lists in its introduction, the seventh is “la nécessité du discours, quand il s'agit de choses très obscures dont les détails doivent être en partie dérobés et en partie révélés”, the necessity of discourse, when it concerns very obscure matters whose details must be partly concealed and partly revealed; and in that case, “le vulgaire ne doit d'aucune manière s'apercevoir de l'endroit où existe la contradiction, et l'auteur quelquefois cherche toute sorte d'expédients pour la dérober”, the vulgar must in no way notice the place where the contradiction lies, and the author sometimes seeks every kind of expedient to conceal it. He adds that the divergences in the present treatise arise from the sixth and seventh causes. This is Averroes's arrangement, carried over from teaching into writing: the book speaks to two audiences at once. Leo Strauss will make these lines the key to a reading of all premodern philosophy (Part Eleven); questionable elsewhere, this reading, where Maimonides is concerned, merely takes the author at his word.

    Spinoza then intervenes, and his response is attested, by name, and of rare violence. In chapter VII of the Theological-Political Treatise, he examines Maimonides's method and judges it inapplicable and harmful: it assumes that the prophets were philosophers, that the clearest literal sense may be tortured in the name of reason, and that one must defer to the learned. He concludes: “Il faut donc absolument rejeter la méthode de Maimonide comme inutile, dangereuse et absurde”, the method of Maimonides must therefore be utterly rejected as useless, dangerous and absurd (ch. VII, trans. Saisset). And in chapter XV he makes it the origin of an error: the first among the Pharisees to declare that Scripture must be bent to the demands of reason “fut Maimonide”, was Maimonides. The break is complete, and it is the true starting point of the modern critique of the Bible. Maimonides accommodated Scripture to reason in order to save it; Spinoza separates them in order to free them both. Scripture teaches not truth but obedience; it therefore has no need to be true in the philosophical sense, and philosophy has no need of it.

    Yet Spinoza owes Maimonides more than he admits. The idea that Scripture speaks according to the capacity of the people and that its images are concessions to their imagination is already in Maimonides; Spinoza takes it up while removing its divine guarantee. Negative theology, which denies God every human predicate, prepares the God of the Ethics, who loves no one and has neither understanding nor will in the human sense. The separation of the sage and the vulgar, for which he reproaches Maimonides in interpretation, he keeps in life: beatitude is for the sage, obedience for the multitude. What he rejects is that the sage should have authority over the meaning of the text, not that there should be sages.

    Where should Maimonides be placed? He does not leave religion and does not claim to: he is the legislator of his community and the guardian of its Law. But within this fidelity, he practises three of the regimes of critique. He treats the representations of God as errors to be corrected; he explains part of worship by its historical function; and he leads the knowledge of God to a silence that closely resembles the experience of the mystics. What he does not admit is that the people should be deprived of the Law. Like Averroes, he divides; but where Averroes divides human beings, he divides the text, and he writes a book that says everything only to the one who knows how to read. The exit from religion, which in Spinoza will be a matter of hermeneutics before it is a matter of metaphysics, begins with this quarrel among readers.

    In literature Franz Kafka, “Vor dem Gesetz” (1915) ; Isaac Bashevis Singer, The Magician of Lublin (1960)

    “Vor dem Gesetz steht ein Türhüter”, before the Law stands a doorkeeper. A man from the country asks to be admitted to the Law; the doorkeeper replies that it is not possible now, and the man waits, for days and years, on a stool beside the open door. Grown old, almost blind, he makes out “im Dunkel einen Glanz, der unverlöschlich aus der Türe des Gesetzes bricht”, in the darkness a radiance that breaks inextinguishably from the door of the Law, and asks his last question: why has no one else asked to be admitted? “Hier konnte niemand sonst Einlaß erhalten, denn dieser Eingang war nur für dich bestimmt. Ich gehe jetzt und schließe ihn”, no one else could be admitted here, for this entrance was meant for you alone; I am going now and I shall shut it.

    Why here: the parable is the seventh cause of contradiction in the Guide raised to the absolute. Maimonides writes a book whose entrance is made for a single reader, the perplexed man capable of reading between the chapters, and which stays closed to the vulgar sitting before the door; Kafka takes away the book and keeps the door. The man from the country is the reader whom the Guide leaves outside, and the doorkeeper is homonymy itself, which admits and refuses in the same word.

    Singer's Yasha, a Jewish magician from Poland, freethinker, seducer and acrobat, ends up voluntarily walled into a brick cell built in his courtyard, become “Jacob the Penitent”, before a God of whom he still knows nothing and to whom he nonetheless never stops speaking. This is negative theology lived from below: of God one knows only what he is not, and one goes on addressing him.

    Sources: Franz Kafka, “Vor dem Gesetz” (1915; reprinted in Ein Landarzt, 1919, and in Der Prozess, ch. 9); Isaac Bashevis Singer, The Magician of Lublin (1960).

    Meister Eckhartc. 1260-1328praying God to be rid of God

    Background: The philosophy of Plotinus: the hypostases, procession and conversion · The thought of Meister Eckhart: detachment, the birth of God in the soul, the trial · Christian mysticism: from Dionysius to John of the Cross and quietism · Medieval Christendom: from the fall of Rome to the stake · Schopenhauer's philosophy: the Will, suffering, compassion, the denial of the will

    The Christian prehistory begins with a scandal. The Dominican Eckhart of Hochheim, master of theology in Paris, preached in Strasbourg and Cologne, in German, to nuns and to lay people, sermons of an audacity without equal. He died during his trial; the bull In agro dominico of John XXII, in 1329, condemned twenty-eight propositions drawn from his works. I do not settle the question of his orthodoxy, which is still debated; I read a sermon that contains, four centuries before the Enlightenment, the most radical critique of the image of God.

    The sermon numbered 52 in Josef Quint's critical edition comments on the first beatitude, “Beati pauperes spiritu”, blessed are the poor in spirit. Eckhart gives there a definition of poverty that rejects every pious definition. In Gustav Landauer's modern German translation (1903): “Das ist ein armer Mensch, der nichts will und nichts weiss und nichts hat”, he is a poor man who wills nothing, knows nothing and has nothing. To will nothing is not even to will to accomplish the will of God: Eckhart specifies that as long as a man's will is to accomplish the most dear will of God, he does not have the poverty of which he speaks, for he still has a will. To know nothing is not even to know that God is at work in oneself; to have nothing, not even to be a place where God might work.

    From this Eckhart draws a prayer: “Darum bitte ich Gott, dass er mich Gottes quitt mache”, therefore I pray God to rid me of God. The Middle High German reads, in Franz Pfeiffer's edition: “hier umbe so bite ich got, daz er mich quit mache gotes” (Deutsche Mystiker des vierzehnten Jahrhunderts, vol. II, Leipzig, 1857, sermon LXXXVII, p. 283, which is sermon 52 in Quint's numbering); I have not checked the text established by Quint (DW II). Eckhart justifies the request by a distinction: the God of whom one must be rid is God as creator, the God who stands over against the creature, the one the creature represents to itself; beyond him there is a being without mode, “über Gott und über Unterschiedenheit”, above God and above all difference, where the soul was before it was created.

    History has read this sentence in two ways. The first, orthodox at least in intention, sees in it negative theology pushed to its limit, that of Pseudo-Dionysius, for whom God surpasses all names, including the name of God. To pray to be rid of God is to pray to be rid of the idol one makes of him, in order to reach the nameless Godhead. The second is modern, and it will make Eckhart an ancestor of the spiritualities without God: detachment, Gelassenheit, becomes an exercise in dispossession that no longer needs any object. Schopenhauer will hail in Eckhart a brother of the sages of India; Simone Weil will speak of decreation.

    Eckhart establishes what modern critics will often forget: the critique of the representation of God, far from being an invention of unbelief, lies at the heart of Christian mysticism. When Feuerbach comes to say that the believers' God is a projection of man, he will be saying what Eckhart says of God the creator, and will draw the opposite conclusion: Eckhart leaves the image of God to enter the Godhead, Feuerbach to return into man. The two gestures have the same form. The confrontation is constructed; it shows at least that the boundary between the critique of religion and spirituality does not run where one thinks.

    In literature Angelus Silesius, Cherubinischer Wandersmann (1657) ; Rainer Maria Rilke, Das Stunden-Buch (1905) ; Robert Musil, Der Mann ohne Eigenschaften (1930-1943)

    Angelus Silesius, a reader of Eckhart and Tauler, set Rhineland mysticism into couplets: “Ich weiß, daß ohne mich Gott nicht ein Nu kann leben; / Werd ich zunicht, er muß von Not den Geist aufgeben”, I know that without me God cannot live an instant; if I come to nothing, he must of necessity give up the ghost (I, 8); and the most famous: “Die Ros ist ohn warum; sie blühet, weil sie blühet, / Sie acht nicht ihrer selbst, fragt nicht, ob man sie siehet”, the rose is without why; it blooms because it blooms, it pays no heed to itself, asks not whether it is seen (I, 289).

    Why here: the first couplet is sermon 52 reduced to two lines, poverty of spirit in which God needs the soul as much as the soul needs him; the second is Gelassenheit become botany, a living without why that asks nothing and expects nothing. Heidegger will comment on the rose in Der Satz vom Grund (1957), and it is through the rose that objectless mysticism passes into the spiritualities without God.

    Rilke, in The Book of Hours (Das Stunden-Buch), gives voice to a monk who turns dependence around: “Was wirst du tun, Gott, wenn ich sterbe? / Ich bin dein Krug (wenn ich zerscherbe?) / Ich bin dein Trank (wenn ich verderbe?) / Bin dein Gewand und dein Gewerbe, / mit mir verlierst du deinen Sinn”, what will you do, God, when I die? I am your pitcher (what if I shatter?), I am your drink (what if I spoil?), I am your garment and your craft; with me you lose your meaning. This is the second reading of Eckhart, the one that makes him an ancestor of the spiritualities without God: a God who exists only in the exercise of the one who bears him. Musil, finally, calls “the other condition” the mystical experience without God that Ulrich and his sister Agathe explore in The Man Without Qualities, with Eckhart open on the table.

    Sources: Angelus Silesius, Cherubinischer Wandersmann, I, 8 and I, 289 (1657); Rainer Maria Rilke, Das Stunden-Buch, “Das Buch vom mönchischen Leben” (written in 1899, published in 1905); Robert Musil, Der Mann ohne Eigenschaften (1930-1943).

    Transition: from the Law to reason

    Background: Aristotle's philosophy: act and potency, causes, the unmoved mover, virtue, contemplation · Medieval Christendom: from the fall of Rome to the stake · Scholasticism and the condemnations: faith and reason in the medieval university

    At the close of the Middle Ages, the critique of religion does not yet exist as a project, but it already has three of its gestures. The first is political: in Plato, Aristotle and Averroes, religion appears for the first time as a function of the city, which the philosopher can judge useful without holding it literally true. The second is therapeutic: Epicurus and Lucretius deliver people from the fear of the gods without denying the gods. The third is apophatic: Plotinus, Maimonides and Eckhart deny of God everything that is said of him, to the point that Feuerbach will see in negative theology a subtle atheism. They share one trait, which will fade in the classical age: they all presuppose an elite, philosophers, sages or mystics, and a multitude left with its images. We must first go back in time to follow the birth of Christianity, which received the God of the Greek philosophers long before the Moderns reworked him and democratized the question.

    Top of the part

    Part Twothe birth of Christianity, between Athens and Jerusalem5 authors

    Background: Biblical chronology: the time of the story and the time of the writing · Christianity in the Roman Empire: from Nero to Diocletian · The Bible: books, canons and languages · From Constantine to Theodosius: Christianity as the religion of the Empire · Why Christianity prevailed: the historians' explanations · Byzantium and Russian Orthodoxy: the other Christianity · The vocabulary of Christian theology: revelation, grace, salvation, original sin · The New Testament: twenty-seven books, their dates and their authors · How the canon was formed: criteria, lists and excluded texts

    The origin of Christianity is not a matter for historians that lies outside our question. Every critique of the Christian religion presupposes a thesis about its birth: Feuerbach thinks it is the projection of the human essence, Nietzsche that it is the work of Paul, Strauss and Bauer that it is a myth, Engels that it is the uprising of the oppressed of the Empire, Onfray that it is a literary fiction. And every refoundation takes up something of this birth, since it was there that the bond was tied between a God of the Law, who came from Jerusalem, and a God of reason, who came from Athens. Tertullian, c. 200, gave the opposition its most famous form: “Quid ergo Athenis et Hierosolymis? quid academiae et ecclesiae?”, what then has Athens to do with Jerusalem, the Academy with the Church? (De praescriptione haereticorum, 7, 9). And he adds, against those who have produced “a Stoic, Platonic and dialectical Christianity” (“Stoicum et Platonicum et dialecticum christianismum”), that after Jesus Christ curiosity is no longer needed (ibid., 7, 11-12). But the question is rhetorical in a sense he did not intend: Athens and Jerusalem already had a great deal in common. Nietzsche, seventeen centuries later, reversed the reproach while keeping it: “Christenthum ist Platonismus für's "Volk"”, Christianity is Platonism for the “people” (Jenseits von Gut und Böse, preface). The formula is polemical, but it points to a fact that historians do not dispute: Christianity thought itself in the categories of Greek philosophy, beginning with that of the Logos. We shall follow this passage from Philo of Alexandria, who reads Genesis with the Timaeus, to Augustine, who turns the God of the Platonists into a God to whom one prays, by way of Celsus and Porphyry, whose critiques, Platonist in character, already contained almost all the arguments of the Enlightenment.

    Philo of Alexandriac. 20 BCE-c. 45/50 CEMoses read with the Timaeus

    Background: Judaism: from the Second Temple to emancipation · Genesis 1 to 3: the creation, Adam and Eve, the fall · The thought of Philo of Alexandria: Genesis read with Plato · The thought of Origen: allegory, the pre-existence of souls, apocatastasis · Councils and the formation of dogma: from Nicaea to Chalcedon · Hermeneutics: from Schleiermacher to Ricoeur · Between the two Testaments: the Maccabees, Enoch, Qumran and apocalyptic expectation · The Gospel of John: the Word made flesh · Messiah, Son of Man, Son of God: the titles of Jesus

    Philo is a Jew of Alexandria, an exact contemporary of Jesus, born into one of the wealthiest families of the community, and in 39-40 a member of the embassy that pleaded the cause of his fellow Jews before the emperor Caligula. He writes in Greek, reads the Bible in the Greek translation of the Septuagint, and comments on it in an immense body of work, almost entirely allegorical. Nothing suggests that he ever heard of Jesus, and none of his treatises mentions the Christian movement. Yet he supplied nascent Christianity with the tool that allowed it to think its God as a philosopher would.

    His project comes down to one assertion, set out at the beginning of the De opificio mundi, his treatise on the creation of the world: Moses is a philosopher, and indeed the first. Moses, he writes, had reached the summits of philosophy very early, and had learned from the oracles of God the most numerous and most important principles of nature (De opificio mundi, 8). Genesis and the Timaeus therefore say the same thing, and when they seem to diverge, it is because the letter of Genesis hides a meaning that allegory must uncover.

    The heart of the doctrine is the Logos. Reading Genesis with the Timaeus requires solving a difficulty that the Timaeus itself leaves open: how can the transcendent God, who has nothing in common with matter, shape the world? Plato placed the Ideas, eternal models, between the demiurge and the world. Philo places them in the mind of God, and he calls this mind in act the Logos. If one wished to speak plainly, he says, one would not say that the intelligible world is anything other than the Logos of God already engaged in creating the world, just as the intelligible city is nothing other than the thought of the architect who plans to build it; and he immediately adds that this is the doctrine of Moses, not his own (De opificio mundi, 24-25). The Logos is thus at once the place of the Ideas, the instrument of creation and the model of man, since man is made “in the image of God”. Philo goes so far as to call it, in a passage of the Questions on Genesis whose Greek original is lost but which Eusebius of Caesarea preserved, the “second God”: nothing mortal could be made in the likeness of the supreme God and Father of the universe, but only in the likeness of the second God, who is his Logos (Quaestiones in Genesim II, 62, quoted by Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel VII, 13).

    A Jew faithful to the Law, who recited every day that God is one, thinks the world on the basis of a divine intermediary who is not God himself and whom he nonetheless names “second God”. In Philo this is not a person, still less a man: the Logos is a function of divine thought, which Philo describes now as a power, now as an archangel, now as the high priest of the world, without ever fixing the metaphor. But a few decades later the prologue of the Gospel of John would write: “Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος”, in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (Jn 1, 1), and then what Philo could never have written: “Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο”, and the Word became flesh (Jn 1, 14). Whether or not Philo directly influenced John, a disputed question, the concept was available, and it was through it that Christianity entered philosophy.

    The allegorical method is the common ancestor of almost all the religious hermeneutics of the West. Philo starts from a principle he holds to be self-evident: God has neither hands, nor anger, nor repentance, and when Scripture ascribes them to him, it speaks the language of men in order to be understood by them. Every narrative therefore has two senses, the literal, which serves the multitude, and the figurative, addressed to those who know how to read. The garden of Eden becomes virtue, the patriarchs become dispositions of the soul, the exodus from Egypt becomes the soul's departure from the body. Philo does not for all that despise the letter: he expressly reproaches the radical allegorists of his time for neglecting the observance of the Law on the pretext of having understood its meaning. The two levels of reading are thus a way of holding together the community and philosophy, the practice of all and the contemplation of a few. One recognizes the division that Averroes would theorize eleven centuries later.

    Philo also left, in the De vita contemplativa, the description of a community of men and women, the Therapeutae, who lived near Lake Mareotis in prayer, the study of the Scriptures and song, withdrawn from the city. Reality or ideal, it is the first image of a spiritual life that is neither the worship of the Temple nor the school of the philosophers, but a form of life governed by contemplation. The Christian monks of Egypt, two centuries later, recognized their ancestors in it, and Eusebius even believed that the Therapeutae were Christians. The confusion is instructive: the form of spiritual life preceded the doctrine that would appropriate it.

    The most instructive fact of his history is his posterity: rabbinic Judaism did not hand him down; the tradition that kept him is Christian. It was Christians of Alexandria, Clement and then Origen, who read him, quoted him, imitated him and copied his manuscripts; it was Christians, such as Eusebius, who preserved for us what we have lost of his Greek text. This is the consensus of historians. Judaism, which was to rebuild itself after the destruction of the Temple in 70 around the Law and its commentary, had no need of a Logos; Christianity, which had to explain how a crucified man could be the son of a single God, needed one vitally. Philo supplied a religion that was not his own with the philosophy it was looking for.

    Philo belongs to the regime of allegory, prior to all the regimes of critique: he does not criticize religion, he translates it into philosophy. This translation has two faces: it shields the Law from the rationalist objection, but it installs in biblical religion a philosopher's God, without passion and without a face. Philo is thus, before Christianity, the inventor of what Heidegger would call onto-theology, applied to the Bible. His allegorical reading also has a price, which Spinoza would make Maimonides, his distant heir, pay (Part One): if one can always read beneath the letter the meaning that reason demands, reason no longer learns anything from Scripture. With regard to the criterion, finally, Philo refounds nothing and demands no new sacrifice; he makes Greek philosophy religious, and biblical religion philosophical.

    In literature Thomas Mann, Joseph und seine Brüder (1933-1943)

    The four novels of Joseph and His Brothers (Joseph und seine Brüder) take up chapters 27 to 50 of Genesis and unfold them over nearly two thousand pages. The prologue, “Descent into Hell”, begins by observing that the well of the past is deep, then goes back from story to story without ever reaching an origin; in the novel, Jacob, Joseph and even the pharaoh Akhenaten know that they are replaying stories already told, and Joseph reads his own life as a myth in the course of fulfilment. Mann said he wanted to take myth back from the obscurantists of his time and turn it towards the human.

    Why here: this is Philo's allegory turned into a novel. Philo read beneath the letter of Moses a meaning that Greek philosophy could approve; Mann reads beneath Genesis a psychology, a history of religions and a morality, and he does so, like Philo, without criticizing the text, by translating it. The regime of allegory did not disappear with Antiquity; it became a literary form, and that form refounds nothing either.

    Sources: Thomas Mann, Joseph und seine Brüder (Joseph and His Brothers), four volumes (1933-1943).

    PTPaul of Tarsusd. c. 64/67Christ crucified, folly to the Greeks

    Background: Judaism: from the Second Temple to emancipation · Paul of Tarsus: the letters, justification, the Law and the new perspective · Why Christianity prevailed: the historians' explanations · Historical-critical exegesis and the quests for the Jesus of history · Engels: dialectical materialism, the history of early Christianity, the reckoning with Feuerbach · Between the two Testaments: the Maccabees, Enoch, Qumran and apocalyptic expectation · The Acts of the Apostles: from Jerusalem to Rome · The letters of Paul: Romans, Corinthians and the others · Sacrifice in the Bible: from Abel's altar to self-offering

    If Philo supplied the concept, Paul supplied the scandal. Still, one must know which Paul one is speaking of. Of the thirteen letters the New Testament attributes to him, historical criticism holds only seven to be authentic: the First Letter to the Thessalonians, the Letter to the Galatians, the two Letters to the Corinthians, the Letter to the Romans, the Letter to the Philippians and the note to Philemon. This is the dominant interpretation, almost a consensus; the others are called deutero-Pauline, written in his school after his death. These seven letters, composed between about 50 and 60, are the oldest Christian texts we have, earlier than all the Gospels. The Acts of the Apostles, which tell his life, are later by at least a generation, composed by the author of the Gospel of Luke with an ancient historian's freedom that calls for caution.

    Paul presents himself as a Jew, and even as an elite Jew. He reminds the Galatians of what his conduct had been “in Judaism”, how he persecuted the Church, and how he “advanced in Judaism beyond many of [his] own age” (Ga 1, 13-14). He does not say that he left Judaism for a new religion; he says that it pleased God “to reveal his Son in me, that I might proclaim him among the nations” (Ga 1, 16). Scholarship in the second half of the twentieth century insisted on this point: the “new perspective on Paul”, inaugurated by E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977), challenged the Lutheran image of a Paul who set Christian grace against a Judaism of legal performance: the Judaism of his time, Sanders shows, was already a religion of the covenant received by grace, and Paul does not leave Judaism, he opens its borders to the nations. Without settling this debate among exegetes, we may note that the presumed founder of Christianity did not think of himself as the founder of a religion.

    What he founds, however, is unheard of, and he knows it. The First Letter to the Corinthians contains the sentence that sums up the encounter of Athens and Jerusalem, and makes it impossible: “ἐπειδὴ καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι σημεῖα αἰτοῦσιν καὶ Ἕλληνες σοφίαν ζητοῦσιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ κηρύσσομεν Χριστὸν ἐσταυρωμένον, Ἰουδαίοις μὲν σκάνδαλον, ἔθνεσιν δὲ μωρίαν”, Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we proclaim Christ crucified, a scandal to Jews and folly to the Gentiles (1 Co 1, 22-23). Paul does not offer a wisdom better than that of the philosophers; he offers a folly, a God who manifests himself in the punishment reserved for slaves. Philo's Logos was the place of the Ideas; Paul's Christ is a condemned man.

    Acts nevertheless tells of an attempt at reconciliation, the scene in which Athens and Jerusalem physically meet. Paul, in Athens, debates with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, who take him to the Areopagus. There he delivers a speech that starts from an altar “to an unknown god”, quotes a Greek poet, “for we are also his offspring”, and declares that God “does not dwell in temples made with hands”; then he announces the judgement and the resurrection of a man, and at that point, says the narrative, “some mocked, and others said: We will hear you again about this” (Ac 17, 22-32). This speech is, according to the dominant interpretation among exegetes, a composition by Luke rather than a transcript, but it rightly shows where the frontier lies. A creator God who does not dwell in temples, the Stoics could understand, and Plato had almost said as much; it is the resurrection of a body that makes the Areopagus laugh. Christianity can speak Greek as long as it speaks of God; it ceases to be Greek as soon as it speaks of the flesh.

    The oldest testimony to the content of the faith is in Paul, and it is a received account rather than a doctrine: the formula of 1 Co 15, 3-5, which we shall meet again in connection with the existence of Jesus, hands down the death of Christ for our sins according to the Scriptures, his burial, his resurrection on the third day and his appearances to Cephas, then to the twelve. Paul writes c. 54; he says he is handing on what he received, probably in Damascus or Jerusalem, in the thirties. And in the Letter to the Galatians he mentions his meeting with Cephas, that is, Peter, and with James, the brother of the Lord (Ga 1, 19). This verse will weigh heavily in the debate on the historical existence of Jesus.

    Two features of Paul's thought matter for our debate. The first is his universalism. “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Ga 3, 28). The sentence does not promise the abolition of slavery or the civil equality of the sexes, and elsewhere Paul sends the slave back to his master; it declares that these distinctions no longer count before God. That is little from the point of view of politics, and it is immense from the point of view of ancient religion, which was always the religion of a people, a city or a station in life. The second feature is his expectation of the end. The oldest letters assume that Christ will return within the lifetime of those to whom they are addressed. The dominant interpretation among historians draws from this a consequence that theologians long refused: Pauline Christianity is first of all an eschatology, an expectation of the imminent end of the world, and not a morality or a metaphysics. Albert Schweitzer, at the beginning of the twentieth century, would make it the key to all research on Jesus.

    Engels, who had read Bruno Bauer closely, drew from these two features an analogy that has enjoyed lasting success. “Die Geschichte des Urchristentums bietet merkwürdige Berührungspunkte mit der modernen Arbeiterbewegung”, the history of early Christianity offers curious points of contact with the modern labour movement: like it, Christianity was originally a movement of the oppressed, and both proclaim an imminent deliverance from bondage and misery (Zur Geschichte des Urchristentums, 1894). Engels adds that Christianity places this deliverance in the beyond and socialism in this world. The analogy is illuminating and dangerous: it illuminates the sociology of the first communities, and announces without meaning to what Löwith would reproach Marxism with, namely that it is a transposed eschatology. Celsus, as we shall see, was already saying with contempt what Engels says with sympathy.

    Did Paul invent Christianity? That is Nietzsche's thesis, for whom Paul is the bearer of bad tidings (Part Seven): Paul “verlegte einfach das Schwergewicht jenes ganzen Daseins hinter dies Dasein”, simply shifted the centre of gravity of that whole existence beyond this existence, into the lie of the risen Jesus, and his need was power (Der Antichrist, § 42). Renan, in his Saint Paul (1869), had already set the Galilean Jesus of the parables against the theologian of Tarsus, with less violence and more melancholy. The comparison is constructed, since Nietzsche does not quote Renan on this point; the two readings converge on a Jesus without doctrine and a Paul without Jesus.

    I believe this thesis is half right. Right, in that Paul made a theology out of an execution, and that the letters take almost no interest in the life of Jesus, in his words, in his deeds: all that counts is the cross and what follows it. Wrong, in that it makes Paul a solitary inventor. Paul says he “received” the formula of 1 Co 15, he keeps company with Peter and James, he quarrels with them over whether converted Gentiles must observe the Law; he joins a movement that existed before him and already believed Jesus risen. And Nietzsche, like Renan, is unaware of what Sanders has shown: for Paul the cross is not the rejection of Judaism, it is its fulfilment for the nations. With regard to the criterion, finally, a phrase from the Letter to the Romans deserves attention: “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your reasonable worship” (Rm 12, 1). Blood sacrifice is replaced by self-offering, and this worship is called logikê, in keeping with the Logos. Paul spiritualizes sacrifice instead of abolishing it. It is an immense advance over the burnt offerings, and it is at the same time the birth certificate of a religion that will be able to demand that the individual offer himself entirely.

    In literature Anatole France, Sur la pierre blanche (1905) ; Níkos Kazantzákis, The Last Temptation (1955)

    In Sur la pierre blanche, Anatole France imagines the proconsul Gallio, brother of Seneca, telling his friends in Corinth about a hearing at which some Jews of the port quarrelled before him: one of them, “fort laid, bancroche et chassieux, nommé Paul ou Saul, originaire de Tarse”, very ugly, bandy-legged and bleary-eyed, named Paul or Saul, a native of Tarsus, an upholsterer by trade, was accused by the head of the synagogue of perverting their law. Gallio dismissed them: “puisqu'il s'agissait uniquement d'une querelle de mots et d'un différend sur les termes de leur loi, ce n'était pas mon affaire”, since it was solely a quarrel about words and a dispute over the terms of their law, it was no business of mine; “Videz vos querelles entre vous comme vous l'entendrez”, settle your quarrels among yourselves as you see fit.

    Why here: the scene expands the verse of Acts (18, 12-17) by showing what the Greek could not see in the “folly” of the cross: not a doctrine to be refuted, but a quarrel about words unworthy of a tribunal. France gives the regime of error its most ironic form, that of a wisdom mistaken about what matters, which treats as a detail the man who, as Nietzsche says, will shift the centre of gravity of existence beyond existence.

    Kazantzákis, in The Last Temptation, pushes Nietzsche's thesis to the point of fable: in the dream in which Jesus has escaped the cross and grown old as a family man, Paul comes to see him and tells him that he will preach Christ crucified and risen all the same, because the world needs that Christ and the man Jesus can do nothing about it. Both the Church of Greece and Rome condemned the book: the fable said too bluntly what the essay judges to be half right.

    Sources: Anatole France, Sur la pierre blanche, “Gallion” (1905); Níkos Kazantzákis, Ο Τελευταίος Πειρασμός (The Last Temptation, 1955).

    Justin Martyrc. 100-c. 165the Logos sown in all human beings

    Background: Christianity in the Roman Empire: from Nero to Diocletian · The religion of the Greek city: sacrifices, festivals, oracles, impiety trials · The thought of Philo of Alexandria: Genesis read with Plato · Justin and the apologists of the 2nd century: Christianity as philosophy · The Acts of the Apostles: from Jerusalem to Rome

    Born in Samaria into a pagan family, Justin sought the truth among the philosophers before finding it, he says, among the prophets. Converted c. 130, he opened a school in Rome where he taught Christianity as a philosophy, wearing the philosopher's cloak, and he died a martyr there c. 165. His two Apologies, addressed c. 150-155 to the emperor Antoninus and to the senate, are the first systematic effort to present the Christian faith to the Greco-Roman world in its own language. They rest on an idea that Philo had prepared and that Justin carries to its conclusion: the Logos that became flesh in Jesus was already present, in part, in all human beings.

    The thesis is stated with a clarity that is still astonishing. Christ, Justin writes, is the Logos in which the whole human race has had a share, and those who lived according to the Logos are Christians, even if they were held to be atheists: among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus and those like them; among the barbarians, Abraham, Elijah and many others (1 Apology, 46). The word “atheists” carries all the weight here. Christians were accused of atheism because they refused the gods of the city; Socrates had been accused for the same reason, and the trial of Socrates becomes the precedent for Christian martyrdom. Justin says so expressly in the Second Apology: Socrates was accused of the same crimes as we are, of introducing new divinities and of not recognizing the gods the city recognized (2 Apology, 10). This is the very crime that the law of the Laws punished: at its birth, Christianity presents itself as the religion of the impious according to Plato and of the just according to Socrates.

    The same chapter contains a quotation over which Celsus and Origen would argue. Justin writes that Socrates urged men to come to know the God unknown to them through the inquiry of reason, saying that it is neither easy to find the Father and maker of all things nor safe, having found him, to declare him to all (2 Apology, 10). This is the Timaeus, which Justin attributes to Socrates: “τὸν μὲν οὖν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς εὑρεῖν τε ἔργον καὶ εὑρόντα εἰς πάντας ἀδύνατον λέγειν”, to find the maker and father of this universe is a task, and having found him, it is impossible to declare him to all (Timaeus 28c). For Justin, Christ did what Plato declared impossible: the Father, inaccessible to the philosophers, made himself known to all.

    The doctrine that gave its name to Justin's thought is that of the Logos spermatikos, the seminal reason. Each of the philosophers, he writes, spoke well insofar as he had a share in the seminal Logos, seeing what was akin to it; and whatever has been well said among all men belongs to us Christians (2 Apology, 13). The formula is double, and its two faces have had two opposite posterities. On the one hand, it is an opening of rare generosity: truth is not the preserve of the baptized, it is sown in all, and one can be a Christian without knowing it. On the other, it is an annexation: everything that is true in others is ours. Justin adds that he professes Christianity not because Plato's teachings are foreign to those of Christ, but because they are not in every respect similar to them (ibid.). Plato saw a part; Christ is the whole.

    Justin also wrote, c. 160, a Dialogue with Trypho, in which he discusses the interpretation of the Scriptures with a cultivated Jew. The book opens with the account of his conversion: he had gone through the schools, Stoic, Peripatetic, Pythagorean, and had settled on Platonism, which promised him the sight of God, when an old man met by the seashore showed him that the prophets knew more than the philosophers. The account is no doubt stylized, but it says the essential: Christianity is not the opposite of philosophy, it is its fulfilment, the only one that keeps its promises. Hegel would take up this scheme by inverting it, since for him it is philosophy that fulfils religion by raising it to the concept; the comparison, which is constructed, shows that the question of which fulfils the other has never ceased to be asked.

    The Dialogue with Trypho also has a dark side: it is one of the first texts in which separation from Judaism becomes a polemic against it: the Law is presented there as a discipline imposed on the Jews because of the hardness of their hearts, and the Church as the true Israel. The doctrine of the seminal Logos, so welcoming towards the Greeks, is much less so towards the Jews, whom it reproaches for having had the Word before their eyes without recognizing it. Christian universalism thus begins with an exclusion, and the long history of Christian anti-Judaism finds one of its roots there.

    An argument that now seems naive has had a long history. Justin asserts that Plato borrowed from Moses his doctrine of creation from formless matter, and even that the passage of the Timaeus in which the world soul is arranged “in the shape of a chi”, crossed within the universe, comes from the bronze serpent that Moses raised in the desert, read by Plato as a cross he did not understand (1 Apology, 59-60). This is the thesis of the “theft of the Greeks”, taken up by Clement of Alexandria and by Eusebius: Greek wisdom is later than Moses and derived from him. Historically false, it answers a polemical necessity: in a world where antiquity confers authority, a religion born under Tiberius had to prove that it was older than Plato.

    Justin made Christianity a philosophy, and it is as a philosopher that he dies, refusing to sacrifice to the gods of the Empire. Martyrdom here is not the sacrificial absolute that the criterion denounces: it is the Roman state, not Justin's doctrine, that demands the sacrifice, and Justin dies for having refused an act of worship. But the doctrine of the seminal Logos contains in germ the other danger: if everything that is true belongs to Christians, those who deny it are not merely in error, they are withholding what does not belong to them. Justin's openness and the intolerance of the following centuries come out of the same sentence.

    In literature Pierre Corneille, Polyeucte (1642) ; Henryk Sienkiewicz, Quo vadis (1896)

    Polyeucte, a newly baptized Armenian nobleman, goes to smash the idols in the middle of a sacrifice and seeks martyrdom. To his wife Pauline he explains the scale of his debts: “Je dois ma vie au peuple, au prince, à sa couronne ; / Mais je la dois bien plus au Dieu qui me la donne : / Si mourir pour son prince est un illustre sort, / Quand on meurt pour son Dieu, quelle sera la mort !”, I owe my life to the people, to the prince, to his crown; / but I owe it far more to the God who gives it me: / if to die for one's prince is an illustrious fate, / when one dies for one's God, what will that death be! (IV, 3). Before his father-in-law, the governor Félix, he declares: “J'ai profané leur temple, et brisé leurs autels”, I have profaned their temple and broken their altars, and to the repeated injunction “Adore-les, ou meurs !”, worship them, or die!, he answers only “Je suis chrétien”, I am a Christian (V, 3).

    Why here: the tragedy stages exactly the case of Justin. It is Rome, through the voice of Félix, that demands sacrifice to the gods and death for whoever refuses it; Polyeucte demands nothing of anyone, he offers his own life. The criterion separates the two: self-offering refounds nothing, the authority that demands it of others does. But Corneille also shows the other face, the one the essay reads in the seminal Logos: the convert who breaks the altars of others already regards their worship as a theft.

    In Quo vadis, Petronius, the arbiter of elegance, observes with an aesthete's curiosity the sect with which his nephew Vinicius becomes infatuated, without ever believing in it; he sees Nero turn the Christians into the torches of his gardens, and chooses his own death, at his banquet, as a man of letters who wants neither Christ nor Caesar. The novel gives the reader of the Dialogue with Trypho what he does not see in Justin: the gaze of the cultivated Roman for whom this martyrdom is stubbornness.

    Sources: Pierre Corneille, Polyeucte, IV, 3 and V, 3 (1642); Henryk Sienkiewicz, Quo vadis (1896).

    Celsus and Origenthe first critique of Christianity, and its answer

    Background: Christianity in the Roman Empire: from Nero to Diocletian · Justin and the apologists of the 2nd century: Christianity as philosophy · Celsus and the True Doctrine: the first philosophical critique of Christianity · The thought of Origen: allegory, the pre-existence of souls, apocatastasis · Councils and the formation of dogma: from Nicaea to Chalcedon · The mysteries and Orphism: Eleusis, Orpheus, Cybele, Isis, Mithras · The apocryphal gospels: Thomas, Peter, Mary, Judas and the others · How the canon was formed: criteria, lists and excluded texts · How the Bible has been read: allegory, the four senses, historical criticism

    Around 178, under Marcus Aurelius, a Platonist philosopher of whom we know almost nothing, Celsus, wrote against the Christians a treatise he entitled Alêthês logos, The True Word. The book is lost. We know it because Origen, around 248, at the request of his patron Ambrose, refuted it sentence by sentence in the eight books of Against Celsus, quoting his adversary at length. Origen says as much in the very preface: he is answering the treatise that was sent to him, which he does not think anyone, however little advanced in philosophy, will accept as a “true word”, as Celsus entitled it (Against Celsus, preface, 4). A complete paradox: the first great anti-Christian pamphlet has reached us only through the piety of a theologian who wanted to destroy it. It is an attested response, the oldest in this essay.

    Celsus's accusations fall into four families. The first targets the person of Jesus: Celsus has a Jew speak, who reproaches Jesus for having invented his virgin birth, for having been born in a village of Judea to a poor spinner driven out by her husband, a carpenter, for adultery; Jesus is said to have hired himself out as a servant in Egypt, to have learned marvellous powers there, and to have come back to proclaim himself a god (Against Celsus I, 28). The father is said to be a soldier named Panthera (I, 32). Celsus then compares the miracles of Jesus to the tricks of the charlatans who, in the marketplaces, for a few obols, drive out demons and cure diseases (I, 68). This is the magician thesis, which denies the divinity of Jesus, not his existence.

    The second family targets faith itself. Celsus reproaches the Christians for wanting neither to give nor to receive a reason for what they believe, and for repeating: do not examine, believe, your faith will save you; and he compares them to the begging priests of Cybele and to soothsayers (I, 9). The third targets their audience. According to Celsus, the Christians say: let no educated, wise or prudent man come to us, but if anyone is ignorant, foolish, uneducated, let him come with confidence; which shows, he concludes, that they neither want nor are able to win over anyone but the simple, the nobodies, slaves, women and children (III, 44). The fourth, the most interesting for us, accuses the Christians of having misunderstood Plato: whatever is good in Scripture, Plato said better, without bombast and without promises (VI, 1), and the Christians who speak of a “supercelestial” God have merely misread the Phaedrus (VI, 19).

    Celsus thus anticipated almost the whole of the modern critique. The thesis of credulity, which demands reasons, is that of Voltaire and d'Holbach. The social thesis, which makes Christianity a religion of slaves and the ignorant, will be Nietzsche's, turned into an accusation of ressentiment, and Engels's, turned into a eulogy of the oppressed. The thesis of borrowing, which makes Christianity a degraded Platonism, announces Nietzsche's formula quoted at the head of this part. And the scandalous genealogy of Jesus, son of a soldier and a repudiated woman, will be taken up by medieval Jewish polemic, then by the libertines. A single argument is missing, and its absence is remarkable: Celsus never claims that Jesus did not exist; on the contrary, he despises him because he lived and was crucified. The first adversary of Christianity, who lived a century and a half after the crucifixion and had every interest in denying whatever he could deny, does not deny that.

    Origen's answer ranks among the great texts of Christian thought because it accepts the adversary's ground. On credulity, Origen answers that, if it were possible for all men to leave the business of life and devote themselves to philosophy, no other method should be followed but that one; but that this is impossible, and that faith is the path of those who cannot philosophize, without Christianity thereby renouncing inquiry and interpretation (I, 9). On the audience, he answers that the ambassadors of truth must seek to win over the greatest number, the simple as well as the intelligent, barbarians as well as Greeks, and that those who turn away from the ignorant as from slaves incapable of following a polished discourse strangely restrict the public good (VI, 1).

    The climax of the dispute is an exchange about the Timaeus. Celsus sends the Christians back to Plato as a better teacher of theology, and quotes the sentence Justin had already quoted: it is hard to find the maker and father of this universe, and having found him, impossible to make him known to all; see, he adds, how divine men seek the way of truth, and how well Plato knew that it was impossible for all to walk in it (VII, 42). Origen answers that these words of Plato are noble and admirable, but that Scripture shows a still greater love of humankind in the Logos of God, who was in the beginning with God and who became flesh, in order to reveal to all what, according to Plato, it was impossible to make known to all (ibid.). The whole difference between Platonism and Christianity lies there. For Celsus, the knowledge of God is the privilege of an elite, and the multitude must keep to the cults of the city. For Origen, it is offered to all, because God himself came down to them.

    Still, one must measure what Origen grants his adversary. Origen is himself a philosopher trained in Alexandria, a pupil, according to Porphyry, of the same Ammonius who was Plotinus's teacher. He reads Scripture according to Philo's method, on three levels, body, soul and spirit, and does not shrink from theses that the Church would later judge unacceptable: the pre-existence of souls, or the hope that all beings, perhaps even the devil, will in the end be restored in God. These doctrines, or those attributed to him, were condemned in the sixth century, long after his death, and most of his Greek work was lost for that reason. The first great Christian theologian, who had answered the first great critique, thus ended up a posthumous heretic. The lesson is twofold: Christian theology was built by borrowing from Greek philosophy its weapons against Greek philosophy, as Celsus accused it of doing; and the institution that came out of it ended up condemning the man who had best defended it, for having thought too much. Eckhart, also condemned after his death, would meet the same fate: the critique of religion has often begun inside theology, among those whom the Church afterwards rejected.

    Celsus, moreover, is not a sceptic. He believes in a supreme God, inaccessible, whom only the wise approach, and in a host of lesser divinities, demons in the Greek sense, who govern peoples and places and to whom it is right to render the honours that custom prescribes. This is therefore not the critique of an unbeliever, but that of a man who cares about the hierarchy of the divine and about traditional piety, and who sees in a religion claiming universality a threat to the order of the world. That is why it seems to me wrong to make him the ancestor of modern atheists. He is the ancestor of those who defend religion for the order it secures, from Voltaire to Maurras and down to the later Onfray, who defends a Christian civilization without sharing its faith. The first adversary of Christianity was a religious conservative.

    The dispute also concerns the city, and in that way it bears directly on our question. At the end of his treatise, Celsus adjures the Christians to help the emperor with all their strength, to work with him to uphold justice, to fight for him and, if need be, under his command; and he urges them to accept the public offices required to uphold the laws and religion (Against Celsus VIII, 73 and 75). Celsus does not ask the Christians to believe in the gods; he asks them to be citizens, that is, to take part in the civil religion without which, he thinks, the Empire dissolves. Origen answers that the Christians help the emperor by their prayers better than soldiers by their arms, and above all that the Christians recognize, in each city, the existence of another homeland, founded by the Logos of God, the Church, whose offices they prefer to serve (VIII, 73 and 75).

    This answer gives birth to an idea that would govern the whole political history of the West: the separation of the religious community from the political community. For Celsus as for Plato, religion is a matter for the city; for Origen, there are two cities, and the higher is not the emperor's. Augustine would give this idea its finished form in the City of God. It has two faces. It frees conscience from the grip of the State, and Bayle, Locke and the Enlightenment would be its distant heirs. But it also creates a second power, the Church, which would in turn be able to demand what the city used to demand.

    Who is right? Justice must first be done to Celsus, whom the Christian tradition has treated as a slanderer. His arguments on credulity and on the borrowings from Platonism are strong, his information on the Jewish polemic of his time precious. But his position rests on the Platonic presupposition par excellence, the division between the philosophers who know and the multitude who believe what the city prescribes for them: Celsus is the last heir of Plato the legislator. Origen, for his part, opens the door to spiritual equality: the God of the philosophers becomes everyone's God, and the slave can know as much as Plato. But he closes, at least in germ, the door to freedom of thought: if the truth is given to all by revelation, the one who refuses it is no longer an ignorant person to be enlightened, he becomes a rebel. The dispute is therefore symmetrical. Celsus defends a political absolute, the gods of the city, to which the individual must sacrifice; Origen defends a revealed absolute, which Christian power would soon impose with the same rigour. Neither of them leaves religion. But from their dispute are born the very idea of a critique of religion by reason and the idea, just as modern, that it must be possible to tell the truth to all.

    In literature Lucian of Samosata, On the Death of Peregrinus (c. 165) ; Gustave Flaubert, La Tentation de saint Antoine (1874)

    Lucian recounts the spectacular suicide of the Cynic Peregrinus, who threw himself onto a pyre at Olympia in 165, and recalls that he had for a time been a Christian in Palestine, a prophet and leader of a community, imprisoned and surrounded by his brethren with extravagant care; the Christians, he writes in substance, despise death and believe themselves immortal, and a clever charlatan can live at their expense. This is, a dozen years before Celsus, the cultivated pagan's view of the sect: simpletons who hold things true without examination.

    In La Tentation de saint Antoine, Flaubert parades before the hermit the heresiarchs, Valentinus, Basilides, Mani, the Ophites and the Circumcellions, then all the gods, who die one after another down to the voice of the God of Israel: “J'étais le Dieu des armées, le Seigneur, le Seigneur Dieu !”, I was the God of hosts, the Lord, the Lord God! His guide, Hilarion, become “beau comme un archange, lumineux comme un soleil”, beautiful as an archangel, luminous as a sun, then reveals himself: “Mon royaume est de la dimension de l'univers ; et mon désir n'a pas de bornes. Je vais toujours, affranchissant[…]”, my kingdom is the size of the universe; and my desire has no bounds. I go on for ever, setting free[…].

    Why here: Flaubert read Celsus in Origen and in the heresiologists, and made a theatre of it. The parade of sects is Celsus's “audience of the ignorant” and “plagiarism” seen from the inside, each heresy holding its truth to be the only one; and Hilarion, Science, who makes the gods die by showing them, is the regime of error in person, with its ambiguity: Anthony takes him for the Devil, and the Devil carries him off. Celsus wanted to save the gods of the city from Christian credulity; Flaubert shows that the science that judges credulity sweeps the gods away with it.

    Sources: Lucian of Samosata, On the Death of Peregrinus, trans. Eugène Talbot (c. 165) ; Gustave Flaubert, La Tentation de saint Antoine, IV and V (1874).

    Porphyry and Augustinethe last adversary and the first synthesizer

    Background: Biblical chronology: the time of the story and the time of the writing · From Constantine to Theodosius: Christianity as the religion of the Empire · Genesis 1 to 3: the creation, Adam and Eve, the fall · Porphyry: the editor of Plotinus and the critic of the Christians · The thought of Augustine: Confessions, City of God, grace, original sin, controversies · Councils and the formation of dogma: from Nicaea to Chalcedon · The prophets of Israel, the exile and the book of Daniel · The vocabulary of Christian theology: revelation, grace, salvation, original sin · How the canon was formed: criteria, lists and excluded texts

    The dispute between Celsus and Origen has a sequel, and it takes place in the same school. Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234-c. 305), disciple and editor of Plotinus, knew Origen in his youth and judged him severely. In a fragment preserved by Eusebius, he relates that Origen, a pupil of Ammonius, the most learned philosopher of his time, had drawn from his teacher a great knowledge of the sciences, but that, in the conduct of his life, he had taken the opposite road, passing from Greek culture to “barbarian audacity” (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI, 19). For a third-century Platonist, Christianity is not a philosophy; it is a barbarism that stole philosophy.

    Of his Against the Christians, written around 270 according to the most common dating (others place it around 300), only fragments quoted by his refuters remain. The most famous concerns the book of Daniel. Jerome reports, in the prologue to his commentary, that Porphyry devoted his twelfth book to denying that Daniel was written by the prophet whose name it bears, and to maintaining that it was composed in Judea in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, so that Daniel did not predict the future but recounted the past (Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, prologue). This is also the conclusion of modern historical-critical exegesis, which dates the composition of Daniel to the years 167-164 BCE. Porphyry was right fifteen centuries before Spinoza and before David Friedrich Strauss, and his method is already theirs: whatever looks too much like a fulfilled prophecy was written after the event.

    Porphyry is nevertheless neither an atheist nor even an enemy of Jesus, and that is what makes his position instructive. Augustine quotes, in the City of God, a passage from his Philosophy from Oracles: the gods, Porphyry writes, have proclaimed Christ most pious and made immortal, and they remember him with praise; but they say that the Christians are polluted, contaminated and entangled in error (“Christum enim dii piissimum pronuntiauerunt et inmortalem factum[…] Christianos uero pollutos[…] et contaminatos et errore implicatos esse dicunt”) (Augustine, De civitate Dei XIX, 23). Jesus is a sage whom his disciples betrayed by making him a god: the thesis that Renan would take up and that Nietzsche would radicalize by setting Jesus against Paul was first formulated by a Neoplatonist.

    Augustine (354-430) answers Porphyry, and his answer settles the form Western theology would take for a thousand years. We have seen that he found among the Platonists the equivalent of the prologue of John, the Word with God, but not the Incarnation (Part One). His whole dialogue with them lies in this lack: they saw the goal without finding the way; they know the Logos, they refuse the Incarnation.

    Book VIII of the City of God draws from this encounter a hierarchy of philosophies. Augustine takes up there Varro's distinction between three theologies, the fabulous theology of the poets, the civil theology of cities and the natural theology of the philosophers, and it is with the philosophers alone that he wants to argue, because if wisdom is God, “uerus philosophus est amator Dei”, the true philosopher is the one who loves God (De civitate Dei VIII, 1). Among them, the Platonists prevail: “Nulli nobis quam isti propius accesserunt”, none have come closer to us than they (VIII, 5). And Augustine adds that he argues with the Platonists because their books are the best known, without ruling out that other sages, of any nation whatever, may have thought the same about God (VIII, 10). One recognizes Justin's seminal Logos, become a victor's courtesy.

    Augustine does more, and it is perhaps his most lasting legacy for spirituality: he shifts the place where God is sought. Plotinus sought the One by climbing above the soul; Augustine seeks him within the soul, and he finds a formula that expresses both movements at once: “tu autem eras interior intimo meo et superior summo meo”, you were more inward than my innermost self, and higher than my highest (Confessions III, 6, 11). The Confessions are the first great book in which a man tells his own life as the path of this inner search. It has been said that modern inwardness, that of Descartes seeking certainty in the cogito and that of Rousseau seeking religion in the heart, is its heir. If so, the spirituality of exercise that Part Twelve will defend as an exit from religion also has a Christian genealogy, and Hadot knew it, recalling what Christian spiritual exercises owed to the philosophical exercises of antiquity.

    Augustine also fixes the relation between faith and reason that the whole of scholasticism would take up. He reads in the Latin translation of Isaiah that unless one believes, one will not understand, and he draws a method from it: believe in order to understand, then understand what one believes. Anselm of Canterbury would make it, in the eleventh century, the motto of a faith seeking understanding, fides quaerens intellectum, and it is within this framework that he would formulate the argument Descartes takes up in the fifth Meditation. The God of the philosophers of the classical age was therefore not born with Descartes: he is the God of Augustine and Anselm, from whom Descartes removes the prior faith so as to keep only the proof.

    The Augustinian synthesis produces the God of whom this whole essay has been speaking from the beginning. It is the God of Plato and Plotinus, immutable, simple, source of being, of truth and of happiness, but endowed with what the Platonists denied him: a will, a history, a love, a grace, a wrath. The Good beyond being becomes a Father who judges and saves. This fusion of the God of the philosophers and the God of the Bible is the major fact of the intellectual history of the Christian West, and the moderns would undo it from two sides. Pascal would undo it from above, by setting the God of Abraham against the God of the philosophers; Heidegger would undo it from below, by showing that the God of metaphysics, cause of itself and ground of beings, has nothing divine about him. Between the two, Spinoza would keep the God of the philosophers while removing from him everything the Bible had given him, and Feuerbach would give back to man everything Augustine had given to God.

    Augustine is also the author who, against the Donatists, justified recourse to the secular arm to bring schismatics back into the Church, commenting on the “compel them to come in” of the parable (Lc 14, 23); this is a fact established by his correspondence, which I do not quote here for lack of having reread it. The God of the philosophers, become a personal God and the God of the Empire, can henceforth demand. Celsus defended the gods of the city against the religion of slaves; two centuries later, the religion of slaves has become the religion of the city, and it has made the law of the Laws its own. The birth of Christianity thus ends in a refoundation in the strict sense, the one Plato had dreamed of and that the Christian emperors, from Constantine to Theodosius, carried out: a rational theology, armed by the State. The whole history of the modern critique of religion would be, in many respects, the history of the defeat of this alliance.

    In literature Henrik Ibsen, Kejser og Galilæer (1873) ; Marcel Proust, Le Temps retrouvé (1927) ; Petrarch, Secretum (c. 1347-1353)

    Emperor and Galilean (Kejser og Galilæer), the drama in ten acts that Ibsen regarded as his major work, follows Julian from the school of Athens to the throne and to death in Persia. The mystic Maximus whispers to him the idea of a “third empire” that would reconcile the empire of the flesh, paganism, and the empire of the spirit, Christianity; Julian believes he is founding it by restoring the gods, and does nothing but persecute, then die, the Galilean having won all the same. This is Porphyry's pagan refoundation turned political: a philosopher emperor who wants to give back to the gods of the city the place the religion of slaves took from them, and who discovers that the sacred cannot be restored by decree.

    Proust, at the end of Le Temps retrouvé, names what involuntary memory has made the narrator discover: “cette réalité que nous risquerions fort de mourir sans l'avoir connue, et qui est tout simplement notre vie, la vraie vie, la vie enfin découverte et éclaircie, la seule vie, par conséquent, réellement vécue, cette vie qui, en un sens, habite à chaque instant chez tous les hommes aussi bien que chez l'artiste”, that reality which we would very likely die without having known, and which is quite simply our life, real life, life at last discovered and illuminated, the only life, therefore, really lived, the life which, in a sense, dwells at every moment in all men as much as in the artist. Why here: it is the “interior intimo meo” of the Confessions without God at the bottom of inwardness. The essay notes that inwardness and the spirituality of exercise have a Christian genealogy; Proust is its purest heir, who keeps the Augustinian movement, turning inward to find the truth, and replaces what is found there with Time and with the work. Petrarch, a millennium before him, had already made Augustine his interlocutor in the Secretum, three days of dialogue in which the saint reproaches the poet for his fame and his love, without quite converting him [résumé].

    Sources: Henrik Ibsen, Kejser og Galilæer (1873) ; Marcel Proust, Le Temps retrouvé, vol. II (1927, posthumous) ; Petrarch, Secretum (c. 1347-1353).
