    Pascal1623-1662the God of Abraham against the God of the philosophers

    Background: The thought of Augustine: Confessions, City of God, grace, original sin, controversies · The thought of Montaigne: the Essays, scepticism, custom, experience · The philosophy of Descartes: doubt, the cogito, God as guarantor of science · The thought of Pascal: the three orders, the wager, Jansenism · The patriarchs: Abraham, the sacrifice of Isaac, Jacob · The prophets of Israel, the exile and the book of Daniel · The vocabulary of Christian theology: revelation, grace, salvation, original sin · The God of the Bible: his names, his images and the formation of monotheism

    On the night of Monday 23 November 1654, from about half past ten in the evening until about half past midnight, Blaise Pascal lived through an experience that he recorded on a sheet of paper, copied onto a piece of parchment, and sewed into the lining of his coat, where it was found after his death. This text, known as the Memorial, bears after the date a single isolated word, “Feu”, fire, and continues thus: “Dieu d'Abraham, Dieu d'Isaac, Dieu de Jacob, / non des philosophes et des savants. / Certitude. Certitude. Sentiment. Joie. Paix.”, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, / not of the philosophers and the scholars. / Certainty. Certainty. Feeling. Joy. Peace.

    These two lines contain a critique of religion that is never ranked among the critiques of religion, because it is made in the name of faith. The God “of the philosophers and the scholars” is the God of Descartes, whom Pascal knew, and whom he did not forgive Descartes for having wanted to do without (fr. 77, quoted above): a demonstrated God, guarantor of the eternal truths, first mover, cause of himself. This God Pascal does not deny; he declares him useless for salvation. The true God is the God of a history, that of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God who reveals himself to persons and not to reasonings. Heidegger will say the same thing of the causa sui (Part Ten); Pascal had said it, without the concept of onto-theology, on that night in 1654. And Jean-Luc Marion, a reader of both Pascal and Heidegger, will make this opposition the centre of God Without Being.

    The Pensées, published in 1670 by Port-Royal from the bundles of papers Pascal left (the order of the fragments is a reconstruction by the editors, and the Léon Brunschvicg edition I quote proposes one among others), develop this critique in three directions.

    The first is the primacy of the heart. “Le cœur a ses raisons, que la raison ne connaît point”, the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know (fr. 277); and the next fragment: “C'est le cœur qui sent Dieu, et non la raison : voilà ce que c'est que la foi : Dieu sensible au cœur, non à la raison”, it is the heart that feels God, and not reason: that is what faith is: God perceptible to the heart, not to reason (fr. 278). The Pascalian “heart” is not feeling in the Romantic sense; it is the faculty that grasps first principles, immediate intuition. But the formula opens a path that Schleiermacher will take, and that leads to religion as experience.

    The second is the hidden God. Pascal takes up the verse of Isaiah, “Vere tu es Deus absconditus” (Is 45, 15), and makes it a thesis: Scripture “dit au contraire que Dieu est un Dieu caché”, says on the contrary that God is a hidden God (fr. 242). One must therefore not seek to prove God from nature, as the apologists do; nature proves nothing, or rather it shows both the presence and the absence of God. Modern man, in the infinite universe, first experiences the void: “Le silence éternel de ces espaces infinis m'effraie”, the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me (fr. 206). Pascal is one of the first Christian thinkers to take the experience of God's absence seriously as a religious experience. Nietzsche, who said he did not read him but loved him, will see in him “das lehrreichste Opfer des Christentums”, the most instructive victim of Christianity (Ecce homo, “Warum ich so klug bin”, § 3); Simone Weil will take up the idea of a God who withdraws.

    The third is the wager, fragment 233, the most famous and the most misread. It is presented as a calculation of interest, and it is one; but the essential lies elsewhere. “Dieu est, ou il n'est pas”, God is, or he is not: reason cannot decide. Yet one cannot not choose: “il faut parier ; cela n'est pas volontaire, vous êtes embarqué”, you must wager; it is not optional, you are embarked. And when the interlocutor objects that he is so made that he cannot believe, Pascal gives him a method: do as those who believe do, “en prenant de l'eau bénite, en faisant dire des messes, etc. Naturellement même cela vous fera croire et vous abêtira”, taking holy water, having masses said, and so on. Quite naturally this will make you believe and will make you like the beasts.

    This “vous abêtira” does not mean “will make you stupid” but “will make you like the beasts”, that is, will submit the machine, the automaton, habit, in place of proud reason. But it says something that all of modern critique will rediscover: belief is acquired through practice, and practice precedes belief. Durkheim will show that rite makes belief and not the reverse; Pascal, for his part, had prescribed it. One sees here how thin the line is between the apologist and the sociologist: the same proposition, that belief is born of habit, serves Pascal to convert and Hume to explain.

    Pascal is therefore not a critic of religion in the sense that Spinoza is, but he radically separates the God of faith from the God of reason, and it is this separation that will make possible, on the one hand, the rational critique of theology (if the God of the philosophers is not the true God, he can be demolished without touching faith), and on the other, a religion of the heart that no longer owes anything to proofs. Kierkegaard, two centuries later, will take up his fight against an overly reasonable Christendom.

    In literature Charles Baudelaire, “Le Gouffre” (1862) ; Jean Racine, Phèdre (1677)

    “Pascal avait son gouffre, avec lui se mouvant”, Pascal had his abyss, moving with him: the first line of Baudelaire's “Le Gouffre” turns the anecdote of the abyss that Pascal is said to have seen open at his side into the very name of modern anguish, which now finds in the sky only a window open onto nothingness.

    Why here: Baudelaire keeps from Pascal the eternal silence of the infinite spaces and loses the God of Abraham who filled it. The abyss without the wager is what fragment 206 becomes when the heart no longer feels anything: the dread remains, the addressee is missing. The poem measures what the essay calls an exit from above, and what happens when the above empties.

    Phèdre is the tragedy of the hidden God as Lucien Goldmann read it in 1955, in the book that bears that title and that places Racine among the writers of Port-Royal: the dominant reading in its day, now disputed, and which I give for what it is. Phèdre, granddaughter of the Sun, lives under the gaze of a heaven that sees everything and never answers: “Soleil, je te viens voir pour la dernière fois !”, Sun, I come to see you for the last time! (I, 3); then, when the sin is consummated, “J'ai pour aïeul le père et le maître des dieux ; / Le ciel, tout l'univers est plein de mes aïeux : / Où me cacher ? Fuyons dans la nuit infernale”, my forebear is the father and master of the gods; / heaven, the whole universe is full of my forebears: / where can I hide? Let us flee into the infernal night (IV, 6). Grace does not come; the heroine is judged by a God who keeps silent. This is the world of the Memorial seen from the side of those who did not have the night of 23 November.

    Sources: Charles Baudelaire, “Le Gouffre”, Les Fleurs du mal, 1868 ed. (poem of 1862); Jean Racine, Phèdre, I, 3 and IV, 6 (1677); Lucien Goldmann, The Hidden God (Le Dieu caché, 1955), for the reading.

    Portrait: Gérard Edelinck, CC BY-SA 4.0

    Spinoza1632-1677God is not someone

    Background: Biblical chronology: the time of the story and the time of the writing · The Bible: books, canons and languages · Spinoza's philosophy: substance, attributes, modes, conatus, kinds of knowledge, the Theological-Political Treatise · The short books: Ruth, Esther, Jonah, Tobit, Judith, Lamentations, Ezra and Nehemiah · Wars of Religion and the birth of toleration: from St Bartholomew's Day to Bayle · The thought of Leo Strauss: natural right, esotericism, Athens and Jerusalem · The thought of Comte-Sponville: materialism, wisdom, spirituality without God · How the Bible has been read: allegory, the four senses, historical criticism

    The Tractatus theologico-politicus (Theological-Political Treatise) appeared in 1670, anonymously, under a false publisher's imprint; the Ethica (Ethics) appeared only after Spinoza's death, in the Opera posthuma of 1677. This gap between what Spinoza published in his lifetime and what he held back matters: the TTP is a book of political combat, the Ethics a system. The critique of religion does not have the same function in the one and in the other, and confusing them produces the most widespread misreading of Spinoza, the one that makes him a masked atheist.

    His fundamental thought is contained in a formula from the preface to the fourth part of the Ethics: “Deus seu Natura”, God, that is, Nature. The full sentence reads: “Ratio igitur, seu causa, cur Deus seu Natura agit, et cur existit, una eademque est”, the reason, or cause, why God, that is, Nature, acts and why he exists is one and the same. The formula does not abolish God; it displaces him. God is not a being separate from the world who wants something for himself; he is the single substance of which all things are modes, and he acts by the sole necessity of his nature. He therefore has neither design, nor anger, nor favour. What is false in religion is not God; it is the image of a God who resembles a king. One recognizes the gesture of Epicurus, but radicalized: the gods of Epicurus were indifferent, the God of Spinoza is impersonal.

    The appendix to the first part dismantles the mechanism of this image. Men are born ignorant of the causes of things and conscious of their desires; they believe themselves free because they do not know what determines them, and they imagine that nature, like them, acts for ends. Hence finalism, and from finalism a God who supposedly arranged everything for man. When such a mind is pressed with questions about the cause of an accident, it goes back from cause to cause “donec ad Dei voluntatem, hoc est ignorantiæ asylum, confugeris”, until you take refuge in the will of God, that is, the asylum of ignorance. The will of God, in vulgar theology, is not an explanation: it is the name that explanation takes when it comes to a halt.

    The TTP adds to this analysis an affective genesis and a political thesis. The preface opens on superstition: if men could manage all their affairs by a sure plan, or if fortune were always favourable to them, they would not be superstitious; but they waver between hope and fear. And Spinoza concludes: “The true cause of superstition, what preserves and sustains it, is therefore fear”. This is the thesis of Lucretius, transposed from physics to the psychology of the passions, and Hume will take it up. As for the political thesis, it lies in the radical separation of faith and philosophy. Philosophy aims at truth; faith “requires not so much truth in its doctrines as piety, that is, what moves the mind to obedience” (ch. XIV). Between the two, “there is no commerce and no affinity” (ch. XIV).

    Here lies Spinoza's originality: he does not ask for religion to disappear. He asks that it cease to lay claim to truth and content itself with what it actually does: securing obedience to a few precepts of justice and charity. Religion becomes a social practice without theoretical content, which the State can regulate and which the philosopher has no need to combat. Spinoza therefore does not leave religion: he puts it in its place. Religion so placed closely resembles Cicero's religio, civic observance without metaphysics, and what Durkheim will call the social function of the sacred. Spinoza thinks of religion, after Polybius and Machiavelli but with another rigour, as a useful institution whose truth matters little.

    For Spinoza keeps, for himself, the name of God, charged with a meaning the vulgar do not suspect, and here the question of spirituality changes the reading. The fifth part of the Ethics culminates in a notion that hasty readers treat as a rhetorical concession and that is the summit of the system: the intellectual love of God. “Mentis Amor intellectualis erga Deum est ipse Dei Amor, quo Deus se ipsum amat”, the mind's intellectual love of God is the very love with which God loves himself (V, prop. 36). This love expects nothing in return, since God loves no one in the human sense; it is the joy that accompanies the knowledge of things in their necessity, sub specie aeternitatis. It affords an experience that Spinoza does not hesitate to describe in terms of eternity: “At nihilominus sentimus experimurque, nos æternos esse”, and nevertheless we feel and experience that we are eternal (V, prop. 23, scholium). And it is not the reward of a virtuous life: “Beatitudo non est virtutis præmium, sed ipsa virtus”, blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself (V, prop. 42).

    This last proposition is Spinoza's deepest answer to religion, deeper than the critique of finalism. Every religion of salvation promises a reward: a paradise, an eternal life, a retribution. Spinoza abolishes the reward by interiorizing it: there is no other salvation than the present joy of understanding. This is what Foucault will call a spirituality: a transformation of the subject that gives it access to the true. And this is why the Ethics can end on a sentence that sounds like a word of wisdom rather than a theorem: “Sed omnia præclara tam difficilia quam rara sunt”, but all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare. The free man, the fourth part says again, “de nulla re minus quam de morte cogitat; et ejus sapientia non mortis, sed vitæ meditatio est”, thinks of nothing less than of death, and his wisdom is a meditation not on death but on life (IV, prop. 67).

    The libertine tradition, and later part of Marxist criticism, read the retention of the name of God as prudence. I believe this reading is wrong. The God of the Ethics is not a pseudonym for Nature meant to deceive the censors; he is what allows Spinoza to think Nature as infinite, necessary and perfect, and to ground a blessedness upon it. What is preserved out of prudence is not the name of God; what is preserved, out of conviction, is the structure of the blessed life. Spinoza is a philosopher of the exit from superstition, not of the exit from the divine. Novalis, in a fragment published after his death by Friedrich Schlegel and Ludwig Tieck, called him “ein Gott-trunkener Mensch”, a God-intoxicated man (Novalis Schriften, vol. II, Berlin, 1802, p. 487).

    This is precisely what his successors will hold against him, and their objections already form a debate. Hegel, in his lectures on the history of philosophy, will say that Spinozism is not an atheism but an acosmism, “Der Spinozismus ist also Akosmismus”, and that there is in him not too little but “zu viel Gott”, too much God (Vorlesungen über die Geschichte der Philosophie, Suhrkamp ed., vol. 20, p. 162-163): far from denying God, he denies the world, which is now no more than a set of modes without consistency. Feuerbach and the Hegelian left, conversely, will read Deus seu Natura as an elegant way of saying that only Nature exists. The real objection, the one that will tell, is a different one: Spinoza explains the illusion by ignorance and fear; he does not explain why man clings to it even when it is shown to him. He describes the error; he does not account for the need for the error. That need will be the object of Feuerbach, Marx and Freud. Nietzsche, finally, who will recognize in Spinoza a precursor, will also mock the “Hocuspocus von mathematischer Form” with which he armours his philosophy (Jenseits von Gut und Böse, § 5): the geometrical form itself will seem to him a mask of the will.

    In literature Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Dichtung und Wahrheit (1814) ; Isaac Bashevis Singer, “The Spinoza of Market Street” (1961) ; Jorge Luis Borges, “Spinoza” (1964)

    In book XIV of Poetry and Truth (Dichtung und Wahrheit), Goethe recounts his encounter with the Ethics: “ich fand hier eine Beruhigung meiner Leidenschaften, es schien sich mir eine große und freie Aussicht über die sinnliche und sittliche Welt aufzutun”, here I found a calming of my passions; a great and free view over the sensible and moral world seemed to open before me. What binds him above all is “die grenzenlose Uneigennützigkeit, die aus jedem Satze hervorleuchtete”, the boundless disinterestedness that shone forth from every proposition, and “jenes wunderliche Wort: „Wer Gott recht liebt, muß nicht verlangen, daß Gott ihn wieder liebe“”, that strange saying: whoever truly loves God must not demand that God love him in return.

    Why here: the “strange saying” is proposition 19 of the fifth part, and Goethe makes of it exactly what the essay reads in Ethics V, 42: not a doctrine but a way of living, “meine Maxime, meine Ausübung”, my maxim, my practice. The poet confirms through use that Spinoza's God is kept out of conviction: no one finds peace with a pseudonym.

    In Singer's story, Dr Fischelson, an old Warsaw scholar who has been rereading the Ethics for thirty years in his garret and believes himself dying, marries his neighbour Dobbe, an illiterate old maid; the wedding night gives him back strength he thought lost, and he murmurs before the stars an apology to the divine Spinoza for having become a fool again. Borges, in a sonnet, shows the lens grinder building God in the half-light with the words of his geometry. Both say what the essay says: blessedness is not a reward, and the sage who loses it by loving someone has betrayed nothing.

    Sources: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Aus meinem Leben. Dichtung und Wahrheit, part three, book XIV (1814) ; Isaac Bashevis Singer, “The Spinoza of Market Street” (1961) ; Jorge Luis Borges, “Spinoza”, El otro, el mismo (1964).

    Portrait: Anonyme, Public domain

    Bayle1647-1706a society of atheists is possible

    Background: The thought of Pierre Bayle: the comet, the Dictionary, toleration · Leibniz's philosophy: monads, pre-established harmony, sufficient reason, theodicy · Analytic philosophy of religion: from the problem of evil to Reformed epistemology · Wars of Religion and the birth of toleration: from St Bartholomew's Day to Bayle

    Pierre Bayle, a French Protestant who took refuge in Rotterdam in 1681 after the suppression of the Protestant Academy of Sedan, published in 1682 a Lettre sur la comète, which became the following year the Pensées diverses sur la comète. The pretext was the passage of the comet of 1680, which popular belief held to be an omen. Bayle first demonstrates that a comet portends nothing; then he arrives at an unexpected argument. If comets were omens sent by God to warn men, they could only strengthen the idolatry of the pagans, who interpreted them as signs from their gods. God would thus have worked a miracle to fortify idolatry. Now is idolatry, Bayle asks, less grave than atheism? And he answers, in the very title of a section: “Que l'Athéisme n'est pas un plus grand mal que l'Idolâtrie”, that atheism is not a greater evil than idolatry (§ CXIV).

    The scandal was immediate, and it provoked an immediate attested response. The pastor Pierre Jurieu, a former friend turned enemy, attacked him precisely on this point; the modern editor quotes his complaint: “On lit le dangereux paradoxe, que l'Athéisme n'est pas un plus grand mal que l'idolâtrie”, one reads the dangerous paradox that atheism is not a greater evil than idolatry. What troubles Jurieu is not so much the theological proposition as its practical consequence: if the atheist is no worse than the idolater, why punish him?

    Bayle goes further, and this is the heart of the matter: he maintains that men act not according to their principles but according to their passions, their temperament and their habits; that belief in God therefore does not prevent Christians from being as vicious as anyone else; and that, conversely, the absence of belief does not prevent one from being virtuous. Hence the conjecture, in § CLXI of the 1749 edition: as regards morals and civil actions, a society of atheists “seroit toute semblable à une société de Paiens. Il y faudroit à la vérité des loix fort severes, et fort bien exécutées pour la punition des criminels. Mais n'en faut-il pas par tout ?”, would be quite like a society of pagans; it would indeed need very severe laws, very well enforced, for the punishment of criminals; but are they not needed everywhere? And Bayle concludes with a sentence that would delight a sociologist: “la Justice humaine fait la vertu de la plus grande partie du monde”, human justice makes the virtue of the greater part of the world.

    Bayle's argument is therefore not an apology for the atheist; it is a sociology before the term existed: men's virtue does not depend on their belief in immortality, it depends on laws, honour, opinion, temperament. Durkheim will draw the opposite consequence: if morality depends on society, and if religion is society worshipping itself, then religion did not die with God. The confrontation with the thesis that posterity attributed to Ivan Karamazov will be conducted in Part Seven.

    Bayle was not an atheist but a sceptical Calvinist, convinced that reason is powerless to establish the truths of faith and that faith must therefore do without reason, which brings him close, by an entirely different path, to Pascal. His defence of the virtuous atheist is a defence of tolerance: if the atheist can be an honest man, the State has no reason to persecute him, and all the less reason to persecute the Protestant or the Jew. The exit from religion he sketches is not an exit from faith; it is an exit from religion as political cement. In this sense he is one of the first to think the exit from religion as the end of a structure of society, not of a belief held by individuals.

    In literature Montesquieu, Persian Letters (1721) ; Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726)

    The story of the Troglodytes, which Usbek tells Mirza in letters XI to XIV, is Bayle's society of atheists turned into a fable, and turned around. A first people, without justice or gods, perishes “par leur méchanceté même”, through their very wickedness; two virtuous families rebuild a happy people whose virtue owes nothing to a Church; then this people, grown numerous, wants a king, and the old man they choose weeps: “Je vois bien ce que c'est, ô Troglodytes ! votre vertu commence à vous peser”, I see well what this is, O Troglodytes! your virtue is beginning to weigh on you; without a ruler, “il faut que vous soyez vertueux, malgré vous”, you must be virtuous in spite of yourselves, but “ce joug vous paroît trop dur”, this yoke seems too hard to you.

    Why here: Montesquieu grants Bayle that a society can be virtuous without religion, and answers him that this virtue does not last, because it is tiring: one gives oneself a king as one gives oneself a god, so as no longer to have to be just by oneself. It is Bayle's “la Justice humaine fait la vertu”, seen from the side of those who ask for its yoke.

    In Swift, the empire of Lilliput has been torn for three generations by the war of the Big-Endians and the Little-Endians: an emperor having cut his finger while opening his egg at the big end, an edict commanded that eggs be broken at the small end, and “it is computed that eleven thousand persons have at several times suffered death, rather than submit to break their eggs at the smaller end”. This is the war of religions reduced to its cause, a rite, and to its effect, the sacrifice demanded of dissenters: Bayle's critique of political cement, in a single paragraph.

    Sources: Montesquieu, Persian Letters, XI-XIV (1721) ; Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels, I, 4 (1726).

    Leibniz1646-1716why something rather than nothing

    Background: The philosophy of Descartes: doubt, the cogito, God as guarantor of science · The thought of Pierre Bayle: the comet, the Dictionary, toleration · Leibniz's philosophy: monads, pre-established harmony, sufficient reason, theodicy · Voltaire: deism, the Infamous, tolerance, Candide · Analytic philosophy of religion: from the problem of evil to Reformed epistemology · Psalms, Job, Qoheleth and the wisdom books

    Leibniz wrote about God all his life, but the two texts in which his thought is summed up are two brief expositions from 1714, written in French during a stay in Vienna: the Principes de la nature et de la grâce fondés en raison, published in 1718 in L'Europe savante, and the Monadology, first published in German translation in 1720, whose French text appeared only in 1840. The only major philosophical work he published in his lifetime is of another kind: the Theodicy: Essays on the Goodness of God, the Freedom of Man and the Origin of Evil, published in Amsterdam in 1710 and born of a controversy with a dead man, Pierre Bayle, who had died four years earlier.

    Leibniz's thought about God comes down to a question, the most famous in modern metaphysics. It is posed in § 7 of the Principes de la nature et de la grâce: “maintenant il faut s'élever à la métaphysique, en nous servant du grand principe, peu employé communément, qui porte que rien ne se fait sans raison suffisante ; c'est-à-dire que rien n'arrive sans qu'il soit possible à celui qui connaîtrait assez les choses de rendre une raison qui suffise pour déterminer pourquoi il en est ainsi, et non pas autrement. Ce principe posé, la première question qu'on a droit de faire sera : Pourquoi il y a plutôt quelque chose que rien ? Car le rien est plus simple et plus facile que quelque chose”, now we must rise to metaphysics, making use of the great principle, little employed as a rule, which holds that nothing happens without a sufficient reason; that is, that nothing happens without its being possible for one who knew things well enough to give a reason sufficient to determine why it is so and not otherwise. This principle laid down, the first question we have the right to ask will be: Why is there something rather than nothing? For nothing is simpler and easier than something.

    Everything hinges on the “for” of the last sentence: nothingness needs no explanation, since it is the simplest state; it is existence that demands one. And this explanation cannot be found in the sequence of contingent things, for each refers to another, to infinity, without any of them accounting for the whole series. The Monadology formulates the principle (“aucun fait ne saurait se trouver vrai ou existant, aucune énonciation véritable, sans qu'il y ait une raison suffisante, pourquoi il en soit ainsi et non pas autrement”, no fact can be true or existent, no statement true, unless there is a sufficient reason why it is so and not otherwise, § 32) and draws the conclusion: “la dernière raison des choses doit être dans une substance nécessaire, dans laquelle le détail des changements ne soit qu'éminemment, comme dans la source, et c'est ce que nous appelons Dieu”, the ultimate reason of things must lie in a necessary substance, in which the detail of changes exists only eminently, as in its source, and this is what we call God (§ 38). It also takes up Descartes' argument and completes it: the ontological proof is valid only if one first shows that the idea of God is possible, that is, non-contradictory, and Leibniz concludes that “Dieu seul ou l'Être nécessaire a ce privilège, qu'il faut qu'il existe, s'il est possible”, God alone, or the necessary Being, has this privilege, that he must exist if he is possible (§ 45).

    The next paragraph contains an attested response to Descartes, and it illuminates the whole difference between the two theologies. “Cependant il ne faut point s'imaginer avec quelques-uns, que les vérités éternelles, étant dépendantes de Dieu, sont arbitraires et dépendent de sa volonté, comme Descartes paraît l'avoir pris et puis M. Poiret”, yet one must not imagine, with some, that the eternal truths, being dependent on God, are arbitrary and depend on his will, as Descartes seems to have taken it, and after him M. Poiret (§ 46). Only contingent truths depend on God's choice; necessary truths depend on his understanding. Leibniz's God does not have the abyss of freedom of the Cartesian God: he is bound by logic, and he chooses according to reasons. He is reason itself become a person. One cannot go further in the rationalization of the divine, and that is why Heidegger, who in 1955-1956 devoted an entire lecture course to the principle of reason, published in 1957 under the title Der Satz vom Grund (The Principle of Reason), will see in Leibniz the thinker in whom onto-theology speaks its name most clearly: in it God is the sufficient reason of beings, the supreme being that grounds all the others.

    This God-as-reason must have reasons for creating this world rather than another, and they can lie only in his goodness. Hence the thesis that made Leibniz famous and ridiculous. Among all possible worlds, God chose the best, for “s'il n'y avait pas le meilleur (optimum) parmi tous les mondes possibles, Dieu n'en aurait produit aucun”, if there were not a best (optimum) among all possible worlds, God would have produced none (Theodicy, I, § 8). Evil is not denied: it is classified, and its presence is justified by the whole. “On peut prendre le mal métaphysiquement, physiquement et moralement. Le mal métaphysique consiste dans la simple imperfection, le mal physique dans la souffrance, et le mal moral dans le péché”, evil may be taken metaphysically, physically and morally; metaphysical evil consists in mere imperfection, physical evil in suffering, and moral evil in sin (I, § 21). Metaphysical evil is inevitable, since every creature is finite; physical evil and moral evil are not necessary, but they are possible, and God permits them because the world that contains them is better, taken as a whole, than any world that would not contain them.

    The Theodicy is an attested response, and its target is named from the preface onwards. Bayle, in his Historical and Critical Dictionary, had maintained that the Manichaeans' objections against the goodness of God were rationally unanswerable, and that one must therefore believe against reason. Leibniz replies that faith and reason cannot contradict each other, since two truths do not contradict each other, and he judges his adversary's position severely: “M. Bayle paraît l'avoir pris tout autrement : il se déclare contre la raison, lorsqu'il se pouvait contenter d'en blâmer l'abus”, M. Bayle seems to have taken it quite otherwise: he declares himself against reason, when he could have contented himself with censuring its abuse (“Discourse on the Conformity of Faith with Reason”, § 46). The debate on religion, at the dawn of the Enlightenment, thus does not run between believers and unbelievers: it runs between two believers, one who separates faith from reason to save faith, the other who unites them to save both. The same preliminary discourse counts among the adversaries of this union an Italian “secte de philosophes”, sect of philosophers, who were called “Averroïstes”, Averroists (§ 7), and we saw in Part One what was really the case with Averroes.

    The meeting with Spinoza belongs to the same picture, and it calls for caution, for Leibniz himself recounted it in a way that minimized its significance. In November 1676, returning from Paris by way of London, Leibniz stopped at The Hague and visited Spinoza, who would die three months later. The Theodicy, thirty-four years afterwards, speaks of it in one offhand sentence: “Je vis M. de la Court, aussi bien que Spinosa, à mon retour de France par l'Angleterre et par la Hollande, et j'appris d'eux quelques bonnes anecdotes sur les affaires de ce temps-là”, I saw M. de la Court, as well as Spinoza, on my return from France by way of England and Holland, and I learned from them some good anecdotes about the affairs of that time (III, § 376). Political anecdotes, then; Leibniz's papers show something else: a note from the same period records that he presented Spinoza with his demonstration of the possibility of the supremely perfect being, and that Spinoza read it. What Leibniz thought at bottom of Spinozism, the preface to the Theodicy states bluntly: Spinoza holds that everything came from the first cause “par une nécessité aveugle et toute géométrique, sans que ce premier principe des choses soit capable de choix, de bonté et d'entendement”, by a blind and wholly geometrical necessity, without this first principle of things being capable of choice, goodness and understanding. The whole of Leibnizian theology can be read as the effort to save the God of reason from the God of necessity: to keep Spinoza's rigour, but to give back to God an understanding, a will and a goodness, that is, everything Spinoza had taken from him.

    This God is not only a principle; he is also the object of a love, and Leibniz has his spirituality, which is that of the optimist. The Principes de la nature et de la grâce end with it: “On peut même dire que dès à présent l'amour de Dieu nous fait jouir d'un avant-goût de la félicité future”, one may even say that even now the love of God gives us a foretaste of future happiness; and this love, though disinterested, produces “une véritable tranquillité de l'esprit ; non pas comme les stoïciens résolus à une patience par force, mais par un contentement présent”, a true tranquillity of mind, not like the Stoics resolved upon a forced patience, but through a present contentment (§ 18). The difference from Stoicism is carefully marked: the Stoic resigns himself to the order, the Leibnizian approves it, because he knows the order is the best. Minds, § 15 says further, are members of the “cité de Dieu”, the city of God, governed by the best of monarchs, “où il n'y a point de crime sans châtiment, point de bonnes actions sans récompense proportionnée”, where there is no crime without punishment, no good action without proportionate reward. The same man spent years, in the last decade of the century, negotiating by letter with Bossuet a project for reuniting the Catholic and Protestant Churches: Leibniz's religion is a religion of reason and concord, which would have the confessions reconciled as truths agree.

    The most famous response to Leibniz is not by a professional philosopher, and it is attested. After the Lisbon earthquake of 1 November 1755, Voltaire wrote a poem on the disaster, then, in 1759, Candide, or Optimism, whose tutor Pangloss teaches “la métaphysico-théologo-cosmolonigologie”, metaphysico-theologo-cosmolonigology, and proves “que, dans ce meilleur des mondes possibles, le château de monseigneur le baron était le plus beau des châteaux”, that in this best of all possible worlds, my lord the baron's castle was the finest of castles (ch. I). After the earthquake and the auto-da-fé that follows it, Candide, flogged and bleeding, wonders: “Si c'est ici le meilleur des mondes possibles, que sont donc les autres ?”, if this is the best of all possible worlds, what then are the others? (ch. VI). And the tale ends on the answer that dismisses metaphysics: “il faut cultiver notre jardin”, we must cultivate our garden (ch. XXX). Rousseau, in a letter to Voltaire of 1756 that we shall meet again, will on the contrary take up the defence of Providence.

    Voltaire caricatures, but he touches a point that the caricature must not make us forget. Theodicy justifies each particular evil by the good of the whole. The criterion asks whether one installs an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded; now theodicy is, in the strict sense, a thought that accepts the sacrifice of the individual to the harmony of the whole, even if it is God, and not man, who decides it. Hegel will transpose theodicy into history, making world history the tribunal where individuals are judged and crushed so that Spirit may advance; and Ivan Karamazov, in Part Seven, will refuse the final harmony if it must be paid for with the tears of a single tortured child. This refusal, a constructed comparison with Leibniz, is the moral response to the Theodicy, as Candide is its ironic response. I believe it strikes truer: what is refused is not the best of worlds, it is the idea that an individual could be counted as a part of the best.

    It would be a mistake to abandon the question of § 7 along with theodicy. Leibniz answered it with God; but the question can outlive the answer. Schelling will take it up in his lectures on the philosophy of revelation, Heidegger will make it the first question of his Introduction to Metaphysics, Bergson will hold it to be a false problem, and Wittgenstein will shift the wonder it expresses towards the very fact that the world is. The last part will gather them around this single question, perhaps the purest form of what may be called a spirituality without religion: wonder before existence, which asks for neither cult, nor dogma, nor sacrifice, and which Leibniz, the most rationalist of philosophers, formulated with the greatest clarity.

    In literature Voltaire, Zadig (1747) ; Alexander Pope, An Essay on Man (1734) ; George Gordon Byron, Cain (1821)

    The penultimate chapter of Zadig turns the Theodicy into a tale. A hermit sets fire to the house of the host who received him and drowns the child of a charitable widow; then he reveals himself to be an angel, Jesrad, and explains: “il n'y a point de mal dont il ne naisse un bien”, there is no evil from which some good is not born, “il n'y a point de hasard ; tout est épreuve, ou punition, ou récompense, ou prévoyance”, there is no chance; all is trial, or punishment, or reward, or foresight. Zadig objects a first time, “s'il n'y avait que du bien, et point de mal ?”, what if there were only good, and no evil?, and a second: “Mais, dit Zadig…”, But, said Zadig…; “Comme il disait mais, l'ange prenait déjà son vol vers la dixième sphère. Zadig, à genoux, adora la Providence, et se soumit”, as he was saying but, the angel was already taking flight towards the tenth sphere; Zadig, on his knees, worshipped Providence, and submitted.

    Why here: twelve years before Candide, Voltaire has already found the answer that matters. It is not Jesrad's argument that is refuted; it is the but that is prevented from finishing: theodicy asks the individual to sacrifice his complaint, and the tale shows the angel flying off at the precise moment the complaint was about to be spoken. Pope, whom Voltaire will target in the Poem on the Lisbon Disaster, had given the same doctrine its most serene formula: “All partial evil, universal good: / And, spite of pride in erring reason's spite, / One truth is clear, whatever is, is right”.

    Byron's Cain gives Zadig's but its tragic form. Cain refuses the inherited fault: “The snake spoke truth; it was the Tree of Knowledge; / It was the Tree of Life: knowledge is good, / And Life is good; and how can both be evil?”; Lucifer, who leads him through the abyss of worlds, says of the Creator: “He is great / But, in his greatness, is no happier than / We in our conflict!”; and before Abel's altar Cain declares: “I will build no more altars, / Nor suffer any”, then kills his brother in the anger the accepted sacrifice arouses in him. This is Ivan Karamazov half a century before Ivan: not the denial of God, but the refusal to count the innocent as a part of the best.

    Sources: Voltaire, Zadig, or Destiny, ch. XX (1747) ; Alexander Pope, An Essay on Man, epistle I (1733-1734) ; George Gordon Byron, Cain, a Mystery (1821).

    Portrait: Christoph Bernhard Francke, Public domain

    Transition: from fear to morality

    On the threshold of the Enlightenment, then, the critique of religion has its principal tools at its disposal, and they come from opposed traditions. From the Epicureans and from Spinoza it inherits the idea that religion is born of fear and of ignorance of causes, and that a knowledge of nature, lived as an exercise, affords a peace that religion promised without giving. From the mystics and from Pascal it inherits the idea that the God of representations and proofs is not the true God, and that the critique of the idol can be an act of faith. From Bayle it inherits the idea that morality does not depend on belief. From Leibniz it receives the barest question, why something rather than nothing, and the obligation to justify God in the face of evil, which Voltaire is about to turn against him. The eighteenth century will combine them in incompatible ways, and Kant, at the century's end, will keep only what is rational in them, that is, morality.

    Top of the part

    Part Fourthe Enlightenment and religion within limits5 authors

    Background: From absolutism to the Revolution: the Church of France, the Enlightenment and the cult of the Supreme Being

    The Enlightenment did not have one doctrine of religion but at least five, which fought one another as fiercely as they fought the Church. Scottish empiricism made religion an object of natural history. French deism kept it as a social restraint. Rousseau refounded it twice, as a religion of the heart and as a civil religion. The materialism of Baron d'Holbach sought to destroy it. Kant's critical philosophy reduced it to morality. These five positions are still ours: we explain religion, we use it, we refound it, we fight it, or we keep what seems reasonable in it. Almost none of them leaves religion without leaving a remainder, and that remainder almost always takes the form of a cult; Hume alone is the exception.

    Hume1711-1776a natural history of belief

    Background: The philosophy of Epicurus: atoms, canonic, pleasure and the remedy for fears · Lucretius and the De rerum natura: nature explained against religion · The thought of Montaigne: the Essays, scepticism, custom, experience · The philosophy of Hume: empiricism, causation, miracles, the natural history of religion · Pascal Boyer: religion explained by cognition · The Gospel of John: the Word made flesh · The God of the Bible: his names, his images and the formation of monotheism

    David Hume published The Natural History of Religion in 1757, in a collection entitled Four Dissertations. His Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, drafted from the 1750s onward and revised until his death, appeared only in 1779, posthumously, through the care of his nephew. The gap between the dates tells of the author's caution: the first book explains religion without judging it; the second judges it, but through the mouths of characters.

    The Natural History changes the question: no longer whether God exists, but where, in human nature, belief in invisible powers comes from. And it starts from a fact that the theologians of his time regarded as a late corruption: “polytheism or idolatry was, and necessarily must have been, the first and most ancient religion of mankind” (section 1). Monotheism is not the origin but a late product, for religion was not born of the contemplation of the order of the world, as the deists believe with their argument from design, but of anxiety. The first religious ideas arose “not from a contemplation of the works of nature, but from a concern with regard to the events of life, and from the incessant hopes and fears, which actuate the human mind” (section 2).

    One recognizes the thesis of Lucretius and Spinoza, fear at the origin of the gods; but Hume adds a dynamic to it. Religions oscillate: “the principles of religion have a kind of flux and reflux in the human mind”, and men have a natural tendency to rise from idolatry to theism, then to sink back from theism into idolatry (section 8). The one and infinite God is too abstract for popular devotion, which gives him intercessors, saints, images; and when these multiply, a reform recalls the divine unity. This law of oscillation is one of the most fertile ideas in the tradition: it anticipates Weber, for whom religious rationalization itself produces disenchantment, and Bergson, for whom dynamic religion always falls back into static religion.

    He adds a comparison that Bayle had prepared and that all liberals would take up: polytheism is tolerant, monotheism intolerant, for a single god suffers no rivals. And he ends on a sceptical observation of great beauty. Having reviewed popular beliefs, which one might readily take for “sick men's dreams”, he concludes: “The whole is a riddle, an ænigma, an inexplicable mystery. Doubt, uncertainty, suspence of judgment appear the only result of our most accurate scrutiny, concerning this subject”. But this very doubt, he adds, would be hard to sustain without a stratagem: setting the superstitions against one another, making them quarrel, and during their fury “happily make our escape, into the calm, though obscure, regions of philosophy”.

    This sentence defines the sceptical exit, and all those that follow are measured against it. Hume does not claim to have refuted religion, proposes nothing in its place, founds no cult. He escapes, while admitting that the region into which he escapes is obscure. He practises the regime of error without drawing a refoundation from it, and he is thus, with Spinoza and Nietzsche, one of the rare authors in this history who leave without refounding, by a path that Spinoza and Nietzsche did not take: not a spirituality, but a suspension. Is it livable? Not all the time, Hume answered, whose sceptical philosopher, in A Treatise of Human Nature, goes back to play backgammon with his friends: “I dine, I play a game of back-gammon, I converse, and am merry with my friends” (I, 4, 7, § 9).

    The Dialogues stage three characters. Cleanthes defends experimental theism: the universe resembles a machine, so it has an author similar to the human mind. Demea defends orthodox a priori theology: God is incomprehensible, and his nature exceeds all analogy. Philo, the sceptic, allies himself by turns with one against the other and demolishes the argument from design: the analogy is weak, since one could just as well compare the universe to an animal or a vegetable, and an imperfect world suggests an imperfect god, or several, or an apprentice. At the heart of the book, in Part X, Philo takes up an ancient argument: “EPICURUS's old questions are yet unanswered. Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?”

    This trilemma, which Hume attributes to Epicurus on the authority of Lactantius (De ira Dei, 13), an attribution now disputed, is the argument that Ivan Karamazov will take up in concrete form, with the tortured children. But Philo does not conclude in favour of atheism. In Part XII he even seems to rally to a minimal form of theism, and he lets fall this sentence, whose irony is undecidable: “To be a philosophical Sceptic is, in a man of letters, the first and most essential step towards being a sound, believing Christian”. A tribute to Pascal, who wished to humble reason to make room for faith, a precaution, or mockery? Critics disagree, and I believe the ambiguity must be left where Hume put it: the sceptic can no more affirm the non-existence of God than his existence, and his exit from religion is an exit from certainty, in one direction as in the other.

    Hume's clearest successor is Kant, who would say that Hume had woken him from his dogmatic slumber (about causality, in the Prolegomena of 1783), and whose Critique of Pure Reason (1781) would take up the critique of the proofs of God's existence. But he would draw from it a conclusion Hume had not envisaged: if theoretical reason cannot prove God, practical reason can postulate him.

    In literature Denis Diderot, Letter on the Blind (1749) ; Laurence Sterne, Tristram Shandy (1759-1767)

    The Letter on the Blind reports the last moments of the blind mathematician Saunderson, to whom a minister holds up the wonders of nature as an objection: “laissez là tout ce beau spectacle qui n'a jamais été fait pour moi ! J'ai été condamné à passer ma vie dans les ténèbres ; et vous me citez des prodiges que je n'entends point, et qui ne prouvent que pour vous”, leave aside all that fine spectacle which was never made for me! I have been condemned to spend my life in darkness, and you cite to me marvels I do not understand, which are proof only for you. The dying man imagines worlds “estropiés, manqués”, crippled, botched, that come together and fall apart, and concludes, turning to the minister: “Voyez-moi bien, monsieur Holmes, je n'ai point d'yeux. Qu'avions-nous fait à Dieu, vous et moi, un pour avoir cet organe, l'autre pour en être privé ?”, look at me well, Mr Holmes, I have no eyes. What had we done to God, you and I, one to have this organ, the other to be deprived of it? The letter earned Diderot three months at Vincennes.

    Why here: this is Part XI of Hume's Dialogues thirty years before Hume, and by another path: Philo refutes the argument from design by logic, Saunderson by the absence of an organ. The proof from the order of the world proves only for those who see the order, and order itself is only “une symétrie passagère ; un ordre momentané”, a passing symmetry, a momentary order. Diderot concludes no more than Hume does: Saunderson dies calling on the God of Clarke and Newton, and we do not know whether he finds him.

    Sterne, an Anglican clergyman and a friend of Hume, gave scepticism its joyful form. Tristram Shandy constantly interrupts itself, and justifies doing so: “Digressions, incontestably, are the sunshine; they are the life, the soul of reading!” (vol. I, ch. 22); and Yorick's sermon, which Corporal Trim reads aloud, teaches that “your conscience is not a law; No, God and reason made the law, and have placed conscience within you to determine” (vol. II, ch. 17). Digression is the suspension of judgment turned into narrative, and Hume would have recognized his backgammon in it: one does not decide, one carries on.

    Sources: Denis Diderot, Lettre sur les aveugles à l'usage de ceux qui voient (1749) ; Laurence Sterne, The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman, vol. I, ch. 22 and vol. II, ch. 17 (1759-1767).

    Portrait: Allan Ramsay, Public domain

    Voltaire1694-1778“it would be necessary to invent him”

    Background: Leibniz's philosophy: monads, pre-established harmony, sufficient reason, theodicy · Voltaire: deism, the Infamous, tolerance, Candide · From absolutism to the Revolution: the Church of France, the Enlightenment and the cult of the Supreme Being

    Voltaire is not an atheist, and he repeated it all his life with an insistence that is not mere caution. He is a deist: he believes in a Supreme Being, architect of the universe and guarantor of morality, and he fights the “Infâme”, the Infamous, that is, superstition, fanaticism and the Church that sustains them. His position is the mirror image of Spinoza's: Spinoza criticizes the vulgar image of God in order to keep an impersonal God; Voltaire criticizes the Church in order to keep a personal God who judges.

    The central text is a verse epistle of 1769 to the anonymous author of the Treatise of the Three Impostors, a clandestine pamphlet that made three frauds of Moses, Jesus and Muhammad. Voltaire grows angry there with militant atheism: “Corrige le valet, mais respecte le maître. / Dieu ne doit point pâtir des sottises du prêtre”, correct the servant, but respect the master; God must not suffer for the follies of the priest. Then he sets out the function of belief in God in lines from which comes the most quoted text of the whole affair:

    “Ce système sublime à l'homme est nécessaire. / C'est le sacré lien de la société, / Le premier fondement de la sainte équité, / Le frein du scélérat, l'espérance du juste.” This sublime system is necessary to man. It is the sacred bond of society, the first foundation of holy equity, the curb of the wicked, the hope of the just.

    And a little further on, the line that became a proverb: “Si Dieu n'existait pas, il faudrait l'inventer. / Que le sage l'annonce, et que les rois le craignent.” If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him. Let the wise man proclaim him, and let kings fear him.

    People always quote the first of these alexandrines, almost never the second, which nonetheless gives it its meaning. Voltaire does not merely say that God is useful to the people; he says that the wise man must proclaim him, and that kings must fear him. This God has a double political function: he restrains the wicked, but also the tyrant, and the rest of the epistle warns kings that if they oppress the innocent, God will judge them. The idea is therefore not, or not only, the cynicism of an aristocrat who would like his servants to believe in God so as not to be robbed, a cynicism Voltaire did formulate elsewhere, but in the mouth of a character, the Englishman A in L'A, B, C (1768): “Je veux que mon procureur, mon tailleur, mes valets, ma femme même, croient en Dieu ; et je m'imagine que j'en serai moins volé et moins cocu”, I want my lawyer, my tailor, my servants, even my wife, to believe in God; and I imagine I shall be less robbed and less cuckolded for it (seventeenth conversation); it is a theory of the moral contract guaranteed by a transcendence.

    Read in the light of what was to come, the formula changes in scope. “If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him”: the line entirely separates the question of God's existence from that of his function. It matters little whether he exists; people must believe in him. This is the programme of Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor, who governs men by miracle, mystery and authority without himself believing in God, and who does so, like Voltaire, in the name of men's good. The novel confirms it: Ivan quotes this line two chapters before the poem (Part Seven).

    Voltairean deism is an exit from religion, in the sense that it abandons dogmas, miracles, Scriptures, the Church. But it keeps what Durkheim will call the function of the sacred: a “sacré lien de la société”, a sacred bond of society. Voltaire emptied religion of its content in order to keep its form, and that form is precisely that of an absolute that binds. It is a refoundation that does not hide itself: it invents God, in full awareness, for his function. This line makes God a necessary artefact.

    In literature Stendhal, The Red and the Black (1830) ; Miguel de Unamuno, San Manuel Bueno, mártir (1931)

    Julien Sorel, at the beginning of The Red and the Black, chooses his career by calculation: “Quand Bonaparte fit parler de lui, la France avait peur d'être envahie ; le mérite militaire était nécessaire et à la mode. Aujourd'hui, on voit des prêtres de quarante ans, avoir cent mille francs d'appointements, c'est-à-dire, trois fois autant que les fameux généraux de division de Napoléon.[…] Il faut être prêtre.” When Bonaparte made a name for himself, France was afraid of being invaded; military merit was necessary and in fashion. Today one sees priests of forty with salaries of a hundred thousand francs, that is, three times as much as Napoleon's famous divisional generals. One must be a priest. Having one day praised Napoleon at a dinner of priests, he binds his arm for two months as a penance.

    Why here: Stendhal describes religion as Voltaire wanted it to be used, but seen from below. The God that kings, justices of the peace and tailors need is a social power; Julien, who does not believe in him, makes a career of him, as the lawyer of L'A, B, C makes a police of him. The seminary at Besançon, later on, completes the demonstration: there hypocrisy is learned as a virtue. “It would be necessary to invent him” has a reverse side: those who invent him are never those who believe in him.

    Unamuno turns the formula around in San Manuel Bueno, mártir: Don Manuel, parish priest of a Castilian village, has lost his faith and goes on preaching it, hearing confessions and consoling, because, he tells his disciple Lázaro in substance, people need to believe in order to live and no truth is worth their peace; he dies a saint in everyone's eyes, and the story ends with his cause for beatification. This is the Grand Inquisitor turned good, a village Voltaire who invents God every Sunday out of charity: the most troubling version of the line, because it asks nothing for itself.

    Sources: Stendhal, Le Rouge et le Noir, I, 5 (1830) ; Miguel de Unamuno, San Manuel Bueno, mártir (1931).

    Portrait: Nicolas de Largillière, CC0

    Rousseau1712-1778the religion of the heart and the catechism of the citizen

    Background: Plato's philosophy: Forms, soul, city, the Good · Rousseau's thought: state of nature, social contract, general will, Emile · From absolutism to the Revolution: the Church of France, the Enlightenment and the cult of the Supreme Being · Evil, Satan and the afterlife: from Sheol to the Last Judgement

    Rousseau occupies in this debate a place that neither Voltaire nor d'Holbach can hold, because he makes two contrary gestures in the same year. In 1762 there appeared Emile, whose Book IV contains the Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar, and The Social Contract, whose penultimate chapter is entitled “De la religion civile”, “On civil religion”. The first text is a radical exit from the Church written by a believer; the second, a precise project for a political religion, twenty-seven years before the Revolution. He leaves the Church and refounds a religion in two books issued by different publishers, which Geneva condemns together.

    The Profession of Faith is a natural religion, but not that of the philosophers. The vicar does not demonstrate God by abstract reasoning; he starts from inner feeling. Before the order of the world, he does not deduce, he experiences: “Je crois donc que le monde est gouverné par une volonté puissante & sage ; je le vois, ou plutôt je le sens, & cela m'importe à savoir”, I believe, then, that the world is governed by a powerful and wise will; I see it, or rather I feel it, and that is what matters for me to know. The “ou plutôt je le sens”, “or rather I feel it”, is the whole difference from Voltaire. Voltaire's God is a clockmaker one infers; the vicar's is a presence one feels. And morality comes neither from a revealed law nor from a calculation of interest; it comes from a faculty that Rousseau hails as an inner divinity: “Conscience ! conscience ! instinct divin ; immortelle & céleste voix, guide assuré d'un être ignorant & borné, mais intelligent & libre ; juge infaillible du bien & du mal, qui rends l'homme semblable à Dieu”, conscience! conscience! divine instinct, immortal and heavenly voice, sure guide of a being ignorant and limited, but intelligent and free; infallible judge of good and evil, who makes man like God.

    This felt God needs no intermediaries, and the Profession of Faith draws an explosive consequence from this. God has spoken, say the revealed religions; the vicar then asks questions all the stronger for being asked by a priest: “Comment cela ? Par des prodiges. Et où sont ces prodiges ? Dans des livres. Et qui a fait ces livres ? Des hommes. Et qui a vu ces prodiges ? Des hommes qui les attestent. Quoi ! toujours des témoignages humains ? toujours des hommes qui me rapportent ce que d'autres hommes ont rapporté ? Que d'hommes entre Dieu & moi !” How so? Through wonders. And where are these wonders? In books. And who made these books? Men. And who saw these wonders? Men who attest them. What! Always human testimony? Always men reporting to me what other men have reported? How many men between God and me! Revelation is a chain of testimony human from end to end. The vicar draws the conclusion: “J'ai donc refermé tous les livres. Il en est un seul ouvert à tous les yeux, c'est celui de la Nature”, so I have closed all the books. There is only one open to all eyes, the book of Nature. External cults, matters of climate, government and national genius, are all of equal worth when they are sincere, for “le culte essentiel est celui du cœur”, the essential worship is that of the heart.

    One might think one was reading Spinoza, and the kinship is real on one point: like the Tractatus, the vicar reduces religion to the practice of justice and charity, and denies miracles any value as proof. But the spirit is the reverse. Spinoza rejects miracles because they would contradict the necessary order of nature, which is God, the vicar because they put men between God and himself: the one speaks in the name of reason, the other in the name of the heart. And the vicar's heart keeps what Spinoza's reason set aside: an immense reverence for the Gospel. This is the most famous page of the Profession of Faith, and it was enough to have it condemned by both camps. The vicar confesses that “la majesté des Écritures m'étonne, la sainteté de l'Évangile parle à mon cœur”, the majesty of the Scriptures astonishes me, the holiness of the Gospel speaks to my heart, and he compares the death of Socrates with that of Jesus: “Oui, si la vie & la mort de Socrate sont d'un Sage, la vie & la mort de Jesus sont d'un Dieu”, yes, if the life and death of Socrates are those of a sage, the life and death of Jesus are those of a God. But he adds at once that this same Gospel “est plein de choses incroyables, de choses qui répugnent à la raison, & qu'il est impossible à tout homme sensé de concevoir ni d'admettre”, is full of incredible things, things repugnant to reason, which no sensible man can conceive or accept, and he concludes with what he himself calls a “scepticisme involontaire”, an involuntary scepticism, which suspends judgment on everything that does not bear on conduct.

    This position, a very coherent one, holds against both its adversaries. Against the philosophers, it maintains that a principled atheism is a presumption as dogmatic as faith, and that one does not live on demonstrations. Against the Churches, it maintains that no one can be damned for not having believed what he could not examine, and that God cannot require of us, as the vicar says, to be so learned. This is the position Kant would take up in 1793 by separating pure religious faith from ecclesiastical faith, and he never hid his debt. In personal notes from the years 1764-1765 he writes that Rousseau set him right and taught him to honour human beings. The response is attested: religion within the boundaries of mere reason is the Profession of Faith translated into the language of critique.

    The judges, for their part, were not mistaken. The Parlement of Paris condemned Emile in June 1762 and issued a warrant for Rousseau's arrest; the book was torn up and burned. A few days later the Small Council of Geneva condemned Emile and The Social Contract. The Archbishop of Paris, Christophe de Beaumont, published a pastoral letter against Emile, to which Rousseau replied in 1763 with his Letter to Christophe de Beaumont. The citizen of Geneva, as he signed his books, was driven from his homeland for having written a religion without a Church.

    Yet in the same year Rousseau wrote the chapter that makes him the great modern theorist of political religion. Chapter VIII of Book IV of The Social Contract begins with a typology. There is the religion of man, “sans Temples, sans autels, sans rites, bornée au culte purement intérieur du Dieu Suprême & aux devoirs éternels de la morale”, without temples, without altars, without rites, limited to the purely inward worship of the Supreme God and to the eternal duties of morality, which is “la pure & simple Religion de l'Evangile, le vrai Théïsme”, the pure and simple religion of the Gospel, true theism: this is the vicar's religion. There is the religion of the citizen, national, with its tutelary gods and its rites prescribed by law. And there is a third, the worst, which gives men two legislations and two homelands: “On peut appeller celui-ci la religion du Prêtre”, this one may be called the religion of the priest, and the example Rousseau gives of it is Roman Christianity.

    The religion of man, however pure, is politically useless, and even harmful, because it detaches hearts from the earthly city. Rousseau goes as far as this sentence, always forgotten when he is made into a sentimental Christian: “Les vrais Chrétiens sont faits pour être esclaves ; ils le savent & ne s'en émeuvent gueres ; cette courte vie a trop peu de prix à leurs yeux”, true Christians are made to be slaves; they know it and are hardly moved by it; this short life has too little value in their eyes. A Christian republic is a contradiction in terms: “chacun de ces deux mots exclud l'autre”, each of these two words excludes the other. Something else is therefore needed, and Rousseau takes the step. “Il y a donc une profession de foi purement civile dont il appartient au Souverain de fixer les articles, non pas précisément comme dogmes de Religion, mais comme sentimens de sociabilité, sans lesquels il est impossible d'être bon Citoyen ni sujet fidele”, there is therefore a purely civil profession of faith whose articles it is for the Sovereign to fix, not exactly as dogmas of religion, but as sentiments of sociability, without which it is impossible to be a good citizen or a faithful subject.

    The articles are listed with the precision of a catechism. The positive dogmas are “L'existence de la Divinité puissante, intelligente, bienfaisante, prévoyante & pourvoyante, la vie à venir, le bonheur des justes, le châtiment des méchans, la sainteté du Contract social & des Loix”, the existence of a powerful, intelligent, beneficent, foreseeing and providing Divinity, the life to come, the happiness of the just, the punishment of the wicked, the sanctity of the social contract and the laws; as for the negative dogmas, Rousseau limits them to one: “c'est l'intolérance”, it is intolerance. One might believe this a minimal and tolerant religion, were it not that the preceding sentence gives the sanction: “Sans pouvoir obliger personne à les croire, il peut bannir de l'Etat quiconque ne les croit pas ; il peut le bannir, non comme impie, mais comme insociable, comme incapable d'aimer sincerement les loix la justice, & d'immoler au besoin sa vie à son devoir. Que si quelqu'un, après avoir reconnu publiquement ces mêmes dogmes, se conduit comme ne les croyant pas, qu'il soit puni de mort ; il a commis le plus grand des crimes, il a menti devant les loix”, without being able to oblige anyone to believe them, it may banish from the State whoever does not believe them; it may banish him, not as impious, but as unsociable, as incapable of sincerely loving the laws and justice, and of sacrificing his life to his duty if need be. If anyone, after publicly acknowledging these same dogmas, behaves as though he did not believe them, let him be punished with death; he has committed the greatest of crimes, he has lied before the laws.

    I know of no text that illustrates my criterion more exactly: one refounds a religion when one installs an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded, and criticism of which becomes sacrilege, and Rousseau writes it out in full. The unsociable man is the one who would be incapable of “immoler au besoin sa vie à son devoir”, sacrificing his life to his duty if need be, and the sanctity of the social contract is a dogma whose betrayal is paid for with one's life. The absolute is no longer God, who appears in the list only as a guarantor; the absolute is the city. Civil religion is a religion of the exit from religion: it takes from the priest the power to damn and gives it to the Sovereign, and replaces hell with exile and the scaffold. The parallel with Plato is constructed: Book X of the Laws had already made belief in the gods a matter of law and punished impiety, and Rousseau, an assiduous reader of Plato, rediscovers the same gesture at the very moment he believes he is founding freedom.

    The project is, moreover, older. Rousseau had formulated it six years earlier, in a letter addressed to Voltaire, and had presented it as a remedy for intolerance. The Letter to Voltaire on Providence, of 18 August 1756, answers the Poem on the Lisbon Disaster, in which Voltaire had mocked optimism in the face of the dead of the 1755 earthquake. Rousseau defends Providence there with one argument that makes one smile and another that strikes home. The argument that makes one smile is that men are responsible for their own ills: nature, he writes, “n'avoit point rassemblé là vingt mille maisons de six à sept étages”, had not assembled twenty thousand houses of six or seven storeys there. The argument that strikes home is existential, and it is the vicar's cry before the vicar: “Non, j'ai trop souffert en cette vie pour n'en pas attendre une autre.[…] Je la sens, je la crois, je la veux, je l'espere, je la défendrai jusqu'a mon dernier soupir”, no, I have suffered too much in this life not to expect another. I feel it, I believe it, I will it, I hope for it, I shall defend it to my last breath. Shortly before comes the proposal that heralds The Social Contract: “Je voudrois donc qu'on eût dans chaque État un code moral, ou une espece de profession de foi civile qui contînt positivement les maximes sociales que chacun seroit tenu d'admettre, & négativement les maximes intolérantes qu'on seroit tenu de rejetter, non comme impies, mais comme séditieuses”, I would therefore wish that each State had a moral code, or a kind of civil profession of faith, containing positively the social maxims everyone would be bound to accept, and negatively the intolerant maxims one would be bound to reject, not as impious but as seditious. And Rousseau invites Voltaire to write it: “Vous nous avez donné dans votre Poëme sur la Religion naturelle le catéchisme de l'homme, donnez-nous maintenant dans celui que je vous propose le catéchisme du citoyen”, you have given us in your Poem on Natural Religion the catechism of man; give us now, in the one I propose to you, the catechism of the citizen. The same letter allows that one may “commencer par exterminer”, begin by exterminating, the religions that attack the foundations of society.

    Voltaire's response is attested, and it is a flat refusal. On 12 September 1756, from Les Délices, he writes: “Mon cher Philosophe, nous pouvons vous & moi, dans les intervalles de nos maux, raisonner en vers & en prose”, my dear Philosopher, you and I can, in the intervals of our ills, reason in verse and in prose; but he begs to be excused for the moment from these “discussions philosophiques qui ne sont que des amusemens”, philosophical discussions that are mere amusements. The real answer came three years later: Candide (1759); Rousseau himself asserted, in Book IX of the Confessions, that the novel was the promised answer to his letter: “Elle n'est autre que le roman de Candide, dont je ne puis parler, parce que je ne l'ai pas lu”, it is none other than the novel Candide, of which I cannot speak, because I have not read it. The quarrel turned to hatred: in 1764 Voltaire anonymously published the Sentiment des citoyens, which revealed to the public that Rousseau had placed his children in the foundling hospital [a known fact]. On the substance, the irony is complete. Voltaire, who wanted God invented to restrain the wicked and the tyrant, and Rousseau, who wanted a catechism of the citizen sanctioned by death, both want a social sacred, and differ only in tone. Voltaire's line and Rousseau's chapter are the two faces of the same refoundation.

    History took care of the implementation, and the confrontation, though constructed, here touches on fact. Robespierre, who venerated Rousseau, had the Convention vote, on 18 Floréal Year II (7 May 1794), a decree by which the French people recognized the existence of the Supreme Being and the immortality of the soul, and instituted festivals every tenth day; the Festival of the Supreme Being was celebrated on 20 Prairial (8 June 1794), a few days before the law of 22 Prairial that accelerated the Terror. I do not believe Rousseau can be held responsible for what others made of him. But one cannot say that the cult of the Supreme Being betrayed the chapter on civil religion: it reproduces its positive dogmas, and the death penalty for civic hypocrisy was not Robespierre's invention.

    Where to place Rousseau? I believe the two texts must be held together, and that one must refuse to choose the “good” Rousseau against the “bad” one. The Savoyard vicar is an admirable exit from the Church: a felt God, without priests or miracles, a morality of conscience, a peaceful scepticism about everything else. The legislator of The Social Contract is an unscrupulous refounder, who knows what he is doing and says so. The link between the two is rigorous: because the religion of man is purely inward, it can found no city; and because no city holds together without the sacred, one must manufacture a sacred that is no longer the priests'. Rousseau saw before Durkheim that society needs to sacralize itself. He was not content to see it, he willed it, and that is why he is an instructive counter-example: a man who leaves the Church through the heart and re-enters religion through the city.

    In literature Victor Hugo, Ninety-Three (1874) ; Anatole France, Les dieux ont soif (1912)

    In Ninety-Three, Cimourdain, a former priest turned delegate of the Committee of Public Safety, explains to his pupil Gauvain, on the eve of having him guillotined, what the Republic must be: “le droit et le devoir parallèles, l'impôt proportionnel et progressif, le service militaire obligatoire, le nivellement, aucune déviation, et, au-dessus de tous et de tout, cette ligne droite, la loi. La république de l'absolu.” Right and duty side by side, proportional and progressive taxation, compulsory military service, levelling, no deviation, and, above all men and all things, that straight line, the law. The republic of the absolute. Gauvain replies that he prefers “la république de l'idéal”, the republic of the ideal: “Au-dessus de la balance il y a la lyre”, above the scales there is the lyre. At the moment Gauvain's head falls, Cimourdain shoots himself through the heart.

    Why here: Cimourdain is the civil religion of The Social Contract made man. He left the Church for the city, and the city has become for him an absolute that demands the sacrifice of the only being he loves, because sparing him would be sacrilege. That he dies at the same stroke changes nothing in the criterion: it is not self-offering that refounds, it is the authority in whose name the offering of others is demanded.

    In Anatole France, the painter Évariste Gamelin, a juror of the Revolutionary Tribunal, professes the faith that Rousseau prescribed for the citizen: “La croyance en un Dieu bon est nécessaire à la morale. L'Être suprême est la source de toutes les vertus, et l'on n'est pas républicain si l'on ne croit en Dieu”, belief in a good God is necessary to morality. The Supreme Being is the source of all virtues, and one is not a republican if one does not believe in God. The atheist Brotteaux, whom the Tribunal will send to the guillotine, had just answered him that “l'humanité copie ses dieux sur ses tyrans”, humanity models its gods on its tyrants: this is Rousseau's single negative dogma, intolerance, applied to the letter.

    Sources: Victor Hugo, Quatrevingt-treize, part three, book VII, ch. 5 and 6 (1874) ; Anatole France, Les dieux ont soif, ch. VI (1912).

    Portrait: Maurice Quentin de La Tour, Public domain

    d'Holbach1723-1789nature against the gods

    Background: D'Holbach: materialism, the Système de la nature, the militant atheism of the Enlightenment

    Paul Henri Thiry, baron d'Holbach, a German naturalized as French, host of a salon frequented by Diderot, Helvétius, Grimm and many others, published the Système de la nature in 1770 under the name of Mirabaud, a perpetual secretary of the Académie française who had died ten years earlier. The first great openly atheist book of European literature, it was condemned to be burned. Voltaire was alarmed by it and answered it in the article “Dieu, dieux” of the Questions sur l'Encyclopédie (fourth part, 1771), in the section “Du Système de la nature”, which opens with an admission: “L'auteur du Système de la nature a eu l'avantage de se faire lire des savants, des ignorants, des femmes”, the author of the System of Nature has had the advantage of being read by the learned, by the ignorant, by women.

    The thesis is a thoroughgoing materialism. Nothing exists but matter in motion, governed by necessary laws; the soul is a function of the body; there is neither freedom, nor immortality, nor God. And religion is explained by ignorance of this nature: “c'est uniquement l'ignorance où l'on fut des causes naturelles et des forces de la nature qui donna la naissance aux dieux”, it was solely ignorance of natural causes and of the forces of nature that gave birth to the gods. Hence the formula that sums up the whole programme: “Si l'ignorance de la nature donna la naissance aux dieux, la connoissance de la nature est faite pour les détruire”, if ignorance of nature gave birth to the gods, knowledge of nature is made to destroy them (II, 1). This is Lucretius without Epicurean piety: the gods are no longer misrepresented, they are phantoms of ignorance.

    On one point d'Holbach directly announces Feuerbach: he describes the mechanism by which man manufactures a god for himself. If he misunderstands nature and needs a god to move it, he is forced to make that god a man of whom he himself is the model; “il croit en faire un dieu en lui donnant ses propres qualités, il croit les rendre plus dignes du souverain monde, en les exagérant”, he believes he makes a god of him by giving him his own qualities, he believes he makes them worthier of the sovereign of the world by exaggerating them, whereas by dint of abstractions and exaggerations he makes them unintelligible (II, 7). Here, in 1770, is the theory of projection that Feuerbach will develop in 1841: God is man raised to infinity. The difference is that d'Holbach sees in it an absurdity, whereas Feuerbach will see in it an unrecognized truth.

    And d'Holbach answers in advance the objection of Jurieu and of Ivan, as Bayle had done, but in terms of utility. The atheist is not a monster: he is “un homme qui connoit la nature et ses loix, qui connoit sa propre nature, qui sçait ce qu'elle lui impose”, a man who knows nature and its laws, who knows his own nature, who knows what it imposes on him, and his experience proves to him that vice harms him and that society is useful to his happiness (II, 12). Morality is founded on enlightened self-interest, not on the fear of hell.
