    The book then does something its militant readers pass over in silence. It ends with an Abrégé du code de la nature in which Nature herself speaks to exhort man; and the author, in a burst of fervour, exclaims: “O nature ! Souveraine de tous les êtres ! Et vous ses filles adorables, vertu, raison, vérité ! soyez à jamais nos seules Divinités ; c'est à vous que sont dus l'encens et les hommages de la terre”, O nature! Sovereign of all beings! And you, her adorable daughters, virtue, reason, truth! be for ever our only Divinities; to you are due the incense and the homage of the earth (II, 14).

    So the book ends with a prayer. Nature is “sovereign”, her daughters are “adorable”, they are our “Divinities”, we owe them “the incense and the homage”. This is not a careless metaphor, it is the very structure of worship, transferred from God to Nature. D'Holbach leaves religion by founding a religion of Nature, just as the French Revolution would found, twenty years later, a cult of Reason and then of the Supreme Being, and as Comte would found a religion of Humanity. Here we have, before Stirner, the proof of what he would say of Feuerbach: our atheists are pious people (Part Six). The comparison is constructed, since Stirner was aiming at his contemporaries, but the formula applies to the baron even better than to them.

    In literature Percy Bysshe Shelley, Queen Mab (1813) ; Sade, Dialogue between a Priest and a Dying Man (1782)

    In canto VII of Queen Mab, the spirit of Ianthe remembers having seen, as a child, an atheist burned who smiled in the flames: “the insensate mob / Uttered a cry of triumph, and I wept. / Weep not, child! cried my mother, for that man / Has said, There is no God”; and the fairy echoes: “There is no God! / Nature confirms the faith his death-groan sealed”. Shelley, expelled from Oxford two years earlier for The Necessity of Atheism, adds to the poem notes in which he rewrites the Système de la nature in English.

    Why here: the line states the paradox of the section. Atheism is uttered as a faith sealed by a martyrdom, and it is Nature that confirms it; the fairy is a priestess. Shelley does in verse what d'Holbach does in his last chapter: he removes God and keeps the adoration.

    Sade, in the Dialogue between a Priest and a Dying Man, written in the keep of Vincennes in 1782, has the priest converted by the dying man. Nature created him “avec des goûts très vifs”, with very lively tastes, there is nothing to expiate, and the libertine ends by calling six women so that the preacher may forget on their breasts “tous les vains sophismes de la superstition”, all the vain sophisms of superstition; the final note observes that he “devint dans leurs bras un homme corrompu par la nature, pour n'avoir pas su expliquer ce que c'était que la nature corrompue”, became in their arms a man corrupted by nature, for having been unable to explain what corrupted nature was. Sade is the only atheist of the century who does not pray to Nature: he conforms to it, and that is why his atheism could never become a religion, nor even a morality.

    Sources: Percy Bysshe Shelley, Queen Mab, VII and notes (1813); D. A. F. de Sade, Dialogue entre un prêtre et un moribond (written in 1782, published in 1926).

    Portrait: Alexander Roslin, Public domain

    Kant1724-1804religion within the boundaries of mere reason

    Background: Kant's philosophy: the three Critiques, the imperative, the postulates, religion · Pietism and German Romanticism: the religion of the heart and of the infinite · German idealism: Kant, Fichte, Schelling, Hegel · Metaphysics and the proofs of the existence of God: from Anselm to Kant · Jürgen Habermas's thought: communicative action, public sphere, postmetaphysical reason, post-secular society · The teaching of Jesus: the Kingdom, the parables, the miracles

    Die Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der bloßen Vernunft (Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason) appeared in 1793, and an enlarged second edition in 1794. The book earned its author a rescript from the King of Prussia, Frederick William II, dated 1 October 1794 and signed by the minister Wöllner; Kant answered by promising, “als Ew. Königl. Maj. getreuester Unterthan”, as Your Royal Majesty's most faithful subject, to abstain entirely from any public discourse on religion, and he later explained that he had chosen this formula deliberately, so as to renounce his freedom of judgement only during the king's lifetime (preface to the Streit der Fakultäten, 1798). Kant's dealings with the censorship, from the moment the first chapters appeared in a journal, are recounted in the introduction to the Kehrbach edition. Kant is the culmination of the German Enlightenment and will be the main target of the following century.

    Kant's principle is laid down at the very outset, in the preface to the first edition: morality does not need religion to found itself, since it rests on the autonomy of practical reason; but it leads necessarily to religion. “Moral also führt unumgänglich zur Religion, wodurch sie sich zur Idee eines machthabenden moralischen Gesetzgebers außer dem Menschen erweitert”, morality thus leads inevitably to religion, through which it extends itself to the idea of a powerful moral lawgiver outside the human being. For reason demands that virtue be crowned by happiness, and only a God can guarantee this agreement that nature does not guarantee. This is the doctrine of the postulates, set out in the Critique of Practical Reason (1788): God, freedom and immortality are not known, they are postulated as conditions of possibility of the highest good. Kant had written in the preface to the second edition of the Critique of Pure Reason (1787) that he had had to abolish knowledge in order to make room for faith: “Ich mußte also das Wissen aufheben, um zum Glauben Platz zu bekommen” (B XXX).

    Hence the definition of religion, which is a complete reversal of the traditional order: “Religion ist (subjectiv betrachtet) das Erkenntniß aller unserer Pflichten als göttlicher Gebote”, religion is, subjectively considered, the recognition of all our duties as divine commands (fourth part, first section). The traditional Christian fulfils his duties because God commands them; the Kantian recognizes as divine duties he already knows through his reason. It is not religion that founds morality, it is morality that adorns itself with a divine name.

    The book then takes up the great Christian dogmas one by one to give them a moral interpretation, and this translation is the model for all those that will follow, from Hegel to Feuerbach and on to Habermas. Original sin becomes “radical evil”, a propensity to evil inscribed in freedom itself, which Kant had first set out in an article of 1792 submitted to the Berlin censorship, as he recounts in a note on his “Censurleiden” published by his biographer Borowski and reproduced by the editor Kehrbach. This evil is not a corrupted nature transmitted by generation, in the manner of Augustine, but a timeless choice of freedom, which subordinates the moral law to self-love. Kant thus keeps from Christianity its darkest anthropology, the one the French Enlightenment had sought to dismiss: man is not naturally good.

    Christ becomes an ideal of reason. “Das Ideal der Gott wohlgefälligen Menschheit”, the ideal of humanity well-pleasing to God, we can represent to ourselves only “unter der Idee eines Menschen”, under the idea of a human being who would not only fulfil all duties but spread good around him and accept every suffering, up to the most ignominious death, for the good of the world (second part). It matters little, Kant says in substance, whether this man existed: the ideal is in our reason, and it is the ideal that we recognize in the Gospel narrative, not the other way round. The whole nineteenth-century quarrel over the life of Jesus is here in germ. Strauss will make the Gospels myths produced by the collective consciousness; Bauer will go so far as to doubt his historicity; Onfray, at the end of this story, will make Jesus a pure concept. Kant had already made historicity indifferent, but for the opposite reason: not to discredit Christianity, but to save its moral core from the hazards of historical criticism.

    Finally the Church becomes an ethical community. Kant calls “ein ethisches gemeines Wesen”, an ethical community, the society of human beings united under laws of virtue, as opposed to the juridical society united under laws of coercion; and he specifies that this concept “ist der Begriff von einem Volke Gottes unter ethischen Gesetzen”, is the concept of a people of God under ethical laws (third part). The invisible Church, that of all people of good will, is the truth of the visible Churches, which are merely historical approximations of it.

    This point is almost always overlooked. Kant does not merely reduce religion to individual morality; he keeps its communal dimension, the one Durkheim will judge essential. The people of God under ethical laws is already, in the terms of 1793, the religion of Humanity that Comte will organize in 1852, with fewer rites and more rigour. It is also what Habermas, in 2001, will call the translation of religious contents into a secular language, and he will explicitly pay tribute to Kant as the first great example of a deconstruction of the truths of faith that secularizes them while saving them. Kant did not abolish the Church; he made it invisible, which is a way of making it universal.

    This reduction has a critical consequence, which Kant draws with a severity that is forgotten: everything in historical religion that exceeds morality falls under suspicion. Kant distinguishes the reiner Religionsglaube, pure religious faith, common to all reasonable human beings, and the Kirchenglaube, ecclesiastical faith, founded on a historical revelation and on Scriptures, which is merely a vehicle. And ecclesiastical faith must be interpreted by pure faith: “Der Kirchenglaube hat zu seinem höchsten Ausleger den reinen Religionsglauben”, ecclesiastical faith has pure religious faith as its highest interpreter (third part, title of section VI). The history of religion is the history of a gradual passage from the first to the second, which is “die Annäherung des Reichs Gottes”, the approach of the kingdom of God (title of section VII).

    The fourth part, the most violent, is entitled “Vom Dienst und Afterdienst unter der Herrschaft des guten Princips oder von Religion und Pfaffenthum”, on service and counterfeit service under the dominion of the good principle, or on religion and priestcraft. There Kant lays down a principle he declares evident: “Alles, was außer dem guten Lebenswandel, der Mensch noch thun zu können vermeint, um Gott wohlgefällig zu werden, ist bloßer Religionswahn und Afterdienst Gottes”, whatever, apart from a good way of life, the human being supposes he can still do to become well-pleasing to God is mere religious delusion and counterfeit service of God. Prayers, pilgrimages, fasts, rites, observances, if they are held to be meritorious in themselves, belong to Fetischmachen, the making of fetishes; and Pfaffenthum, clericalism, is the constitution of a Church “sofern in ihr ein Fetischdienst regiert”, insofar as a fetish service reigns in it.

    Let us measure the critique contained in this text by a man brought up as a Pietist Lutheran: Kant turns almost all actual religious practice into fetishism. He applies to Christian worship the vocabulary of the fetish, which Marx, a reader of Charles de Brosses (Du culte des dieux fétiches, 1760), will rediscover to speak of the commodity. He anticipates Bergson's distinction between static and dynamic religion, and Barth's between religion and faith. And yet he does not leave religion: he keeps its core, God as moral lawgiver, immortality as hope, Christ as the ideal of humanity well-pleasing to God.

    This is where the three objections of the following century strike. Schleiermacher, in 1799, will answer that religion is neither a knowledge nor a morality, but an intuition and a feeling, and that by reducing it to morality one has missed it entirely; the reply targets Kant without naming him, and it opens the regime of experience. Hegel will answer that the postulated God is an empty God, a Sollen, an ought-to-be that never is, and that true religion is the one in which the infinite is reconciled with the finite. And Nietzsche, much later, will formulate the hardest objection: Kantian morality has not left religion, it is the Christian religion, become invisible because it has disguised itself as reason. In The Antichrist (§ 10), he will say that German philosophy is “eine hinterlistige Theologie”, an underhanded theology, and that “Der Erfolg Kants ist bloß ein Theologen-Erfolg”, Kant's success is merely a theologian's success. The response is attested, though a century late. Kant believed he had reduced religion to morality; Nietzsche replies that he sacralized morality.

    In literature Heinrich von Kleist, Michael Kohlhaas (1810) ; Victor Hugo, “La Conscience” (1859)

    Michael Kohlhaas begins with the portrait of a horse dealer from Brandenburg, “einer der rechtschaffensten zugleich und entsetzlichsten Menschen seiner Zeit”, one of the most upright and at the same time most terrible men of his age, who might have passed for the model of the good citizen “wenn er in einer Tugend nicht ausgeschweift hätte. Das Rechtgefühl aber machte ihn zum Räuber und Mörder”, had he not gone to excess in one virtue: his sense of justice made him a robber and a murderer. For two horses mistreated by a country squire, Kohlhaas raises a band, burns Wittenberg, has himself called the lieutenant of the archangel Michael, is brought back to submission by Luther, obtains justice and mounts the scaffold, satisfied [summary].

    Why here: Kohlhaas is the categorical imperative made man, the moral law without the starry heavens. Kleist had written to his fiancée in March 1801 that reading Kant had just robbed him of the certainty of ever attaining truth, and that his life was shattered by it; nine years later, he stages a man for whom right is the absolute that Kant placed within us, and who demands of everyone, and of himself, the sacrifice a religion would demand. Religion within the boundaries of reason has its possible refoundation: Justice with a capital letter.

    Hugo, in “La Conscience”, has Cain flee before an eye open in the sky, from town to town, behind walls, all the way to the tomb: “On fit donc une fosse, et Caïn dit : ‘C'est bien !’ / Puis il descendit seul sous cette voûte sombre ; / Quand il se fut assis sur sa chaise dans l'ombre / Et qu'on eut sur son front fermé le souterrain, / L'œil était dans la tombe et regardait Caïn”, so they dug a pit, and Cain said: ‘It is well!’ / Then he went down alone beneath that dark vault; / When he had sat down on his chair in the shadow / And they had closed the vault above his brow, / The eye was in the tomb and was looking at Cain. It is Kant's inner tribunal in an image, and Rousseau's “instinct divin”, divine instinct: a God who is no longer anything but a gaze, and from whom one does not escape by closing the door.

    Sources: Heinrich von Kleist, Michael Kohlhaas (1810); Victor Hugo, “La Conscience”, La Légende des siècles, first series (1859).

    Portrait: Becker, Public domain

    A constructed debate: can morality do without God?

    Background: The thought of Pierre Bayle: the comet, the Dictionary, toleration · The philosophy of Hume: empiricism, causation, miracles, the natural history of religion · Voltaire: deism, the Infamous, tolerance, Candide · Dostoevsky's work: the Karamazovs, Demons, polyphony

    It remains to set face to face the answers of the Enlightenment to the question that will haunt Ivan Karamazov and that Bayle had already asked: if God does not exist, does morality still hold? The confrontation is constructed; each of these authors took a position, and their positions map out all the possible solutions.

    Bayle answers that morality holds through society: laws, honour and opinion make the virtue of the greatest number, and a society of atheists would be like a society of pagans, provided the laws were severe. Hume answers, across the whole of his moral work, that morality holds through sentiment: sympathy, utility, the approval that agreeable and useful characters arouse in us, have no need of a divine lawgiver; religion, far from supporting morality, often corrupts it by substituting frivolous observances for it. D'Holbach answers that morality holds through enlightened self-interest: the atheist knows nature and knows that vice harms him. Voltaire answers that morality does not hold without God, at least for the people and for kings: there must be a judge, otherwise the scoundrel and the tyrant have no curb; and if this judge did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him. Kant, finally, answers that morality holds without God, since it rests on the autonomy of reason, but that it cannot understand itself without God, since it demands an agreement of virtue and happiness that only a God guarantees.

    Ivan's question thus receives, as early as the eighteenth century, five answers, only one of which proves him right: Voltaire's. The other four maintain that morality survives God, because it rests on society (Bayle), on sentiment (Hume), on self-interest (d'Holbach) or on reason (Kant). But what does each put in God's place? Bayle puts human Justice, that is, the State; d'Holbach Nature, which he ends by invoking as a divinity; Kant Reason, which postulates God; Voltaire an invented God. Only Hume puts something that does not have the form of an absolute: a human sentiment, variable, fragile, and which promises nothing. That is why I take Hume, and not d'Holbach, to be the one who truly leaves religion in the Enlightenment: he is the only one who replaces God with no capital letter.

    Dostoevsky, a century later, will know or retain only Voltaire's answer, turned against him: if God is necessary to morality, and if God does not exist, then everything is permitted. The other four will seem to him the tricks of philosophers.

    In literature Denis Diderot, Conversation of a Philosopher with the Maréchale de \\\* (1776) ; Victor Hugo, Les Misérables (1862)

    The maréchale is astonished that the atheist Crudeli, who is Diderot, has the morals of a believer: “Pourquoi non, quand il est honnête homme ?”, why not, when he is an honest man? She asks what will be put in the place of religion to frighten the wicked; he replies: “Quand je n'aurais rien à mettre à la place, ce serait toujours un terrible préjugé de moins ; sans compter que, dans aucun siècle et chez aucune nation, les opinions religieuses n'ont servi de base aux mœurs nationales”, even if I had nothing to put in its place, it would still be one terrible prejudice the fewer; not to mention that in no century and among no nation have religious opinions served as the basis of national morals.

    Why here: it is the debate of this section played in two voices. The maréchale sides with Voltaire, Crudeli with Bayle and with Hume, with a nuance the essay retains: he puts nothing in its place, not even d'Holbach's Nature. Diderot is, with Hume, the only one of the Enlightenment who answers the question without a capital letter.

    In Hugo, Bishop Myriel visits the member of the Convention G., who is dying an outlaw and who has “voté la fin du tyran”, voted for the end of the tyrant. The old man, an atheist in the bishop's eyes, states his creed: “L'infini est. Il est là. Si l'infini n'avait pas de moi, le moi serait sa borne ; il ne serait pas infini ; en d'autres termes, il ne serait pas. Or il est. Donc il a un moi. Ce moi de l'infini, c'est Dieu.”, the infinite is. It is there. If the infinite had no self, the self would be its limit; it would not be infinite; in other words, it would not be. Now it is. Therefore it has a self. This self of the infinite is God. The bishop, at the end, finds only one thing to ask of him: “Votre bénédiction, dit l'évêque. Et il s'agenouilla”, your blessing, said the bishop. And he knelt. The priest asks for the blessing of the member of the Convention, “un quasi-régicide”, an almost-regicide, according to Hugo: two moralities, two absolutes, which recognize each other without merging, and neither of which asks the other to sacrifice itself. This is Hugo's answer to the question of the section, and it is not an argument: it is a gesture, like the kiss Christ gives the Inquisitor.

    Sources: Denis Diderot, Entretien d'un philosophe avec la maréchale de \\\* (1776); Victor Hugo, Les Misérables, I, 1, 10, “L'évêque en présence d'une lumière inconnue” (1862).

    Transition: from reason to experience

    The Enlightenment thus ran through every way of leaving religion by reason. Only Hume, having escaped into the obscure regions of philosophy, refounds nothing, at the price of a suspension that is hard to sustain. Voltaire kept God for his function; d'Holbach destroyed the gods only to end with a prayer to Nature; Kant reduced religion to morality and made morality a religion. The generation of Romanticism and German idealism draws a radical conclusion from this: if reason can neither found nor destroy religion, it is because religion is not a matter of reason. A matter of feeling, Schleiermacher will say; of the concept, Hegel will reply, but of a concept that contains feeling and goes beyond it. Between these two answers the modern critique of religion will be born.

    Top of the part

    Part Fivefeeling and concept4 authors

    Background: Pietism and German Romanticism: the religion of the heart and of the infinite · From the Judges to the Kings: Samuel, Saul, David and Goliath, Solomon and the Temple · German idealism: Kant, Fichte, Schelling, Hegel · The nineteenth century: the Church against modernity, theology before criticism

    Kant had believed he could hold religion at bay by lodging it within the boundaries of mere reason: a moral faith, without dogma claiming to know, without worship claiming to please God. Religion was saved because it was reduced, and it is this reduction that the next generation finds intolerable, from two opposite sides. Some will say that Kant missed religion because he folded it back onto morality, whereas it is first of all a matter of sensibility, of intuition, of a lived relation to the infinite: this is Schleiermacher. Others will say that Kant missed it because he forbade reason to know the absolute, whereas religion already says, in the form of images, what philosophy can think in the form of concepts: this is Hegel. The first opens the way to the modern spiritualities of experience, the second to the philosophies that claim to preserve religion by surpassing it. From their clash, and then from Strauss's application of the Hegelian method to the Gospel narratives, the Hegelian left will emerge, and everything that follows, from Feuerbach to Comte, answers their question: is religion first a feeling or first a truth?

    Friedrich Schleiermacher1768-1834religion as sense and taste for the infinite

    Background: Kant's philosophy: the three Critiques, the imperative, the postulates, religion · Pietism and German Romanticism: the religion of the heart and of the infinite · Schleiermacher's thought: the Speeches, the Glaubenslehre, hermeneutics · Hermeneutics: from Schleiermacher to Ricoeur · Barth's theology: the Römerbrief, dialectical theology, the Church Dogmatics

    In 1799, in Berlin, the Über die Religion. Reden an die Gebildeten unter ihren Verächtern (On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers) appeared without the author's name. Their author was a young pastor at the Charité hospital, a familiar of Friedrich Schlegel's Romantic circle, and the title already states the whole design: the book is not addressed to believers but to those who despise religion in the name of culture. It does not seek to prove God to them, but to show them that what they despise is something other than religion: a failed metaphysics and a catechism morality, which they are right to despise, but which are not religion.

    The fundamental thought fits into one line of the second speech, the most famous in the book: “Praxis ist Kunst, Spekulation ist Wissenschaft, Religion ist Sinn und Geschmack fürs Unendliche”, practice is an art, speculation is a science, religion is sense and taste for the infinite. And a little earlier: “Ihr Wesen ist weder Denken noch Handeln, sondern Anschauung und Gefühl”, its essence is neither thinking nor acting, but intuition and feeling. Kant had brought religion back to action (morality); rationalist metaphysics had brought it back to thought (the proofs of God). Schleiermacher gives it a third province, irreducible to the other two: experience. “Religion haben, heißt das Universum anschauen”, to have religion is to intuit the universe.

    The word Anschauung does not designate a mystical vision in the sense of an ecstasy cut off from ordinary life. It designates the subject's receptivity to what exceeds it, the moment when, in any perception whatever, the finite lets itself be grasped as an expression of the infinite. Schleiermacher describes it with the precision of a phenomenologist before the term existed: it is the first instant of every perception, before intuition and feeling separate, when sense and its object are, so to speak, fused into each other. He calls it “Jener erste geheimnisvolle Augenblick”, that first and mysterious instant, and he adds that it is indescribable and passes very quickly. Religion consists in recapturing this instant and recognizing it in the religious activity of the soul.

    Three consequences follow.

    The first concerns God. If religion is intuition of the universe, the idea of God is only one modality of it among others, one way of representing to oneself the unity of what one intuits. In 1799 Schleiermacher draws from this a conclusion that caused scandal and that he softened in later editions: “so müßt Ihr auch zugeben, daß eine Religion ohne Gott besser sein kann, als ein andre mit Gott”, you must also admit that a religion without God can be better than another with God. One could hardly announce more plainly what the twentieth century will call spirituality without God. The hero of this religion without God is named: Spinoza. The second speech pays him a tribute that has remained famous: “Opfert mit mir ehrerbietig eine Locke den Manen des heiligen verstoßenen Spinoza!”, offer with me, reverently, a lock of hair to the shades of the holy, outcast Spinoza! And further on: “voller Religion war Er und voll heiligen Geistes”, he was full of religion and full of holy spirit. The atheist par excellence in the eyes of Europe becomes, from a pastor's pen, the saint of true religion: what is impiety in the light of dogma becomes piety in the light of experience.

    The second consequence concerns Scripture and the institution. If religion is a living experience, the sacred text is only its trace. Schleiermacher has an admirable sentence here: “Jede heilige Schrift ist nur ein Mausoleum der Religion ein Denkmal, daß ein großer Geist da war, der nicht mehr da ist”, every holy scripture is only a mausoleum of religion, a monument attesting that a great spirit was there who is there no longer. And he concludes: “Nicht der hat Religion, der an eine heilige Schrift glaubt, sondern der welcher keiner bedarf, und wohl selbst eine machen könnte”, the one who has religion is not the one who believes in a holy scripture, but the one who needs none and could well write one himself. The miracle undergoes the same displacement: it is no longer a departure from the laws of nature, but the religious name for any event whatever, once it is perceived in its relation to the infinite. Everything is a miracle for whoever has the religious sense, and nothing for whoever lacks it.

    The third consequence concerns eternity. Religion does not promise a life after death; it gives, here, an eternity that is not a duration. Schleiermacher says so in a formula that Spinoza could have signed and that Wittgenstein will rediscover in the Tractatus (6.4311; the comparison is mine): “Mitten in der Endlichkeit Eins werden mit dem Unendlichen und ewig sein in einem Augenblick, das ist die Unsterblichkeit der Religion”, in the midst of finitude to become one with the infinite and to be eternal in a moment, that is the immortality of religion.

    The Reden are not a mere Romantic effusion. Schleiermacher is a rigorous theologian, and his great dogmatics, Der christliche Glaube (The Christian Faith, 1821-1822, second edition 1830-1831), will systematize the intuition of 1799 in a soberer form: piety is defined there as the feeling of absolute dependence, schlechthinniges Abhängigkeitsgefühl (1830 spelling: schlechthiniges), the Leitsatz of § 4 stating that we know ourselves to be “schlechthin abhängig”, absolutely dependent, that is, in relation with God. The passage from the intuition of the universe to the feeling of dependence is not without significance. The intuition of 1799 was active, almost aesthetic; the feeling of dependence is passive, it expresses creatureliness. But the principle remains the same: religion has its seat in the immediate feeling of self, not in knowledge or in the will.

    This position is, I believe, the first modern attempt to leave institutional religion without leaving lived religion, and as such it prefigures the whole contemporary shift from religion to spirituality. Schleiermacher dismisses dogma, the text, the miracle in the vulgar sense, personal immortality and even, in 1799, the necessity of God; he keeps experience. Not as a private matter: the last speeches insist on the religious community, on the Church as the free communication of intuitions, and on the plurality of positive religions, each being a singular way of intuiting the universe. He does not found a new religion; he claims to unveil the essence of all of them.

    The objection will come from two sides. Hegel will reproach him for having reduced religion to a feeling, that is, to what is most subjective, most arbitrary and most animal in man. Feuerbach, later, will take the lesson in the other direction: if religion is feeling, and if feeling is human, then God is human feeling objectified. Schleiermacher unintentionally opened the door to anthropological reduction: the feeling of the infinite, detached from all objective truth, can always be reinterpreted as a feeling of self. Schleiermacher must be given his best defence here: he never said that the infinite was a product of feeling; he said that feeling was the place where the infinite gives itself. But his theory contains no means of distinguishing these two theses. This is the structural weakness of every spirituality of experience, which we shall find again in William James and in Rudolf Otto: experience proves that one feels, it does not prove what one feels.

    In literature Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Faust (1808) ; Friedrich Hölderlin, Hyperion (1797) ; William Wordsworth, “Tintern Abbey” (1798)

    The Speeches on Religion appeared in 1799; the three texts that follow frame them within ten years and say the same thing in verse. In Martha's garden, Gretchen puts to Faust the question that German has since called the Gretchenfrage: “Nun sag, wie hast du's mit der Religion?”, tell me, how do you stand with religion? Faust answers with a refusal of names: “Erfüll davon dein Herz, so groß es ist, / Und wenn du ganz in dem Gefühle selig bist, / Nenn es dann, wie du willst, / Nenn's Glück! Herz! Liebe! Gott / Ich habe keinen Namen / Dafür! Gefühl ist alles; / Name ist Schall und Rauch, / Umnebelnd Himmelsglut”, fill your heart with it, great as it is, and when you are wholly blissful in the feeling, then call it what you will, call it happiness, heart, love, God; I have no name for it; feeling is everything; the name is sound and smoke, clouding the glow of heaven. And Gretchen: “Ungefähr sagt das der Pfarrer auch”, the pastor says roughly that too.

    Wordsworth, the year before the Speeches, felt above the Wye “A presence that disturbs me with the joy / Of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime / Of something far more deeply interfused, / Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, / And the round ocean, and the living air, / And the blue sky, and in the mind of man”. Hölderlin, two years earlier, opened Hyperion on the same wish: “Eines zu sein mit Allem, das ist Leben der Gottheit, das ist der Himmel des Menschen. Eines zu sein mit Allem, was lebt, in seliger Selbstvergessenheit wiederzukehren ins All der Natur, das ist der Gipfel der Gedanken und Freuden”, to be one with all, that is the life of the godhead, that is the heaven of man; to be one with all that lives, to return in blissful self-forgetfulness into the All of nature, that is the summit of thoughts and joys.

    Why here: “Sinn und Geschmack fürs Unendliche”, “Anschauung und Gefühl”: the generation of 1798 wrote Schleiermacher's religion before him, in Germany and in England, and Goethe gave its refutation in the same scene. Gretchen's “the pastor says roughly that too” is Hegel's objection, a feeling that has no criterion; and Faust, who does not believe, uses this speech to seduce the girl who does. The regime of experience is born in a garden, between a man who refuses to name and a woman who asks for a name.

    Sources: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Faust. Der Tragödie erster Teil, “Marthens Garten” (1808) ; Friedrich Hölderlin, Hyperion oder der Eremit in Griechenland, I (1797) ; William Wordsworth, “Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey”, Lyrical Ballads (1798).

    Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel1770-1831religion surpassed and preserved

    Background: The philosophy of Hegel: dialectic, the Phenomenology, Absolute Spirit, religion and concept · German idealism: Kant, Fichte, Schelling, Hegel · The philosophy of history: from Augustine to Löwith · The Passion and the Resurrection: the four accounts and what history retains

    Hegel arrived in Berlin in 1818; Schleiermacher was already teaching there, and the two men, colleagues at the university, cordially detested each other. Their quarrel is not a faculty anecdote: it sets against each other the two great answers to Kant. To understand it, one must start from Hegel's thesis on religion.

    Hegel does not hold religion to be false: it says the true, and even the absolute true, but in an inadequate form. Religion and philosophy have, in his view, the same content: the absolute, spirit, God. They differ in form: religion presents this content in the form of Vorstellung, representation, that is, in images, narratives, sensible figures and external relations: a Father who sends his Son, a Son who dies and rises again, a Spirit who descends upon a community. Philosophy presents the same content in the form of the Begriff, the concept, that is, in thought that grasps the inner necessity of what the image sets side by side. The Vorlesungen über die Philosophie der Religion (Lectures on the Philosophy of Religion), delivered in Berlin in 1821, 1824, 1827 and 1831 and published after his death, say so unambiguously: there is no question whatever of philosophy overturning religion, for “vielmehr ist die Religion eben der wahrhafte Inhalt nur in Form der Vorstellung”, religion is rather precisely the true content, only in the form of representation. And Hegel adds that humanity did not have to wait for philosophy to receive the consciousness of truth.

    The word that sums up this relation is Aufhebung, untranslatable because it unites three senses that English keeps apart: to cancel, to preserve, to raise up. Philosophy “sublates” religion: it cancels its representational form, preserves its content, and raises it to the form of the concept. This is a first figure of our question: Hegel leaves religion, since the religious form is declared inferior and provisional, but while preserving it entirely, since its whole content passes into philosophy. Neither a naive believer nor a critic of religion, he wants an exit that is a preservation. The whole Hegelian left will be born from the question whether this preservation is sincere.

    Within this framework belongs an early text whose legacy is immense. In 1802, in Glauben und Wissen (Faith and Knowledge), published in the Kritisches Journal der Philosophie that he edited with Schelling in Jena, Hegel attacks the philosophies of Kant, Jacobi and Fichte, which he accuses of having abandoned the knowledge of God to faith and thereby separated the finite from the infinite. The conclusion of the text formulates, eighty years before The Gay Science, the death of God. The pure concept, Hegel writes, must designate the “unendlichen Schmerz”, the infinite grief, on which the religion of modern times rests, namely the feeling that “Gott selbst ist tot”, God himself is dead. This feeling, he adds, had only been expressed empirically by Pascal, whose words he quotes about a nature that “marque partout un Dieu perdu et dans l'homme et hors de l'homme”, everywhere marks a lost God, both within man and outside man. Philosophy must restore, the same sentence goes on, the “spekulativen Karfreitag”, the speculative Good Friday, “in der ganzen Wahrheit und Härte seiner Gottlosigkeit”, in the whole truth and harshness of its godlessness, so that the highest totality may rise again “in die heiterste Freiheit ihrer Gestalt”, into the most serene freedom of its shape.

    Two remarks are called for. The first is philological. This “Gott selbst ist tot” is usually linked to the Lutheran Good Friday hymn O Traurigkeit, o Herzeleid, whose second stanza is by Johann Rist (1641). In Glauben und Wissen, Hegel does not quote this hymn: he quotes Pascal. In the Lectures on the Philosophy of Religion, on the other hand, he makes the connection himself: “Gott selbst ist todt, heißt es in jenem lutherischen Liede”. And he comments in the same place, on the death of Christ, that it is the “fürchterlichste Gedanke”, the most dreadful thought, that all that is eternal and all that is true is not, that negation is in God himself. The connection with the hymn, presented by tradition as a commentators' hypothesis, is thus made by Hegel himself, but in the Lectures and not in the text of 1802.

    The second remark is one of substance. For Hegel, the death of God is not an event in the history of unbelief; it is a moment of the concept, and precisely the moment of negativity within the absolute itself. God dies in Christ, and this death is overcome in the resurrection, that is, in the Spirit of the community: a Good Friday that calls for an Easter Sunday. When Nietzsche takes up the formula, he will keep its grief and remove its resurrection. The whole history of the critique of religion in the nineteenth century is played out, on my reading, in the interval between Hegel's speculative Good Friday and the murder without resurrection of the madman of The Gay Science.

    The quarrel with Schleiermacher is an attested response. In 1822, Hegel wrote a preface to the book of his disciple Hermann Friedrich Wilhelm Hinrichs, Die Religion im inneren Verhältnisse zur Wissenschaft (Religion in Its Inner Relation to Science). The first volume of Schleiermacher's Glaubenslehre had just appeared, with its definition of piety by the feeling of dependence. Hegel did not name his colleague, but all Berlin understood. If religion, he writes, is grounded in man only on a feeling, then this feeling has no other determination than to be the feeling of his dependence, “und so wäre der Hund der beste Christ, denn er trägt dieses am stärksten in sich, und lebt vornehmlich in diesem Gefühle”, and so the dog would be the best Christian, for he bears this feeling most strongly within him and lives chiefly in this feeling. And he adds: “Auch Erlösungsgefühle hat der Hund, wenn seinem Hunger durch einen Knochen Befriedigung wird”, the dog also has feelings of redemption, when a bone brings satisfaction to his hunger. The next sentence gives the positive thesis: in religion, spirit rather finds its liberation.

    The sarcasm is cruel, but it contains a serious argument against every spirituality of experience. A feeling, as such, is indeterminate; it can have any content whatever; it contains in itself no criterion of truth. The feeling of dependence is felt by the dog towards its master, and by the servile subject towards his tyrant. If religion is only feeling, nothing allows us to distinguish piety from servility. Hegel demands that religion be thought, that is, that it have a true content that reason can recognize. It is the same demand that makes him scorn, in the Phenomenology of Spirit (1807), the “beautiful soul” that, “um die Reinheit seines Herzens zu bewahren”, in order to preserve the purity of its heart, flees contact with actuality.

    Should we side with Hegel against Schleiermacher? On the argument yes, on the conclusion no. Hegel saw clearly: a religion founded on feeling alone is defenceless against psychological reduction, and Feuerbach will prove it. But his conclusion, that philosophy possesses the truth of religion better than religion itself, generates a symmetrical and graver danger. If philosophy is the truth of religion, the philosopher is the true priest and the system the completed dogma: Hegel leaves religion only by making philosophy a higher religion, that of those who understand. This is already the structure of the Averroist division: there are those who have representation, the people, and those who have the concept, the wise. Hegel does not govern believers, but he understands them better than they understand themselves, and that is another form of sovereignty.

    The ambiguity of Aufhebung remains fertile, and it is what breaks the school apart after 1831. If philosophy preserves the content of religion, is it religion that is saved, or philosophy that takes its place? The Hegelian right will answer that Hegel demonstrated the truth of Christianity; the left will answer that he pronounced its dissolution. The words “left” and “right” come from this debate, and it is Strauss who will introduce them, in connection with Christ.

    In literature Jean Paul, Siebenkäs (1796) ; Germaine de Staël, De l'Allemagne (1813)

    The “Speech of the dead Christ, from the top of the edifice of the world, that there is no God” (“Rede des toten Christus vom Weltgebäude herab, daß kein Gott sei”) is a “flower piece” inserted into the novel Siebenkäs: the dreamer wakes in a churchyard at midnight, the dead rise from their graves, and Christ descends upon the altar: “alle Toten riefen: »Christus! ist kein Gott?« Er antwortete: »Es ist keiner.«[…] »Ich ging durch die Welten, ich stieg in die Sonnen und flog mit den Milchstraßen durch die Wüsten des Himmels; aber es ist kein Gott.[…] ich hörte nur den ewigen Sturm, den niemand regiert«”, all the dead cried out: Christ! is there no God? He answered: There is none. I went through the worlds, I climbed into the suns and flew with the Milky Ways through the deserts of heaven; but there is no God; I heard only the eternal storm that no one governs. To the children who ask whether they have no father: “Wir sind alle Waisen, ich und ihr, wir sind ohne Vater”, we are all orphans, I and you, we are without a father. Then the sleeper wakes: “Meine Seele weinte vor Freude, daß sie wieder Gott anbeten konnte”, my soul wept for joy that it could worship God again. Mme de Staël freely translated the dream in De l'Allemagne, under the title “Un Songe” (A Dream): “les morts s'écrièrent : Ô Christ ! n'est-il point de Dieu ? Il répondit : Il n'en est point.[…] j'ai regardé dans l'abîme et je me suis écrié : Père, où es-tu ? mais je n'ai entendu que la pluie qui tomboit goutte à goutte dans l'abîme, et l'éternelle tempête, que nul ordre ne régit, m'a seule répondu”, the dead cried out: O Christ! is there no God? He answered: There is none; I looked into the abyss and cried out: Father, where are you? but I heard only the rain falling drop by drop into the abyss, and the eternal storm, which no order rules, alone answered me; to the dead children who ask whether they have no father, Christ answers: “Nous sommes tous orphelins, moi et vous nous n'avons point de père”, we are all orphans, I and you, we have no father, and the world collapses. She stops there, without the awakening, and comments: it seems to her beautiful “de transporter ainsi au-delà de la tombe l'horrible effroi que doit éprouver la créature privée de Dieu”, thus to carry beyond the grave the horrible dread that the creature deprived of God must feel.

    Why here: six years before “Gott selbst ist tot”, a novelist had put the death of God into the mouth of Christ, and it was through Mme de Staël that the image passed into France, to Nerval, to Vigny, to Musset. The difference between the two versions is the whole stake of the section: in Jean Paul, the dream ends with an awakening and a God regained, as the speculative Good Friday ends with a resurrection; in Mme de Staël, the dream remains without awakening, and it is this version that Nietzsche will keep. The death of God with sublation or without sublation: Hegel and his left, already, in two translations of the same dream.

    Sources: Jean Paul, Siebenkäs, “Erstes Blumenstück” (1796) ; Germaine de Staël, De l'Allemagne, part two, ch. XXVIII (1813).

    David Friedrich Strauss and Bruno Bauer1808-1874; 1809-1882myth and imposture

    Background: Historical-critical exegesis and the quests for the Jesus of history · David Friedrich Strauss: The Life of Jesus, myth, The Old Faith and the New · Bruno Bauer: the critique of the Gospels, the Berlin Free Ones, the Jewish question · The Young Hegelians: from the critique of religion to the critique of politics · The New Testament: twenty-seven books, their dates and their authors · The Gospel of Mark: the oldest account · The apocryphal gospels: Thomas, Peter, Mary, Judas and the others · Messiah, Son of Man, Son of God: the titles of Jesus

    In 1835 and 1836 the two volumes of Das Leben Jesu, kritisch bearbeitet (The Life of Jesus, Critically Examined) appeared in Tübingen. Their author, twenty-seven years old, who had heard Hegel in Berlin shortly before his death, would lose his post at the Tübingen seminary because of the book, and a professorship in Zurich would be withdrawn from him in 1839 under popular pressure. Rarely has a work of scholarship caused such a scandal, and rightly so: it raises, with all the resources of philology, the question that runs all the way to Onfray, that of the historical value of the gospel narratives.

    Strauss's answer comes down to one notion: myth. Before him, two readings were at odds. The supernaturalist reading took the miracles as facts; the rationalist reading, that of a Paulus, also took them as facts, but natural and misunderstood ones: Jesus did not walk on the water, he walked along the shore, and the disciples saw wrongly. Strauss dismisses both readings alike, because both assume that the Gospels report events. He proposes a third way: the gospel narratives are myths, that is, according to the definition he gives in the introduction, “nichts Andres, als geschichtartige Einkleidungen urchristlicher Ideen, gebildet in der absichtslos dichtenden Sage”, nothing other than history-like clothings of early Christian ideas, formed in legend that composes without intention.

    Everything hangs on the adverb absichtslos, without intention. Myth is not a lie: it has no author who knows he is inventing. It arises in a community that awaits a Messiah and that, convinced Jesus was he, tells his life according to the features the Scriptures attributed to the Messiah: birth in Bethlehem, descent from David, the healings foretold by Isaiah. The narrative is not fabricated to deceive; it is produced by faith itself, which cannot picture the Messiah otherwise. This notion ruins at a stroke the old Enlightenment hypothesis of priestly imposture, found in the clandestine treatise of the Three Impostors and which Voltaire only half shook off. The evangelists are not forgers; they are believers who think in images.

    But Strauss does not stop there, and this is what makes him more than a philologist. In the preface he asserts that his critique leaves the heart of faith intact: “Den inneren Kern des christlichen Glaubens weiss der Verfasser von seinen kritischen Untersuchungen völlig unabhängig”, the author knows the inner core of the Christian faith to be entirely independent of his critical inquiries. The supernatural birth, the miracles, the resurrection and the ascension, he adds, “bleiben ewige Wahrheiten, so sehr ihre Wirklichkeit als historischer Fakta angezweifelt werden mag”, remain eternal truths, however much their reality as historical facts may be doubted. One recognizes the Hegelian structure: the narrative is the representation, the eternal truth is the concept.

    And what is this concept? The Schlussabhandlung, the concluding dissertation, states it in pages that are, in my view, the true starting point of Feuerbach. Strauss asks whether the idea of the unity of divine and human nature must have been realized once, in one individual, and never again. He answers that this is not how the idea realizes itself: it does not like to pour all its fullness into a single specimen; it unfolds in a multiplicity of individuals. Then comes the thesis: “Das ist der Schlüssel der ganzen Christologie, dass als Subjekt der Prädikate, welche die Kirche Christo beilegt, statt eines Individuums eine Idee, aber eine reale, nicht Kantisch unwirkliche, gesetzt wird”, this is the key to the whole of Christology: as the subject of the predicates the Church assigns to Christ, one posits, instead of an individual, an idea, but a real one, not unreal in the Kantian manner. And the idea is named: “Die Menschheit ist die Vereinigung der beiden Naturen, der menschgewordene Gott”, humanity is the union of the two natures, God become man. Strauss goes on: humanity is the worker of miracles, since spirit subdues nature ever more; it is the sinless one, it is the one that dies, rises again and ascends to heaven.

    We can see what has happened. Strauss has performed the operation Feuerbach will theorize six years later: he has transferred the predicates of Christ to the human species, to the Gattung. The very word Gattung appears in his text: the properties the Church attributes to Christ contradict one another in an individual; they agree “in der Idee der Gattung”, in the idea of the species. Feuerbach's divinized Man is already there, in 1836, from the pen of a Hegelian who believes he is saving Christianity. The most radical historical criticism of its time thus ends, not in the abolition of the divine, but in its transfer onto humanity. The English reception confirms it in its own way: Strauss's first English translator (1846) would also be Feuerbach's translator in 1854, Marian Evans, who was to become George Eliot. The title of her translation of Feuerbach presents her precisely as “Translator of "Strauss's Life of Jesus"”.

    Bruno Bauer goes further, and in another direction. First a theologian of the Hegelian right, he moved to the extreme left at the end of the 1830s, lost his venia legendi in Bonn in 1842, and argued in his Kritik der evangelischen Geschichte der Synoptiker (1841-1842) that the Gospels are not the product of a collective legend, as Strauss held, but the conscious literary work of one author, the evangelist Mark, on whom the others depend. Against Strauss's absichtslos, then, there is an author, an intention, a creation; hence, in the late Bauer, doubts about the historical existence of Jesus himself. Engels, who had known Bauer in his Berlin days, paid him a qualified tribute in 1882 in “Bruno Bauer und das Urchristentum”. He judges the dependence of the Gospels on one another irrefutably demonstrated, and concedes that, since the content of the Gospels proves almost entirely unverifiable historically, “so daß man selbst die geschichtliche Existenz eines Jesus Christus für fraglich erklären kann”, one may even declare the historical existence of a Jesus Christ doubtful. But Engels rejects the Enlightenment conclusion that Bauer comes close to: one is not done with a religion that subjugated the Roman Empire “indem man sie einfach für von Betrügern zusammengestoppelten Unsinn erklärt”, by simply declaring it nonsense patched together by impostors. It must be explained by its historical conditions.

    Strauss and Bauer thus trace, as early as the 1840s, the two paths between which the whole historical criticism of Christianity will oscillate, down to Onfray. For Strauss, the narratives are myths born of a community's faith, and their kernel of truth is an idea; for Bauer, they are a literary creation behind which there may be no one at all. The first path leads to a religion of humanity, the second to a thesis of non-existence, and neither leaves religion: the first transfers it, the second reduces it to a fiction whose power remains to be explained, which Bauer does not do and for which Engels reproaches him. As we saw in Part Two, Michel Onfray's Théorie de Jésus takes up, without always knowing it, Bauer's path while lending it Strauss's vocabulary: Jesus “as a concept”.

    Strauss's story has an epilogue, which prompts an attested response from Nietzsche. Nearly forty years after Das Leben Jesu, Strauss published Der alte und der neue Glaube (The Old Faith and the New, 1872). In it he asks four questions: are we still Christians? do we still have a religion? how do we conceive the world? how do we order our life? To the first he answers no. To the second he answers “ja oder nein, je nachdem man es verstehen will”, yes or no, depending on how one wishes to understand it: there remains a piety towards the universe, “dieselbe Pietät, wie der Fromme alten Stils für seinen Gott”, the same piety as the old-style believer feels for his God, a feeling of dependence on the All, which the Darwinian science expounded in the next chapter does not abolish but orients. The most feared critic of Christianity ends by proposing a religion of the universe, bourgeois and comfortable, in which Beethoven and Haydn take the place of liturgy. In 1873 the young Nietzsche devoted to him the first of his Unzeitgemäße Betrachtungen, David Strauss, der Bekenner und der Schriftsteller (David Strauss, the Confessor and the Writer), in which he makes him the type of the “Bildungsphilister”, the cultivated philistine. Nietzsche does not reproach Strauss for being too critical, but for not being critical enough: he has done away with the Christian God and kept Christian morality intact, without seeing that the one does not stand without the other, the first statement of the objection that The Gay Science will make famous. Strauss thus travels in a single lifetime the movement I describe over a century: from the critique of dogma to a substitute religion.

    In literature George Eliot, Middlemarch (1871-1872) ; Alfred Tennyson, In Memoriam A. H. H. (1850)

    Marian Evans was twenty-six when she completed, in 1846, the English translation of Strauss's Leben Jesu, followed by that of Feuerbach in 1854; having become George Eliot, she put into Middlemarch a scholar who is the reverse of Strauss. Mr Casaubon devotes his life to “the Key to all Mythologies”, a work meant to trace all the myths of the world back to a corrupted primitive revelation; he dies without having written it, because he knows no German and the Germans have already made his project obsolete.

    Why here: Casaubon looks beneath the myths for a revelation, Strauss finds in them a community that believes; the novel makes pre-critical erudition into a domestic tragedy, and German criticism into a rumour arriving from abroad. Dorothea, who marries Casaubon to serve this Key, is the reader of Strauss that George Eliot had been, and the novel leads her to what the essay calls the religion of humanity, without God and without a Key.

    Tennyson, in In Memoriam, gave Victorian England the formula of its crisis, just as Strauss was reaching it in English: “There lives more faith in honest doubt, / Believe me, than in half the creeds” (XCVI). The line is the exact contemporary of the transfer Strauss performs: faith leaves the dogmas, and it must go somewhere; in Tennyson, into doubt itself; in Strauss, into humanity; in both cases the place does not remain empty.

    Sources: George Eliot, Middlemarch (1871-1872) ; Alfred Tennyson, In Memoriam A. H. H., XCVI (1850).

    Portrait: Hermann Günther, Public domain

    Portrait: Auteur inconnu, Public domain

    Ernest Renan1823-1892the god become an incomparable man

    Background: Historical-critical exegesis and the quests for the Jesus of history · Ernest Renan: the Life of Jesus, science, the nation · From the Judges to the Kings: Samuel, Saul, David and Goliath, Solomon and the Temple · Positivism and scientism: science as a substitute religion in the nineteenth century · The Gospel of Mark: the oldest account · The nineteenth century: the Church against modernity, theology before criticism · The teaching of Jesus: the Kingdom, the parables, the miracles

    The Vie de Jésus (The Life of Jesus) appeared in Paris in 1863. Its author had left the seminary of Saint-Sulpice in 1845; he was a philologist of the Semitic languages, and he had just been suspended from his chair at the Collège de France for having, in his inaugural lecture of 1862, called Jesus “un homme incomparable”, an incomparable man. A great publishing success, the book sold tens of thousands of copies within a few months, was translated throughout Europe and provoked hundreds of refutations.

    Renan does three things at once, and they must be told apart to understand why Nietzsche would hate him and Dostoevsky would fight him.

    The first is a principle of method, laid down in the introduction with a clarity the Germans had lacked. Renan imagines a wonder-worker presenting himself, and a commission of scholars checking his miracle under controlled, repeatable conditions. Never, he observes, has a miracle occurred under such conditions; the wonder-worker has always chosen his subject, his setting, his audience; and most often it is the people themselves, “par suite de l'invincible besoin qu'il a de voir dans les grands événements et les grands hommes quelque chose de divin”, owing to their invincible need to see something divine in great events and great men, who create the legends after the fact. Hence the principle: “un récit surnaturel ne peut être admis comme tel, qu'il implique toujours crédulité ou imposture, que le devoir de l'historien est de l'interpréter et de rechercher quelle part de vérité, quelle part d'erreur il peut receler”, a supernatural narrative cannot be accepted as such, it always implies credulity or imposture, and the historian's duty is to interpret it and to seek out what share of truth and what share of error it may conceal. Renan, like Strauss, looks for the truth behind the narrative, but his method is positivist, not Hegelian: the supernatural is excluded on principle, not by dialectic. And the word “imposture” reappears, alongside “credulity”.

    The second is an experience, which Renan recounts with an emotion that did much for the book's success. In 1860-1861 he travelled in Galilee on an archaeological mission. The agreement of texts and places, the harmony of the gospel ideal with the landscape, were for him “comme une révélation”, like a revelation. He goes on: “J'eus devant les yeux un cinquième évangile, lacéré, mais lisible encore, et désormais, à travers les récits de Matthieu et de Marc, au lieu d'un être abstrait, qu'on dirait n'avoir jamais existé, je vis une admirable figure humaine”, I had before my eyes a fifth gospel, torn but still legible, and from then on, through the narratives of Matthew and Mark, instead of an abstract being one would say had never existed, I saw an admirable human figure. The sentence is aimed at Bauer's thesis: against the abstract being one would say had never existed, Renan sets the human figure recovered in Galilee, and he is thus the anticipated adversary of all the mythicists.

    The third is a cult. The Vie de Jésus is not a cold book: it ends in a genuine doxology. Having said that we moderns labour without reaping, Renan concludes: “Mais quels que puissent être les phénomènes inattendus de l'avenir, Jésus ne sera pas surpassé. Son culte se rajeunira sans cesse; sa légende provoquera des larmes sans fin; ses souffrances attendriront les meilleurs coeurs; tous les siècles proclameront qu'entre les fils des hommes, il n'en est pas né de plus grand que Jésus”, but whatever the unexpected phenomena of the future may be, Jesus will not be surpassed. His cult will renew its youth unceasingly; his legend will draw tears without end; his sufferings will move the best hearts; every century will proclaim that among the sons of men there has been born none greater than Jesus. Christ ceases to be God; he becomes the greatest of men; and his cult is declared eternal. Renan is a pure example of an exit from religion that preserves it in the form of admiration. It is Christianity minus the supernatural, that is, a religion of the great man.

    Two attested responses measure what is at stake. The first is Nietzsche's, who read Renan with growing hostility. In Der Antichrist (written in 1888, published in 1895), he writes: “Herr Renan, dieser Hanswurst in psychologicis, hat die zwei ungehörigsten Begriffe zu seiner Erklärung des Typus Jesus hinzugebracht, die es hierfür geben kann: den Begriff Genie und den Begriff Held”, Monsieur Renan, that buffoon in psychologicis, has brought to his explanation of the type of Jesus the two most unfitting concepts there could be: the concept of genius and the concept of hero. And in Götzen-Dämmerung (completed in 1888, published in January 1889), he goes further: what is the use of all the free thought, modernity and mockery, “wenn man mit seinen Eingeweiden Christ, Katholik und sogar Priester geblieben ist!”, when one has remained, in one's entrails, a Christian, a Catholic and even a priest! Renan believes he has left the Church; he has merely changed altars.

    The second response is Dostoevsky's. In A Writer's Diary of 1873, he recalls Renan, who, unlike Belinsky, stopped before the figure of Christ, proclaiming in his book “полной безверия”, full of unbelief, the Vie de Jésus, that Christ nonetheless remains “идеал красоты человеческой”, the ideal of human beauty. The connection with Renan is attested, and we know that the figure of a too human Christ, reduced to morality and admiration, is one of Dostoevsky's constant targets.

    Renan opens a possibility that what follows will take up again and again: that of a spirituality without the supernatural, centred on an exemplary figure. Jesus becomes a master of life, like Socrates or the Buddha. The contemporary spiritualities that make Christ a sage, of which Frédéric Lenoir gave a popular version at the beginning of the twenty-first century under the title Le Christ philosophe (2007), are the direct heirs of Renan. Nietzsche's objection reaches them all: to admire Jesus as a genius or a hero is to misunderstand him twice, as God and as man. Between Renan and Nietzsche lies the whole difference between an exit that preserves religion as a cult of the great man and a genealogy that refuses every cult.

    In literature Marcel Proust, Pastiches et mélanges (1919)

    In L'Affaire Lemoine, Proust tells the same swindle, an engineer claiming to manufacture diamonds, in the manner of nine writers. The Renan pastiche lends the author of the Vie de Jésus his indulgence towards the impostor and his lyricism of the future: “Patience donc ! Humanité, patience. Rallume encore demain le four éteint mille fois déjà d'où sortira peut-être un jour le diamant ! Perfectionne, avec une bonne humeur que peut t'envier l'Éternel, le creuset où tu porteras le carbone à des températures inconnues de Lemoine et de Berthelot. Répète inlassablement le sto ad ostium et pulso, sans savoir si jamais une voix te répondra : ‘Veni, veni, coronaberis’”, patience then! Humanity, patience. Light again tomorrow the furnace already put out a thousand times, from which the diamond will perhaps one day come forth! Perfect, with a good humour the Eternal may envy you, the crucible in which you will bring carbon to temperatures unknown to Lemoine and Berthelot. Repeat tirelessly the sto ad ostium et pulso, without knowing whether a voice will ever answer you: ‘Veni, veni, coronaberis’.

    Why here: Proust caught with a perfect ear what Nietzsche aimed at in a word, the priest “in one's entrails”. The art of pastiche is to keep the music while changing the object: Renan applying to a stock-market affair the fervour, the patience and the Latin quotations he reserved for Humanity is the cult of the great man become style, and style become cult. Humanity is addressed there with the familiar “thou”, as Nature was by d'Holbach, and promised a coronation.

    Sources: Marcel Proust, Pastiches et mélanges, “L'Affaire Lemoine”, VIII, “par Ernest Renan” (1919; the first pastiches appeared in Le Figaro in 1908).

    Portrait: Antoine Samuel Adam-Salomon, Public domain

    Transition: from a quarrel of schools to the break

    Schleiermacher shifted religion towards experience, to the point of admitting a religion without God; Hegel towards the concept, to the point of making philosophy its truth. Strauss transferred the predicates of Christ to humanity; Renan made Christ the greatest of men and declared his cult eternal. None of them wants to destroy religion; all want to save it by transforming it, and all transform it into something that keeps the place of the absolute: the universe, Spirit, Humanity, the great man.

    Against this caution there rises, from 1841 onwards, the generation of the Young Hegelians, who take Hegel's Aufhebung and Strauss's transfer at their word and draw the consequence their masters did not dare to draw: if God is man, then one must say so, and stop worshipping him under another name. But in saying so, they merely displace worship once more.

    Top of the part

    Part Sixthe Hegelian left and its adversaries6 authors

    Background: The Young Hegelians: from the critique of religion to the critique of politics · The nineteenth century: the Church against modernity, theology before criticism

    In 1840 Frederick William III of Prussia died; his son, Frederick William IV, a pietist romantic, brought Schelling to Berlin to combat “die Drachensaat des Hegelschen Pantheismus”, the dragon's seed of Hegelian pantheism. The Young Hegelians lost their posts, their journals were banned, and the critique of religion became for them the necessary form of political critique in a state that called itself Christian. This is the context of the German texts in this part, published between 1841 and 1845 in a climate of censorship and exile. At the same moment, in Copenhagen and in Paris, two authors who could not be more opposed, Kierkegaard and Comte, answered the same question by opposite routes, one by returning to faith against Christendom, the other by founding a religion without God. And in Frankfurt an old philosopher ignored for thirty years, Schopenhauer, proposed a mysticism without God that would shape Nietzsche's youth.

    Ludwig Feuerbach1804-1872the secret of theology

    Background: Exodus: Moses, the departure from Egypt, Sinai and the Law · David Friedrich Strauss: The Life of Jesus, myth, The Old Faith and the New · Feuerbach's thought: The Essence of Christianity, the species, love, nature · Max Stirner and The Ego and Its Own: the Ego against the spectres · Engels: dialectical materialism, the history of early Christianity, the reckoning with Feuerbach · The thought of Luc Ferry: transcendental humanism, the Man-God, the revolution of love · Evil, Satan and the afterlife: from Sheol to the Last Judgement

    This whole debate pivots on Feuerbach, who must be followed at greater length than is usually done. He is reduced to a formula, theology is anthropology, and to a book, Das Wesen des Christentums. But his thinking about religion extends over twenty years, from 1830 to 1851, and it moves: it starts from death, passes through Christianity, takes on Hegel, defends itself against Stirner and ends in nature. At every stage our question returns: did the man who dissolved God into man abolish religion, or did he displace it?

    The first book, published anonymously, cost its author his career. The Gedanken über Tod und Unsterblichkeit (Thoughts on Death and Immortality) appeared in Nuremberg in 1830. Feuerbach, then a Privatdozent at Erlangen, denies personal immortality in it: the individual is finite, and what is infinite in him, reason, love, spirit, does not belong to him as his own; death is the act by which the individual returns to the infinite what was not his. The author was quickly identified, and he would never be appointed professor. This starting point sheds light on everything else: the first object of Feuerbach's critique is not God but the beyond, and his first gesture is not to deny the infinite but to take it away from the individual and give it to the species. The young Hegelian of 1830 is still a pantheist of spirit, and it will take him ten years to make the species no longer Spirit, but man.

    Das Wesen des Christentums (The Essence of Christianity) appeared in Leipzig, published by Otto Wigand, in 1841. It struck a whole generation as a liberation, and Engels still remembered it in 1886 in his Ludwig Feuerbach und der Ausgang der klassischen deutschen Philosophie: “Die Begeisterung war allgemein: Wir waren alle momentan Feuerbachianer”, the enthusiasm was general: we were all Feuerbachians for the moment. The words “for the moment” already tell what followed.

    The thesis is stated in the preface to the first edition: the book means to show “daß das Geheimniß der Theologie die Anthropologie ist”, that the secret of theology is anthropology. The abridged formula of the textbooks, “die Theologie ist Anthropologie”, is not in the first edition in that form, and the difference is no small one: the word Geheimnis says that theology hides what it is and must be deciphered. George Eliot, in her 1854 translation made from the second German edition, keeps the word: “the secret of theology is anthropology”.

    The deciphering rests on a theory of consciousness. Man differs from the animal because he is conscious not only of himself as an individual but of his species, his Gattung, that is, of the infinity of his essence: reason, will, love. This infinite essence the finite individual cannot recognize as his own: he projects it outside himself and worships it under the name of God. Hence the central formula: “Das Bewußtsein Gottes ist das Selbstbewußtsein des Menschen”, the consciousness of God is the self-consciousness of man. The mechanism is precise: man, and this for Feuerbach is the secret of religion, objectifies his essence, then makes himself the object of this objectified essence transformed into a subject; he thinks of himself as an object, but as the object of an object, of another being. All the divine predicates are human predicates raised to infinity: God is love, and it is human love that is worshipped without knowing it.

    The book tests the thesis dogma by dogma, and it was this testing, more than the thesis, that made its success. The first part, entitled “Die Religion in ihrer Uebereinstimmung mit dem Wesen des Menschen”, religion in its agreement with the essence of man, reads each mystery as the secret of a human reality. The incarnation is the secret of love: God becomes man because love drives him to it, and the love that commands God is higher than he is, which Feuerbach writes with a boldness that announces the conclusion: “Die Liebe ist Gott selbst und außer ihr ist kein Gott”, love is God himself and apart from it there is no God. Prayer is the secret of the heart that knows no limits: “Das Gebet ist die Selbsttheilung des Menschen in zwei Wesen”, prayer is the self-division of man into two beings, a dialogue of man with himself, with his heart. The miracle is the secret of desire: “Das Wunder ist eine Creatio ex nihilo”, the miracle is a creation out of nothing, for whoever makes wine from water makes wine from nothing; and its truth is simple: “Aber was ist das Wunder? Ein realisirter supranaturalistischer Wunsch”, but what is the miracle? A supernaturalist wish fulfilled.

    The second part reverses the lighting: “Die Religion in ihrem Widerspruch mit dem Wesen des Menschen”, religion in its contradiction with the essence of man. For the projection is not innocent: placed outside man, his essence escapes his criticism and turns against him. The central chapter, the last before the conclusion, is “Der Widerspruch von Glaube und Liebe”. Love, says Feuerbach, is universal and unites all men; faith is particular and separates those who believe from those who do not. “Der Glaube ist also wesentlich parteiisch”, faith is therefore essentially partisan; “Der Glaube kennt nur Feinde oder Freunde, keine Unparteilichkeit”; and the consequence is necessary: “Der Glaube ist wesentlich intolerant”, faith is essentially intolerant. The flames of hell, he adds, are only the sparks of the furious glance that faith casts on unbelievers. This chapter is the real point of the book: Feuerbach does not reproach Christianity for being false, but for betraying its own heart, love, for the sake of faith, from which love must be wrested.

    The second edition, in 1843, adds a preface containing Feuerbach's most quoted sentence in the twentieth century, because Guy Debord made it the epigraph of The Society of the Spectacle (1967). I give it in Eliot's translation, made from that edition: the present age “prefers the sign to the thing signified, the copy to the original, fancy to reality, the appearance to the essence”; and for that age, the criticism that dispels illusion is a profanation, “for in these days illusion only is sacred, truth profane”. The sentence says that Feuerbach knew himself to be a profaner and held profanation to be a duty of truth.

    Feuerbach owes to Strauss the transfer of the predicates to the species, but he does away with the Hegelian Spirit of which Strauss's humanity was the realization: there is only man, sensuous and natural. He owes to Schleiermacher the idea that religion has its seat in feeling, but where Schleiermacher saw the place where the infinite gives itself, he sees the place where man gives himself the infinite. The reduction Hegel feared is accomplished.

    There remained Hegel, with whom Feuerbach settles accounts in two short texts that are perhaps more important than the great book. The Vorläufige Thesen zur Reform der Philosophie (Provisional Theses for the Reform of Philosophy), written in 1842 and published in 1843 in Switzerland, because of Prussian censorship, in Arnold Ruge's Anekdota, open with a sentence that extends the diagnosis of 1841: “Das Geheimnis der Theologie ist die Anthropologie, das Geheimnis aber der spekulativen Philosophie die Theologie”, the secret of theology is anthropology, but the secret of speculative philosophy is theology. Hegel did not go beyond religion, he rationalized it. “Die Hegelsche Philosophie ist der letzte Zufluchtsort, die letzte rationelle Stütze der Theologie”, Hegelian philosophy is the last refuge, the last rational support of theology, and Feuerbach adds with biting irony that, just as Catholic theologians once became Aristotelians to fight Protestantism, Protestant theologians will have to become Hegelians to fight atheism. Hence the method, which fits in one line: “Wir dürfen nur immer das Prädikat zum Subjekt, und so als Subjekt zum Objekt und Prinzip machen”, we need only ever make the predicate the subject, and thus, as subject, the object and the principle. Hegel says: Spirit thinks; Feuerbach: man thinks, and Spirit is only his thought. This is the inversion that Marx, thirty years later, would still claim in the afterword to Capital, by setting back on its feet a dialectic that was standing on its head.

    The Grundsätze der Philosophie der Zukunft (Principles of the Philosophy of the Future), of 1843, give the positive version. The first paragraph states the meaning of the whole modern age: “Die Aufgabe der neueren Zeit war die Verwirklichung und Vermenschlichung Gottes”, the task of the modern age was the realization and humanization of God. The philosophy of the future will be sensualist: real being is sensuous being, and truth lies not in the thinking self but in the relation between two sensuous beings, the I and the Thou. “Der natürliche Standpunkt des Menschen, der Standpunkt der Unterscheidung in Ich und Du, Subjekt und Objekt ist der wahre, der absolute Standpunkt”. Here one recognizes, eighty years before Buber's Ich und Du (1923), the philosophy of dialogue; Buber acknowledged this debt, which I note without quoting it, not having checked the passage.

    Paragraph 60 states plainly what the book of 1841 implied. “Einsamkeit ist Endlichkeit und Beschränktheit, Gemeinschaftlichkeit ist Freiheit und Unendlichkeit”, solitude is finitude and limitation, community is freedom and infinity; and Feuerbach concludes: man by himself is man, in the ordinary sense; man with man, “die Einheit von Ich und Du ist Gott”, the unity of I and Thou is God. This is not a metaphor. The Theses had said it of the new philosophy: it has made the attribute the substance, the predicate the subject, and thereby “die neue Philosophie ist die realisierte Idee, die Wahrheit des Christentums”, the new philosophy is the realized idea, the truth of Christianity; and Feuerbach specifies: “Aber eben weil sie das Wesen des Christentums in sich hat, gibt sie den Namen des Christentums auf”, but precisely because it has the essence of Christianity within it, it gives up the name of Christianity. This sentence is the centre of our question: Feuerbach does not claim to abolish Christianity, but to keep its essence and give up its name.

    Criticism therefore has a positive task: not to destroy religion, but to retranslate it, to give back to man what he has alienated. The necessary turning point of history, says the last chapter of 1841, is the avowal “daß das Bewußtsein Gottes nichts andres ist als das Bewußtsein der Gattung”, that the consciousness of God is nothing other than the consciousness of the species. And he draws the practical rule from it: if the essence of man is the supreme being of man, then the first and highest law must be the love of man for man. “Homo homini Deus est”, man is a God to man, “dieß ist der oberste praktische Grundsatz”, this is the supreme practical principle, and it is the “Wendepunkt der Weltgeschichte”, the turning point of world history. The formula reverses the homo homini lupus of the Hobbesian tradition.

    Hasty readers miss the essential point: Feuerbach does not merely say that human relations are good, he says that they are holy.
