The Inquisitor is exactly what one obtains when one leaves God while keeping religion: an atheist who holds faith to be indispensable to men, and who governs it out of love for them. He is the political culmination of the Feuerbachian critique, a religion of humanity administered by those who know. He is also, by a comparison I construct, a transposition of Comte as high priest of Humanity: a spiritual power that does not believe in the supernatural, but knows that men need worship, mystery and direction. But Comte believes in his Great Being; the Inquisitor believes only in the weakness of men. The Inquisitor is a Comte who has become lucid, and therefore tragic.

    And Christ's answer is not an argument. He is silent, then: “тихо целует его в его бескровные девяностолетние уста”, he kisses him gently on his bloodless ninety-year-old lips; Mongault: “le Prisonnier s'approche en silence du nonagénaire et baise ses lèvres exsangues”, the Prisoner silently approaches the old man of ninety and kisses his bloodless lips. The kiss refutes nothing: it refuses to enter the order of justification, which is the Inquisitor's. One may see in it an answer of another order, which is neither a thesis nor an institution, but a gesture, a way of being before the other: what the twentieth century will call spirituality, what remains of the religious once dogma and the Church are taken away.

    The answer of the whole novel is of the same order. Book VI, devoted to the starets Zosima, opposes to Ivan not a theodicy but a form of life, which comes down to two sentences. That of Zosima's younger brother, Markel, as he is dying: “всякий пред всеми за всех и за всё виноват”, each is guilty before all, for all and for everything. And that of Zosima on hell: “Отцы и учители, мыслю: "Что есть ад?" Рассуждаю так: "Страдание о том, что нельзя уже более любить"”, fathers and teachers, I ask myself: what is hell? the suffering of no longer being able to love; Mongault: “la souffrance de ne plus pouvoir aimer”, the suffering of no longer being able to love. This is not a proof of God, but the description of a way of existing in which Ivan's question is transformed without being resolved. The novel does not say that Ivan is wrong; it says that one cannot live in his position, and that whoever wants to live in it goes mad.

    This answer is strange in relation to the series. Spinoza answered the need for God with knowledge, Feuerbach with reappropriation, Marx with the transformation of the world, Comte with the organization of a cult. Zosima answers with a conversion of the gaze, which does not abolish evil but changes the subject's relation to evil. It is not a doctrine that could be set against Ivan's, it is an exercise, in the sense in which Hadot will speak of the spiritual exercises of Antiquity. The comparison is constructed; it announces the last part of this essay: the answer the novel opposes to the Inquisitor's religion is not another religion, it is a spirituality. Within the novel itself, moreover, this Christianity is suspect to the institution: Zosima's corpse smells, against the expectation of the faithful who hoped for a miracle, and the scandal shows that his faith has nothing to do with miracle, mystery and authority.

    Dostoevsky also saw the other outcome of the death of God, the man who makes himself god. This is Kirillov, in Besy (Demons, 1871-1872), the engineer who kills himself to prove his freedom and to become god, according to the logic he states himself: “Если нет бога, то я бог”, if there is no God, then I am god. The Inquisitor and Kirillov sketch the two possible refoundations: religion without God administered by a few, and the divinization of man. Nietzsche, who would read Les Possédés in the French translation by Victor Derély (Plon, 1886) and copy passages from it into his notebooks from November 1887 to March 1888, without knowing The Brothers Karamazov, and Camus, who would know them very well, would each take them up in their own way.

    In this series, Dostoevsky does not receive objections: he hands them out. Nietzsche would salute him in Götzen-Dämmerung, “Streifzüge” 45: Dostoevsky is “des einzigen Psychologen, anbei gesagt, von dem ich Etwas zu lernen hatte”, the only psychologist, incidentally, from whom I had something to learn. Nietzsche discovered Dostoevsky in February 1887, in a bookshop in Nice, through a French translation published under the title L'Esprit souterrain (trans. Halpérine-Kaminsky and Ch. Morice, Plon, 1886). He thus discovered Dostoevsky without the book in which the encounter would have been most evident; yet he would take up as genealogy what Dostoevsky had staged as drama.

    In literature Herman Melville, Billy Budd (1924) ; Victor Hugo, Les Misérables (1862)

    In Billy Budd, completed on the eve of Melville's death and published in 1924, the young foretopman Billy, falsely accused of mutiny by the master-at-arms Claggart, kills him with a blow of his fist, unable to speak. Captain Vere, who knows the innocence of his heart, cries out: “Struck dead by an angel of God. Yet the angel must hang!” He convenes a drumhead court, himself argues against the judges' pity in the name of the law of war and the order of the ship, and has Billy hanged at dawn; Billy dies blessing him [summary].

    Why here: Vere is the Grand Inquisitor in uniform, and Melville made him a good man. He knows that truth is on the side of the innocent, and he sacrifices him to the peace of the multitude, because, he says in substance, the men of the crew would not understand his being spared. This is the mechanism the essay describes with Girard and that the Inquisitor administers: a victim designated so that order may hold. Billy's blessing is Christ's kiss, a gesture that is not an argument.

    Javert, in Les Misérables, after Jean Valjean has spared him at the barricade and he in turn has let Valjean go, discovers two roads: “Il voyait devant lui deux routes également droites toutes deux, mais il en voyait deux ; et cela le terrifiait, lui qui n'avait jamais connu dans sa vie qu'une ligne droite”, he saw before him two roads, both equally straight, but he saw two; and that terrified him, he who had never in his life known anything but one straight line; he feels “que quelque chose d'horrible pénétrait dans son âme, l'admiration pour un forçat”, that something horrible was entering his soul, admiration for a convict, and throws himself into the Seine. This is the other face of the Inquisitor: the law as absolute, which does not survive the encounter with a grace it can neither punish nor understand. Smerdyakov, whom the essay reads with Bayle, has no such excuse.

    Sources: Herman Melville, Billy Budd, Sailor (written from 1886 to 1891, published in 1924); Victor Hugo, Les Misérables, V, 4, 1 (1862).

    Portrait: Vasily Perov, Public domain

    Nietzsche1844-1900the death of God as a task

    Background: Paul of Tarsus: the letters, justification, the Law and the new perspective · Ernest Renan: the Life of Jesus, science, the nation · Schopenhauer's philosophy: the Will, suffering, compassion, the denial of the will · The philosophy of Nietzsche: tragedy, genealogy, will to power, eternal return, overman · Marcel Gauchet's thought: the disenchantment of the world, the exit from religion, democracy · The Passion and the Resurrection: the four accounts and what history retains · The teaching of Jesus: the Kingdom, the parables, the miracles · The letters of Paul: Romans, Corinthians and the others · Messiah, Son of Man, Son of God: the titles of Jesus

    We must begin with Schopenhauer, for it was against his first master that Nietzsche forged his relation to the divine. The debt, as we have seen, is immense and openly claimed. In 1887, in Book V of The Gay Science, he pays him a tribute that bears directly on our question: “Schopenhauer war als Philosoph der erste eingeständliche und unbeugsame Atheist, den wir Deutschen gehabt haben: seine Feindschaft gegen Hegel hatte hier ihren Hintergrund”, Schopenhauer was, as a philosopher, the first avowed and inflexible atheist that we Germans have had: this was the background of his hostility towards Hegel (FW 357). And he adds that “Die Ungöttlichkeit des Daseins galt ihm als etwas Gegebenes, Greifliches, Undiskutierbares”, the non-divine character of existence was for him something given, tangible, beyond discussion.

    The sentence is historically very precise. Nietzsche sees in Schopenhauer's hostility towards Hegel a religious quarrel: Hegel, with his reason in history and his final reconciliation, remained a theologian in disguise, whereas Schopenhauer had had the courage to look at a world without providence. The same § 357 goes on to make Hegel the great delayer of atheism, the one who tried to persuade the Germans of the divinity of existence by means of the historical sense. Nietzsche thus places Schopenhauer on the side of probity and Hegel on the side of the reprieve granted to God. The response is attested, and it fixes the starting point: the question of God's existence is settled; what remains is to know what one does with existence once it is admitted that it is not divine.

    It is on this point that Nietzsche breaks with his master. Schopenhauer drew a moral conclusion from the absence of God: since existence has no meaning, the will to live must be denied, and pity, which recognizes the suffering of all that lives, is the supreme virtue. Nietzsche sees in this conclusion the subtlest survival of Christianity. In Der Antichrist, § 7, he grants Schopenhauer the diagnosis only to turn it around: “Schopenhauer war in seinem Recht damit: durch das Mitleid wird das Leben verneint, verneinungswürdiger gemacht”, Schopenhauer was right in this: through pity, life is denied, made more worthy of denial; and the next sentence defines pity as “die Praxis des Nihilismus”, the practice of nihilism. The atheist Schopenhauer had kept the Christian morality of pity and the Christian ideal of asceticism: he had left God without leaving religion, and his piety, which Feuerbach directed towards Man, was directed in his case towards renunciation.

    The Genealogie der Moral (On the Genealogy of Morality, 1887) carries the critique all the way to the person. In § 6 of the third essay, Nietzsche quotes Schopenhauer's description of aesthetic contemplation, in which one celebrates “den Sabbat der Zuchthausarbeit des Wollens”, the Sabbath of the penal servitude of willing, and he asks: supposing that Schopenhauer was a hundred times right for his own person, “was wäre damit für die Einsicht ins Wesen des Schönen getan?”, what would thereby have been gained for insight into the essence of the beautiful? In § 7, he goes further: Schopenhauer would have fallen ill, would have become a pessimist, “ohne seine Feinde, ohne Hegel, das Weib, die Sinnlichkeit und den ganzen Willen zum Dasein, Dableiben”, without his enemies, without Hegel, woman, sensuality and the whole will to exist, to stay there. The pessimist needed what he denied.

    Die fröhliche Wissenschaft (The Gay Science) appeared in 1882; the fifth book was added in the second edition of 1887. The gap matters: the death of God is first announced (Book III), then, five years later, interpreted (Book V). The usual mistake is to read § 125 as an atheist thesis. It is the opposite: a scene that holds the atheists up to ridicule.

    Book III opens, in § 108, with a parable: after the Buddha's death, his shadow was still shown in a cave for centuries. “Gott ist tot: aber so wie die Art der Menschen ist, wird es vielleicht noch jahrtausendelang Höhlen geben, in denen man seinen Schatten zeigt”, God is dead, but given the way men are, there will perhaps be caves for thousands of years yet in which his shadow is shown. The whole programme is there. The death of God is not the end of religion; it is the beginning of a long survival of its shadows. That the parable starts from the Buddha is not without significance: it was through Schopenhauer that Nietzsche knew Buddhism, and it is the Schopenhauerian shadow, that of a religion without God founded on the denial of the will, that is targeted at the same time as the Christian shadow.

    § 125 stages the “tolle Mensch”, the madman, who runs into the marketplace in broad daylight with a lantern, crying that he is looking for God. Those who surround him and mock him are precisely unbelievers. It is to them that he announces: “Wir haben ihn getötet, ihr und ich!”, we have killed him, you and I. The atheists of the marketplace believe that the absence of God is a settled matter, just one more opinion; the madman knows that it is an event, and a murder, whose consequences have not yet been measured. He then asks our question: “Welche Sühnefeiern, welche heiligen Spiele werden wir erfinden müssen?”, what festivals of atonement, what sacred games shall we have to invent? Henri Albert: “Quelles expiations, quels jeux sacrés serons-nous forcés d'inventer ?[…] Ne sommes-nous pas forcés de devenir nous-mêmes des dieux pour du moins paraître dignes des dieux ?”, what atonements, what sacred games shall we be forced to invent?[…] Must we not ourselves become gods, if only to appear worthy of it? The exit from religion calls of itself for a new religion. Nietzsche says so in 1882, and in the form of a question.

    No one arranged the meeting between this question and Dostoevsky's scene. The madman asks whether we shall not have to become gods to be worthy of the murder; that is Kirillov's position. He asks what sacred games we shall have to invent; that is the position of the Inquisitor and of Comte. The two paths of refoundation, which Dostoevsky had embodied in two characters, Nietzsche formulates as two questions in the same paragraph. The comparison is constructed, since Nietzsche had not read Demons in 1882; the convergence of two minds that did not yet know each other is all the more significant.

    For Nietzsche, the shadows of God are everywhere one does not look for them. In morality first: people have stopped believing in the Christian God, but they go on believing in the value of pity, equality and disinterestedness, which have meaning only through him; this is the reproach he makes to Schopenhauer, and it will be the one he makes to the socialists, the democrats and the positivists. In language next: “wir werden Gott nicht los, weil wir noch an die Grammatik glauben”, we shall not be rid of God so long as we still believe in grammar (Götzen-Dämmerung, “Die "Vernunft" in der Philosophie”, 5), for grammar imposes a subject behind every act, a substance behind every becoming, and God is the supreme subject. In science finally, and this is the hardest blow.

    § 344, in Book V, is entitled “Inwiefern auch wir noch fromm sind”, in what sense we too are still pious. The will to truth, the refusal to be deceived and to deceive, the demand on which science rests, is not itself scientific: it is a faith. And Nietzsche confesses: “daß auch wir Erkennenden von heute, wir Gottlosen und Antimetaphysiker, auch unser Feuer noch von dem Brande nehmen, den ein jahrtausendealter Glaube entzündet hat, jener Christen-Glaube, der auch der Glaube Platos war, daß Gott die Wahrheit ist, daß die Wahrheit göttlich ist”; Albert: “nous aussi, nous qui cherchons aujourd'hui la connaissance, nous les impies et les antimétaphysiques, nous empruntons encore notre feu à l'incendie qu'une foi vieille de mille années a allumé, cette foi chrétienne qui fut aussi la foi de Platon et qui admettait que Dieu est la vérité et que la vérité est divine”, that we too, the seekers after knowledge of today, we godless ones and anti-metaphysicians, still take our fire from the blaze kindled by a faith thousands of years old, that Christian faith which was also the faith of Plato, that God is truth, that truth is divine.

    The Genealogie der Moral draws the same conclusion by another path, and turns it into a thesis on the history of Christianity that anticipates the theories of secularization by a century. In § 24 of the third essay, Nietzsche observes that no philosophy has yet asked whether the will to truth itself needs a justification, because the ascetic ideal dominated all philosophy, “weil Wahrheit als Sein, als Gott, als oberste Instanz selbst gesetzt wurde, weil Wahrheit gar nicht Problem sein durfte”, because truth was posited as being, as God, as the highest authority itself, because truth was not allowed to be a problem at all. In § 27, he takes the step. Honest atheism, far from opposing the ascetic ideal, is its last form: “er ist die Ehrfurcht gebietende Katastrophe einer zweitausendjährigen Zucht zur Wahrheit, welche am Schlusse sich die Lüge im Glauben an Gott verbietet”, it is the awe-inspiring catastrophe of a two-thousand-year discipline in truth, which in the end forbids itself the lie of belief in God. And he states its law: “Alle großen Dinge gehen durch sich selbst zugrunde, durch einen Akt der Selbstaufhebung”, all great things perish through themselves, through an act of self-suppression. Christianity as dogma perished of its own morality; Christianity as morality must in turn perish of its own truthfulness, when that truthfulness asks what any will to truth is worth. Nietzsche indeed quotes himself: the formula about the two-thousand-year discipline already appears word for word in § 357 of The Gay Science, in connection with Schopenhauer's atheism, followed by this sentence: “Man sieht, was eigentlich über den christlichen Gott gesiegt hat: die christliche Moralität selbst”, one sees what really triumphed over the Christian God: Christian morality itself. The atheism of the admired master thus becomes a fruit of the Christian conscience, and Schopenhauer finds himself, once again, among the pious.

    Nietzsche is describing here a Christianity that destroys itself out of fidelity to itself; what Marcel Gauchet will call, in 1985, the “religion de la sortie de la religion”, the religion of the exit from religion. The comparison is constructed, and Part Eleven will take it up again; Gauchet's thesis is already formulated, in genealogical terms, in a paragraph of 1887. Nietzsche even adds, in parentheses, that the same development took place in India, independently, with the Buddha, which makes the exit from religion through truthfulness a law of the ascetic religions, and not a Christian peculiarity.

    Hence the conclusion of the Genealogy, which gives the whole of religious history its psychological foundation: the ascetic ideal expresses a fundamental fact of the human will, “lieber will noch der Mensch das Nichts wollen, als nicht wollen”, man would rather will nothingness than not will (III, 28); Albert: “l'homme préfère encore avoir la volonté du néant que de ne point vouloir du tout”. It is at this point that Nietzsche answers Schopenhauer. Schopenhauer believed that one could stop willing; Nietzsche shows that the denial of the will is still a willing, turned towards nothingness. Religion is not an error of the intellect, as in Spinoza, nor a projection of the essence, as in Feuerbach, nor the sigh of the oppressed, as in Marx; it is the form taken, for want of anything better, by the will to give suffering a meaning. As long as this will finds no other object, it will return to the ascetic ideal under new names.

    Here Nietzsche escapes Stirner's objection, and that is why I place him with Spinoza among those who do not refound a religion. He does not claim to have left it: he knows, and he says, that his own critique is made with Christian fire. This knowledge is not a weakness of his position, it is its strength: the atheist who believes himself free of all faith is the man of the marketplace who laughs at the madman; the one who knows where his fire comes from can at least choose what he does with it.

    There remains Jesus, who separates Nietzsche from all his supposed heirs, and who sets him head-on against the great biographer of the century. Renan's Life of Jesus (1863) had made Christ a genius and a hero, an incomparable man before whom humanity was to bow; the last page of the book invites the moderns, “éternels enfants”, eternal children, to bow “devant ces demi-dieux”, before these demigods. Renan left dogma while keeping the cult: Christ was no longer God, but he remained the object of an adoration, transferred from the supernatural to moral genius. This is a refoundation in the sense of this essay, and Nietzsche denounces it with a violence that is not merely a matter of temperament: he calls Renan, as we saw in Part Five, a buffoon in psychology, and says he remained a priest in his very bowels.

    The response, which is attested, targets the gesture that Feuerbach, Strauss and Renan had in common: leaving the supernatural while keeping the veneration. But Nietzsche is not content to unmask Renan: he proposes another Jesus. Der Antichrist (The Antichrist), written in 1888 and published in 1895, is one of the most violent books written against Christianity, but its violence is aimed at Paul and the Church, not at Jesus. For the vocabulary of the hero and the genius, Nietzsche substitutes a word in which one usually hears Dostoevsky, though Nietzsche does not name him here: “das Wort Idiot” (§ 29). He imagines this type in “eine Welt, wie aus einem russischen Romane” (§ 31). And he states: “im Grunde gab es nur einen Christen, und der starb am Kreuz”, in truth there was only one Christian, and he died on the cross; Albert: “au fond il n'y a eu qu'un seul chrétien, et il est mort sur la croix” (§ 39). Christianity is the work of Paul, that “Dysangelist”, bearer of bad tidings (§ 42), who made the death of Jesus into a doctrine of judgement and eternal life. Nietzsche, moreover, does not doubt for a moment that Jesus existed.

    Nietzsche's Jesus is an “idiot” in Dostoevsky's sense, that is, a being incapable of resistance, of resentment and of dogma, who lives in an inner kingdom and does not preach it. This portrait resembles, and not by chance, the silent Christ of “The Grand Inquisitor”, and the Church that betrayed him resembles the Inquisitor's. The comparison is constructed, since Nietzsche did not know the poem. Dostoevsky and Nietzsche nevertheless agree on one point: historical Christianity, the institution, dogma and authority, is the negation of the practice of Jesus. They part ways on what follows. Dostoevsky believes that this practice can still be lived, and that is Zosima; Nietzsche judges it beautiful and impossible, the symptom of a gentle decadence, and looks elsewhere.

    Where does he look? This is the question, too often forgotten behind the hammer, of Nietzschean spirituality. At the beginning of Book IV of The Gay Science (§ 276), for the new year 1882, Nietzsche makes a wish; Albert: “Je veux apprendre toujours davantage à considérer comme la beauté ce qu'il y a de nécessaire dans les choses”, I want to learn more and more to see as beautiful what is necessary in things, then: “Amor fati : que cela soit dorénavant mon amour. Je ne veux pas entrer en guerre contre la laideur. Je ne veux pas accuser, je ne veux même pas accuser les accusateurs”, Amor fati: let that be my love from now on. I do not want to wage war against ugliness. I do not want to accuse, I do not even want to accuse the accusers, and finally: “je veux, quelle que soit la circonstance, n'être une fois qu'affirmateur !”, I want, whatever the circumstance, some day to be only a Yes-sayer! Here one can measure the closeness to Spinoza and the distance from him. Like Spinoza, Nietzsche wants to love necessity; but where Spinoza loved it because he understood it, Nietzsche loves it without justifying it. Amor fati is not a knowledge, it is an exercise of the will, a discipline of affirmation. This is what Ivan refused in advance: to love fate is to love the child's tear as well.

    The other image of this spirituality is that of noon. In Götzen-Dämmerung, the chapter “Wie die "wahre Welt" endlich zur Fabel wurde” tells in six stages the history of an error, that of the true world opposed to the apparent world, from Plato to positivism. At the last stage, the abolition of the true world brings with it that of the apparent world, and Nietzsche punctuates: “Mittag; Augenblick des kürzesten Schattens; Ende des längsten Irrthums; Höhepunkt der Menschheit; INCIPIT ZARATHUSTRA”, noon; moment of the shortest shadow; end of the longest error; high point of humanity; here begins Zarathustra. The shortest shadow: this is the answer to § 108 of The Gay Science, where the shadow of God was to last for thousands of years. Noon is the hour when the shadows of God disappear, not because they have been fought, but because the sun is at its highest. Nietzschean spirituality is not a replacement religion; it is the attempt to live at the hour when there is no longer any world behind the world. Camus, as we shall see, will make of it the “pensée de midi”, the thought of noon.

    The objection awaiting Nietzsche will come from his most attentive reader. Nietzsche wanted to overturn Platonism: to put life above truth, becoming above being, value above fact. But to overturn a hierarchy is still to think in its terms. “Value”, the “will to power”, the “eternal return” are answers to the metaphysical question par excellence: what are beings as a whole? Nietzsche would then be, not the first philosopher to have left metaphysics, but the last metaphysician. One can also put to him a simpler objection, which Dostoevsky might have formulated: are not amor fati and the overman, in their turn, figures of Kirillov, the man who makes himself god? And is not Zarathustra, with his discourses, his disciples and his parables, one more religion? Nietzsche himself feared so, since he wrote, at the end of his conscious life, that there was “Nichts in mir von einem Religionsstifter”, nothing in him of a founder of religion, and: “Ich will keine „Gläubigen“”, I want no “believers”.

    These objections will come in the twentieth century, with Heidegger and Camus. In the meantime another response arises, which comes neither from the novelists nor from the philosophers: religion becomes an object of science, and this science, which many awaited as a weapon against it, will discover that the sacred does not let itself be dismissed so easily.

    In literature Gérard de Nerval, “Le Christ aux Oliviers” (1844) ; Algernon Charles Swinburne, “Hymn to Proserpine” (1866) ; Thomas Mann, Doktor Faustus (1947)

    Nerval set Jean Paul's dream in five sonnets, having read it in Madame de Staël. Christ, in the Garden of Olives, wakes his sleeping disciples: “Mes amis, savez-vous la nouvelle ? / J'ai touché de mon front à la voûte éternelle ; / Je suis sanglant, brisé, souffrant pour bien des jours ! // Frères, je vous trompais : Abîme ! abîme ! abîme ! / Le dieu manque à l'autel où je suis la victime… / Dieu n'est pas ! Dieu n'est plus !’ Mais ils dormaient toujours !”, My friends, do you know the news? / I have touched the eternal vault with my brow; / I am bloodied, broken, suffering for many days! // Brothers, I was deceiving you: Abyss! abyss! abyss! / The god is missing from the altar where I am the victim… / God is not! God is no more!’ But still they slept! In the fifth sonnet, Caesar questions Jupiter Ammon about “ce nouveau dieu qu'on impose à la terre”, this new god being imposed upon the earth, and “l'oracle invoqué pour jamais dut se taire”, the oracle invoked had to fall silent for ever.

    Why here: thirty-eight years before the madman of The Gay Science, a poet has the death of God announced by the son, in the public square, to men who are asleep; this is already § 125, with its atheists of the marketplace who do not understand what they have done, and with the same suspicion: the one who announces the news is the victim, and the altar remains.

    Swinburne, in the “Hymn to Proserpine”, gives voice to a pagan of Rome after the proclamation of Christianity as the religion of the state: “Thou hast conquered, O pale Galilean; the world has grown grey from thy breath.” This is “Dionysus against the Crucified” twenty years before Ecce Homo, and spoken from the side of the vanquished; Nietzsche read the English with contempt, and yet it was an Englishman who found the line. Thomas Mann, finally, gave Nietzsche the body of a musician, Adrian Leverkühn, who makes with the devil the pact of inspiration in exchange for love, composes a cantata that “takes back” the Ninth Symphony, and collapses into madness in 1930; the book was written while Germany was collapsing in its turn. The novel is the tragic version of the objection the essay raises: a genealogy that wants to refuse everything ends by making a pact with what it refused.

    Sources: Gérard de Nerval, “Le Christ aux Oliviers”, Les Chimères (1844; collection of 1854); Algernon Charles Swinburne, “Hymn to Proserpine”, Poems and Ballads (1866); Thomas Mann, Doktor Faustus (1947).

    Portrait: Friedrich Hermann Hartmann, Public domain

    Top of the part

    Part Eightthe sciences of religion and spiritual experience7 authors

    Background: The sociology of religion: from Comte to secularization theory · Hermeneutics: from Schleiermacher to Ricoeur · Positivism and scientism: science as a substitute religion in the nineteenth century

    Between 1900 and 1932, in barely a generation, religion changes its intellectual status. Until then, philosophers judged it: true or false, useful or harmful, alienating or consoling. From now on, scholars describe it. The sociologist asks what function it fulfils in the group, the psychologist from what experience it proceeds, the historian of religions what it has in common from one culture to another. This shift, neutral in appearance, is not neutral. For in ceasing to ask whether religion is true, the science of religion often discovers that it is necessary, and it rediscovers, under new names, the question of this essay.

    Two families take shape, and they answer each other. The first, sociological, is that of Durkheim and Weber: religion is a collective fact, bound up with the cohesion of groups or with the rationalization of conduct, and its apparent disappearance raises the question of what replaces it. The second, psychological and phenomenological, is that of James, Otto, Freud and Bergson: religion is first of all an individual experience, a feeling, an emotion, and the question becomes that of its value. It is in this second family that the notion of spirituality is born, in the modern sense: a religious experience distinguished from the institution, from dogma and sometimes from God himself. The two families cross constantly. Durkheim cites James; Otto discusses James and Schleiermacher; Freud replies to Romain Rolland, a reader of the Indian mystics; Bergson discusses Durkheim and cites James. Never has the dialogue between authors been so dense or so well attested.

    Durkheim1858-1917one does not leave the sacred

    Background: The sociology of religion: from Comte to secularization theory · The anthropology of religion: from Tylor to Girard · Rousseau's thought: state of nature, social contract, general will, Emile · Durkheim's sociology: the social fact, anomie, the Elementary Forms · From absolutism to the Revolution: the Church of France, the Enlightenment and the cult of the Supreme Being

    The Elementary Forms of Religious Life appeared in 1912. The book studies Australian totemism, but its true object is religion in general, grasped in what Durkheim takes to be its simplest form. Its thesis is stated from the introduction onward: “la religion est une chose éminemment sociale”, religion is an eminently social thing. Religious representations are collective representations that express collective realities; rites are ways of acting that arise within assembled groups.

    The definition of religion, given in the first chapter of Book I and quoted in the prologue, does not contain the word God, and that is its first bold stroke. The centre is no longer the divine, it is the sacred, and the sacred is defined by a separation: “Les choses sacrées sont celles que les interdits protègent et isolent ; les choses profanes, celles auxquelles ces interdits s'appliquent et qui doivent rester à distance des premières”, sacred things are those which prohibitions protect and isolate; profane things, those to which these prohibitions apply and which must remain at a distance from the former. Buddhism, a religion without a personal god, fits into this definition without difficulty; and, as we shall see, many things that do not call themselves religious fit into it too.

    Where does the sacred come from? From society itself, which in moments of gathering experiences itself as a force superior to individuals, and which projects this force onto an emblem: the totem, then the god. Book II says so bluntly: rites, by tightening the bonds that attach the faithful to their god, really tighten those that unite the individual to society, “puisque le dieu n'est que l'expression figurée de la société”, since the god is only the figurative expression of society. The god of the clan, Durkheim adds, can be nothing other than the clan itself, but hypostatized.

    One might think one was reading Feuerbach transposed from the species to the group. God was, for Feuerbach, only the projected human essence; he is, for Durkheim, only society represented. The comparison is constructed (Durkheim never cites Feuerbach), and the conclusions are opposed. Feuerbach wanted to repatriate the projected essence and dissolve religion into anthropology; Durkheim concludes that if religion expresses society, it is not an illusion, it is true in its own way. “Il n'y a donc pas, au fond, de religions qui soient fausses. Toutes sont vraies à leur façon : toutes répondent, quoique de manières différentes, à des conditions données de l'existence humaine”, there are thus, at bottom, no religions that are false. All are true in their own fashion: all answer, though in different ways, to given conditions of human existence. The believer is mistaken about the object of his worship; he is not mistaken about the force he feels. This is what makes Durkheim a formidable adversary of every critique of religion as error. Spinoza, Feuerbach, Onfray treat religion as a false representation; Durkheim answers them that religion is not first of all a representation.

    The conclusion of the book develops this point, drawing on the testimony of believers themselves and citing in a note William James's The Varieties of Religious Experience. Believers, Durkheim writes, feel that the true function of religion “n'est pas de nous faire penser, d'enrichir notre connaissance[…] mais de nous faire agir, de nous aider à vivre”, is not to make us think, to enrich our knowledge[…] but to make us act, to help us live. And: “Le fidèle qui a communié avec son dieu n'est pas seulement un homme qui voit des vérités nouvelles que l'incroyant ignore ; c'est un homme qui peut davantage”, the believer who has communed with his god is not merely a man who sees new truths of which the unbeliever is ignorant; he is a man who is capable of more. What is at stake is clear. If religion were a form of knowledge, science could replace it, and Durkheim indeed grants that, as regards knowledge, “la pensée scientifique n'est qu'une forme plus parfaite de la pensée religieuse”, scientific thought is only a more perfect form of religious thought. But if religion is a force for action, science does not replace it, for science always remains at a distance from action: faith, Durkheim writes, is “avant tout un élan à agir”, above all an impetus to act, and science, however far one pushes it, is never enough for that.

    The culmination of the demonstration is a historical fact that Durkheim invokes twice: the French Revolution. In Book II he writes that society's aptitude for setting itself up as a god or for creating gods “ne fut nulle part plus visible que pendant les premières années de la Révolution”, was nowhere more visible than during the first years of the Revolution, when things purely secular by nature, “la Patrie, la Liberté, la Raison”, the Fatherland, Liberty, Reason, were transformed into sacred things; and he goes on: “Une religion tendit d'elle-même à s'établir qui avait son dogme, ses symboles, ses autels et ses fêtes”, a religion tended of itself to become established, which had its dogma, its symbols, its altars and its feasts. This is, given by a sociologist in 1912, a demonstration of the thesis of this essay: the most radical exit from the Christian religion that France has known produced, almost immediately, a new religion. The “sacred games” that Nietzsche's madman announced, the Revolution had already invented.

    The general conclusion of the book draws from this a prophecy that answers Comte point by point, in attested fashion, and which must be quoted almost in full. Durkheim begins with an affirmation of principle: “Il y a donc dans la religion quelque chose d'éternel qui est destiné à survivre à tous les symboles particuliers dans lesquels la pensée religieuse s'est successivement enveloppée”, there is thus in religion something eternal that is destined to outlive all the particular symbols in which religious thought has successively wrapped itself. No society can do without reaffirming its collective sentiments in common, and he asks what essential difference separates an assembly of Christians celebrating the life of Christ from a gathering of citizens commemorating the institution of a new moral charter. Then comes the diagnosis of the present: “les anciens dieux vieillissent ou meurent, et d'autres ne sont pas nés. C'est ce qui a rendu vaine la tentative de Comte en vue d'organiser une religion avec de vieux souvenirs historiques, artificiellement réveillés : c'est de la vie elle-même, et non d'un passé mort que peut sortir un culte vivant”, the old gods are growing old or dying, and others are not yet born. This is what made vain Comte's attempt to organize a religion out of old historical memories, artificially revived: it is from life itself, and not from a dead past, that a living cult can emerge. And the prophecy: “Un jour viendra où nos sociétés connaîtront à nouveau des heures d'effervescence créatrice au cours desquelles de nouveaux idéaux surgiront”, a day will come when our societies will know once again hours of creative effervescence in the course of which new ideals will arise, and the conclusion: “Il n'y a pas d'évangiles qui soient immortels et il n'y a pas de raison de croire que l'humanité soit désormais incapable d'en concevoir de nouveaux”, there are no gospels that are immortal, and there is no reason to believe that humanity is henceforth incapable of conceiving new ones.

    Durkheim proves Comte right on substance and wrong on method. Comte was right to think that no society lives without a cult; he was wrong to believe that a cult can be manufactured by decree, with a calendar of great men. Religions are not invented, they arise from collective effervescence. The consequence admits of no appeal: one does not leave the sacred, one changes it. The exit from the Christian religion is not an exit from religion, it is an interregnum, a “phase de transition et de médiocrité morale”, a phase of transition and moral mediocrity, while we wait for the gods that are not yet born.

    I take Durkheim's position to be one of the two strongest objections to the very idea of an exit from religion, and a disturbing objection. It is strong because it is founded on an analysis of the social function of the sacred, and not on a preference; it is disturbing because the “hours of creative effervescence” that Durkheim longed for in 1912 did come, and they took the form of the political religions of the twentieth century, with their mass festivals, their dogmas, their symbols and their altars. Durkheim obviously did not wish for the totalitarianisms, but his theory gave no means of distinguishing a fruitful effervescence from a murderous one. This is the point at which Bergson, twenty years later, will attack him.

    In literature Émile Zola, Lourdes (1894) ; Louis-Ferdinand Céline, Journey to the End of the Night (1932)

    Lourdes follows a white train of the sick and the priest Pierre Froment, who has lost his faith and accompanies a paralysed childhood friend. Zola, who had made the journey in 1892 with his notebooks, describes the mechanics of the miracle as a contagion: the stories of cures passed around the carriage, the Magnificat; “Les habitants du village vont en foule attendre la miraculée sur la route, pendant que les cloches sonnent à la volée ; et, quand on la voit sauter lestement de la voiture, des cris, des sanglots de joie éclatent, on entonne le Magnificat”, the villagers go in a crowd to wait on the road for the woman miraculously healed, while the bells ring out in full peal; and when she is seen jumping nimbly down from the carriage, cries and sobs of joy burst out, and the Magnificat is struck up; and Pierre himself, in the heat of the carriage, feels that “la contagion agissait, il ne savait plus bien où s'arrêtaient le réel et le possible”, the contagion was at work, he no longer quite knew where the real ended and the possible began.

    Why here: this is the collective effervescence of The Elementary Forms described eighteen years before the book, by a novelist who observes it as an unbeliever and who undergoes its effect. The miracle of Lourdes is not, for Zola, an individual error; it is a social force, “la contagion du mystère”, the contagion of mystery, which produces the sacred through gathering, and from which even the faithless priest is not protected. Durkheim would say that Zola saw the god being born from the crowd, and that he was wrong to believe that one is cured of it by knowing it.

    Céline shows the same effervescence from the side where Durkheim did not look. Bardamu, at the beginning of Journey to the End of the Night, enlists on a whim behind a passing regiment, and discovers within a few weeks that the Fatherland is a sacred that demands the death of millions of men without anyone asking anything of it in return; he decides to be a coward, alone against the crowd, and the novel is the story of this desertion from all absolutes: war, the colony, the factory, medicine for the poor. The essay says that the French Revolution sacralizing the Fatherland is a demonstration of the thesis; Céline gives its counterproof: a man who refuses the effervescence of 1914, and who is left, precisely, with no sacred at all.

    Sources: Émile Zola, Lourdes, first day, IV and V (1894); Louis-Ferdinand Céline, Journey to the End of the Night (1932).

    Portrait: Auteur inconnu, Public domain

    Weber1864-1920disenchantment and the return of the gods

    Background: The sociology of religion: from Comte to secularization theory · The philosophy of Nietzsche: tragedy, genealogy, will to power, eternal return, overman · The Protestant Reformation: Luther, Calvin and the break-up of Christendom · Weber's sociology: ideal types, rationalization, charisma, value neutrality · Hebrews, James, Peter, John, Jude: the other letters

    Max Weber approaches religion from the other end. What interests him is not the cohesion of the group but the rationalization of conduct, and to express it he coined the most famous phrase in the sociology of religion, “Entzauberung der Welt”, the disenchantment of the world. The word appears in Die protestantische Ethik und der Geist des Kapitalismus (The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism), published in 1904-1905; the phrase only enters it in the revision of 1920. In the revised version, Weber speaks of “Jener große religionsgeschichtliche Prozeß der Entzauberung der Welt”, that great process in the history of religion which is the disenchantment of the world, which begins with ancient Jewish prophecy; and he adds that “Die radikale Entzauberung der Welt ließ einen anderen Weg als die innerweltliche Askese innerlich nicht zu”, the radical disenchantment of the world inwardly allowed no other path than asceticism within the world.

    “Disenchantment” is not first of all the loss of faith; it is the elimination of magic as a means of salvation. The enchanted world is one in which mysterious forces can be manipulated by rites, sacraments, formulas. Disenchantment is the work of the religions themselves: Hebrew prophecy, which condemns magic, then Calvinist Puritanism, which abolishes the sacraments as means of salvation and leaves the believer alone before a hidden God. Disenchantment is thus, as in Nietzsche, a self-suppression of the religious by the religious. The convergence with § 27 of the Genealogy is not fortuitous: Weber had read Nietzsche, and he alludes to him, as we shall see.

    The result of this process is described in a dark page of The Protestant Ethic. The Puritan ascetic wanted to work in a calling; we are compelled to do so. Concern for external goods was to lie on the shoulders of the saint like a light cloak, “Aber aus dem Mantel ließ das Verhängnis ein stahlhartes Gehäuse werden”, but fate turned the cloak into a casing as hard as steel. And Weber contemplates, for the “last men” of this cultural development, the truth of a terrible saying: “Fachmenschen ohne Geist, Genußmenschen ohne Herz: dies Nichts bildet sich ein, eine nie vorher erreichte Stufe des Menschentums erstiegen zu haben”, specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart: this nullity imagines it has climbed to a level of humanity never before attained. The “letzten Menschen”, in quotation marks in the text, are those of the prologue of Zarathustra; the allusion to Nietzsche is transparent, but Weber does not name him.

    But it is in the lecture Wissenschaft als Beruf (Science as a Vocation), delivered in Munich in 1917 and published in 1919, that Weber poses the question of our essay without circumlocution. He first defines disenchantment there: not that we know more than the savage about our conditions of life, but that we believe there are “prinzipiell keine geheimnisvollen unberechenbaren Mächte”, in principle no mysterious incalculable powers, and that everything can be mastered by calculation; “Das aber bedeutet: die Entzauberung der Welt”, but this means: the disenchantment of the world. Then he asks whether this process has a meaning, and it is Tolstoy he summons, reporting his answer: science is meaningless because it gives no answer to the only question important for us, “Was sollen wir tun? Wie sollen wir leben?”, what shall we do? how shall we live?

    Weber's answer is original: disenchantment has not abolished the gods. It has multiplied them. “Die alten vielen Götter, entzaubert und daher in Gestalt unpersönlicher Mächte, entsteigen ihren Gräbern, streben nach Gewalt über unser Leben und beginnen untereinander wieder ihren ewigen Kampf”, the many old gods, disenchanted and hence in the form of impersonal powers, rise from their graves, strive for power over our lives and begin again their eternal struggle with one another. The true, the beautiful, the good, the sacred, the nation, the class: so many ultimate values that can no longer be ranked by a higher authority. Life, Weber writes, knows only “den ewigen Kampf jener Götter miteinander”, the eternal struggle of those gods with one another, that is to say the impossibility of deciding between the ultimate standpoints on life, and hence the necessity of choosing.

    The gap with Durkheim is clear. Durkheim awaited new gods, born of a collective effervescence that would remake the unity of society. Weber observes that the gods have already returned, but in the plural, and that they will remake no unity. The exit from monotheism is not an exit from religion, it is a return to polytheism, a polytheism of values without temples or sacrifices, but not without victims. The thesis of our essay takes a new form here: one does not refound a religion, one refounds several, which wage war on one another.

    Weber offers no consolation. He distinguishes the man who remains in science, accepting that he will receive from it no answer to the question of meaning, from the one who returns to faith. The latter must accomplish what Weber calls, in quotation marks, the “„Opfer des Jntellekts"”, the sacrifice of the intellect; and he adds that the capacity to accomplish this virtuoso performance is “das entscheidende Merkmal des positiv religiösen Menschen”, the decisive mark of the positively religious man. Weber does not despise this sacrifice: he judges it morally superior to the false reconciliation of those who dare not choose, and he concludes: “Wer dies Schicksal der Zeit nicht männlich ertragen kann, dem muß man sagen: Er kehre lieber, schweigend, ohne die übliche öffentliche Renegatenreklame, sondern schlicht und einfach, in die weit und erbarmend geöffneten Arme der alten Kirchen zurück”, to whoever cannot bear this fate of the age like a man, one must say: let him rather return, in silence, without the usual public advertisement of the renegade, but plainly and simply, into the arms of the old Churches, opened wide and mercifully.

    What he refuses, on the other hand, is the third way, that of the prophets of the lectern and the manufacturers of religion. To those who await new prophets and new saviours, he recalls the song of the watchman of Edom, in the book of Isaiah: “Wächter, wie lang noch die Nacht? Der Wächter spricht: Es kommt der Morgen, aber noch ist es Nacht”, watchman, how much longer the night? The watchman says: the morning comes, but it is still night. Weber refuses both the return to the Church for himself and the manufacture of a new Church. He saw, like Nietzsche, that the exit from religion calls forth replacement religions, and he refused to give in to them, at the price of a solitude he does not hide.

    Weber's position is honest, and hard to live. It escapes the reproach that Stirner addressed to the pious atheists, since it refuses any hierarchy of values grounded in the last instance; but it pays for this refusal with a kind of tragic heroism, that “like a man” which today sounds like a pose. One may wonder whether the ethic of responsibility, with its austere grandeur, is not itself an inner-worldly asceticism: the last form of the Puritanism Weber had described, applied this time to the absence of God. Weber would then be the last Puritan, as Nietzsche saw in Schopenhauer the last Christian.

    In literature Daniel Defoe, Robinson Crusoe (1719) ; Franz Kafka, Das Schloß (1926) ; Friedrich Schiller, “Die Götter Griechenlands” (1788)

    Robinson, alone on his island, keeps his accounts with God like a merchant: he draws up two columns, “Evil” and “Good”, and sets each misfortune against its compensation: “I am cast upon a horrible, desolate island, void of all hope of recovery. But I am alive; and not drowned, as all my ship's company were.” Why here: Weber cited Defoe in The Protestant Ethic as the type of inner-worldly asceticism, and the page proves it: grace is verified by an account book, and the shipwrecked Puritan rebuilds in three weeks a business, a set of accounts and a calendar.

    Kafka wrote the steel casing without naming it. “Es war spät abends, als K. ankam. Das Dorf lag in tiefem Schnee. Vom Schloßberg war nichts zu sehen, Nebel und Finsternis umgaben ihn, auch nicht der schwächste Lichtschein deutete das große Schloß an”, it was late in the evening when K. arrived; the village lay deep in snow; nothing could be seen of the Castle hill, fog and darkness surrounded it, not even the faintest glimmer of light indicated the great Castle. And the mayor, further on, explains the administration that never makes mistakes: “Es gibt nur Kontrollbehörden. Freilich, sie sind nicht dazu bestimmt, Fehler im groben Wortsinn herauszufinden, denn Fehler kommen ja nicht vor”, there are only control authorities; of course, they are not meant to find errors in the crude sense of the word, for errors do not occur. The Castle is Weberian bureaucracy become destiny: “no mysterious incalculable powers”, Weber said, and yet a power that no one reaches, and whose files have taken the place of grace.

    Schiller, finally, had mourned in 1788 the gods of Greece driven out by the one God and by reason, and a nature “stripped of its gods” that now serves only the law of gravity: this is Entzauberung before the word, and the poem scandalized the Pietists because it already said that monotheism had begun the disenchantment that science completes. Weber will cite the “old gods” rising from their graves; Schiller had seen them go down into them.

    Sources: Daniel Defoe, Robinson Crusoe (1719); Franz Kafka, Das Schloß, ch. 1 and 5 (written in 1922, published in 1926); Friedrich Schiller, “Die Götter Griechenlands” (1788).

    Portrait: Ernst Gottmann, Public domain

    William James1842-1910religion as experience

    Background: The psychology and psychoanalysis of religion: from James to experimental psychology · Durkheim's sociology: the social fact, anomie, the Elementary Forms · The thought of William James: pragmatism, psychology, religious experience · Bergson's philosophy: duration, intuition, the élan vital, the Two Sources · Received revelations: spiritism, channeling, the Christ Letters · Quantum mysticism, synchronicity and the law of attraction

    With William James, the ground shifts. The Varieties of Religious Experience, published in 1902, brings together the Gifford Lectures delivered in Edinburgh in 1901-1902. The book is the founding charter of what would later be called spirituality.

    From the second lecture onward, James distances himself from religion as an institution: his definition, quoted in the prologue and presented as arbitrary, relates religion to the individual in his solitude, where Durkheim related it to the Church. For Durkheim, the religious individual is a product of the group; for James, the religious group is a fallout, a second-hand routine, of the original experiences of a few individuals. Durkheim cites James in his conclusion, but in order to turn the Jamesian definition against itself: the strength that faith gives comes from the collective. The dialogue is attested, and it bears on the point that concerns us: can religion exist without a community? If James is right, a spirituality without a Church is possible; if Durkheim is right, it is only a weakened reflection of a collective cult.

    James's method, a pragmatist one, takes shape against an adversary he calls “medical materialism”. He gives a cruel description of it: medical materialism “finishes up Saint Paul by calling his vision on the road to Damascus a discharging lesion of the occipital cortex, he being an epileptic”. James does not deny that religious states have physiological correlates; he denies that the origin of a state decides its value. He borrows his criterion from the Gospel, and from Jonathan Edwards: “By their fruits ye shall know them, not by their roots.”

    This answer holds, by anticipation, against all the genealogical critiques of our series. Feuerbach explained religion by projection, Marx by misery, Nietzsche by ressentiment, Freud will do so by infantile desire: to all of them James replies in advance that origin does not settle value. For Freud, who writes twenty-five years later, the confrontation is constructed: to say that belief in God arises from the need for paternal protection says nothing about the truth or the fruitfulness of that belief. Freud knows this, moreover, since he will carefully distinguish illusion from error.

    The most famous lectures of the book contrast two religious types, healthy souls and sick souls. James takes from Francis Newman the distinction between “the once‐born and the twice‐born”. The former live in a spontaneous optimism, without awareness of evil; the latter have passed through melancholy, the sense of sin or of the absurd, and have found peace only at the price of a second birth. James invites his audience to turn their backs on the “once‐born and their sky‐blue optimistic gospel” in order to listen to the “sick souls”. This typology illuminates our whole series: Ivan Karamazov is the sick soul par excellence, who refuses the sky-blue gospel of final harmony; Comte and Renan, with their religion of Humanity and of genius, are “once-born”. The question of spirituality then arises differently: it is not a matter of knowing whether one believes, but whether one has passed through evil.

    At the summit of religious experience, James places mysticism, to which he devotes the sixteenth and seventeenth lectures. He draws out four marks. The first is ineffability: the subject says at once that his state “defies expression”, that its quality must be directly experienced and cannot be imparted. The second is the noetic quality: although similar to feelings, mystical states seem to those who live them to be also states of knowledge, “states of insight into depths of truth unplumbed by the discursive intellect”. The third is transiency, the fourth passivity. This description, empirical and non-confessional, makes it possible to recognize a kinship between Eckhart, Teresa of Ávila, the Sufi mystics, the Vedantic texts and certain testimonies of natural or induced experience. It grounds the possibility of a comparative spirituality, detached from any particular Church.

    The conclusion is at once cautious and bold. James distinguishes what is common to all religious experiences from what he calls the “over‐beliefs” proper to each tradition. And what is common fits into a formula: “the fact that the conscious person is continuous with a wider self through which saving experiences come”; this content, he adds, seems to him “literally and objectively true as far as it goes”. And he ends by translating into schematic language what he calls the instinctive belief of mankind: “God is real since he produces real effects.”

    James's position is generous, and fragile. It is generous because it takes religious experience seriously without demanding adherence to a dogma; it makes it possible to think a spirituality that is neither a Church nor an illusion. It is fragile because the criterion of fruits says nothing about content: the fanatic too produces real effects. And it raises a question that James leaves open: is the “wider self” God, the unconscious, nature, society? Durkheim answered society, Freud will answer the unconscious, Bergson will answer the élan vital. James leaves the question to the over-beliefs, and that, at bottom, is the very definition of modern spirituality: an experience that is certain, whose object remains undetermined.

    In literature Walt Whitman, Leaves of Grass (1855) ; Leo Tolstoy, Confession (1882)

    James ranks Whitman among the once-born souls, those whose religion is a form of health; “Song of Myself” is its profession of faith: “Why should I wish to see God better than this day? / I see something of God each hour of the twenty-four, and each moment then, / In the faces of men and women I see God, and in my own face in the glass, / I find letters from God dropt in the street, and every one is sign'd by God's name, / And I leave them where they are.”

    Tolstoy is, for James, the exemplary sick soul and “twice-born”, and he quotes him at length: “I felt, says Tolstoy, that something had broken within me on which my life had always rested, that I had nothing left to hold on to, and that morally my life had stopped.[…] Behold me then, a man happy and in good health, hiding the rope in order not to hang myself to the rafters of the room where every night I went to sleep alone.”

    Why here: the two texts are the very material of the Varieties, and they give the reader what the essay identifies as James's strength and fragility. Whitman finds God in faces without asking anything of anyone; Tolstoy finds him again in the faith of the peasants after having wanted to die; the criterion of fruits absolves them both, and says nothing about what they saw. “By their fruits ye shall know them, not by their roots”: the letter in the street and the hidden rope are fruits; of the root, pragmatism knows nothing, and says so.

    Sources: Walt Whitman, “Song of Myself”, 48, Leaves of Grass (1855); Leo Tolstoy, Исповедь (Confession, 1882), quoted in the translation given by William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience, lectures VI-VII (1902).

    Portrait: Alice Boughton, Public domain

    Rudolf Otto1869-1937the numinous and the wholly other

    Background: Schleiermacher's thought: the Speeches, the Glaubenslehre, hermeneutics · Phenomenology: from Husserl to the theological turn · Rudolf Otto and The Idea of the Holy: the numinous, the wholly other, comparative mysticism · Jung's psychology: archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, Answer to Job · Levinas's philosophy: the other, the face, ethics as first philosophy, the Talmud

    Rudolf Otto's Das Heilige (The Idea of the Holy) appeared in 1917, the same year as Weber's lecture on science. The two texts answer each other without knowing it: Weber records disenchantment, Otto describes what, in the sacred, resists all rationalization. The book's subtitle, Über das Irrationale in der Idee des Göttlichen und sein Verhältnis zum Rationalen, on the irrational in the idea of the divine and its relation to the rational, says what matters.

    Otto, a Lutheran theologian at Marburg, begins with an operation on vocabulary. The word “heilig”, holy, has become a moral term in German: the holy is the perfectly good. Yet this moral sense overlays an older one, which religious languages preserve and which must be isolated. For this Otto coins a word: “Ich bilde hierfür zunächst das Wort: das Numinöse, (wenn man von omen ominös bilden kann, dann auch von numen numinös)”, for this I first form the word: the numinous (if one can form ominös from omen, one can also form numinös from numen). And he adds that since this category is “vollkommen sui generis”, entirely sui generis, it cannot be defined in the strict sense, but only “erörterbar”, open to being discussed and suggested.

    Hence a singular method, which makes Das Heilige a book of spirituality as much as of the history of religions. At the beginning of the third chapter, Otto invites his reader to recall a moment of strong religious emotion, and warns: “Wer das nicht kann oder solche Momente überhaupt nicht hat, ist gebeten, nicht weiter zu lesen”, whoever cannot do so, or has never had such moments at all, is asked to read no further. The sentence, famous and often mocked, is nonetheless consistent with the thesis: if the numinous is a primary datum, one can speak of it only to someone who has felt it, as one cannot speak of colours to the blind. The consequence is considerable. If Otto is right, every critique of religion that treats it as a theory or a function misses its object: the critic who has never felt the numinous does not know what he is talking about.

    The numinous is described through its effects on the soul. Otto reduces them to a formula that has become classic, “das mysterium tremendum”, the mystery that makes one tremble, to which is added the “fascinans”, what attracts and enraptures. The divine is at once terrifying and fascinating; it repels and it attracts. And above all it is the “ganz Andere”, the wholly other, something that does not belong to the circle of our reality. The numinous is not a being greater than the others; it is of another order.

    Otto answers Schleiermacher at the centre of chapter 3, and the response is attested. Otto acknowledges his predecessor's discovery: “Ein sehr bemerkenswertes Element solchen Erlebnisses hat Schleiermacher glücklich herausgegriffen: das Gefühl der „Abhängigkeit"”, Schleiermacher happily singled out a very remarkable element of such experience: the feeling of “dependence”. But he levels two reproaches at him. The first is that this feeling, as Schleiermacher describes it, is not sufficiently distinguished from other feelings of natural dependence, of powerlessness or inadequacy. Otto therefore proposes another name: “Ich suche nach einem Namen für die Sache und nenne es Kreaturgefühl, das Gefühl der Kreatur, die in ihrem eigenen Nichts versinkt und vergeht gegenüber dem, was über aller Kreatur ist”, I look for a name for the thing and call it creature-feeling, the feeling of the creature that sinks and vanishes into its own nothingness before that which is above all creatures. The second reproach goes deeper: Schleiermacher started from the feeling of self and inferred God from it, as a cause; Otto holds that the feeling of dependence is a secondary effect, which presupposes the primary experience of an external object. “Das Gefühl einer „schlechthinnigen Abhängigkeit" meiner hat zur Voraussetzung ein Gefühl einer „schlechthinnigen Unnahbarkeit" seiner”, the feeling of an “absolute dependence” of myself presupposes a feeling of an “absolute unapproachability” of him.

    The correction reaches far. Schleiermacher, by grounding religion in the feeling of the subject, had unwittingly opened the way to Feuerbach: if religion is a feeling of man, it can be traced back to man. Otto closes this way. Religious feeling is not a feeling of self; it is the response to an object that is not the self. The Feuerbachian critique of projection is thus circumvented, not by an argument but by a description: the numinous gives itself as what precedes the subject. I am not entirely convinced; but the question of leaving religion changes its nature. If the numinous is an a priori category of the mind, as the chapters that the book's table of contents entitles “Das Heilige als Kategorie a priori” assert, then one cannot leave it, any more than one can leave the category of causality. One can only let it lie fallow or cultivate it.

    Otto also answers, in an attested way, William James, whom he cites several times. He borrows testimonies of religious experience from James's book, but reproaches him for having collected them “ohne selber auf das „Irrationale", das in ihnen zittert, acht zu haben”, without himself paying attention to the “irrational” that trembles in them. James, a pragmatist, judges experience by its fruits; Otto, a phenomenologist before the term, wants to grasp it in its own content. And he targets Kant and religious humanism when he evokes, with visible irony, those who seek to build themselves a “Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der reinen Vernunft” or of “Humanität”. Kant's title and the humanism of Humanität, in which one may also hear Comte's religion of Humanity, which Otto does not name, are dismissed together to the shelf of religions without the numinous, that is, for Otto, of religions that are not religions.

    Otto's book is one of the strongest defences of the irreducibility of the religious that the twentieth century produced, and it is also, paradoxically, one of the main sources of spirituality without a Church. For if the numinous is a universal experience, prior to dogmas, it can be felt outside any confession, in nature, art, music, solitude. Otto did not want this, since he thought Christianity the highest form of the sacred; but his category escaped his theology. It nourished Eliade as much as contemporary spiritualities, and one may wonder whether Romain Rolland's “oceanic feeling”, to which Freud would reply, is not a variant of it. I believe so: it is a numinous without tremendum, a pure fascinans.

    In literature William Blake, “The Tyger” (1794) ; Herman Melville, Moby-Dick (1851) ; Rainer Maria Rilke, Duineser Elegien (1923)

    “Did He who made the lamb make thee?” The question of Blake's “Tyger”, in the Songs of Experience, has no answer in the poem: the same God forged gentleness and terror, and the poet does not ask why, he asks who, before a fire “burning bright, / In the forests of the night”.

    Why here: this is Otto's tremendum before the word, and without theology. The tiger is neither good nor evil, it is wholly other, and the adoration it arouses is neither moral nor rational; Blake wrote in six stanzas what Otto would reproach Kant and humanism for having forgotten.

    Melville, in chapter 42 of Moby-Dick, “The Whiteness of the Whale”, asks why whiteness appals: “is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows, a colourless, all-colour of atheism from which we shrink?” Otto's numinous is described here at its barest: a mysterium tremendum without content, in which the sacred and nothingness are indistinguishable, and of which the white whale is the idol. Rilke, finally, opens the Duino Elegies with a cry that has no addressee: “Wer, wenn ich schriee, hörte mich denn aus der Engel / Ordnungen?[…] Denn das Schöne ist nichts / als des Schrecklichen Anfang, den wir noch grade ertragen, / und wir bewundern es so, weil es gelassen verschmäht, / uns zu zerstören. Ein jeder Engel ist schrecklich”, who, if I cried out, would hear me among the orders of angels? for beauty is nothing but the beginning of terror, which we can still just bear, and we admire it so because it serenely disdains to destroy us. Every angel is terrible: the fascinans and the tremendum in the same line, in a poet who no longer had a God to whom to ascribe them.

    Sources: William Blake, “The Tyger”, Songs of Experience (1794) ; Herman Melville, Moby-Dick, ch. 42 (1851) ; Rainer Maria Rilke, Duineser Elegien, I (1923).

    Portrait: Photographe inconnu, Public domain

    Freud1856-1939illusion and the oceanic feeling

    Background: The psychology and psychoanalysis of religion: from James to experimental psychology · Exodus: Moses, the departure from Egypt, Sinai and the Law · Feuerbach's thought: The Essence of Christianity, the species, love, nature · Oedipus: the oracle, the Sphinx, the plague of Thebes · Freud's psychoanalysis: the unconscious, Oedipus, Totem and Taboo, illusion, Moses · Ricoeur's philosophy: symbol, suspicion, text, narrative · Jung's psychology: archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, Answer to Job · Narcissus and Echo: the reflection, the voice, narcissism

    Die Zukunft einer Illusion (The Future of an Illusion) appeared in 1927. It is the text that fulfils, in our series, the regime of illusion, and its concept must first be made precise, for Freud is subtler than his readers. An illusion is not an error. “Eine Illusion ist nicht dasselbe wie ein Irrtum, sie ist auch nicht notwendig ein Irrtum”, an illusion is not the same thing as an error, nor is it necessarily an error. What defines illusion is its motivation: “Wir heißen also einen Glauben eine Illusion, wenn sich in seiner Motivierung die Wunscherfüllung vordrängt, und sehen dabei von seinem Verhältnis zur Wirklichkeit ab”, we therefore call a belief an illusion when wish-fulfilment comes to the fore in its motivation, and in doing so we disregard its relation to reality.

    The distinction answers, without naming it, the reproach James addressed to medical materialism. Freud does not claim to have shown that God does not exist; he shows that belief in God would be held even if it were false, because it answers a wish. This is a new regime in our series, distinct from Spinozist error and Feuerbachian projection: religion is not false knowledge, it is a belief whose strength does not come from knowledge.

    What wish? That of the child in distress. Freud reconstructs the genesis: the adult, facing the overwhelming forces of nature and fate, finds himself again in a situation he has already known, that of the child before his parents, and above all before the father, “dessen Schutzes man aber auch sicher war”, of whose protection one was also sure. The man who discovers that he will always remain a child before the world “verleiht diesen die Züge der Vatergestalt, er schafft sich die Götter”, lends these powers the features of the father figure, he creates gods for himself. Das Unbehagen in der Kultur would restate the thesis in one sentence: “Ein ähnlich starkes Bedürfnis aus der Kindheit wie das nach dem Vaterschutz wüßte ich nicht anzugeben”, I could not point to any need arising from childhood as strong as the need for a father's protection. Religion then becomes, in a formula that caused a scandal, “die allgemein menschliche Zwangsneurose”, the universal obsessional neurosis of humanity, arising, like the child's, from the Oedipus complex.

    Like Feuerbach, Freud makes God a human production; but where Feuerbach saw in it the projected essence of man, to be reappropriated, Freud sees a remnant of childhood, to be outgrown. Freud does not cite Feuerbach in these two books; the confrontation, which is constructed, measures a reversal of value: Feuerbach's God was man writ large, Freud's is man writ small.

    The objection Freud raises against himself is the classic objection of the defenders of useful religion: can man live without religious consolation? Will the masses, deprived of God, not believe that everything is permitted? Freud answers with a pedagogy. Infantilism exists to be outgrown: “Der Mensch kann nicht ewig Kind bleiben, er muß endlich hinaus ins „feindliche Leben"”, man cannot remain a child for ever, he must at last go out into “hostile life”. And against consolation he sets another power, weaker but more tenacious: “die Stimme des Intellekts ist leise, aber sie ruht nicht, ehe sie sich Gehör geschafft hat”, the voice of the intellect is soft, but it does not rest until it has gained a hearing.

    To designate the power that is to replace religion, Freud writes: “Unser Gott Λόγος”, our god Logos; and he specifies in a note that he borrows the divine pair “Λόγος-᾽Ανάγκη”, Logos and Ananke, from the Dutch writer Multatuli. Further on, he concedes: “unser Gott Λόγος ist vielleicht nicht sehr allmächtig, kann nur einen kleinen Teil von dem erfüllen, was seine Vorgänger versprochen haben”, our god Logos is perhaps not very almighty, he can fulfil only a small part of what his predecessors promised. The vocabulary is deliberate, and Freud knows it to be ironic; it is no less symptomatic for that. To say what replaces God, Freud finds no other word than god: a more modest god, a more honest one, but a god all the same, with his “predecessors”. This is the thesis of our essay, pronounced by the man who most resolutely wanted to refute it.

    The book ends with a famous sentence, which is at once an act of faith and a profession of humility: “Nein, unsere Wissenschaft ist keine Illusion. Eine Illusion aber wäre es zu glauben, daß wir anderswoher bekommen könnten, was sie uns nicht geben kann”, no, our science is no illusion. But it would be an illusion to believe that we could get elsewhere what it cannot give us. Freud's own criterion can be turned against him. Is this confidence in science not itself a belief in which wish-fulfilment comes to the fore? Freud had asked himself the question in the book, asking whether our conviction that we can know reality through science has “eine bessere Begründung”, a better foundation. He answered yes, because science corrects itself; but Nietzsche, in § 344 of The Gay Science, had already shown that this will to truth was a faith: Freud's god Logos is the latest avatar of the God-as-truth of Plato and of Christianity.

    The response that matters here came from a friend, not a philosopher. Romain Rolland (1866-1944), who had received The Future of an Illusion, answered Freud in a letter of 5 December 1927. He reproached him for not having grasped the true source of religiosity, which according to him was neither dogma nor consolation, but a particular feeling, that of eternity, without perceptible bounds and as it were oceanic. Rolland was then preparing his books on Ramakrishna and Vivekananda, and he spoke as a connoisseur of Indian mysticism. Freud answered publicly, in the first chapter of Das Unbehagen in der Kultur (Civilization and Its Discontents, 1930). There he summarizes his friend's letter, which describes “ein Gefühl wie von etwas Unbegrenztem, Schrankenlosem, gleichsam „Ozeanischem"”, a feeling as of something unlimited, unbounded, as it were “oceanic”, and which he glosses: “Also ein Gefühl der unauflösbaren Verbundenheit, der Zusammengehörigkeit mit dem Ganzen der Außenwelt”, a feeling, then, of an indissoluble bond, of belonging to the whole of the external world. A note, added later, lifts the anonymity: since the publication of The Life of Ramakrishna and The Life of Vivekananda (1930), Freud no longer needs to conceal that the friend in question is Romain Rolland.

    Then Freud makes an admission of disarming honesty: “Ich selbst kann dies „ozeanische" Gefühl nicht in mir entdecken”, I myself cannot discover this “oceanic” feeling in myself. He does not deny that it exists in others; he explains it by a return to primary narcissism: the infant does not distinguish its ego from the world, and the oceanic feeling would be the survival, in certain adults, of this “primäre Ichgefühl” (I reproduce the inflected form of the text), primary ego-feeling, whose ideational contents would be precisely “die der Unbegrenztheit und der Verbundenheit mit dem All”, those of limitlessness and of a bond with the All. But he refuses to see in it the source of religion. The source remains, for him, infantile helplessness and longing for the father: “Für die religiösen Bedürfnisse scheint mir die Ableitung von der infantilen Hilflosigkeit und der durch sie geweckten Vatersehnsucht unabweisbar”, for religious needs, their derivation from infantile helplessness and the longing for the father it arouses seems to me irrefutable.

    With this exchange, the question of religion becomes that of spirituality. Rolland defends a religiosity without a personal God, without dogma, without a Church: a feeling of unity with the Whole, which he holds to be universal and finds as much in Spinoza as in the Indian mystics. Freud opposes to it a religion that is always that of the father, of protection and of guilt. Both are right, and that is why the debate matters. Freud is right about the instituted religions, whose infantile mainspring he describes accurately. Rolland is right to say that there is something else, an experience Spinoza would have recognized. But Freud is perhaps right a second time, and that is his real strength: the oceanic feeling, if it is a remnant of primary narcissism, is still a form of childhood, a way of denying the separation of the ego and the world. Spirituality without God would then be only a religion without a father, but not without a mother.

    Freud, moreover, encountered Dostoevsky, which closes a loop. In 1928 he contributed, as a preface to a German edition of the drafts of The Brothers Karamazov, an essay, “Dostojewski und die Vatertötung”, Dostoevsky and parricide, in which he reads the novel in the light of the murder of the father. The novel whose centre is a parricide, and whose question is the death of God, is thus read by the man who makes God the figure of the father. Freud saw what Dostoevsky had staged: that the death of God and the death of the father are one and the same affair, and that guilt does not die with them.

    In literature Franz Kafka, Brief an den Vater (1919) ; Hans Christian Andersen, “The Little Match Girl” (1845)
