    The Letter to His Father, which Kafka wrote in 1919 and never delivered, opens with a question: “Du hast mich letzthin einmal gefragt, warum ich behaupte, ich hätte Furcht vor Dir”, you asked me recently why I claim to be afraid of you; and it describes a father whose greatness fills the world: “Manchmal stelle ich mir die Erdkarte ausgespannt und Dich quer über sie hin ausgestreckt vor”, sometimes I imagine the map of the world spread out, and you stretched across it. The father's Judaism is described there as a nothing handed down with reproach, and the son says he found in the temple only a vague boredom and shame [summary].

    Why here: this is The Future of an Illusion written from the child's side, by a contemporary of Freud in Prague. The father is immense, inaccessible, arbitrary, and the religion that comes from him is a fear; Kafka does not need Freud to say so, and Freud did not need Kafka to find it. But the letter also shows the limit the essay points out: in Kafka the fear of the father produces no consolation, it produces The Trial; infantile helplessness explains the fear, it does not explain why one seeks refuge in it.

    Andersen's little match girl, barefoot in the snow on the last evening of the year, strikes her matches one by one and sees in each flame a stove, a roast goose, a Christmas tree, then her dead grandmother, the only person who ever loved her; she strikes them all to hold her back, and the grandmother carries her away “where there is neither cold, nor hunger, nor fear”; she is found dead in the morning, smiling. This is Freud's illusion in its exact definition, a belief commanded by a wish, and his reservation about Rolland in an image: what the child sees in the flame is not the father, it is the grandmother. Religion without a father, but not without a mother.

    Sources: Franz Kafka, Brief an den Vater (written 1919, published 1952) ; Hans Christian Andersen, “Den lille Pige med Svovlstikkerne” (1845).

    Portrait: Max Halberstadt, Public domain

    Bergson1859-1941static religion and dynamic religion

    Background: Christian mysticism: from Dionysius to John of the Cross and quietism · Durkheim's sociology: the social fact, anomie, the Elementary Forms · Bergson's philosophy: duration, intuition, the élan vital, the Two Sources

    The Two Sources of Morality and Religion, published in 1932, is Bergson's last great book, and probably the work of interwar French philosophy that poses our question most directly. It presents itself as a response both to Durkheim, whom it discusses explicitly, and to James, whom it cites and whose intuition it extends. It attempts to hold the two families together, the sociological and the mystical, by tracing them to two distinct sources.

    Bergson begins, in the second chapter, with an observation that could be Spinoza's or Onfray's: “Le spectacle de ce que furent les religions, et de ce que certaines sont encore, est bien humiliant pour l'intelligence humaine. Quel tissu d'aberrations !”, the spectacle of what religions were, and of what some still are, is truly humiliating for human intelligence. What a tissue of aberrations! But he draws from it a question that neither Spinoza nor Onfray asks with the same rigour: how could an intelligent being have believed such things, and why has he never been cured of them? The answer is not ignorance, since humanity clings to them all the more as experience and reasoning contradict them. It is a function. “La vérité est que la religion, étant coextensive à notre espèce, doit tenir à notre structure”, the truth is that religion, being coextensive with our species, must pertain to our structure.

    Bergson calls this function fabulatory. Intelligence, which is proper to man, has a dissolving power: it shows the individual that he could prefer his own interest to that of the group, and it also reveals to him that he will die. Nature, which produced intelligence, had to produce a counterweight at the same time. This counterweight is religious fables: “la religion est donc une réaction défensive de la nature contre le pouvoir dissolvant de l'intelligence”, religion is thus a defensive reaction of nature against the dissolving power of intelligence. And the fabulating function did not first serve the novel or the theatre: “la religion était la raison d'être de la fonction fabulatrice”, religion was the raison d'être of the fabulating function. The “static religion” thus produced “attache l'homme à la vie, et par conséquent l'individu à la société, en lui racontant des histoires comparables à celles dont on berce les enfants”, binds man to life, and consequently the individual to society, by telling him stories comparable to those with which children are lulled to sleep.

    The kinship with Durkheim is manifest, and Bergson acknowledges it. He cites the Durkheimian thesis that religious representations are the work of the collective mind, and he accepts it in part: “Nous admettrons volontiers, quant à nous, l'existence de représentations collectives, déposées dans les institutions, le langage et les mœurs”, for our part we shall readily admit the existence of collective representations, deposited in institutions, language and customs. But he rejects its consequence. For Durkheim, society is the sole source of the sacred. For Bergson, it is only one source, and the least lofty. Static religion is that of closed societies, which preserve themselves by defending themselves; it is infra-intellectual, natural, and it turns on the spot. The book's first chapter had already contrasted the closed soul, which turns in a circle with its society, and the open soul, whose love extends to the whole of humanity, “aux animaux, aux plantes, à toute la nature”, to animals, to plants, to all of nature. Between the nation and humanity, Bergson writes, lies the whole distance from the finite to the indefinite: no gradual extension of social solidarity leads from one to the other. A leap is needed.

    This leap, the mystics accomplished. “Dynamic religion”, inward and supra-intellectual, is born of a few exceptional individuals who regained contact with the creative impetus of life. Bergson defines mysticism precisely: “l'aboutissement du mysticisme est une prise de contact, et par conséquent une coïncidence partielle, avec l'effort créateur que manifeste la vie. Cet effort est de Dieu, si ce n'est pas Dieu lui-même”, the culmination of mysticism is a contact, and consequently a partial coincidence, with the creative effort that life manifests. This effort is of God, if it is not God himself. And what the mystics say, when one tries to put it in a formula, is simple: “Dieu est amour, et il est objet d'amour : tout l'apport du mysticisme est là”, God is love, and he is the object of love: the whole contribution of mysticism lies there. Bergson adds that the mystics unanimously testify “que Dieu a besoin de nous, comme nous avons besoin de Dieu”, that God needs us, as we need God, and he draws from this a vision of creation as “une entreprise de Dieu pour créer des créateurs”, an undertaking of God to create creators.

    Bergson's thesis matters because it separates two things that most of our authors confused. There is static religion, produced by society to defend itself; it is fabulating, and it deserves all the criticisms that have been addressed to it, from Spinoza to Freud. And there is mysticism, which is not a religion but the living source of which religions are the cooling. Bergson says it in an image: “Nous nous représentons donc la religion comme la cristallisation, opérée par un refroidissement savant, de ce que le mysticisme vint déposer, brûlant, dans l'âme de l'humanité”, we therefore picture religion as the crystallization, brought about by a skilful cooling, of what mysticism deposited, burning hot, in the soul of humanity. One can then leave static religion, and one must, without leaving mysticism. Leaving religion does not call for another religion; it calls for a return to the source.

    Bergson here answers, in a constructed way, all the authors of our series. To Durkheim he answers that society explains only static religion, and does not account for the love of humanity. To Freud, whom he does not cite but knows, he answers that the fabulating function is indeed a defence, but does not exhaust the religious. To Nietzsche he answers that the “overman” already exists, and that his name is the mystic: Bergson cites the sages of Greece, the prophets of Israel, the Arahants of Buddhism and the saints of Christianity as the exceptional men in whom open morality has been embodied. To William James, finally, he pays explicit tribute, quoting at length his testimony on the San Francisco earthquake, and he extends his intuition by giving the “wider self” a name, the creative effort of life.

    The last pages carry the question onto the terrain of technical civilization, with a strange topicality. Bergson asserts there that “la mystique appelle la mécanique”, mysticism calls for mechanics, because man will detach himself from matter only by leaning on it; but he adds that the converse is true: “le corps agrandi attend un supplément d'âme, et que la mécanique exigerait une mystique”, the enlarged body awaits a supplement of soul, and mechanics would require a mysticism. The book ends with this sentence: “L'humanité gémit, à demi écrasée sous le poids des progrès qu'elle a faits. Elle ne sait pas assez que son avenir dépend d'elle”, humanity groans, half crushed beneath the weight of the progress it has made. It does not know well enough that its future depends on itself; and it is for humanity to decide whether it wants to make the effort required “pour que s'accomplisse, jusque sur notre planète réfractaire, la fonction essentielle de l'univers, qui est une machine à faire des dieux”, so that the essential function of the universe, which is a machine for making gods, may be fulfilled, even on our refractory planet.

    This ambiguous sentence sums up, in my view, the whole difficulty of this part. A machine for making gods: Bergson means that the universe tends to produce beings capable of creation and love, mystics, divine men. But one can also hear the echo of the question of Nietzsche's madman, “must we not ourselves become gods?”, and the echo of Kirillov. Bergson believes he escapes the divinization of man because the god that is made in us is the creative impetus and not the self. I believe he does escape it, but narrowly, and at the price of a metaphysics of life that few readers today are prepared to follow. The fact remains that Bergson gives systematic form to the distinction on which the rest of this essay will live: closed religion, which one can and must leave, and open spirituality, which one does not leave because it is not an institution but a movement.

    In literature Marcel Proust, Swann's Way (1913) ; Charles Péguy, The Portal of the Mystery of Hope (1911)

    Proust's madeleine is the experience of duration that Bergson described in concepts, and the narrator draws from it the conclusion philosophy does not dare to draw: “toutes les fleurs de notre jardin et celles du parc de M. Swann, et les nymphéas de la Vivonne, et les bonnes gens du village et leurs petits logis et l'église et tout Combray et ses environs, tout cela qui prend forme et solidité, est sorti, ville et jardins, de ma tasse de thé”, all the flowers in our garden and those in M. Swann's park, and the water lilies of the Vivonne, and the good folk of the village and their little dwellings and the church and all of Combray and its surroundings, all of this, taking shape and solidity, sprang, town and gardens alike, from my cup of tea.

    Why here: Proust always denied being a Bergsonian, and yet he is one on the point that matters for the essay: the past is not abolished, it endures, and an exercise of attention, here an involuntary one, restores it whole. This is dynamic religion without mysticism and without God, the impetus that creates out of what seemed dead; and it is also the limit the essay notes in Bergson, a metaphysics of life that few readers follow to the end, but that every reader of Proust has felt once.

    Péguy, Bergson's pupil, put the impetus into a little girl: “La petite espérance s'avance entre ses deux grandes sœurs et on ne prend pas seulement garde à elle”, little hope walks forward between her two big sisters and no one even notices her, faith and charity, and “Cette petite espérance qui n'a l'air de rien du tout”, this little hope who looks like nothing at all, is the one who leads the other two. The Portal is a Christian poem, written the same year as The Perception of Change; it expresses Bergson's dynamic religion twenty years before The Two Sources, from the believer's side, and with the same thesis: what lives in a religion is not what is fixed but what moves forward, and that cannot be instituted.

    Sources: Marcel Proust, Du côté de chez Swann, “Combray”, I (1913) ; Charles Péguy, Le Porche du mystère de la deuxième vertu (1911).

    Portrait: Henri Manuel, Public domain

    Ricoeur1913-2005critique passed through

    Background: The thought of Marx: historical materialism, alienation, ideology, fetishism · Hermeneutics: from Schleiermacher to Ricoeur · Freud's psychoanalysis: the unconscious, Oedipus, Totem and Taboo, illusion, Moses · Ricoeur's philosophy: symbol, suspicion, text, narrative

    Paul Ricoeur comes last, by design: he is the first reader of this part. The gesture that made him famous consists in looking together at three authors we have met separately, Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, and giving them a common name. Ricoeur places them in a single school, the school of suspicion, and tradition has retained, on the basis of his book, the phrase “maîtres du soupçon” (masters of suspicion). The book is De l'interprétation. Essai sur Freud, published by Seuil in 1965. His biographical position explains nothing but situates everything: Ricoeur is a Protestant, trained in the French Reformed tradition and a reader of Barth; his five years of captivity in Pomerania are years of reading, of Jaspers and of Husserl; he would later write the preface to the French translation of Bultmann, and the “Préface à Bultmann” (Preface to Bultmann) is reprinted in Le Conflit des interprétations (1969). A believer, then, who chose to read the hardest atheists not as adversaries to be refuted, but as masters whose school must be followed.

    What do these three masters do? All three practise what Ricoeur calls interpretation as an exercise of suspicion. Their common gesture is to doubt, no longer the thing, as Descartes did, but consciousness itself: what consciousness believes it sees, believes, wills, is not what is at play within it. Religion, for Marx, expresses the world upside down; for Nietzsche, it expresses weakness under the name of virtue; for Freud, it expresses the child's desire under the name of Providence. In all three cases, the manifest meaning is the effect of a latent meaning that must be deciphered, and understanding goes by way of a detour. Ricoeur calls this common discipline a “science médiate du sens” (mediate science of meaning), which he opposes to the “conscience immédiate du sens” (immediate consciousness of meaning).

    This grouping puts our own map to the test. We have distinguished three regimes where Ricoeur sees one school: the symptom in Marx, value in Nietzsche, illusion in Freud. Is he right to merge them? I believe he is right as to method and wrong as to object. As to method, the unity is real: all three treat belief as a doctored text whose hidden author must be found, the class, the weak will, the infantile desire. As to object, the distinction holds: Marx does not want to cure the individual, he wants to change the world that needs opium; Freud does not want to change the world, he wants the individual to stop being a child; Nietzsche wants neither, he wants new values to be created. Ricoeur's grouping shows what the three share against religion; our regimes show what separates them in the manner of leaving it, and that is where refoundation is decided.

    But the heart of the book is a conflict. Opposite the hermeneutics of suspicion, he sets another hermeneutics, that of the restoration of meaning, whose model he finds in the phenomenology of religion, in Van der Leeuw and in Eliade: an interpretation that listens to the symbol instead of unmasking it, and that lets itself be told by it something it did not know. Ricoeur thus describes two opposed dispositions, a willingness to listen and a willingness to suspect. Both are legitimate, and neither can absorb the other. The sentence that condenses this conflict says that we are “ces hommes qui n'ont pas fini de faire mourir les idoles et qui commencent à peine d'entendre les symboles”, those men who have not finished putting the idols to death and who are barely beginning to hear the symbols.

    This is where the notion that made Ricoeur's fortune comes in, though he rarely uses it: the “seconde naïveté” (second naïveté). It appears for the first time at the end of La Symbolique du mal (1960), in a concluding chapter whose title is already a thesis, “Le symbole donne à penser” (the symbol gives rise to thought). The starting diagnosis is the forgetting of the sacred peculiar to modernity: the first naïveté, that of the believer who lives in the symbol without reflecting on it, has become impossible for us. But Ricoeur refuses to conclude that the symbol is dead. Not having consulted the French text of 1960, I quote the English translation by Emerson Buchanan: “we can, we modern men, aim at a second naïveté in and through criticism”, and it is “by interpreting that we can hear again”; “beyond the desert of criticism, we wish to be called again”; and this second naïveté is meant to be the postcritical equivalent of the precritical hierophany.

    What Ricoeur proposes, then, is a faith that has passed through critique, not a faith that has avoided it. The distinction bears directly on our question. Kierkegaard too wanted a faith that would owe nothing to historical criticism; Barth too wanted a faith that would not be a religion. But both placed themselves out of reach of suspicion, by the leap or by Revelation. Ricoeur agrees to remain exposed to it. He does not say to Freud: you are wrong about religion. He says to him: you are right about one religion, that of the protecting father and the judge, and it is precisely this religion that must die. In the lecture “Religion, athéisme, foi” (Religion, atheism, faith), reprinted in Le Conflit des interprétations, he distinguishes, I summarize without quoting, two cores of religion that modern atheism rightly destroys: the god of accusation, whom Nietzsche unmasked as an invention of ressentiment, and the god of consolation, whom Freud unmasked as a desire for protection. What remains after this double destruction, if anything remains, is neither the moral God nor the providential God. It is a word one listens to, a call that promises nothing.

    Freud defined illusion by its motivation, the belief in which the fulfilment of a wish comes to the fore, and he loyally added that this does not settle its truth. Ricoeur takes Freud at his word: if the Freudian critique bears on the motivation of belief and not on its object, it does not close the question of the object, it purifies it. A belief that has renounced the protecting father, that has mourned consolation, escapes Freudian suspicion by definition, since the infantile wish no longer comes to the fore in it. Freud showed that the religion of the child is an illusion; he did not show, and did not claim to show, that there is no other. Ricoeur's reading of Freud is attested; the argument I draw from it here is a reconstruction, but it rests on the very letter of The Future of an Illusion and turns Freud's own loyalty against him.

    The same reply can be made to the regime of the symptom. Marx said that religion is the protest against real distress at the same time as its expression; Ricoeur hears in the second half of the sentence what Marxism wanted to forget there. If religion is also a protest, then its critique cannot consist solely in dissolving it; it must also hear what it protests against. The hermeneutics of suspicion, pushed to the end, destroys the content of the symbol; the hermeneutics of listening gathers what the symbol said and suspicion could not hear. Our essay has practised this double gesture from the beginning without naming it: we have dismantled the refoundations, but we have also taken seriously what each of them was seeking.

    There is, however, an objection, and it is a strong one. Is the second naïveté not a first naïveté that gives itself a good conscience? One passes through critique, says Ricoeur; but one comes out of it with the same symbols, fault, defilement, exile, promise, and reinvests them with a new meaning. Is this not what Hegel did, whom we reproached for translating religion into concept the better to preserve it? Is it not what Strauss did, who discovered in myth a truth of humanity? Ricoeur knows the objection, since he knows Hegel closely. His reply, I believe, comes down to one word: he does not claim that the second naïveté is a form of knowledge. Hegel completed religion in absolute knowledge; Ricoeur leaves it incomplete in interpretation, which has no end. The symbol gives rise to thought; it does not give rise to knowledge. And this difference is the one that separates, in our essay, refoundation from the exception.

    For that is indeed where Ricoeur must be classed. He does not leave religion: he remained a believer, and he never hid that his faith preceded his philosophy, although he always took care not to bring it in as an argument. But neither does he refound a religion in the sense of the criterion. He installs no absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual could be demanded; on the contrary, he installs the individual in an infinite task of interpretation in which no absolute lets itself be possessed. Having entered the school of his adversaries, he never entirely left it: a rare position, which I believe more honest than that of most apologists as well as most critics. It has its price, which is instability: the second naïveté is always in danger of falling back into the first, or of dissolving into suspicion. Ricoeur accepts this, and this acceptance makes him, at the end of this part, a fair interlocutor of the three masters he named.

    Ricoeur leaves a question for what follows. If the critique of religion can be passed through, if listening is possible after suspicion, then the exit from religion is not an event, but a path that can be travelled in both directions. Heidegger, Barth, Weil, Levinas, Marion all attempted, each in his or her own way, this return beyond critique. The question will each time be the same: is this return a second naïveté that knows what it is doing, or a refoundation that forgets it?

    In literature Charles Baudelaire, “Correspondances” (1857) ; Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, Le Petit Prince (1943)

    “La Nature est un temple où de vivants piliers / Laissent parfois sortir de confuses paroles ; / L'homme y passe à travers des forêts de symboles / Qui l'observent avec des regards familiers”: Nature is a temple where living pillars sometimes let out confused words; man passes through it across forests of symbols that watch him with familiar looks. Why here: Baudelaire's sonnet says in four lines what Ricoeur, after Eliade, calls the world of the symbol, and what he reproaches the masters of suspicion for having ceased to hear. The temple has no priest, the words are confused, and the symbols watch whoever passes through them: the symbol gives rise to thought, and it does not need to be believed in order to speak. Baudelaire, who was no untroubled believer, is the poet of the second naïveté, the one that knows the pillars are trees and hears them all the same.

    The fox in Le Petit Prince teaches the child that rites are necessary, because they make one day different from the others, and that one sees rightly only with the heart, what is essential being invisible to the eyes; the child thus learns that his rose, like five thousand others, is unique because he has tamed it. This is Ricoeur's lesson reduced to a fable: rite and symbol are not errors about the world, they are what makes a world habitable, and one can know this without ceasing to practise them. The tale has become a secular Scripture, read in schools and at funerals; the essay would say that it is a second naïveté that has found its book.

    Sources: Charles Baudelaire, “Correspondances”, Les Fleurs du mal, IV (1857) ; Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, Le Petit Prince, ch. XXI (1943).

    Portrait: Jmendrik, CC0

    Assessment of Part Eight: suspicion and experience

    Background: Weber's sociology: ideal types, rationalization, charisma, value neutrality

    The landscape has changed profoundly. The sciences of religion have not confirmed the expectation of the Enlightenment, which hoped to see religion dissolve under the light of knowledge. Durkheim showed that one does not leave the sacred; Weber, that the gods return in the plural; Freud, that God is replaced by a god Logos; Otto, that the numinous is a category of the mind; James and Bergson, that mystical experience outlives all Churches; and Ricoeur gave this landscape its name, the school of suspicion, by showing that one can pass through it without going back or settling in it. The debate no longer bears on the existence of God, but on two new questions: that of the social function of the sacred, which the political religions of the twentieth century will make tragic, and that of spiritual experience, which theology and philosophy will each take up in its own way. These sciences make inevitable a question that Part Nine takes up in its own right: why do people believe? Part Ten will then open in this double context; Camus, in particular, will measure there what the divinization of history costs, akin to that sacralization of society which Durkheim had described without fearing it. The twentieth century thus begins with the discovery that man without God is not man without religion.

    Top of the part

    Part Ninewhy do people believe? Need, function, cognition9 authors

    Background: The psychology and psychoanalysis of religion: from James to experimental psychology · The anthropology of religion: from Tylor to Girard · The cognitive science of religion: why gods are easy to think · Analytic philosophy of religion: from the problem of evil to Reformed epistemology · René Girard's mimetic theory

    Until now, the essay has asked how one leaves religion, almost never why one enters it; and yet this is the question the reader asks first: why does the human being need religion, or, when he no longer wants it, spirituality? The word “need” already contains the answer. To speak of need is to suppose a constant lack, inscribed in human nature, which religion fills and which would come back to claim its due if religion were abolished: that is Durkheim's thesis, and it is what the thesis of this essay calls into question. I shall therefore speak rather of a disposition: something in the mind, in existence and in common life makes religious belief easy, frequent, sometimes almost irresistible, and the task is to take its springs apart without deciding in advance that they call for a god. The philosophers we have met drew a first map of them: fear, desire, lament, helplessness, society, the fabulating function, the need for meaning. Two formulas set the tone. Feuerbach: “Der Wunsch ist der Ursprung, ist das Wesen selbst der Religion”, the wish is the origin, it is the very essence of religion. Freud: religious ideas were born “aus dem Bedürfnis, die menschliche Hilflosigkeit erträglich zu machen”, from the need to make human helplessness bearable. The human sciences of the twentieth century put the question again with fieldwork, experiments and figures: Tylor and Frazer looked for the origin of religion in an error of reasoning, Malinowski in anxiety before what one does not master, Jung in a natural function of the psyche, Girard in violence and sacrifice; then will come the psychology of death, the sociology of meaning and of memory, the cognitive sciences and the comparative surveys, which a constructed debate will bring face to face.

    Tylor and Frazer1832-1917; 1854-1941religion as primitive philosophy

    Background: The anthropology of religion: from Tylor to Girard · The cognitive science of religion: why gods are easy to think · The philosophy of Hume: empiricism, causation, miracles, the natural history of religion · The mysteries and Orphism: Eleusis, Orpheus, Cybele, Isis, Mithras · Tylor and Frazer: animism, survivals, The Golden Bough · Pascal Boyer: religion explained by cognition

    The anthropology of religion was born in England, in the last third of the nineteenth century, from an ambition that resembles that of the Scottish Enlightenment: to make belief an object of natural history, going back from its most complex forms to its simplest. Edward Burnett Tylor, a Quaker by upbringing, without a university degree, a traveller in Mexico and then the first holder of a chair of anthropology at Oxford, published in 1871 the two volumes of Primitive Culture. The book bears as its epigraph a French sentence by Président de Brosses, the inventor of the word “fetishism”: “ce n'est pas dans les possibilités, c'est dans l'homme même qu'il faut étudier l'homme”, it is not in possibilities, it is in man himself that man must be studied. A whole programme: not to speculate on what man ought to have believed, but to look at what he believes.

    Tylor starts from a difficulty of definition, and his solution would weigh on the whole of the following century. To require, before speaking of religion, belief in a supreme god, in a judgement after death, in idols or sacrifices, is to exclude many peoples from it and to confuse it with some of its developments. One must therefore, says Tylor, posit “as a minimum definition of Religion, the belief in Spiritual Beings”. This belief he calls animism, and he reconstructs its genesis by a line of reasoning that Durkheim would summarize. The man of the origins dreams; at night he sees himself travelling far away, conversing with the absent or the dead; he concludes that there is in him a double, a soul, capable of leaving the body. From the human soul one passes to the souls of animals and things, from these to spirits, from spirits to gods. Religion is first of all a philosophy: a theory, false but rational, worked out by a savage philosopher to explain sleep, dreams, sickness and death.

    Tylor accepts both consequences of this thesis. The first is that there is no people without religion, if one adopts the minimum definition: belief in spirits is universal, which makes religion a trait of humanity and not an invention of priests. The second is that this primitive philosophy is an error, and that its remains live on in modern societies in the form of “survivals” which must be identified and rooted out. Tylor says so bluntly on the last page of his book: ethnography has the office, harsher and at times painful, of exposing “the remains of crude old culture which have passed into harmful superstition” and marking them out for destruction; that is why “the science of culture is essentially a reformer's science”. One recognizes the first regime of this essay, the regime of error, in its evolutionist version: religion is true as a universal fact, false as a theory, and progress dissolves it.

    James George Frazer, more than twenty years younger, gave this school its monument and its public. The Golden Bough appeared in two volumes in 1890 and swelled to twelve in the third edition (1906-1915), before the abridgement of 1922 that would make it a bedside book for generations of writers. Frazer starts there from a riddle of detail, the priest of Diana at Nemi who attains his office only by killing his predecessor, and draws from it a fresco of human thought in three ages. In the first, man believes he can act on nature through magic, which rests on two laws of the association of ideas, similarity and contiguity. Frazer gives its most famous formula: legitimately applied, these laws produce science; illegitimately applied, they produce magic, “the bastard sister of science”. In the second age, man discovers that nature does not obey him, and he turns to powers that must be prayed to. Frazer then defines religion as “a propitiation or conciliation of powers superior to man which are believed to direct and control the course of nature and of human life”. In the third age, science recovers, against religion, the magical idea of a regular order of nature, but this time founded on observation. The book closes on this movement of thought, which goes, “on the whole”, “from magic through religion to science”.

    Two features concern this essay directly. Frazer is, first, cautious about the last word. The laws of nature are themselves only hypotheses, and “in the last analysis magic, religion, and science are nothing but theories of thought”, so that science may one day be superseded by a more perfect hypothesis. Next, and above all, The Golden Bough is an immense repertory of sacrificed kings, of gods who die and are reborn, and of public scapegoats, human or animal, laden with the ills of the community before being driven out or killed. Frazer does not say in so many words that the Passion of Christ belongs to this series, but the whole book suggests it, and his readers understood it so: it is one of the sources of the mythicist thesis examined in connection with the birth of Christianity. Girard would take up this repertory and reverse its meaning.

    This anthropology was refuted from three sides, and each refutation opens a path that what follows will take. Durkheim, first, sets against it an argument that I believe is decisive against intellectualism. If the animist theory were true, he writes, one would have to admit that religious beliefs are “représentations hallucinatoires, sans aucun fondement objectif”, hallucinatory representations without any objective foundation, born of “une sorte de délire qui le saisit régulièrement chaque jour”, a sort of delirium that seizes him regularly every day, and one could not understand how such an aberration has run through the whole of human history. An institution so universal and so lasting cannot rest on a mere error; it must answer to something real, which Durkheim finds in society. Wittgenstein, next, reproaches Frazer for making his “savages” into bad physicists (Part Ten). Malinowski, finally, would reproach the two Englishmen for having studied religion in their libraries, and would show in the field that magic is not a false science but a technique for dealing with anxiety.

    Tylor and Frazer's answer is the simplest: people believe because they are mistaken, and they will stop believing when they know. It is the answer of the Enlightenment carried into ethnography, with the same weakness as in d'Holbach: it explains why a belief is born, not why it lasts when one knows it to be false. Tylor nevertheless left a gain that no one has undone: belief in invisible beings is universal. The cognitive sciences, at the end of the twentieth century, would take up his question almost in his own terms, asking no longer whether this belief is true, but why a human mind produces it so easily.

    In literature Joseph Conrad, Heart of Darkness (1899) ; Victor Hugo, “Ce que dit la bouche d'ombre” (1856) ; T. S. Eliot, The Waste Land (1922)

    In Heart of Darkness, Marlow discovers that Kurtz, the exemplary agent sent to the Congo to bring light, has had himself worshipped: he presided “at certain midnight dances ending with unspeakable rites, which[…] were offered up to him, do you understand? to Mr. Kurtz himself”. His report to the Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs, seventeen pages long, ends with a scrawled postscript: exterminate all the brutes [summary].

    Why here: Conrad writes at the moment when The Golden Bough is turning divine kings into survivals; Kurtz is one of Frazer's divine kings manufactured by a European of Tylor's generation, and the novel turns the thesis of survival around: “primitive philosophy” is not behind us, it waits at the end of the river, and it is the man of the Enlightenment who settles into it. Religion as an error to be dispelled becomes, in a single season, religion as a power to be exercised.

    Hugo, in “Ce que dit la bouche d'ombre”, has a spectre dictate to him, on Jersey, a cosmology in which matter is a punishment and nothing is inanimate: “Arbres, roseaux, rochers, tout vit ! Tout est plein d'âmes”, trees, reeds, rocks, everything lives! Everything is full of souls. This is Tylor's animism written by a poet who believes in it, fifteen years before Primitive Culture: proof that the “survival” survives among the moderns too. T. S. Eliot, finally, built The Waste Land on The Golden Bough, which he names in his notes together with Jessie Weston's book on the Grail: the myth of the wounded king and the barren land, which Frazer explained, becomes the form of the poem. Frazer wanted to reduce myth to an error; the twentieth century made it a structure, and poetry took it up where anthropology left it.

    Sources: Joseph Conrad, Heart of Darkness, II (1899) ; Victor Hugo, “Ce que dit la bouche d'ombre”, Les Contemplations, VI, 26 (1856) ; T. S. Eliot, The Waste Land and its notes (1922).

    Portrait: Elliot & Fry, Public domain

    Portrait: Antoine Bourdelle, photo Didier Descouens, Public domain

    Malinowski1884-1942magic begins where mastery ends

    Background: The anthropology of religion: from Tylor to Girard · Malinowski: fieldwork, functionalism, magic, science and religion · Norris and Inglehart: existential security, the World Values Surveys · Heracles: the labours, the choice, the apotheosis

    Bronisław Malinowski, born in Kraków, trained in physics and philosophy before coming to anthropology through reading The Golden Bough, spent most of the years 1915-1918 in the Trobriand Islands, off New Guinea, living among those he studied. On this experience he founded the method of participant observation, and from it he drew, on our question, a short essay, “Magic, Science and Religion”, which appeared in 1925 in a collective volume edited by Joseph Needham, Science, Religion and Reality.

    Malinowski first ruins Frazer's thesis with a fact. The Trobrianders do not confuse magic with technique. They know perfectly well that a garden grows because it has been dug, weeded and fenced, and they do all this with the care of good farmers; magic is added to work, it does not replace it. But it is not added everywhere, and here observation becomes experiment, in the example that every textbook has cited since. In the villages on the inner lagoon, fishing is done by poisoning, in an easy and perfectly reliable way; on the shores of the open sea, it is dangerous, and its yield depends on the uncertain passage of shoals of fish. Now, “in the Lagoon fishing, where man can rely completely upon his knowledge and skill, magic does not exist, while in the open-sea fishing, full of danger and uncertainty, there is extensive magical ritual to secure safety and good results”.

    The conclusion shifts the whole question. Magic is not an erroneous science, born of a badly conducted association of ideas; it is man's answer to the zones where his knowledge no longer suffices, where chance, danger and death decide. Its function, writes Malinowski, is “to ritualise man's optimism, to enhance his faith in the victory of hope over fear”. We find again the fear and hope that Hume placed at the origin of religion, but their sign is reversed. For Hume, fear produced terrible gods, and religion was a sickness of the mind; for Malinowski, the rite produces confidence, and this confidence has a vital value. The sailor who recites his formula before leaving the channel is not mistaken about the sea; he is giving himself the courage to go out on it.

    Religion, which Malinowski distinguishes from magic, is born of the most extreme of these zones. “Of all sources of religion, the supreme and final crisis of life, death, is of the greatest importance”. Before the death of someone close, man is torn between attachment and terror, the wish to keep the dead and the horror of the corpse; funeral rites give form to this ambivalence, and belief in immortality chooses, between the two answers suggested by the instinct of self-preservation, the answer of hope. “Religion saves man from a surrender to death and destruction”. And Malinowski concludes against Tylor: the true kernel of animism is not the observation of dreams, it is “the deepest emotional fact of human nature, the desire for life”. The soul is not a savage philosopher's hypothesis; it is a refusal.

    Malinowski finally opposes Durkheim, and his criticism is all the more interesting in that he does him justice. He rejects the idea of a “collective soul” and maintains that, in the societies he observed, religion arises to a large extent from purely individual sources, that crowds do not always produce religion, and that their effervescence is often entirely profane. He acknowledges, however, that Durkheim's school asked the right questions: why are religious acts almost always collective, and why are beliefs obligatory for all members of the tribe? His answer: religion, born of individual anxiety, is taken up by the group because the group, too, needs to survive the death of its members: funerals are the moment when society reconstitutes itself around a loss. We thus have, in 1925, a psychology and a sociology of religion reconciled around death, which announces Ernest Becker's psychology of death.

    A year later, in Myth in Primitive Psychology (1926), Malinowski extended the same analysis to myth. Myth, he says in substance, is not among the Trobrianders an explanation of natural phenomena, as the mythologists of the nineteenth century believed, nor a learned allegory; it is a “charter”, a narrative that founds and guarantees a present order, a prerogative, a rite, a rule of marriage or of property. Myth does not answer curiosity, it answers contestation: it says why things must be as they are. Religion therefore answers not only the anxiety of the individual before chance and death; it also answers a group's need to justify its order, which joins by another route the civil religion of Plato and of Rousseau, and announces the sociology of Peter Berger.

    Malinowski's position seems to me solid, and work he could not have known has confirmed it. It explains what neither Tylor nor Frazer explained: why belief does not retreat as knowledge advances, but only as uncertainty retreats. It makes religion not an error but an answer to a situation, and this answer varies with the situation. This is the hypothesis that Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart would put to the test on a world scale. But it leaves open the question that concerns this essay: if religion is the ritualized optimism of those who face danger, does it still have a function when danger is mastered, and what then remains, if not death itself, which nothing masters?

    In literature Jean de La Fontaine, “Le Chartier embourbé” (1668) ; Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea (1952)

    La Fontaine's carter, stuck in the mud in Lower Brittany, “loin / De tout humain secours”, far from all human help, first swears, then calls on Hercules. A voice answers him in the night: “Hercule veut qu'on se remue, / Puis il aide les gens.” (Hercules wants people to bestir themselves, then he helps them.) It has him clear the mud from the wheels, break the stone, fill in the rut, and when the cart moves off again, it concludes: “Aide-toi, le Ciel t'aidera”, help yourself, and Heaven will help you.

    Why here: the fable says in thirty lines what lagoon fishing and open-sea fishing say. Where knowledge and effort suffice, the god sends man back to his shovel; prayer begins only at the edge of what man does not master, and La Fontaine, as a moralist, would like that edge to recede.

    Hemingway's Santiago (The Old Man and the Sea) holds to the same division, but on the side of the open sea. Alone in his skiff, hooked to a fish he cannot yet see, he tells himself that he is not religious, promises ten Our Fathers and ten Hail Marys if he catches the fish, and starts reciting them mechanically without letting go of the line. Magic, says Malinowski, ritualizes optimism: the old man fishes with his hands and prays with the rest.

    Sources: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, book VI, 18, “Le Chartier embourbé” (1668) ; Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea (1952).

    Portrait: Photographe inconnu, LSE Library, No restrictions

    Jung1875-1961the religious function of the psyche

    Background: The psychology and psychoanalysis of religion: from James to experimental psychology · Gnosis and Gnosticism: from Valentinus to Hans Jonas and Voegelin · Psalms, Job, Qoheleth and the wisdom books · Rudolf Otto and The Idea of the Holy: the numinous, the wholly other, comparative mysticism · Freud's psychoanalysis: the unconscious, Oedipus, Totem and Taboo, illusion, Moses · Jung's psychology: archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, Answer to Job · Quantum mysticism, synchronicity and the law of attraction

    Carl Gustav Jung is the most famous of Freud's disciples to have broken with him, and religion lies at the centre of this break. The son of a pastor, brought up in a parsonage in the canton of Basel and nourished on a keen aversion to his father's theology, he had been designated by Freud as his heir, the “crown prince” of psychoanalysis, according to a formula found in their correspondence. The break was consummated in 1912-1913, after the publication of Wandlungen und Symbole der Libido (Transformations and Symbols of the Libido), in which Jung extended the libido beyond sexuality and read myths as expressions of a general psychic energy. Freud could not accept this, because the extension took the edge off his theory of religion: if the libido is any psychic energy whatever, religious desire is no longer the repetition of an infantile desire, it is a desire in its own right.

    Jung's thesis is simple to state and difficult to assess. The human psyche possesses by nature a religious function, which is not the residue of a neurosis but a normal activity of the soul, as natural as sexuality or aggressiveness. This function expresses itself in images that recur, with striking constancy, in the myths, dreams, visions and delusions of the most distant peoples and ages: these are the archetypes, empty forms of the collective unconscious that the particular representations of each culture fill. The most important of them is the Self, the image of psychic totality, which Jung recognizes in Christ, the Buddha, the mandala, the philosophers' stone of the alchemists. The process by which the individual enters into relation with this totality, which he calls individuation, is for him the psychological equivalent of what religions called salvation. He set it out for the general public in the Terry Lectures at Yale, in 1937, published the following year under the title Psychology and Religion.

    The Yale lectures contain a definition that concerns this essay directly, because it chooses, between the two etymologies of religio examined in the prologue, Cicero's against Lactantius's. Religion, says Jung, is the careful and scrupulous observation of what Rudolf Otto called the numinosum, a power that seizes the subject rather than being produced by him. The choice is not innocent: Cicero's religio was a scruple, an attentiveness, a rereading; it presupposed neither dogma nor a personal God. In taking it up, Jung makes religion an attitude of consciousness before what exceeds it, and he can say, without contradiction from his point of view, that a man with no denomination is religious if he takes his dreams and symbols seriously. Otto's Wholly Other becomes, in Jung, a region of the psyche.

    The gap with Freud is clear. For Freud, religion is an illusion, which humanity must outgrow as the child outgrows its dependence; for Jung, it is a function, and the man who represses it pays the price. He formulated this conviction in a clinical observation for which he has often been reproached: among his patients over thirty-five, he says in substance in an essay of 1932, there is not one whose ultimate problem was not that of finding a religious attitude towards life again, which has nothing to do, he specifies, with membership of a denomination or a Church. The neurosis of modern man would be a sickness of the loss of meaning, and psychotherapy would take over from spiritual direction.

    This function is not a belief. Jung repeats that he speaks as an empiricist, of what the soul produces, and not as a theologian, of what exists outside it; but the empiricism he claims constantly overflows its own limits.

    One formula has fixed this position in people's memories, and it also shows what is disquieting about it. In 1959, the BBC broadcast a long interview of Jung by John Freeman, recorded in his house at Küsnacht. Freeman asks him whether he believes in God. Jung hesitates, then answers: “I know. I don't need to believe. I know”. The sentence caused a scandal on both sides: believers heard in it a gnostic pride that replaces faith with knowledge; unbelievers, a profession of faith disguised as science. Jung himself had to specify in letters that he was speaking of the experience of a psychic reality, not of a metaphysical demonstration.

    Jung's boldest book on this ground is also his latest. In Antwort auf Hiob (Answer to Job, 1952), he reads the book of Job as the moment when man, just and suffering, becomes morally superior to a God who crushes him to win a wager; the Incarnation would be this God's answer to his own injustice, the necessity for him to become man in order to attain the consciousness that his creature has revealed to him. The book scandalized theologians, and with reason: it makes God a developing psychic image that needs human consciousness in order to know itself. But it touches, unexpectedly, the question that the conclusion of this essay leaves open, that of the lament of the oppressed creature. Jung takes Job's side against God, as Ivan Karamazov took the child's side against universal harmony; only, instead of concluding in favour of revolt, he concludes in favour of a transformation of the divine. This is yet another way of keeping religion, by making it absorb its own critique.

    The main objection came from a believer, and the response is attested. In 1952, Martin Buber published in the review Merkur an essay, “Religion und modernes Denken”, taken up in Eclipse of God (New York, Harper, 1952), then in the German edition, Gottesfinsternis (Eclipse of God, Zurich, Manesse, 1953). In it he accuses Jung of two things: of psychologism, since God is there no more than an image of the soul, and of gnosis, since the relation to the living God, which for Buber is an encounter with an external Thou, is replaced by the knowledge of an inner content. Jung replied in the same review with an “Antwort an Martin Buber”, to which Buber responded. The debate is, at bottom, that of mysticism and gnosis, of faith and knowledge. Jung claims to assert nothing about God in himself, but only about the image of God in the psyche; Buber answers that this reservation is an evasion, and that a god who exists only as a psychic function is not a god but an instrument.

    I believe Buber is right, but for a reason that is not exactly his. The danger of Jung, in the light of this essay's criterion, is not that he denies God; it is that he makes religion necessary without making it true. If the soul needs religious symbols as the body needs food, one cannot leave religion, only change symbols, and the therapist becomes the guardian of this necessity. It is Durkheim's position transposed from society to the psyche, and it has the same effect: it makes the question of this essay idle. It nevertheless has a consequence that Jung did not see. A religious function detached from all truth and all institution can be filled with anything at all, including what Jung called, in 1936, in an essay on Wotan, the awakening of an archaic god in the German soul, which he described, in my view, more than he fought it. A religion of the unconscious demands no explicit sacrifice; nor does it offer any criterion for refusing the sacrifice that an awakened archetype would demand. Jung was right against Freud on one point: the religious disposition is not merely infantile. He was wrong to believe that it was, in itself, a wisdom. His most popular notion, synchronicity, set out in 1952 with the physicist Wolfgang Pauli, showed it after him: we shall meet it again, at the end of Part Twelve, at the heart of the spiritualities that ask quantum physics to guarantee that the Universe is sending us signs.

    In literature Hermann Hesse, Demian (1919) ; Herman Melville, Moby-Dick (1851)

    Demian, published under a pseudonym just after the war, tells of the adolescence of Emil Sinclair between the bright world of home and the dark world of the street, under the guidance of a schoolfellow, Max Demian, who teaches him to read Cain differently and reveals to him the god Abraxas, at once God and devil; the image of the bird that fights its way out of the egg, and flies towards Abraxas, is its emblem. Hesse wrote the book after an analysis with Josef Bernhard Lang, a pupil of Jung, in 1916-1917, and met Jung himself only in 1921; the novel is the first Jungian fiction: individuation, shadow, Self, archetypes, without a single term of the doctrine.

    Why here: the reader sees in it what Buber reproached Jung for. Abraxas is worshipped by no one, he is “realized” by Sinclair; the god is no longer a Thou, but a content of the soul to be integrated, and religion becomes necessary without becoming true, exactly as the essay says of Jung. The novel also bears its date: the bird that breaks the egg of the world, in 1919, in Germany, speaks of something other than a psyche.

    For Answer to Job, Melville had already written the character. Ahab, in chapter 36, answers Starbuck, who accuses him of blasphemy: “To me, the white whale is that wall, shoved near to me. Sometimes I think there's naught beyond. But 'tis enough. He tasks me; he heaps me; I see in him outrageous strength, with an inscrutable malice sinewing it.[…] Talk not to me of blasphemy, man; I'd strike the sun if it insulted me”. Jung would say that Job is morally superior to the God who crushes him; Ahab had thought it, and he had made of this superiority a hunt. Jung's book is an Answer to Job; Moby-Dick is Ahab's answer, and it ends at the bottom of the sea.

    Sources: Hermann Hesse, Demian. Die Geschichte von Emil Sinclairs Jugend (1919) ; Herman Melville, Moby-Dick, ch. 36, “The Quarter-Deck” (1851).

    Girard1923-2015the sacred is born of sacrifice

    Background: From Cain to Babel: the fratricide, the Flood, the tower · The anthropology of religion: from Tylor to Girard · The patriarchs: Abraham, the sacrifice of Isaac, Jacob · Dionysus and the Bacchae: the foreign god, madness, dismemberment · Oedipus: the oracle, the Sphinx, the plague of Thebes · Freud's psychoanalysis: the unconscious, Oedipus, Totem and Taboo, illusion, Moses · René Girard's mimetic theory · Ernest Becker: the denial of death, the heroic system, the escape from evil · The Passion and the Resurrection: the four accounts and what history retains · Sacrifice in the Bible: from Abel's altar to self-offering · Evil, Satan and the afterlife: from Sheol to the Last Judgement

    René Girard is the author in this part who bears most directly on the thesis. Trained at the École des chartes, he left in 1947 to teach in the United States, where he spent his whole career, notably at Johns Hopkins, at Buffalo and then at Stanford, and he came to anthropology through literature. His first book, Deceit, Desire and the Novel (1961), starts from an observation about the great novelists, Cervantes, Stendhal, Flaubert, Proust and Dostoevsky: their characters never desire an object directly; they desire it because someone else desires it. Don Quixote wants to be a knight because Amadis was one; Emma Bovary loves through the novels she has read. Human desire is not a straight line between a subject and an object but a triangle whose apex is a model. Girard calls this desire mimetic.

    Girard recounted that while writing the last page of Deceit, Desire and the Novel, on the final conversion of the heroes who renounce desire according to the other, he himself underwent, at the end of the 1950s, a conversion that brought him back to the Catholicism of his Avignon childhood. The biography does not explain the thesis, but it says where the author speaks from: Girard speaks as a believer. Elected to the Académie française in 2005, he remained admired by theologians, debated by anthropologists, and more or less ignored by the philosophers of the French university.

    The discovery would have remained a thesis of literary criticism without its consequence. When the model is distant, like Amadis for Don Quixote, imitation is harmless. When the model is close, desiring the same object in the same world, he becomes a rival, the rival an obstacle, and the obstacle an even more fascinating model. Mimetic desire breeds rivalry, and rivalry too spreads by imitation: each imitates the other's violence, differences fade, and the whole community slides towards what Girard calls the mimetic crisis, a war of all against all in which nothing any longer distinguishes the adversaries. This is the hypothesis of his second book, Violence and the Sacred (1972), and it is there that Girard encounters religion.

    How does a community get out of it? Girard answers with a hypothesis that nothing allows us to observe, but which he believes he can read in myths the world over. The violence of all against all, because it is mimetic, can suddenly turn into the violence of all against one. It is enough for an individual, singled out by some trait or other, an infirmity, a strangeness, a royal position, to draw the accusations upon himself; imitation does the rest, and the unanimous community turns against him and kills him. This collective murder has a miraculous effect: peace returns, since all the violence has been discharged onto a single victim. The community, which does not understand what has happened, attributes the return of peace to the victim itself. The victim was guilty, since it was killed; it is beneficent, since its death saved everyone. It becomes sacred, that is, at once accursed and divine. Girard sums up the thesis in a sentence that has become famous, which makes violence the true heart and secret soul of the sacred.

    All archaic religion proceeds, according to Girard, from this victimage mechanism. Myth is the story of the lynching told from the point of view of the lynchers, who do not know that they have killed an innocent: the god in it is always guilty of something, of incest like Oedipus, of a fault like the Pharmakos. Rite is the controlled repetition of the founding murder, on a substitute victim, human or animal, so as to reproduce its pacifying effects: this is sacrifice. Prohibitions are the measures taken to prevent the return of the crisis, by separating what mimetic desire tends to confuse. The gods, finally, are deified victims. Girard here takes up all of Frazer's material, his sacrificed kings and his scapegoats, but he reverses its interpretation: where Frazer saw an error of reasoning, Girard sees a necessary misrecognition, without which the mechanism would not work. If the lynchers knew that their victim was innocent, peace would not return.

    Girard builds his demonstration on Oedipus the King, which shows how he reads a myth. Thebes is ravaged by plague, the image of the crisis in which differences fade; the city looks for the culprit; Oedipus and Tiresias, then Oedipus and Creon, accuse each other in a series of symmetrical exchanges in which each becomes the double of the other. And the city at last finds its culprit, the lame stranger who became king, who has committed the two undifferentiating crimes par excellence, parricide and incest, the crimes that confuse generations and places. Oedipus is driven out, the plague ceases. For Girard, Sophocles' tragedy is half lucid: it shows the symmetry of the accusations and lets us suspect that Oedipus's guilt might be a collective verdict rather than a fact; but in the end it confirms it, and the myth it takes up never doubts it for a moment. The case of Oedipus throws light, by contrast, on that of Socrates, whom the trial for impiety likewise singles out to the unanimity of a city in crisis; and Plato, as we have seen, wrote the law that would have condemned him a second time. The comparison is constructed: the city of the philosophers was not safe from the mechanism it believed it had mastered.

    Ten years later, The Scapegoat (1982) applies the same grid to texts that no one takes for myths. Girard starts from a poem by Guillaume de Machaut, which tells how, in the middle of the fourteenth century, the Jews were accused of poisoning the wells during the Black Death and were massacred. The modern reader does not hesitate for a second: the plague is real, the accusation false, the massacre real. From this Girard draws what he calls the “stereotypes of persecution”: a crisis that effaces differences, undifferentiating crimes imputed to the victims, signs that single them out, minorities, the infirm, foreigners, and the collective violence itself. If we know how to read these stereotypes in a medieval text, he asks, why not in myths, which display all of them? The strength of the argument is methodological: it does not ask us to invent an original murder; it asks us to treat myths as we treat chronicles of persecution, by taking the side of the victim. The last great book, I See Satan Fall Like Lightning (1999), gives this reversal its biblical name: Satan, in the Gospels, is the accuser, the principle of mimetic desire and of the unanimous crowd, and his fall is the end of his power to accuse without being unmasked.

    One can see why Girard matters to this essay. The criterion I have proposed says that a religion is refounded when an absolute is installed in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded. Girard says more: religion is born of the sacrifice of an individual to the unanimity of the group. What the essay described as a symptom of refoundation would be the birth certificate of every religion. If the sacred is collective violence transfigured, then each time an exit from religion singles out a victim, Plato's impious man, the citizen who violates Rousseau's civil religion, the class enemy, the traitor to the Nation, it reproduces the founding gesture and refounds, literally, a religion. Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor is not only a parable of power; he is, in Girardian terms, the priest who manages the victimage mechanism and who protects the crowd from the truth.

    But Girard also reverses the thesis, and it is there that he becomes truly original. There are, according to him, texts that tell the lynching from the point of view of the victim, and that proclaim its innocence: those of the Bible. Joseph, sold by his brothers, is innocent; Job, accused by his friends, is innocent; Isaiah's suffering servant is innocent; the Psalms give voice to the man whom the crowd assails. The Gospels complete this unveiling: the Passion is a unanimous lynching, in which even the disciples fail, but it is told by those who know that the victim is innocent, and who proclaim it. Christianity, for Girard, is therefore not one more sacrificial religion; it is the revelation of the sacrificial mechanism, the revelation of “things hidden since the foundation of the world” (Mt 13, 35), which give their title to the book of 1978, written in dialogue with two psychiatrists, Jean-Michel Oughourlian and Guy Lefort. This revelation has a historical consequence: once unveiled, the mechanism no longer works, since it required misrecognition. The societies that have received the Gospels can no longer reconcile themselves at the expense of a victim without knowing, at least dimly, that they are committing an injustice. Hence the modern concern for victims, which Girard regards as the deepest legacy of Christianity, and hence also, for want of a regulating mechanism, the rise of a violence that nothing any longer contains, the theme of his last book, Battling to the End (2007).

    For a long time Girard refused to call the Passion a sacrifice, precisely because it unveiled sacrifice; at the end of a long exchange with the Jesuit theologian Raymund Schwager, he finally accepted the word in a new sense, that of the gift of self that refuses violence instead of undergoing it. This dispute over vocabulary is not secondary: it means that Christianity, for Girard, is at once the exit from sacrificial religion and a religion, which is the very thesis of Marcel Gauchet, whom we shall read in the part on secularization: Christianity as the religion of the exit from religion. The comparison is constructed, for the paths differ, Gauchet starting from political history and Girard from the anthropology of desire; yet the two bodies of thought share the same weakness, which is to make Christianity the end point of the religious history of humanity.

    Girard responded, in attested fashion, to several authors in this essay. Against Freud, he takes up in Violence and the Sacred the hypothesis of Totem und Tabu (1912-1913), the original murder of the father by the horde of sons, and he pays tribute to him for having glimpsed the founding murder; but he reproaches him for having tied it to sexual desire and to the father, instead of to mimetic rivalry and to the arbitrary victim. Against Durkheim, he accepts that the sacred is social, but he refuses the idea that society worships itself in it: what the community worships is its own violence transfigured, and the reverse side of Durkheimian unanimity is a corpse. It is against Nietzsche that his response goes furthest. Nietzsche had ended Ecce homo with the formula “Dionysos gegen den Gekreuzigten”, Dionysus against the Crucified. Girard takes up the formula as the title of an essay and agrees with Nietzsche on the diagnosis: the difference between Dionysus and Christ does not lie in the story, for both die under the blows of a crowd; it lies in the point of view, since the Dionysian myth takes the side of the lynchers and the Gospel that of the victim. Nietzsche saw this better than the theologians, and he chose Dionysus, that is to say the crowd. From this Girard draws a grave charge against Nietzsche: the will to power that despises compassion for the weak is the return, in philosophy, of the persecutors' point of view.

    There remain the objections of the anthropologists. The first concerns method: a founding mechanism that leaves traces only in the myths that conceal it is, by construction, unverifiable, and any absence of a victim in a myth can be read as further proof of concealment. The second concerns universality: many societies practise sacrifice as an exchange, a gift, a meal shared with the gods, without the lynching scene being found in it, and field ethnologists have often reproached Girard for treating the ethnographic material as Frazer did, by selective comparisons. The third concerns closure: a theory that makes its own religion the key to all the others lays itself open to the suspicion of having been constructed to lead there. These objections are strong, and Girard has not, I believe, entirely answered them.

    In this immense construction two storeys must be separated, one of which carries my conviction and the other not. The first is anthropological: mimetic desire, the crisis, the singling out of a scapegoat, the misrecognition that allows the crowd to believe itself innocent. It is a hypothesis, unverifiable in its originary version, but of considerable descriptive power, and the history of the twentieth century, with its designated victims and its unanimous crowds, has given it terrible confirmations. It gives the criterion of this essay an anthropological foundation. The second storey is apologetic: the Bible and the Gospels would be the only revelation of this mechanism, and Christianity the only way out. It seems to me much more fragile. It neglects the other traditions that have thought the innocence of the victim or refused sacrifice, Greek tragedy itself, which sometimes lets the victim's lament be heard, or the refusal of blood sacrifice among the prophets, which Girard indeed ties to the Bible, but also the wisdoms of India or China, which he hardly examines. And it makes historical Christianity, which had its stakes and its Inquisitors, the vehicle of a revelation it has betrayed so often that Dostoevsky could imagine Christ condemned a second time by his Church. Girard replies that the Church betrayed the Gospels, and that betrayal presupposes revelation. So be it. But then the exit from sacrifice no longer belongs to a religion: it belongs to anyone who refuses to join the crowd, believer or not. I shall draw the consequence of this in the conclusion, against Girard's apologetics and with his anthropology.

    In literature Euripides, The Bacchae (405 BCE) ; Jean de La Fontaine, “Les Animaux malades de la peste” (1678) ; Shirley Jackson, “The Lottery” (1948)

    In The Bacchae, the messenger tells what the women of Thebes, possessed by Dionysus, are doing on Cithaeron: “tu aurais vu une d'elles déchirer en deux, de ses mains, une génisse aux lourdes mamelles et mugissante ; et d'autres mettaient les vaches en lambeaux ; et tu aurais vu les côtes et les pieds fourchus sauter de toutes parts, et les morceaux, suspendus aux sapins, dégoutter de sang”, you would have seen one of them tear in two, with her hands, a lowing heifer with heavy udders; and others were rending the cows to shreds; and you would have seen ribs and cloven hooves flying on every side, and the pieces, hanging from the fir trees, dripping with blood. Then it is King Pentheus, who has come to spy on them, who is torn to pieces by his own mother, Agave; she returns in triumph with the head she believes to be a lion's, and her father Cadmus slowly brings her back to reason, until the cry: “Non ! Mais je tiens la tête de Pentheus, malheureuse !”, No! But I am holding the head of Pentheus, wretched woman that I am!

    Why here: this is the text on which Girard built Violence and the Sacred, and one need only read it to see why. The unanimous crowd, the victim first royal and then a beast, the god who demands and who feeds on the lynching, the misrecognition that lets the mother carry the head as a trophy: the whole mechanism is there, and Euripides shows it at the moment when Athens is dying. “Dionysus against the Crucified” is not a formula: it is this scene against another.

    La Fontaine turned the scapegoat into a fable. Plague strikes the animals; the lion proposes that each confess his faults and that the guiltiest be sacrificed; the powerful absolve one another, and it is the donkey, who grazed the grass of a meadow, that is condemned: “A ces mots on cria haro sur le baudet”, at these words they all cried out against the donkey; the moral: “Selon que vous serez puissant ou misérable, / Les jugemens de Cour vous rendront blanc ou noir”, according as you are powerful or wretched, / the judgements of the Court will make you white or black. Shirley Jackson, in 1948, described the same rite in an American village, on the June morning when lots are drawn, with slips of paper in a black box, for the woman whom the whole village, its children included, will stone so that the harvest may be good; The New Yorker received more indignant letters than for any other story. The fable and the story show what Girard holds to be universal and what the ethnologists dispute: the victim designated by the crowd, and the crowd that does not see itself.

    Sources: Euripides, The Bacchae, trans. Leconte de Lisle (405 BCE) ; Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, VII, 1 (1678) ; Shirley Jackson, “The Lottery”, The New Yorker, 26 June 1948.

    Portrait: Vicq, Public domain

    BBecker1924-1974religion as heroism against death

    Background: The psychology and psychoanalysis of religion: from James to experimental psychology · Oedipus: the oracle, the Sphinx, the plague of Thebes · Ernest Becker: the denial of death, the heroic system, the escape from evil

    Ernest Becker was neither a theologian nor a professional philosopher, but an American cultural anthropologist who had spent his career on the margins of the university, dismissed or barely tolerated from one post to the next. The Denial of Death appeared in 1973; Becker died of cancer in March 1974, and the book received the Pulitzer Prize for general non-fiction two months later. This chronology made the book's legend: written by a man who knew he was dying and who drew from it a theory of the whole of culture. But the legend must not hide the thesis, which gives our question an answer that neither Feuerbach nor Freud had formulated in this form.

    The thesis can be put in a few words, and I paraphrase it for want of having consulted the original text: the idea of death, and the terror it inspires, haunt the human animal more than anything else, and they are the mainspring of its activity. Man is the only animal that knows it will die; Bergson had written as much in 1932 in almost identical terms, “Les animaux ne savent pas qu'ils doivent mourir”, animals do not know that they must die, and he already drew from it a function of religion, “une réaction défensive de la nature contre la représentation, par l'intelligence, de l'inévitabilité de la mort”, a defensive reaction of nature against the representation, by the intelligence, of the inevitability of death. Becker does not cite Bergson, and the encounter is my doing; but it shows that the intuition is not peculiar to American psychology. Becker adds to it an anthropology of the hero. Man is a living contradiction: a mind capable of representing the infinite, housed in a body that decays. Unable to look this contradiction in the face, he covers it over with what Becker calls a causa sui project, the effort to be one's own cause, and with heroism, that is, the conviction of having a worth that outlasts death. Every culture is then a hero system: a set of roles, stories and rites that allows each person to believe himself important beyond his own disappearance.

    Religion is, for Becker, the vastest of these systems, and his position is not a simple reduction. Becker starts from Freud, but he corrects him through Otto Rank, the former disciple whom Freud had rejected, and through Kierkegaard. From Rank he retains that the fear of death is more fundamental than sexuality, and that the Oedipus complex itself is a causa sui project, the child's desire to become his own father. From Kierkegaard he retains the analysis of anxiety as the dizziness of freedom before nothingness, and the conclusion that the only honest way out is faith, which acknowledges dependence instead of denying it. The book's last chapter is ambiguous: Becker judges there that religion in the Kierkegaardian sense, the faith that accepts creatureliness, is the highest heroism, because it alone does not lie about the human condition. He is no apologist; he says only that, if one must choose a vital lie, the one that admits itself as such is better than those that do not know themselves. This is Pascal's position, which Becker arrives at without having sought it: Pascalian divertissement is the mechanism of denial he describes, “les hommes n'ayant pu guérir la mort, la misère, l'ignorance, ils se sont avisés, pour se rendre heureux, de n'y point penser”, men, having been unable to cure death, wretchedness and ignorance, have taken it into their heads, in order to be happy, not to think about them.

    The posthumous book Escape from Evil (1975) draws from this anthropology a consequence that bears directly on the criterion. People who live by hero systems cannot bear others to contest them, for contestation reopens the question the system was meant to close. Social evil then arises from the denial of death: others are sacrificed to prove to oneself that one will not die, enemies are designated so that one's own symbolic immortality remains uncontested. This is a theory of sacrifice, which meets Girard's by another path: the two men did not read each other, as far as I know, and the comparison is constructed. For the one, sacrifice protects the individual against death; for the other, it protects the community against its own violence. In both cases, religion is inseparable from a victim.

    Experimental psychology has sought to put this thesis to the test. From 1986 onwards Jeff Greenberg, Sheldon Solomon and Tom Pyszczynski drew from it a terror management theory: worldviews and self-esteem would serve as a buffer against death anxiety, and being reminded of death (mortality salience) should strengthen attachment to one's worldview and hostility towards those who contest it. In the founding experiment, in 1989, judges first invited to think about their own death set heavier bonds for a prostitute: “judges recommended especially harsh bonds for a prostitute when mortality was made salient” (A. Rosenblatt et al., Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 57, 1989, p. 681-690, abstract). But a large coordinated replication, Many Labs 4 (R. Klein et al., Collabra: Psychology 8, 2022), dealing with another classic experiment of the theory (Greenberg et al., 1994), did not find the effect, across seventeen laboratories and 1,550 participants. The theory is not thereby refuted, but one of its most cited effects is wavering, and it can no longer be taken as established.

    Becker first gives a precise answer to the question “why do people believe?”: because we die, and we know it. Then a consequence that meets the thesis of this essay: if every culture is a hero system against death, then the exits from religion that install a new absolute, History, the Nation, Race, Civilization, are not accidents; they are replacement hero systems, which promise symbolic immortality to those who serve them and refuse it to those who contest them. The sacrifice criterion here receives a psychological explanation. But Becker leaves open a question he does not resolve: can one live without a vital lie? Lucretius answered yes, provided one understands that death is nothing to us; Becker does not believe so, and this is what leads him back to Kierkegaard. I believe he is wrong on this point, or rather that he confuses two things: the need for meaning, which is universal, and the need for immortality, which perhaps is not. The spiritualities of exercise, from Spinoza to Hadot, do not deny death; they seek to look at it without lying to themselves.
