    Transition: from explanation to ordeal

    The human sciences have explained religion; they have not dissolved it. They have shown that belief has universal springs, cognitive, existential and social, that its intensity varies with the security of existence, and that the need it satisfied, for meaning, for bonds and for protection, survives God. But explanation leaves untouched the question that the twentieth century poses with a new urgency. If religion is not an error that science corrects, but a human response to a human condition, what becomes of that response when God falls silent? The thinkers of the next part are no longer content to explain: they put religion to the test, from within and from without, believers and unbelievers together. All of them had read, directly or not, the explainers of religion. None of them believed that explanation was enough.

    Top of the part

    Part Tenthe twentieth century, God after metaphysics10 authors

    Background: Phenomenology: from Husserl to the theological turn · The vocabulary of Christian theology: revelation, grace, salvation, original sin · Twentieth-century Christian theology: dialectical, existential, Catholic, death of God · The Gospel of John: the Word made flesh

    Part Nine showed that explaining belief does not dissolve it; Part Eight had already rehabilitated, with Bergson, James and Otto, the mystic whom nineteenth-century critique regarded as a sick man, a dreamer or an exploiter. The question of this essay has thus shifted ground. We no longer ask only whether dogmas are true, what Churches are for, which desire beliefs satisfy. We ask what becomes of an experience, and whether it survives the ruin of the representations that long framed it: can one keep spirituality while losing religion, or religion while losing the God of the philosophers?

    The twentieth century answers in a way that no critic of the previous century had foreseen. It does not merely produce atheists more consistent than Feuerbach. It produces, and this is the major fact, a theological critique of religion, and a religious critique of God. The atheists, for their part, take atheism as a starting point rather than a conclusion, and ask what it costs; others seek the divine outside being, or the mystical outside language.

    This shift is decisive. Until now, the exit from religion was made against religion, and one could ask whether it did not refound another. From now on, it is also made from within religion, and one can ask the reverse question: is the critique of religion not, at least sometimes, the work of faith itself? If so, the simple opposition between believers and unbelievers, from which we were still starting, no longer holds. The dividing line runs elsewhere: between those who want an absolute that is available, possessed, usable, and those who renounce it, whether they pray or not.

    Heidegger1889-1976God and metaphysics die together

    Background: Aristotle's philosophy: act and potency, causes, the unmoved mover, virtue, contemplation · Phenomenology: from Husserl to the theological turn · The philosophy of Nietzsche: tragedy, genealogy, will to power, eternal return, overman · Metaphysics and the proofs of the existence of God: from Anselm to Kant · The thought of Heidegger: Dasein, Being and Time, the turn, technology, 1933 · The Gospel of John: the Word made flesh

    Heidegger's texts are protected by copyright, and I have been unable to check any of them against a printed edition: the quotations that follow are given from concordant secondary sources, with their provenance, or from an online reproduction of the German text; they will have to be verified against the Gesamtausgabe before any publication.

    I begin with Heidegger, not because he is the most important, but because almost all the other authors in this part situate themselves in relation to the configuration he named onto-theology. The word does not designate an error of this or that philosopher, but the very structure of Western metaphysics since Plato and Aristotle, which comes down to a double question: what are beings as beings, what is common to everything that is, and what is the supreme being, the one that grounds all the others? The first question is ontological, the second theological, and metaphysics is both at once: it thinks being as ground, and the ultimate ground as a supreme being. What philosophers have called God is the name of this ground.

    The essay “Nietzsches Wort "Gott ist tot"” (Holzwege, 1950), the substance of which, according to Heidegger's own note, was read several times in 1943 before small circles, drawing on the lectures on Nietzsche given at Freiburg between 1936 and 1940, turns Nietzsche against himself. The word “God”, in Nietzsche, does not designate only the Christian God, but the supersensible world in general, Ideas, ends, values. Hence: “Das Wort ›Gott ist tot‹ bedeutet: die übersinnliche Welt ist ohne wirkende Kraft. Sie spendet kein Leben. Die Metaphysik, d.h. für Nietzsche die abendländische Philosophie als Platonismus verstanden, ist zu Ende.” The death of God is not an episode in the history of religions; it is the end of Western metaphysics, which Nietzsche pronounces without seeing that he still belongs to it. To think beings as will to power and the world as values to be posited is to complete metaphysics, not to leave it. The reversal of Platonism remains Platonic: it puts life where Plato put the Idea, but still thinks in terms of hierarchy and value, and “value” is for Heidegger the last avatar of the Platonic Good, become a mere condition posited by the will for its own growth. The essay ends on a sentence that strikes the reason of the Enlightenment as much as faith: “Das Denken beginnt erst dann, wenn wir erfahren haben, daß die seit Jahrhunderten verherrlichte Vernunft die hartnäckigste Widersacherin des Denkens ist”, thinking begins only when we have experienced that reason, glorified for centuries, is the most stubborn adversary of thinking.

    This reading strikes the whole series of Parts Six, Seven and Eight. If Heidegger is right, Feuerbach, Marx, Nietzsche and Freud did not leave religion, not because they kept a residue of piety, as Stirner maintained, but because they remained metaphysicians. Feuerbach replaces God with the human essence: he changes the ground, he does not renounce grounding. Marx replaces providence with the laws of history, Nietzsche the Idea with the will to power: the same structure. Freud replaces God with the Logos, and says so, as we have seen, with disarming frankness. Stirner's objection bore on the content of the absolute; Heidegger's bears on its form. One can empty the absolute of all theological content and remain within onto-theology, as long as one thinks the real on the basis of a first principle that accounts for it. The critique of religion by reason is, in this respect, the continuation of philosophical theology by other means.

    The second text is the lecture “Die onto-theo-logische Verfassung der Metaphysik”, collected in Identität und Differenz (1957). The God of the philosophers is there the ultimate ground, and its proper name is causa sui. But such a god has nothing divine about it: “Zu diesem Gott kann der Mensch weder beten, noch kann er ihm opfern. Vor der Causa sui kann der Mensch weder aus Scheu ins Knie fallen, noch kann er vor diesem Gott musizieren und tanzen”, to this god man can neither pray nor offer sacrifice; before the causa sui, man can neither fall to his knees in awe, nor play music and dance before this god. And Heidegger adds that god-less thinking, “das gott-lose Denken, das den Gott der Philosophie, den Gott als Causa sui preisgeben muß”, which must give up the god of philosophy, is “dem göttlichen Gott vielleicht näher”, perhaps closer to the divine god.

    The sentence says that philosophical atheism, the critique of the God-as-ground, is not opposed to religion: it perhaps clears the place for a god who would no longer be that of the philosophers. The critique of religion becomes, in Heidegger, a critique of philosophical theology in favour of waiting. As early as 1927, in “Phänomenologie und Theologie”, he separated the two domains radically: theology is “eine positive Wissenschaft”, a positive science, and “als solche daher von der Philosophie absolut verschieden”; faith is the mortal enemy, “Todfeind”, of philosophy, and a Christian philosophy is a “hölzernes Eisen”, a wooden iron, a square circle. The gesture recalls Spinoza, but reverses its meaning: Spinoza separated in order to free philosophy from theology, Heidegger separates in order to free the divine from philosophy.

    Heidegger thus gives, three centuries later, a history and a reason to the opposition that Pascal's Memorial drew between the God one encounters and the God one demonstrates (Part Three); a constructed comparison, for I have not verified that Heidegger cites Pascal in this text.

    A text from 1951, less well known and sharper, confirms this meaning. At a seminar held in Zurich on 6 November 1951, Heidegger answers students who question him on the relation between being and God. His answers, recorded in volume 15 of the Gesamtausgabe, settle a persistent misunderstanding: “Sein und Gott sind nicht identisch, und ich würde niemals versuchen, das Wesen Gottes durch das Sein zu denken”, being and God are not identical, and I would never attempt to think the essence of God by way of being. Then: “Wenn ich noch eine Theologie schreiben würde, wozu es mich manchmal reizt, dann dürfte in ihr das Wort »Sein« nicht vorkommen”, if I were still to write a theology, as I am sometimes tempted to do, the word “being” would not be allowed to appear in it. And finally: “Der Glaube hat das Denken des Seins nicht nötig”, faith has no need of the thinking of being.

    These three sentences undo the lazy reading that makes “being” a substitute for God, an impersonal divinity for philosophers disappointed with Christianity. Being is not God, and faith has no need of it. The critique of onto-theology therefore does not aim to replace the God of the philosophers with being, which would be to refound a metaphysics; it aims to restore to faith its own source, which is not reason, and to thinking its own task, which is not to ground God. The young Heidegger had been a seminarian and a student of Catholic theology at Freiburg before writing to Engelbert Krebs, in January 1919, that epistemological insights had made “das System des Katholizismus problematisch und unannehmbar”, the system of Catholicism problematic and unacceptable to him, “nicht aber das Christentum und die Metaphysik”, but not Christianity and metaphysics; it is not insignificant that his most radical critique of metaphysics is formulated as a service rendered to the divine rather than as its liquidation.

    Hence Heidegger's last public word on the question, the interview given to Der Spiegel in September 1966 to Rudolf Augstein and Georg Wolff, published at his wish after his death, in issue 23 of 31 May 1976, under the title “Nur noch ein Gott kann uns retten”, only a god can still save us. In W. J. Richardson's English translation, he declares that philosophy cannot bring about any immediate change in the state of the world, that the only possibility left to us is to prepare, through thinking and poetry, a readiness for the appearance of the god or for his absence in the decline.

    This formula is made to say too much or too little. Too much, when one sees in it a late conversion, a return of the old thinker to the faith of his childhood: nothing in the interview names the Christian God, and the indefinite article, “ein Gott”, is deliberate. Too little, when one sees in it a quip: Heidegger says in earnest that neither technology, nor politics, nor philosophy can answer the distress of the age, and that thinking can only prepare. The structure is that of waiting. It is not unrelated to the Gelassenheit of the small volume bearing that title (1959), which brings together the Messkirch address of 1955 and a conversation written in 1944-1945: a letting-be, a serenity that renounces willing, and a word that Heidegger deliberately takes over from Meister Eckhart (gelâzenheit) while shifting its meaning, since it is no longer a matter of surrendering one's own will to the divine will but of leaving willing behind.

    The objection is obvious, and I believe it is right. Heidegger saw that the critique of religion by reason remains caught in the metaphysics it believes it has overcome. But he draws from this a waiting without content, a piety without object, a religion without dogma or Church whose priest is the thinker and whose sacred text is Hölderlin. One does not leave religion by announcing a god to come: one founds one, a vague one, and perhaps a dangerous one, since it does not say what it is waiting for. The objection still needs to be made precise, otherwise it would fall under the reproach Heidegger levels at his critics, that of judging thinking by the yardstick of calculating reason. I do not reproach him for waiting, but for not saying who waits and in whose name. Pascal waited too, but he knew what he was waiting for, and his waiting was governed by a Scripture, a Church, a prayer. Spinoza waited for nothing, and his beatitude was actual. Heidegger waits without object or rule, and it is this indeterminacy that could, in 1933, allow itself to be filled by a historical object: one cannot pretend that the commitment of 1933 and the Black Notebooks do not exist, since they show what a thinking that waits for the saviour was able to recognize, once, in real history. A spirituality without content is not for all that without an absolute: it is an empty absolute, available to whoever wishes to occupy it. This is the lesson that Part Eleven will find again in Blumenberg, under the name of the reoccupation of positions.

    Heidegger nevertheless established what no one in this part will call into question: the critique of the God of the philosophers is not the critique of God, and can be its opposite. The Protestant theologians of his time had understood this before him, and often better than he did.

    In literature Franz Kafka, “Eine kaiserliche Botschaft” (1919) ; Friedrich Hölderlin, “Patmos” (1803) ; Paul Celan, “Todtnauberg” (1967)

    “Der Kaiser, so heißt es, hat Dir, dem Einzelnen, dem jämmerlichen Untertanen, dem winzig vor der kaiserlichen Sonne in die fernste Ferne geflüchteten Schatten, gerade Dir hat der Kaiser von seinem Sterbebett aus eine Botschaft gesendet”, the emperor, so it is said, has sent a message from his deathbed to you, the individual, the wretched subject, the tiny shadow that has fled into the farthest distance before the imperial sun, to you of all people. The messenger sets out, vigorous, tireless; but the halls, the stairways, the courtyards, the palaces nested one within another are endless, “und so weiter durch Jahrtausende[…] Niemand dringt hier durch und gar mit der Botschaft eines Toten. Du aber sitzt an Deinem Fenster und erträumst sie Dir, wenn der Abend kommt”, and so on through millennia; no one gets through here, least of all with the message of a dead man. But you sit at your window and dream it to yourself, when evening comes.

    Why here: the parable is Heideggerian waiting seen by a man who does not give himself up to it. A dead god has sent a message that will never arrive; the one who waits for it dreams it; and Kafka says neither that the message exists nor that it does not. “Nur noch ein Gott kann uns retten” is the sentence of the man at the window; the essay's objection, a waiting without content of which one does not know who waits or in whose name, is the sentence of the narrator.

    Heidegger made Hölderlin the sacred text of this waiting, and “Patmos” in particular, whose lines on danger and what saves he commented on endlessly; the poem, written for the Landgrave of Homburg, speaks of the nearness of the god and the difficulty of grasping him, and asks that the letter be kept, “der feste Buchstab”, when the god has withdrawn. Celan, finally, went up to Todtnauberg in 1967, drank the water of the well with the wooden star, wrote in the visitors' book a line that hoped for “a coming word in the heart” of the thinker, and put into the poem the waiting for that word, which did not come. Two waitings face to face on the same mountain path; the Jewish poet's had a content.

    Sources: Franz Kafka, “Eine kaiserliche Botschaft”, Ein Landarzt (1919) ; Friedrich Hölderlin, “Patmos” (1803) ; Paul Celan, “Todtnauberg”, Lichtzwang (1967, published 1970).

    Portrait: Willy Pragher, CC BY-SA 3.0

    Wittgenstein1889-1951that the world is

    Background: Analytic philosophy of religion: from the problem of evil to Reformed epistemology · Tylor and Frazer: animism, survivals, The Golden Bough · Wittgenstein's philosophy: the Tractatus, language games, ethics and the mystical

    Ludwig Wittgenstein never wrote a book on religion, nor even an article: a few pages of the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, a lecture of 1929 published after his death, notebooks, remarks on a book of anthropology, conversations reported by his students. Yet he occupies in our debate a place that no one else can hold: that of a man who closed, with unprecedented rigour, the possibility of saying anything whatever about God, and who left open, with the same rigour, the place of what cannot be said.

    The Tractatus, written during the war, published in German in 1921 and in a bilingual edition in London in 1922, ends with a series of propositions whose sequence is the argument. First, the sense of the world cannot lie in the world: “Der Sinn der Welt muss ausserhalb ihrer liegen. In der Welt ist alles wie es ist und geschieht alles wie es geschieht; es gibt in ihr keinen Wert”, the sense of the world must lie outside it; in the world everything is as it is and everything happens as it happens; in it there is no value (6.41). Next, God does not show himself in the facts: “Wie die Welt ist, ist für das Höhere vollkommen gleichgültig. Gott offenbart sich nicht in der Welt”, how the world is, is completely indifferent for what is higher; God does not reveal himself in the world (6.432). Then the central proposition: “Nicht wie die Welt ist, ist das Mystische, sondern dass sie ist”, it is not how the world is that is the mystical, but that it is (6.44). And the conclusion: “Es gibt allerdings Unaussprechliches. Dies zeigt sich, es ist das Mystische”, there is indeed the inexpressible; it shows itself, it is the mystical (6.522).

    It would be wrong to see in this a concession made to religion by a positivist. Wittgenstein is not Carnap, and the Vienna Circle was mistaken in taking him for an ally. The Tractatus does not say that what cannot be said does not exist; it says that what matters most cannot be said. “Wir fühlen, dass selbst, wenn alle möglichen wissenschaftlichen Fragen beantwortet sind, unsere Lebensprobleme noch gar nicht berührt sind”, we feel that even when all possible scientific questions have been answered, the problems of our life have not been touched at all (6.52). And the solution of the problem of life, adds 6.521, is seen in the vanishing of this problem: that is why, Wittgenstein asks, those to whom the sense of life became clear after long doubt could not say what this sense consisted in. The last proposition, “Wovon man nicht sprechen kann, darüber muss man schweigen”, what one cannot speak about, one must keep silent about (7), is not contempt, but a form of respect.

    Two less cited propositions bear more directly on our question. The first concerns the modern view of the world: “Der ganzen modernen Weltanschauung liegt die Täuschung zugrunde, dass die sogenannten Naturgesetze die Erklärungen der Naturerscheinungen seien”, the whole modern view of the world rests on the illusion that the so-called laws of nature are the explanations of natural phenomena (6.371); “So bleiben sie bei den Naturgesetzen als bei etwas Unantastbarem stehen, wie die älteren bei Gott und dem Schicksal”, so the moderns stop at the laws of nature as at something inviolable, as the ancients did at God and fate (6.372). The thesis of this essay is here applied to science: the exit from religion through science installed a new inviolable in place of the old one. Freud, a few years later, would call it “our god Logos”. The comparison is constructed: Wittgenstein denies science the status of ultimate explanation that Freud granted it, and that is why he cannot put it in God's place.

    The second concerns eternity: “Wenn man unter Ewigkeit nicht unendliche Zeitdauer, sondern Unzeitlichkeit versteht, dann lebt der ewig, der in der Gegenwart lebt”, if by eternity one understands not infinite temporal duration but timelessness, then he lives eternally who lives in the present (6.4311). The preceding sentence says that death is not an event of life, and the following one that the immortality of the soul would solve no riddle. One hears Epicurus, for whom death is nothing to us, and Spinoza, for whom we feel and experience that we are eternal: Wittgenstein rediscovers ancient wisdom and the fifth part of the Ethics by the most improbable path, that of logic.

    The lecture on ethics, delivered at Cambridge in 1929 and published in 1965 in the Philosophical Review, gives this experience a content. To convey what he calls absolute value, Wittgenstein describes the experience that is for him the experience par excellence: “I believe the best way of describing it is to say that when I have it I wonder at the existence of the world”; and he adds that he is then inclined to use such phrases as “how extraordinary that anything should exist”. Further on, he redescribes it as seeing the world as a miracle, distinguishing the relative miracle, what science has not yet explained, from the absolute miracle; when we look at a fact scientifically, he says, everything miraculous about it disappears. But he adds at once that the expression of this wonder is nonsense, since one cannot wonder that a thing is without being able to imagine its not being, and one cannot imagine the world not being. The wonder is real, and its formulation is a misuse of language: it is this double affirmation, held to the end, that makes Wittgenstein singular.

    Here appears the question that Part Twelve will take up: why is there something rather than nothing? Leibniz had posed it as the first question we have the right to ask; Schelling and Heidegger would take it up as the fundamental question of metaphysics. Wittgenstein receives it as a wonder, not as a question, and refuses to answer it, because there is nothing there to answer.

    The war notebooks of 1914-1916 show that this silence was not indifference. In them Wittgenstein identifies God with the meaning of life, and prayer with thinking about this meaning; to believe in God is to see that the facts of the world are not everything. We also know, from the concordant testimony of his friends, that during the war he carried Tolstoy's The Gospel in Brief and recommended it to those around him. His student Maurice Drury reports that he said he was not a religious man, but could not help seeing every problem from a religious point of view. These are only recollections, but they agree with the Tractatus.

    One last text concerns the anthropology of religion of Part Nine. In 1931, Wittgenstein read James Frazer's The Golden Bough and set down remarks on it that were published in 1967. He reproaches Frazer for explaining magical rites as errors, false hypotheses about causality, and turns the accusation around: it is Frazer who is primitive, more savage than most of his savages, since he cannot imagine a practice that is not a failed technique. The man who burns an effigy does not believe he is acting on the enemy as the doctor acts on a fever; he is expressing something, and the rite satisfies by expressing. This is a radical critique of the regime of error, from Lucretius to d'Holbach and Frazer: religion is not bad physics. Durkheim had seen this in his own way, making the rite the act by which a society represents its own strength to itself; Wittgenstein goes further, since he refuses even the functional explanation, which remains an explanation. Freud, who explained religion by infantile desire, would fall under the same reproach. The confrontation with Durkheim and Freud is constructed; the one with Frazer is attested.

    Where should Wittgenstein be placed with regard to the criterion? He refounds nothing, and could refound nothing, since any doctrine about what is higher falls into nonsense: no cult, no morality, no community. But neither does he leave religion in the sense in which d'Holbach or Freud wanted to leave it, since he keeps intact, and even protects against science, the place of wonder, of meaning and of what shows itself. I regard him as a mystic without God and without doctrine, in the sense in which he uses the word: someone who experiences the world as a limited whole, wonders that it is, and falls silent. His position is stricter than that of Spinoza, who still spoke of God, and than that of Camus, who spoke of the absurd: Wittgenstein denies himself even the name. His silence is not an answer to the question of religion; it is the refusal to let an answer occupy the place of the question.

    In literature Rabindranath Tagore, The King of the Dark Chamber (1914) ; Leo Tolstoy, “The Three Hermits” (1886) ; Georg Trakl, Gedichte (1913)

    Wittgenstein read Tagore at the Vienna Circle, in 1927, when he preferred reading poems to arguing with Schlick, and he translated The King of the Dark Chamber with Yorick Smythies. Queen Sudarshana, in the play, can meet her husband the king only in a room without light; she complains of it to her maid: “But why should this room be kept dark?”; “Because otherwise you would know neither light nor darkness.[…] You can meet others in the lighted rooms: but only in this dark room can you meet your lord.”; and when she wants a lamp brought in: “How can I bring light to a place which he would have kept always dark!”

    Why here: the play is the Tractatus put on stage, 6.522 and 7: what is highest shows itself only where nothing can be said, and to want to light it up is to lose it. The king has no form, and the queen, who demands to see him, runs off with a false king covered in gilt, the idol of the lighted rooms. Wittgenstein did not explain why he loved the play; the dark chamber explains it for him.

    Tolstoy, whom Wittgenstein carried in his knapsack in 1916, tells in “The Three Hermits” of a bishop who, at sea, lands on an island where three hermits pray saying only: “You are three, we are three, have mercy on us”; he teaches them the Lord's Prayer with difficulty, sails away, and sees them at night running over the water behind the ship to tell him they have forgotten the prayer; the bishop crosses himself and answers that theirs is enough. It is the remark on Frazer as a tale: the rite is not a false hypothesis, it expresses, and the bishop is Frazer converted. Trakl, finally, whose poems Wittgenstein said he did not understand but whose tone made him happy, is the last piece of evidence: a meaning that shows itself without being said.

    Sources: Rabindranath Tagore, The King of the Dark Chamber, II (1914, after Raja, 1910) ; Leo Tolstoy, “Три старца” (“The Three Hermits”, 1886) ; Georg Trakl, Gedichte (1913).

    Portrait: Moritz Nähr, Public domain

    Barth1886-1968religion is the affair of godless man

    Background: Feuerbach's thought: The Essence of Christianity, the species, love, nature · Kierkegaard's thought: the stages, anxiety, despair, Abraham, the attack on Christendom · The Protestant Reformation: Luther, Calvin and the break-up of Christendom · Barth's theology: the Römerbrief, dialectical theology, the Church Dogmatics · The Churches and the totalitarian regimes: Barmen, the concordats, state atheism · The letters of Paul: Romans, Corinthians and the others · Hebrews, James, Peter, John, Jude: the other letters

    Karl Barth is the greatest Protestant theologian of the twentieth century, and the first theologian of that century, in this essay, to maintain that the critique of religion is not a weapon against faith but a demand of faith. His position is all the more singular in that he formulates it in Feuerbach's own terms, having read Feuerbach closely and taken him seriously as almost no theologian before him had.

    Trained in German liberal theology, the heir of Schleiermacher, Barth broke with it during the First World War, when he saw his teachers, Harnack and Herrmann among them, sign the “Aufruf an die Kulturwelt” of 4 October 1914, known as the Manifesto of the Ninety-Three, by which German intellectuals declared their solidarity with the war; Barth would say that he had discovered there, “with horror”, the names of almost all his German teachers. The theology that had made religion an expression of human consciousness, of feeling, of culture, seemed to him to have handed God over to man. His Römerbrief (The Epistle to the Romans, 1919, recast in 1922) proclaims, on the contrary, the infinite qualitative difference between God and man. The expression comes from Kierkegaard, and Barth says so himself in the preface to the second edition: if he has a “system”, it consists in keeping in view what Kierkegaard called the “unendlichen qualitativen Unterschied” of time and eternity; the commentary itself speaks of the “qualitativen Unterschieds von Gott und Mensch, Gott und Welt”, the qualitative difference between God and man, God and world. God is not the extension of our aspirations; he is the Wholly Other, who can be known only if he reveals himself, and who reveals himself in Jesus Christ, not in religion.

    It is in this context that paragraph 17 of the Kirchliche Dogmatik (Church Dogmatics) must be read, in volume I/2, published in 1938. Its title is already a thesis: “Gottes Offenbarung als Aufhebung der Religion”, the revelation of God as the Aufhebung of religion. The word is Hegel's, and Barth plays on it deliberately: it means at once abolition and elevation, suppression and preservation at a higher level. The central sentence of the paragraph is this: “Religion ist Unglaube; Religion ist eine Angelegenheit, man muß geradezu sagen: die Angelegenheit des gottlosen Menschen”, religion is unbelief; religion is an affair, one must say it outright: the affair of godless man.

    By “religion”, Barth means the human attempt to grasp God by one's own means: to represent him, to win him over, to justify oneself before him through works, rites, thoughts. Now this attempt is, in the eyes of revelation, the contrary of faith. Faith receives; religion takes. Faith listens to a word that comes from elsewhere; religion manufactures a god to its own measure. Barth makes no exception for Christianity: the Christian religion is a religion like the others, and as such it is unbelief. It is “true” only by grace, as a sinner is righteous only when justified. Barth uses an image: revelation illuminates the Christian religion as the sun illuminates a region of the earth, without changing its nature.

    The kinship with Feuerbach is not fortuitous. Barth devoted an essay to him in 1927, “Ludwig Feuerbach”, published in the journal Zwischen den Zeiten and then collected in Die Theologie und die Kirche (1928); it is this text which, translated into English, serves as the introductory essay to the 1957 American reissue of George Eliot's translation of The Essence of Christianity. In it Barth grants Feuerbach a victory that the apologists of the nineteenth century had always refused him: Feuerbach is “mit seiner Religionsdeutung auf der ganzen Linie Recht”, right all along the line with his interpretation of religion, at least “sofern sie sich auf die Religion als Erfahrung des bösen und sterblichen Menschen bezieht”, insofar as it bears on religion as the experience of evil and mortal man. This is an attested reading: a theologian concedes the point to theology's most feared critic.

    But he concedes it on religion, and therein lies the whole subtlety of the manoeuvre. Yes, religion is projection; yes, the God whom man represents to himself is only his own essence enlarged; yes, the theology that starts from man, from his feeling or his consciousness, like Schleiermacher's, necessarily ends in anthropology. Barth even draws from this an argument against the whole of liberal theology: Feuerbach is the truth of Schleiermacher. Only, revelation is not religion. It is not a product of consciousness; it comes from elsewhere, and it is precisely for this reason that it judges religion. Feuerbach's critique, turned around, becomes an instrument for purifying faith.

    The boldness of the move is considerable. Feuerbach believed he had dissolved theology into anthropology. Barth replies: you have dissolved religion, and you were right to do so; faith was not in what you dissolved. It is the reverse of Stirner's operation: Stirner showed that the atheist remained pious; Barth shows that the pious man, as religious, is an atheist, “gottlos”, without God.

    The objection is well known, and it was formulated as early as the 1960s: Barth removes revelation from critique by declaring it out of reach, but this removal holds only for someone who already believes. John Glasse, in “Barth on Feuerbach” (Harvard Theological Review 57, 1964), and others after him have argued that the Barthian answer is intelligible only from within faith. Feuerbach could reply that “revelation” is the most refined projection of all: the one that declares itself unprojected. And a reader of Nietzsche would add that the distinction between religion and faith is itself a religious gesture, the one by which the priest reserves for himself the truth he denies to others.

    I believe, however, that Barth scores a point that this objection does not erase. He establishes that the critique of religion is not, by nature, a critique of transcendence; it can be a critique of the appropriation of transcendence. What he condemns in religion is man making use of God, and this condemnation meets, by an entirely different road, what Spinoza said of the vulgar who imagine a God in their own image, what Marx said of opium, what Nietzsche said of the priest. Our question then takes a new form: leaving religion without founding another might perhaps be possible if one agrees not to leave faith. It is a wager that most of our authors would refuse, and one that an unruly pupil of Barth was to push to its most extreme consequences.

    In literature Georges Bernanos, The Diary of a Country Priest (1936) ; Franz Kafka, Der Prozess (1925)

    The curé of Ambricourt, in The Diary of a Country Priest, keeps the tally of his failures: a parish that is bored, a body that is falling apart, conversations in which he convinces no one, and a countess from whom he wrests, an hour before her death, the consent she was refusing God. He dies in the home of a former fellow seminarian who has left the priesthood, without a priest, and his last words, reported in a letter from that friend, are: “Qu'est-ce que cela fait ? Tout est grâce”, what does it matter? All is grace. Why here: Bernanos wrote the Dogmatics I/2 as a novel. What the curé possesses, his pastoral method, his reasons, his health, is the affair of man and serves no purpose; what acts passes through him without his knowing it, and the only sentence that counts is the one that strips him of all merit. “Religion ist Unglaube” is not a theologian's thesis; it is the diary of a man to whom religion gave nothing and from whom faith took everything.

    In the cathedral of The Trial, the prison chaplain tells Josef K. the parable of the door of the Law, discusses every possible reading of it with him, and concludes: “Das Gericht will nichts von dir. Es nimmt dich auf, wenn du kommst, und es entläßt dich, wenn du gehst”, the court wants nothing from you; it receives you when you come and dismisses you when you go. This is Barth's infinite qualitative difference, seen from below: an authority that expects nothing, that can be neither swayed nor understood, and before which every “religion”, every step the accused takes, is a misunderstanding. Kafka does not say that this court is God; Barth would say that the God of religion is this court, and that faith begins when one stops pleading.

    Sources: Georges Bernanos, Journal d'un curé de campagne (1936) ; Franz Kafka, Der Prozess, ch. 9, “Im Dom” (written 1914-1915, published 1925).

    Portrait: Hans Lachmann, CC BY-SA 3.0 de

    Bonhoeffer1906-1945living before God without God

    Background: The Protestant Reformation: Luther, Calvin and the break-up of Christendom · Barth's theology: the Römerbrief, dialectical theology, the Church Dogmatics · The thought of Bonhoeffer: The Cost of Discipleship, the Ethics, the prison letters · Twentieth-century Christian theology: dialectical, existential, Catholic, death of God · The Churches and the totalitarian regimes: Barmen, the concordats, state atheism

    Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a Lutheran pastor trained in Berlin, close to Barth without being his disciple, joined the Confessing Church against the Nazi takeover of German Protestantism, then the resistance circles preparing the elimination of Hitler. Arrested in April 1943, he was executed at the Flossenbürg camp on 9 April 1945, a few weeks before the end of the war. The letters he wrote from Tegel prison to his friend Eberhard Bethge, published by Bethge in 1951 under the title Widerstand und Ergebung (Resistance and Submission), contain some of the most debated pages in the theology of the century.

    The starting point is an observation, formulated in the letter of 30 April 1944: “Wir gehen einer völlig religionslosen Zeit entgegen; die Menschen können einfach, so wie sie nun einmal sind, nicht mehr religiös sein”, we are moving towards a completely religionless time; people as they now are simply cannot be religious any more. This observation is not a lament: Bonhoeffer does not regret the religious age and does not wish to restore it. He asks what becomes of Christ in a world that no longer needs religion.

    By “religion” he means neither faith nor Christianity as such, but a certain way of believing, settled in the Christian West, which rests on three features: metaphysics, which places God in a world behind the world; inwardness, which lodges him in the secret of the individual soul; and above all recourse to God at the limits, where human knowledge and power fail. It is this last feature that he designates by the word Lückenbüßer, the stopgap. The God of religion is the one called upon when we no longer know, when we no longer can, when we die. Now, as science, technology, medicine and politics push back these limits, this God retreats: a God of the gaps, he loses a province with every human advance.

    In the letter of 16 July 1944, the most famous, Bonhoeffer retraces the history of modern autonomy, from Herbert of Cherbury to Grotius, from Descartes to Kant, and concludes: “Gott als moralische, politische, naturwissenschaftliche Arbeitshypothese ist abgeschafft, überwunden; ebenso aber als philosophische und religiöse Arbeitshypothese (Feuerbach!)”, God as a moral, political, scientific working hypothesis has been abolished, overcome; but so too as a philosophical and religious working hypothesis (Feuerbach!). Feuerbach's name, in parentheses and followed by an exclamation mark, is an attested mention. Bonhoeffer does not refute Feuerbach: he records him as an irreversible stage in the history of consciousness, behind which there is no going back.

    In the same letter, Bonhoeffer takes up Grotius's formula, “etsi deus non daretur”, as if God were not given. Grotius had used it to say that natural law would hold even if God did not exist. Bonhoeffer turns it into a maxim of Christian life: one must live in the world as if God were not given. And he adds the sentence that caused a scandal: “Vor und mit Gott leben wir ohne Gott. Gott läßt sich aus der Welt herausdrängen ans Kreuz, Gott ist ohnmächtig und schwach in der Welt und gerade und nur so ist er bei uns und hilft uns”, before God and with God we live without God. God lets himself be pushed out of the world and onto the cross; God is powerless and weak in the world, and precisely thus, and only thus, is he with us and does he help us.

    This thought overturns, term by term, the critique of the nineteenth century. Feuerbach said: God is the projection of human power; man strips himself of his strengths in order to adore them in an all-powerful being. Bonhoeffer replies: the God of the cross is not all-powerful; he is weak, he lets himself be driven out, and it is this very weakness that makes him a God and not a projection. Marx said: religion consoles for powerlessness. Bonhoeffer replies: faith is not the recourse of the powerless; it is the life of the adult, who no longer needs God to plug the holes in his knowledge. Nietzsche said: Christianity is a religion of pity, which preserves the weak. Bonhoeffer replies: Christianity is participation in the suffering of God in the world, not an escape from the world.

    Two days later, on 18 July 1944, Bonhoeffer returns to the idea of a world come of age, “mündig gewordene Welt”, an expression that echoes the Kantian definition of the Enlightenment as emergence from the state of immaturity. This world come of age is, he writes, “gottloser und darum vielleicht gerade Gott-näher als die unmündige Welt”, more godless, and for that very reason perhaps closer to God than the world not yet come of age.

    A misreading must first be set aside. Bonhoeffer did not preach an atheist Christianity, nor a “death of God” in the sense of the American theologians of the 1960s who would claim him as their own. He believes in God, he prays, he dies a Christian. What he rejects is religion as a historical form of faith, and he seeks a “non-religious interpretation” of biblical concepts. I have not verified that the exact phrase “religionsloses Christentum”, religionless Christianity, appears in the letters, although it circulates everywhere under his name; I therefore give it as a received summary, not as a quotation.

    Bonhoeffer also distinguishes himself from Barth, and the distinction is attested. In the letters of May and June 1944, he reproaches his elder with an “Offenbarungspositivismus”, a positivism of revelation: Barth was right to criticize religion, but he put in its place a revelation to be taken or left, a block of dogmas that must be swallowed whole. This is, in theological terms, the very objection that Feuerbach could have made to Barth: revelation declared out of reach becomes a new positivity, a new law. Bonhoeffer is no gentler with Bultmann, who wanted to demythologize the New Testament: “Bultmanns Ansatz ist eben im Grund doch liberal”, Bultmann's approach is, at bottom, liberal after all. To demythologize is still to reduce faith to what modern man can accept: it is to do Schleiermacher over again.

    Bonhoeffer thus attempts a narrow path between two failures: that of liberal theology, which dissolves faith into culture, and that of Barth, which freezes it into positive revelation. The dogmaticians who followed him doubted that it was practicable, and history seemed to prove him wrong on one point at least: the forecast of a “completely religionless” time turned out to be false, since the last third of the twentieth century saw religion return everywhere in forms Bonhoeffer had not foreseen. But this empirical refutation does not touch the heart of his thought, which is not a sociological prophecy: faith does not need religion, and the fading of religion can be an opportunity for it.

    Here we have the radical form of the Christian answer to our question. Can one leave religion without founding another? Yes, Bonhoeffer answers, on condition of not leaving Christ. The exit from religion is not the end of faith but its purification, and this purification passes through the acceptance of a weak, absent, crucified God. It will be objected, and I object, that this weak God looks very much like a projection of the condition of the prisoner of Tegel: a man reduced to powerlessness, who turns his powerlessness into a place of divine presence. But the objection turns back on itself: if projection produces a powerless God, without glory, who does not console and guarantees nothing, it is no longer the projection Feuerbach described, the one that gave God all the perfections man denied himself. It is, on the contrary, a dispossession. And it was this dispossession that a French philosopher, who died in the same year as Bonhoeffer's arrest, had pushed further.

    In literature Albert Camus, The Plague (1947) ; Graham Greene, The Power and the Glory (1940)

    In The Plague, Father Paneloux preaches twice. The first sermon, at the beginning of the epidemic, explains the scourge as a deserved punishment, and the narrator reports its opening: misfortune, the Jesuit says in substance, you have deserved it. Then Paneloux witnesses, with Doctor Rieux, the death agony of the child of Judge Othon, whose death is described hour by hour; Rieux flings at him that this child, at least, was innocent. The second sermon no longer says “you” but “we”, and it asks that one believe everything or deny everything, accept the child's death because one cannot understand it; Paneloux dies shortly afterwards, of an illness that is perhaps not the plague, and his record card reads: doubtful case.

    Why here: Paneloux is the theologian who carries out, without knowing it, the programme of the Tegel letters. The first sermon is the stopgap God and the God of explanations, the one Bonhoeffer dismisses; the second is the weak God who guarantees nothing and does not console, before whom one must live “etsi deus non daretur”. Camus, an unbeliever, wrote the trajectory that Bonhoeffer, a believer, was travelling in prison in the same year; and he judged it: Rieux works, Paneloux dies, and the novel does not say which of the two is right, only which one remains.

    Greene, in The Power and the Glory, follows in Mexico a nameless priest, a drunkard, the father of a child, hunted by an atheist and upright lieutenant, who goes on saying Mass because he is the last; he gives himself up in order to hear a dying man's confession, and he is shot. The unworthy priest and the virtuous policeman are the two faces of a God who no longer helps by his omnipotence but by his weakness: in Greene, the Church holds by a man who hardly believes in it any more, and that is why it holds.

    Sources: Albert Camus, La Peste, II and IV (1947) ; Graham Greene, The Power and the Glory (1940).

    Portrait: Auteur inconnu, CC BY-SA 3.0 de

    Simone Weil1909-1943atheism as purification

    Background: The thought of Meister Eckhart: detachment, the birth of God in the soul, the trial · Christian mysticism: from Dionysius to John of the Cross and quietism · Antigone: the law of the city and the unwritten laws · The thought of Bonhoeffer: The Cost of Discipleship, the Ethics, the prison letters · The thought of Simone Weil: attention, affliction, decreation, rootedness · The Trojan War: Iphigenia at Aulis, the wrath of Achilles, Priam · Matthew and Luke: the infancy, the Sermon on the Mount, the parables · The thought of Iris Murdoch: the novels, the Good, attention · The teaching of Jesus: the Kingdom, the parables, the miracles · The letters of Paul: Romans, Corinthians and the others

    Simone Weil died at Ashford, in England, on 24 August 1943, at the age of thirty-four. An agrégée in philosophy, a pupil of Alain, a factory worker at Alsthom and at Renault, a short-lived combatant in the Spanish Civil War, she had, from 1937 and 1938 onwards, mystical experiences that she describes with extreme sobriety, without ever asking for baptism. She remains on the threshold of the Church, out of fidelity, she says, to everything the Church has excluded. She published no book in her lifetime. Gravity and Grace (1947) is a compilation of fragments drawn from her notebooks, chosen, ordered and titled by Gustave Thibon, to whom she had entrusted her notebooks in 1942; the chapter titles and their order are his. What one quotes, then, are fragments, not a composed doctrine.

    One of these chapters is entitled “L'athéisme purificateur”, purifying atheism. It opens with a paradox that Weil accepts without trying to resolve it: “Cas de contradictoires vrais. Dieu existe, Dieu n'existe pas. Où est le problème ? Je suis tout à fait sûre qu'il y a un Dieu, en ce sens que je suis tout à fait sûre que mon amour n'est pas illusoire. Je suis tout à fait sûre qu'il n'y a pas de Dieu, en ce sens que je suis tout à fait sûre que rien de réel ne ressemble à ce que je peux concevoir quand je prononce ce nom. Mais cela que je ne puis concevoir n'est pas une illusion”, a case of contradictories that are both true. God exists, God does not exist. Where is the problem? I am quite sure that there is a God, in the sense that I am quite sure my love is not illusory. I am quite sure that there is no God, in the sense that I am quite sure nothing real resembles what I can conceive when I pronounce that name. But that which I cannot conceive is not an illusion.

    Weil does not say that God exists in one way and does not exist in another, according to a convenient scholastic distinction. She says that both propositions are true, and true together. God exists, in the sense that the love that turns towards him is not an illusion. God does not exist, in the sense that everything I can represent to myself under that name is false. The negation bears on the representation, the affirmation on the orientation. And this double truth leads to the most quoted sentence of the chapter: “Il y a deux athéismes dont l'un est une purification de la notion de Dieu”, there are two atheisms, one of which is a purification of the notion of God.

    What is the other? Weil does not name it, but the context points to it: the atheism that denies God in order to put man in his place, the humanist atheism of Feuerbach and Comte. That one is not a purification; it is one more idolatry. Weil says so elsewhere in the same chapter, with a severity that meets Stirner by an entirely different road: “Les erreurs de notre époque sont du christianisme sans surnaturel. Le laïcisme en est la cause”, the errors of our age are Christianity without the supernatural. Secularism is the cause of them. Christianity without the supernatural is the religion of Humanity, Christian morality kept without God, which Nietzsche mocked in the English “atheists” and which Stirner denounced in Feuerbach. Weil rejects it, but in the name of the supernatural, not in the name of the Unique One.

    Purifying atheism, by contrast, denies the false God, and Weil specifies what it is: “La religion en tant que source de consolation est un obstacle à la véritable foi : en ce sens l'athéisme est une purification. Je dois être athée avec la partie de moi-même qui n'est pas faite pour Dieu. Parmi les hommes chez qui la partie surnaturelle d'eux-mêmes n'est pas éveillée, les athées ont raison et les croyants ont tort”, religion as a source of consolation is an obstacle to true faith: in this sense atheism is a purification. I must be an atheist with the part of myself that is not made for God. Among those in whom the supernatural part of themselves has not been awakened, the atheists are right and the believers wrong.

    This fragment matters to our question, for it answers Marx directly. Marx said that religion is the opium of the people, the consolation of the oppressed creature. Weil adopts this as her own, and draws from it a conclusion he had not envisaged: what Marx criticized as illusion, Weil criticizes as idolatry. And among those who have no experience of the supernatural, the atheist is right against the believer, because the believer without experience adores an image. In the same chapter: “Entre deux hommes qui n'ont pas l'expérience de Dieu, celui qui le nie en est peut-être le plus près”, between two men who have no experience of God, the one who denies him is perhaps the closer to him. The confrontation is constructed, and the biography warrants it: Weil read Marx, she was a trade-union and revolutionary activist, and her critique of religious consolation is a Marxist critique turned towards the supernatural.

    Weil also proposes a practice: “Un mode de purification : prier Dieu, non seulement en secret par rapport aux hommes, mais en pensant que Dieu n'existe pas”, one mode of purification: to pray to God, not only in secret with regard to men, but thinking that God does not exist. The formula meets, across six centuries, Eckhart's prayer quoted in Part One, to ask God to be freed of God. It also meets Bonhoeffer, living before God as if God were not given, and Heidegger, for whom godless thinking is perhaps closer to the divine God. These convergences are constructed confrontations, with no established reading of one by another; but their concordance, within the space of fifteen years, from 1942 to 1957, says something about the age: the critique of religion had ceased to be the monopoly of unbelievers.

    The metaphysical heart of this thought is the notion of decreation. The chapter bearing that title opens thus: “Décréation : faire passer du créé dans l'incréé. Destruction : faire passer du créé dans le néant. Ersatz coupable de la décréation”, decreation: to make something created pass into the uncreated. Destruction: to make something created pass into nothingness. A guilty substitute for decreation. Then: “La création est un acte d'amour et elle est perpétuelle. À chaque instant notre existence est amour de Dieu pour nous. Mais Dieu ne peut aimer que soi-même. Son amour pour nous est amour pour soi à travers nous. Ainsi, lui qui nous donne l'être, il aime en nous le consentement à ne pas être”, creation is an act of love and it is perpetual. At every instant our existence is God's love for us. But God can love only himself. His love for us is love for himself through us. Thus he who gives us being loves in us the consent not to be.

    God, in creating, withdrew: he renounced being everything so that something other than himself could exist. Weil writes it in a single line: “Dieu renonce, en un sens, à être tout. Nous devons renoncer à être quelque chose. C'est le seul bien pour nous”, God renounces, in a sense, being everything. We must renounce being something. That is the only good for us. Spirituality is then neither the flourishing of the self nor its divinization, but the imitation of the divine withdrawal: the self must consent not to be, so that God may pass through it.

    The gap with Part Six is total. Feuerbach wanted to give back to man the predicates he had alienated in God; Weil wants man to renounce even those he believes he possesses. Stirner founded his cause on nothing, and this nothing was the creative self, “das schöpferische Nichts”. Weil founds hers on a nothing of another nature: the consent of the self to efface itself. Both start from nothingness, but in opposite directions: Stirner's nothingness is a power that consumes, Weil's an absence that lets through.

    This thought provides, in my view, a fine instrument for distinguishing a spirituality that serves as opium from one that does not: consolation. It is not a second criterion of refoundation, which remains the absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded; it is an indicator. Every thought that consoles, promises, guarantees a reward, whether heavenly, as with Nietzsche's priests, or historical, as with the Marxists, keeps religion's function as opium. A spirituality that does not console, that accepts misfortune without justifying it and consents without hoping for compensation, escapes it. Weil says so in another fragment of the collection: “Il ne faut pas avoir de consolation”, one must not have consolation.

    The objection is serious. This spirituality of consent, of renunciation, of decreation, resembles feature for feature what Nietzsche called the ascetic ideal: the will turned against itself, which would rather will nothingness than not will. I believe the objection is partly right, and it would be dishonest to set it aside in the name of the admiration Weil inspires. But it misses the essential point. The ascetic ideal, according to Nietzsche, gives a meaning to suffering; it makes it bearable by interpreting it as punishment or as trial. Weil refuses precisely that: she gives no meaning to misfortune, she refuses to let one be given. Misfortune is neither a punishment nor a means; it is the condition of the creature subject to necessity, and the only right attitude is to look at it without disguising it. In this sense Weil is closer to Spinoza than to Saint Paul: she wants to see necessity as it is.

    I therefore hold Weil to be the principal believing candidate for the rank of exception, alongside Spinoza, Hume, Nietzsche and Wittgenstein. She does not leave religion, since she believes. But she leaves consoling religion, the religion that founds and guarantees, and she does so while keeping the name of God and denying every representation of God. She is, with Eckhart, the proof that a spirituality can be a critique of religion from within.

    In literature Homer, Iliad (8th century BCE) ; Sophocles, Antigone (c. 442 BCE)

    Weil wrote in 1939 that the Iliad is the poem of force, and that its only gentleness lies in the moments when force stops. The last book is where this happens: Priam, led by night by Hermes, enters Achilles' tent and kisses his hands; “Souviens-toi de ton père, ô Akhilleus égal aux dieux ! Il est de mon âge et sur le seuil fatal de la vieillesse.[…] Un seul défendait ma ville et mes peuples, Hektôr, que tu viens de tuer tandis qu'il combattait pour sa patrie.[…] Respecte les dieux, Akhilleus, et, te souvenant de ton père, aie pitié de moi qui suis plus malheureux que lui, car j'ai pu, ce qu'aucun homme n'a encore fait sur la terre, approcher de ma bouche les mains de celui qui a tué mes enfants !”, remember your father, godlike Achilles, who is of my age, on the grim threshold of old age; the one son who guarded my city and my people, Hector, you have just killed as he fought for his country; revere the gods, Achilles, and, remembering your father, pity me, who am more wretched than he, for I have done what no other man on earth has done, and raised to my lips the hands of the man who killed my sons. Achilles gently pushes him away: “Comment as-tu osé venir seul vers les nefs des Akhaiens et soutenir la vue de l'homme qui t'a tué tant de braves enfants ? Ton cœur est de fer”, how did you dare come alone to the ships of the Achaeans and face the eyes of the man who killed so many of your brave sons? Your heart is of iron; “et ils se souvenaient tous deux ; et Priamos, prosterné aux pieds d'Akhilleus, pleurait de toutes ses larmes le tueur d'hommes Hektôr ; et Akhilleus pleurait son père et Patroklos”, and the two of them remembered; and Priam, huddled at the feet of Achilles, wept without restraint for man-slaying Hector; and Achilles wept for his father, and for Patroclus.

    Why here: Weil reads in this scene what the essay retains from her, the refusal to give a meaning to misfortune. Priam does not ask why, Achilles explains nothing; each of the two weeps for his own dead, without consolation and without theodicy, and that is the poem's only justice. Misfortune here is neither punishment nor trial; it is the condition of the creature subject to force, and the pity that arises for an instant between the killer and the father is the exact contrary of the ascetic ideal: it does not interpret.

    Weil taught Antigone to the workers of Rosières in 1936, to show them, she wrote, that a two-thousand-year-old tragedy concerned them. Antigone answers Creon, who reproaches her for honouring the rebel brother: “Je suis née non pour une haine mutuelle, mais pour un mutuel amour”, I was born not to share in hatred but to share in love; and he: “Si ta nature est d'aimer, va chez les morts et aime-les. Tant que je vivrai, une femme ne commandera pas”, if love is your nature, go down to the dead and love them; while I live, no woman shall rule. This is the essay's criterion in its ancient form: the city that demands a sacrifice, and a woman who offers her life without demanding anyone else's, in the name of an unwritten law she has no word to name. Weil saw the supernatural in it; the essay sees in it the self-offering that refounds nothing, and the refusal of the scapegoat before Girard.

    Sources: Homer, Iliad, XXIV, trans. Leconte de Lisle (8th century BCE) ; Sophocles, Antigone, trans. Leconte de Lisle (c. 442 BCE) ; Simone Weil, “L'Iliade ou le poème de la force” (1940-1941) and “Antigone” (1936), for the reading.

    Portrait: Auteur inconnu, Public domain

    Bataille1897-1962experience without God, and atheology

    Background: The thought of Simone Weil: attention, affliction, decreation, rootedness · Bataille's thought: expenditure, the accursed share, sovereignty, the College of Sociology

    Georges Bataille was a librarian at the Bibliothèque nationale; he converted to Catholicism in 1914 and spent a year at the seminary of Saint-Flour before entering the École des chartes in 1918, then became an atheist, an adversary and later a fellow traveller of surrealism, a founder of reviews and secret societies, and a passionate reader of Nietzsche at a time when Nietzsche was suspected in France of Nazism. During the war he undertook a Summa Atheologica: the title parodies the Summa theologiae of Thomas Aquinas and announces an enterprise of the same scope, but in the opposite direction. The project, left unfinished, comprises Inner Experience (1943), Guilty (1944) and On Nietzsche (1945).

    The word “atheology” is thus Bataille's, and it matters for our story, since Michel Onfray would take it up in 2005 for his Traité d'athéologie. Onfray declares that he borrows it from Bataille's project. A theologian who reviewed the Traité, Emilio Brito, observes that Onfray borrows the word but does not use it in the same sense. The observation seems to me correct. For Onfray, atheology is a rational critique of the monotheisms, a dismantling of their lies. For Bataille, it is the search for an experience that has the form of mystical ecstasy but refers to no God.

    The first volume of the Summa gives, a few pages after its opening, a definition: “J'appelle expérience un voyage au bout du possible de l'homme”, I call experience a journey to the end of what is possible for man. And Bataille had fixed its meaning from the first page: he has in mind “moins à l'expérience confessionnelle, à laquelle on a dû se tenir jusqu'ici, qu'à une expérience nue, libre d'attaches, même d'origine, à quelque confession que ce soit”, less the confessional experience to which one has had to keep until now than a naked experience, free of ties, even of origin, to any confession whatever. Inner experience is thus that of the mystics, the wrenching away, the ecstasy, the loss of self, but delivered from its confessional framework. It leads to no God, to no salvation, to no knowledge, but to non-knowledge, to night, to what Bataille calls the impossible.

    The kinship with Weil has a history: the two met in the early 1930s, in Boris Souvarine's Cercle communiste démocratique and around his review La Critique sociale, and Bataille drew a barely veiled portrait of Weil in the figure of Lazare in Blue of Noon, finished in 1935 and published in 1957. Like Weil, Bataille wants an experience without any representation of God, and the loss of the self. But where Weil consents not to be so as to let God pass through, Bataille loses himself for the sake of losing himself, letting nothing pass through; where she seeks decreation, he seeks expenditure, transgression, excess. His sacred is not that of a love which withdraws, but that of the festival, of sacrifice, of eroticism and of death. It comes from Durkheim and Mauss, whom Bataille read closely, more than from Saint John of the Cross.

    The response that follows is attested. In 1943, Jean-Paul Sartre published in the Cahiers du Sud a review of Inner Experience under an ironic title, “Un nouveau mystique” (“A New Mystic”). In it he reproaches Bataille for remaining a shamefaced Christian, a mystic who has lost God but keeps the posture of the believer. He writes in particular: “Dieu est mort : n'entendons pas par là qu'il n'existe pas, ni même qu'il n'existe plus. Il est mort : il nous parlait et il se tait, nous ne touchons plus que son cadavre”, God is dead: let us not take this to mean that he does not exist, nor even that he no longer exists. He is dead: he used to speak to us and he is silent, we now touch only his corpse. The sentence describes Bataille as Sartre sees him: a man who lives in mourning for God, who touches the corpse, and who turns this mourning into an experience. For Sartre, this is an imposture: one does not leave religion by prolonging indefinitely one's mourning for God. Bataille would reply in an appendix to On Nietzsche in 1945.

    I believe that Sartre is right on one point and wrong on the essential one. He is right when he notes that Bataille keeps the whole structure of Christian mysticism: asceticism, the dark night, ecstasy, the language of the impossible. But Sartre is wrong when he concludes that it is an imposture. Bataille does not claim to have overcome religion through reason; he claims that the experience religion used to frame can be lived outside it, and that it is truer there. This is William James's thesis, turned towards night rather than towards light, and Sartre, for whom consciousness is always transparent to itself, could not hear it.

    Bataille gave this experience a theory, in a book written around 1948 and published after his death, Theory of Religion (1973). I have read no extract from it; according to the publishers' presentations, religion is understood there as the search for a lost intimacy, the intimacy of the animal with the world, which labour, the tool and discursive thought have broken. If that is indeed the thesis, it places Bataille in a singular position: religion is neither an error, nor a symptom, nor an illusion of desire, but the memory of a continuity that man lost in becoming man. And the exit from religion is not progress; it is the completion of the rupture.

    I hold Bataille to be a witness of capital importance, but not an exception. He does not refound a religion in the sense of Comte or the late Heidegger: he promises nothing, awaits nothing, organizes nothing. But he refounds a sacred, that of transgression, and this sacred has its rites, the festival, eroticism, sacrifice, and its officiants, the members of the secret society Acéphale which he founded in 1936 and which lasted until 1939. Bataille's atheology is not an exit from the religious; it is its radicalization outside God. It confirms, unexpectedly, the thesis of Durkheim set out in Part Eight: one can do without God, one cannot do without the sacred.

    In literature Charles Baudelaire, “The Litanies of Satan” (1857) ; Joris-Karl Huysmans, Là-bas (1891) ; D. A. F. de Sade, Juliette (1797)

    “Ô toi, le plus savant et le plus beau des Anges, / Dieu trahi par le sort et privé de louanges, / Ô Satan, prends pitié de ma longue misère !”, O thou, the most learned and the fairest of the Angels, / God betrayed by fate and deprived of praise, / O Satan, take pity on my long misery! The refrain returns fifteen times in “The Litanies of Satan”, and the prayer is addressed to “Toi qui sais tout, grand roi des choses souterraines”, Thou who knowest all, great king of things underground, the patron of pariahs, of the condemned and of inventors. Why here: the poem is a liturgy, with its responses and its closing prayer, and it inverts the Mass without leaving it. This is the sacred of transgression that the essay recognizes in Bataille: one does not leave the cult, one reverses its address, and the rite remains.

    Huysmans, in Là-bas, has Durtal, the writer investigating Gilles de Rais, attend a black mass celebrated in a Parisian chapel by an apostate priest, Canon Docre, before hysterical women, with the profanation of the hosts; Durtal comes away sickened, and Huysmans would go from there to the Trappists. The novel shows what Durkheim would say of Acéphale: a secret society that needs a god to profane in order to have a sacred. Sade, finally, from whom Bataille learned everything, has his libertines say that crime is the only means of offending a nature that takes no offence, and blasphemy the only pleasure left to one who no longer believes: atheology before the word, and its contradiction, since one still needs a God in order to outrage him.

    Sources: Charles Baudelaire, “Les Litanies de Satan”, Les Fleurs du mal, “Révolte” (1857) ; Joris-Karl Huysmans, Là-bas, ch. XIX (1891) ; D. A. F. de Sade, Histoire de Juliette (1797).

    Sartre1905-1980atheism as a starting point

    Background: Dostoevsky's work: the Karamazovs, Demons, polyphony · Existentialism: from Kierkegaard to Sartre, believers and atheists · Bataille's thought: expenditure, the accursed share, sovereignty, the College of Sociology · Sartre's philosophy: being-in-itself, being-for-itself, freedom, bad faith, commitment · The Atreids: Agamemnon, Clytemnestra, Orestes and the Erinyes

    Sartre is not a thinker of religion. He wrote no book on it, and his atheism is not the outcome of a critique but a premise. That is what makes him valuable here: he marks the moment when atheism ceases to be a thesis to be demonstrated and becomes a situation to be assumed. He is the hurried heir of the whole series, the one who takes for granted what Feuerbach, Marx and Nietzsche had conquered, and who asks what it costs.

    The programmatic formula is found in the lecture given in Paris on 29 October 1945 and published the following year, Existentialism Is a Humanism: “L'existentialisme n'est pas autre chose qu'un effort pour tirer toutes les conséquences d'une position athée cohérente”, existentialism is nothing other than an effort to draw all the consequences of a coherent atheist position. The important word is “cohérente”, coherent. Sartre reproaches the atheists of the nineteenth century, and he expressly targets the “professeurs français” (French professors) who, “vers 1880” (around 1880), wanted to “constituer une morale laïque” (establish a secular morality), in short “tout ce qu'on appelle en France le radicalisme” (everything that in France is called radicalism), for having suppressed God while keeping everything else: a human nature, an a priori morality, values inscribed in an intelligible heaven. This is, in Sartrean terms, Stirner's objection to Feuerbach and Nietzsche's to the freethinkers, but formulated in the name of a consequence rather than a genealogy: if God does not exist, there is no human nature, since there is no God to conceive it; existence precedes essence; man is nothing other than what he makes of himself; he is condemned to be free, and without excuse.

    It is in this context that Sartre invokes Dostoevsky, and one must be exact, for it was established above that the formula “if God does not exist, everything is permitted” does not appear in this proverbial form in the Karamazovs. Sartre writes, in Existentialism Is a Humanism: “Dostoïevsky avait écrit : ‘Si Dieu n'existait pas, tout serait permis.’ C'est là le point de départ de l'existentialisme”, Dostoevsky had written: “If God did not exist, everything would be permitted.” That is the starting point of existentialism. Sartre thus attributes to Dostoevsky a formula manufactured by the reception, and makes it the starting point of a philosophy. It is an exemplary case of what tradition makes a text say: Ivan puts forward a conditional thesis, which Smerdyakov takes seriously and which the novel puts to the test; Sartre makes it an axiom.

    Yet the use Sartre makes of the formula matters more than the misattribution. For Ivan, and for the adversaries of atheism, “everything is permitted” is a threat: without God, no more morality. For Sartre, it is a liberation that is at the same time a burden: everything is permitted, so nothing is guaranteed, so I am responsible for everything. The absence of God does not abolish morality; it abolishes its guarantees, and lays on each choice the weight of a universal legislation. Sartre turns Ivan around as Bonhoeffer turned Feuerbach around: what was an objection becomes a task.

    There is, finally, in The Words (1964), the autobiography of his childhood, a sentence saying that atheism “est une entreprise cruelle et de longue haleine”, is a cruel and long-drawn-out undertaking. The context is that of the writer who realizes that literature had been for him a salvation, a substitute religion, and who must rid himself of it. The admission carries weight: the most declared atheist of his time acknowledges that he refounded a religion, that of writing, and that it took him decades to notice.

    Sartre is thus a witness for the prosecution of our thesis, and a lucid witness. He shows that the exit from religion is never secured, that it is an “entreprise”, an undertaking, and that it remains unfinished even in the man who proclaimed it finished. But I do not count him among the exceptions. His atheism is all of a piece, without spiritual remainder, and that is its limit: Sartre sees in religion only an escape from freedom, bad faith, and grants it nothing of what Marx still granted it, protest, nor of what James or Bergson granted it, experience. Ph. Cabestan observes that Sartre remains indifferent to the death of God as an event, unlike Heidegger. One can go further: for Sartre, the death of God is not an event, because God never lived. This is the position of the man of the marketplace in § 125 of The Gay Science, that of the unbelievers who laugh at the madman.

    Heidegger, moreover, replied to the 1945 lecture in the Letter on Humanism (Brief über den Humanismus, written in 1946, published in 1947), rejecting the existentialism and the humanism attributed to him. The response is attested: Heidegger reproaches Sartre for remaining a metaphysician by simply inverting the order of essence and existence, the very reproach he had made to Nietzsche. Sartre's coherent atheism remains, in his eyes, within onto-theology: it has replaced God with human freedom as foundation.

    In literature Jean-Paul Sartre, The Flies (1943) ; Jean-Paul Sartre, The Devil and the Good Lord (1951)

    Sartre put his lecture on the stage, before and after delivering it. In The Flies, Orestes returns to Argos, where Jupiter reigns through remorse and Aegisthus governs through fear; he kills Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, then refuses Jupiter his repentance: the men of Argos are his men, he must open their eyes, and he leaves taking the flies, the Erinyes, far from the city. In The Devil and the Good Lord, Goetz, a warlord, wagers first on absolute evil, then on absolute good, founds a City of the Sun which is massacred, and discovers that God has never answered him: there are only men, he concludes, and he takes command of the rebel peasants.

    Why here: the two plays are the very movement of Existentialism Is a Humanism, and they show the remainder the essay points out. Orestes and Goetz leave God through an act, not through a demonstration, and they keep from religion the form of sacrifice: Orestes carries off the flies like a voluntary scapegoat, Goetz takes upon himself the evil of all. Sartre wanted to draw all the consequences of a coherent atheist position; his heroes draw them by taking up the role of the redeemer, and this is what the essay calls the religion of writing, avowed in The Words: an atheist who can think of freedom only as a passion.

    Sources: Jean-Paul Sartre, Les Mouches (1943) ; Jean-Paul Sartre, Le Diable et le bon Dieu (1951).

    Portrait: T1980, CC BY 3.0

    Camus1913-1960revolt and measure

    Background: Max Stirner and The Ego and Its Own: the Ego against the spectres · Kierkegaard's thought: the stages, anxiety, despair, Abraham, the attack on Christendom · Dostoevsky's work: the Karamazovs, Demons, polyphony · Prometheus and Pandora: the sharing of the sacrifice, fire, evil · Sisyphus and the underworld: Hades, Tantalus, the Danaids · Sartre's philosophy: being-in-itself, being-for-itself, freedom, bad faith, commitment · The thought of Camus: the absurd, revolt, the cycles

    Camus is the only author in this part who himself composed, before this essay, a genealogy of the exit from religion covering almost all our authors. The Rebel (1951) devotes chapters to Stirner, to Ivan Karamazov, to Nietzsche, to Marx, to Hegel, to Sade, to the regicides and deicides of the Revolution. Camus is therefore not only an author to be placed, but a competitor, whose answer to the same question must be discussed.

    The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) set out from the absurd: the confrontation between the human call for meaning and the unreasonable silence of the world. Religion there is one of the temptations to be refused: that of the “saut”, the leap, for which Camus reproaches Kierkegaard and Shestov, and which consists in making the absurd itself a path towards God. Camus asks that one live in the absurd without leaving it either through suicide or through faith, and he ends on the image of Sisyphus going back down towards his rock: “La lutte elle-même vers les sommets suffit à remplir un cœur d'homme. Il faut imaginer Sisyphe heureux”, the struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy. The happiness of Sisyphus promises nothing, justifies nothing: it is, avant la lettre, a spirituality without consolation, in the sense in which Weil spoke of it in the very year Camus published this book.

    The Rebel shifts the question from the absurd to revolt. The central formula is a cogito: “Je me révolte, donc nous sommes”, I rebel, therefore we are. Revolt is not a solitary act: it discovers, in the very refusal, a value common to all men, something in me that must not be violated and that is also in the other. And it has a metaphysical form: “La révolte métaphysique est le mouvement par lequel un homme se dresse contre sa condition et la création tout entière”, metaphysical revolt is the movement by which a man rises up against his condition and the whole of creation.

    It is here that Camus meets Ivan Karamazov, and his reading joins that of Part Seven. Ivan, Camus writes, “inaugure l'entreprise essentielle de la révolte qui est de substituer au royaume de la grâce celui de la justice”, inaugurates the essential undertaking of revolt, which is to substitute for the kingdom of grace that of justice. Ivan does not deny God; he judges him, in the name of justice, and returns his ticket. But this revolt contains in germ its own perversion: if justice replaces grace, and if man is the sole judge, man may permit himself anything in the name of justice.
