Camus says it bluntly: “A ce ‘tout est permis’ commence vraiment l'histoire du nihilisme contemporain”, with this “everything is permitted” the history of contemporary nihilism truly begins.

    The thesis of the book is therefore this. Metaphysical revolt, just in its principle, becomes criminal when it forgets its limit. It begins by contesting God in the name of man; it ends by divinizing man, then history, and by killing in the name of this new divinity. Camus describes the outcome of this drift through an enumeration: “Le cynisme, la divinisation de l'histoire et de la matière, la terreur individuelle ou le crime d'Etat”, cynicism, the divinization of history and of matter, individual terror or state crime. The divinization of history: that, in Camus, is the name of what this essay calls the refoundation of a religion. Marxism, for him, has not left religion; it has replaced the kingdom of God with the end of history, and reproduces, with the Inquisition removed and the camps added, the structure of collective salvation.

    The encounters between Camus and our authors are attested by the book's very table of contents: one chapter is entitled “L'Unique” (“The Unique One”), on Stirner (p. 84), another “Nietzsche et le nihilisme” (“Nietzsche and Nihilism”, p. 88), others “Les régicides” (“The Regicides”, p. 143) and “Les déicides” (“The Deicides”, p. 168). Camus read Stirner, Nietzsche, Hegel, Marx, and Dostoevsky with a fervour that would lead him, in 1959, to adapt for the stage Les Possédés, the title under which Demons was then known in France. With them he builds a genealogy of nihilism that resembles, on many points, the one this essay has proposed: Stirner pushes revolt to absolute egoism; Nietzsche sees nihilism and wants to overcome it through the yes to life, but his doctrine would be misappropriated; Marx turns revolt into a religion of history.

    Against this drift, Camus proposes a thought of the limit, which he calls “pensée de midi”, the thought of noon, in reference to the Mediterranean, to Greek light, to measure. The last part of the book closes on a sentence that condenses everything: “Au midi de la pensée, le révolté refuse ainsi la divinité pour partager les luttes et le destin communs”, at the noon of thought, the rebel thus refuses divinity in order to share the common struggles and destiny. To refuse divinity: not only that of God, but that which the rebel is tempted to attribute to himself. Measured revolt contests God without making itself God, refuses grace, but also history as supreme tribunal. It remains on a human scale, in solidarity with other men, without promise.

    The book provoked one of the most violent quarrels of the postwar period. Francis Jeanson, in Les Temps modernes, published in 1952 a severe article, “Albert Camus ou l'âme révoltée” (“Albert Camus, or the Rebel Soul”); Camus replied with a letter to the review's director dated 30 June 1952, and Sartre in turn replied to him, which consummated the break between the two men. For Jeanson and Sartre, Camus, by refusing revolutionary violence in the name of a morality of measure, places himself outside history, in the purity of a beautiful soul, and his thought of noon is a disguised religious position: eternal morality against concrete history. For Camus, on the contrary, it is Sartre's thought, which accepts violence in the name of the end of history, that is religious: it sacrifices present men to future men, as the inquisitors sacrificed bodies to the salvation of souls.

    I believe that Camus is right on the substance and Sartre on a point of method. On the substance, Camus saw, two years after Meaning in History and without depending on Löwith, that the philosophies of history refound an eschatology, and that this eschatology authorizes murder. He saw that the exit from religion, when it claims to found a collective salvation on history, is more murderous than the religion it leaves, because it no longer has a beyond to limit its demands here below. On method, Sartre is right to reproach him for judging history from above: the thought of noon has no institution, no politics, no grip on reality. It is an individual wisdom presenting itself as a collective answer.

    For our question, Camus is a new serious candidate for exception, after Spinoza, Hume, Nietzsche and Wittgenstein, and alongside Weil. He does not refound a religion: he expressly refuses divinity, of God as of man, and he refuses consolation, since Sisyphus is happy without hope. Yet he keeps what resembles a spirituality: the beauty of the Mediterranean world, solidarity, Greek measure, lucid acceptance. Is that enough to say that he has left religion without founding another? I believe so, with one reservation. The “pensée de midi” is a myth, in the sense in which Camus himself likes the word, and this myth has its sacred geography, the Mediterranean, and its golden age, Greece. Camus divinizes neither man nor history; but he aestheticizes a nature and a culture, and this aestheticization is perhaps the most discreet form of refoundation. I leave the question open for the conclusion.

    In literature Albert Camus, The Stranger (1942) ; André Malraux, Man's Fate (1933) ; René Char, Leaves of Hypnos (1946)

    At the end of The Stranger, the chaplain enters the cell of the condemned Meursault and wants to make him pray; Meursault seizes him by the collar and shouts at him that none of his certainties is worth one hair of a woman's head, that nothing matters, and that from the depths of his future the same breath had been rising towards him across the years; once the chaplain has gone, he opens himself for the first time to the tender indifference of the world, and finds himself happy.

    Why here: this is The Myth of Sisyphus as a character, and the barest version of what the essay calls a spirituality without consolation. Meursault refounds nothing; he does not replace God with Man or with History, he consents to an indifferent world and finds joy in it, and he asks no one to die for it. The chaplain, for his part, would like him to weep, that is, to console himself; Meursault's refusal is the reservation that Weil formulates on the side of faith.

    Malraux, in Man's Fate, stages the other pole, the “we” of revolt. Katow, in the yard where the Shanghai insurgents wait to be burned alive in the boiler of a locomotive, gives his cyanide to two terrified young Chinese men, and walks to his death without it. This is the freely consented self-offering that the essay's criterion does not touch, and it is “I rebel, therefore we are”: the solidarity that founds a community without dogma, at the moment when there is nothing left to gain. Char, in Leaves of Hypnos, his notebooks from the maquis, gave this revolt without a heaven its maxims, while refusing to make a doctrine of it.

    Sources: Albert Camus, L'Étranger, II, 5 (1942) ; André Malraux, La Condition humaine, VI (1933) ; René Char, Feuillets d'Hypnos (1946).

    Portrait: United Press International, Public domain

    Levinas1906-1995ethics as an optics of the divine

    Background: Judaism: from the Second Temple to emancipation · The thought of Maimonides: the Guide for the Perplexed, the Mishneh Torah, prophecy · Phenomenology: from Husserl to the theological turn · Rudolf Otto and The Idea of the Holy: the numinous, the wholly other, comparative mysticism · Levinas's philosophy: the other, the face, ethics as first philosophy, the Talmud · The God of the Bible: his names, his images and the formation of monotheism

    With Emmanuel Levinas, the critique of onto-theology changes its source. Heidegger had diagnosed onto-theology and sought the way out in another thinking of being. Levinas, one of the first to introduce Husserl and Heidegger into France, starts from the same diagnosis and draws the opposite conclusion: it is not the forgetting of being that disfigured God, it is being itself. The God of the philosophical tradition was thought of as a supreme being, then as the being of beings; in both cases he was caught up in ontology, and that was his undoing. One must therefore look for a God uncontaminated by being, in the phrase of the foreword to Of God Who Comes to Mind (1982). The title of the great book of 1974, Otherwise than Being or Beyond Essence, states the programme: not to be otherwise, but otherwise than being.

    This God is found neither in a mystical experience nor in a supernatural revelation, but in the most everyday relation there is, the relation to the other person. Totality and Infinity (1961) starts from a text we read in Part Three, Descartes's third Meditation. There Descartes discovers in himself an idea he could not have produced, the idea of the infinite, which exceeds him; and he concludes that there is in him, in a certain way, the perception of the infinite, that is, of God, before that of the finite, that is, of himself (the Latin sentence is quoted in Part Three). Levinas keeps the structure and changes the content. The idea of the infinite is a thought that thinks more than it thinks, a content that overflows its container. And this structure is encountered not first in the proof of God, but in the face of the other, which always exceeds the idea I form of it.

    The face is the central notion, and it must be understood in the strictest sense: not a form one sees, but a nakedness that speaks. In a text of 1952, “Ethics and Spirit”, collected in Difficult Freedom (1963), Levinas writes that the face is inviolable, that these eyes, absolutely without protection, oppose possession with an absolute resistance, and that the temptation of murder is inscribed in this resistance; and he concludes: to see a face is already to hear “Tu ne tueras point”, “Thou shalt not kill”. The commandment is not added to the face by a law, it is the face itself; and it is only there that God can be thought: everything I can hear coming from God or going towards him, God who is invisible, must have come to me through this unique voice.

    Hence the formula that condenses all of Levinas, and which is a precise answer to our question: “Ethics is an optic”. Ethics is not the corollary of the vision of God, it is that very vision, so that everything I know of God must find an ethical expression. Levinas adds an example that directly concerns Maimonides, whom we read in Part One: the knowledge of God we can have is expressed, according to Maimonides, in the form of negative attributes; it receives a positive meaning from the moral statement “God is merciful”, which means “be merciful like him”. The attributes of God are given not in the indicative, but in the imperative. A text of 1961, published in L'Arche, says it more sharply: ethics is an optics of the divine; no relation with God is direct or immediate; the divine can be manifested only through the neighbour; and for a Jew, incarnation is neither possible nor necessary.

    Feuerbach, for whom the truth of theology is anthropology, added, in the Grundsätze der Philosophie der Zukunft (1843), that the unity of I and Thou is God (§ 60, quoted in Part Six), and that “die wahre Dialektik ist kein Monolog des einsamen Denkers mit sich selbst, sie ist ein Dialog zwischen Ich und Du”, true dialectic is not a monologue of the solitary thinker with himself, it is a dialogue between I and Thou (§ 62). Levinas seems to say the same thing, and says the opposite. For Feuerbach, the Thou refers me to humanity, to the species, to the common essence we share; the relation is symmetrical, and God dissolves into it. For Levinas, the face of the other refers me to a height I do not share, to an irreducible asymmetry: the other is not another self, he is situated, Levinas says, in a dimension of height, in the ideal, in the divine. Martin Buber, in Ich und Du (1923), had already thought of the relation as the place where the Eternal lets himself be encountered; Levinas always acknowledged this priority, and always reproached him for the reciprocity of the relation, which erases height. The confrontation with Feuerbach is constructed, the one with Buber attested in Levinas's work; both show that the same word, the Thou, can found an exit from religion or a new religion depending on whether it is thought of as symmetrical or asymmetrical.

    This thought has a name in Difficult Freedom: “a religion for adults”, the title of an essay of 1957. There Levinas joins, unexpectedly, the most radical critiques this essay has encountered. Judaism, he writes, disenchanted the world, by contesting the idea that religions arose from enthusiasm and the sacred. Enthusiasm is possession by a god; the numinous, the sacred in Otto's sense, envelops and transports man beyond his powers, and true freedom is offended by this uncontrollable surplus. The sentence is uncompromising: the sacred that envelops and transports me is a violence. One recognizes Weber's vocabulary, and one hears a direct reply to Rudolf Otto: the mysterium tremendum, far from being the heart of religion, is what true religion must free itself from.

    Levinas pushes the paradox to its limit. Monotheism, measured against the divine that the mythical gods embodied, is nothing but atheism. The destruction of the numinous sacred carries the risk of atheism, and this risk must be run: it is a great glory for the Creator to have set on its feet a being who affirms him after having contested and denied him. Monotheism surpasses and integrates atheism, but it is impossible unless one has reached the age of doubt, solitude and revolt. The critique of religion is therefore not the enemy of faith, but its condition. One also understands why Levinas, in the same text, finds Simone Weil as an adversary, since she sought in pagan myths the forms of the true God. The same essay rejects the Plotinian exit: against the philosophy that proclaims, with Plotinus, that the soul will go towards nothing other than itself, Judaism teaches a real transcendence, a relation with Him without whom the soul cannot stand. Plotinus, whom we read in Part One, is targeted here by name: this is an attested response.

    In 1961, the year of Totality and Infinity, Levinas published a short occasional piece, “Heidegger, Gagarin and Us”, collected in Difficult Freedom. In it he targets the prestigious current of modern thought that came from Germany, which would have man rediscover the world, rootedness, landscape, place. Technology, on the contrary, tears us away from the Heideggerian world and from the superstitions of Place; what matters most in Gagarin's feat is that he left Place, and that for an hour a man existed outside any horizon. Judaism did not sublimate idols, it demanded that they be destroyed; like technology, it demystified the universe. The confrontation is attested, and of a violence that the urbanity of the tone does not hide: for Levinas, the sacred of place, of soil and of blood is the very essence of paganism, and the thinking of being is its last learned form. Levinas, a prisoner of war while his family was being murdered in Lithuania, had admired Sein und Zeit and seen its author join the Nazi party in 1933.

    The criterion makes Levinas hard to classify. He seems to escape refoundation without difficulty: he installs neither Church, nor cult, nor dogma, and his religion for adults is defined precisely against the enthusiasm that carries the individual outside himself. But he demands something else, which resembles a sacrifice. In a radio commentary of 1955, “Loving the Torah More than God”, devoted to Zvi Kolitz's text attributed to Yossel Rakover, a fighter of the Warsaw ghetto, he writes that to love the Torah more than God means precisely to have access to a personal God against whom one can rebel, that is, for whom one can die. And Otherwise than Being pushes responsibility for the other as far as substitution, as far as the hostage: I am responsible for the other to the point of answering for his fault, without reciprocity.

    Is this an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded? I do not think so, without being entirely sure. To die for a God against whom one rebels is a self-offering, which the criterion does not reach. The reason lies in the nature of this absolute: neither an idea, nor a nation, nor a class, nor a Church, but the singular face of the other human being, this one, now. The sacrifice the criterion denounces consists in immolating individuals to an abstraction; Levinasian responsibility consists in never sacrificing an individual to an abstraction, even that of the common good. One may judge this demand crushing, and I believe it is: an infinite responsibility, without reciprocity, is a burden no life can carry, and Levinas knows it, since he introduces the “third party”, justice and the State to measure it. But it does not refound a religion in the sense in which Comte founded one. Levinas offers a spirituality that has mourned the sacred, and that finds the divine in the prohibition of murder. It is, with Ricoeur, a demanding form of faith that has passed through critique; and it is, against Heidegger and against Marion, an exit from onto-theology that passes not through being but through the other.

    In literature Vasily Grossman, Life and Fate (1960) ; Leo Tolstoy, “Master and Man” (1895)

    In Life and Fate, the notebook of Ikonnikov, a holy fool held in a German camp, sets against the Good of doctrines, which has always ended by killing in its name, “the small kindness”, that of an old peasant woman who brings bread to an enemy soldier, without reason, without witness and without future; this kindness without ideology, the notebook says, is the only one that has never been defeated, because it has never fought. Levinas commented on it in his last interviews as the only form of goodness that has not become a regime.

    Why here: it is the face before theory. The Good with a capital letter, History, Party, Nation, is the sacrificial absolute the essay denounces; the small kindness is responsibility for the other reduced to a gesture, which founds nothing, demands nothing of anyone, and saves one man at a time. Grossman, whose mother was killed in Berdichev, writes this notebook against the two secular religions of his century, and Levinas recognizes his ethics in it because it is there without doctrine.

    Tolstoy, in “Master and Man”, takes a merchant, Vasily Andreyevich, out into a snowstorm with his servant Nikita, where they lose their way; after trying to flee alone on horseback, he comes back and lies down full length on the freezing peasant, to warm him with his body; he dies in the night, and his last feeling is this: “He remembered that Nikita was beneath him, and that it was he, Vasily Andreyevich, who had warmed and revived Nikita. He listened and heard his servant breathing, and even faintly snoring. ‘He is alive,’ he said to himself triumphantly, ‘so I am alive again in him!…’”. This is the substitution of Otherwise than Being, the one-for-the-other to the point of dying in his place, written by a heterodox Christian in 1895; and it is also the essay's reservation: an infinite demand, which Tolstoy turns into a happy death, and which ordinary life cannot live by.

    Sources: Vasily Grossman, Жизнь и судьба (Life and Fate, written in 1960, published in 1980), Part Two, Ikonnikov's notebook; Leo Tolstoy, “Хозяин и работник” (“Master and Man”, 1895).

    Portrait: Bracha L. Ettinger, CC BY-SA 2.5

    Marionb. 1946the idol and the icon

    Background: Phenomenology: from Husserl to the theological turn · The thought of Heidegger: Dasein, Being and Time, the turn, technology, 1933 · The philosophy of Jean-Luc Marion: the idol and the icon, givenness, the saturated phenomenon

    Jean-Luc Marion closes this part with a reversal. A Catholic philosopher, a phenomenologist, a pupil of Beaufret in the preparatory class for the École normale supérieure and of Derrida at the École itself, in the rue d'Ulm, a specialist in Descartes, he published in 1982 God Without Being, which takes the Heideggerian critique of onto-theology seriously and turns it in favour of faith. If the God of metaphysics is only an idol, faith has lost nothing by his death: it can at last think of God otherwise than as the supreme being.

    The central distinction of the book is that of the idol and the icon. The idol is not a false god in the ordinary sense; it is a way of seeing. It stops the gaze and sends back to it its own measure, like an invisible mirror. The gaze that produces the idol is filled: it sees what it can see, it sees God at its own height. The icon, on the contrary, does not let itself be seen: it looks at the one who looks at it, and decentres him. Marion applies this distinction to concepts: “Quand une pensée philosophique énonce, de ce qu'elle nomme alors ‘Dieu’, un concept, ce concept fonctionne exactement comme une idole”, when a philosophical thought states a concept of what it then calls “God”, this concept functions exactly like an idol. The God of the philosophers is a conceptual idol, and Marion defines it in Heidegger's very terms: “l'idole conceptuelle a un site, la métaphysique, une fonction, la théologie dans l'onto-théo-logie, et une définition, la causa sui”, the conceptual idol has a site, metaphysics, a function, theology in onto-theo-logy, and a definition, the causa sui.

    Marion nevertheless goes further than Heidegger, and it is here that the attested response takes shape. Heidegger, in denouncing onto-theology, did not free God from being; he only changed the order of subordination. For him, God can appear only within the horizon of being, as the divine that shows itself to meditative thinking; he remains subject to the question of being. Marion sees in this a second idolatry, subtler than the first. Hence his thesis: “Dieu ne se dit pas d'abord et à partir de l'Être”, God is not said first of all and on the basis of Being. God is said on the basis of love, of agapè, of the gift, which precedes being and cannot be reduced to it. According to an academic thesis, Marion even crosses out the word “God”, to signify that the name does not name a being.

    The Zurich seminar here takes on its full significance. Marion relies on Heidegger's declaration that a theology, if he were to write one, should not contain the word “being”. He takes Heidegger at his word: since Heidegger himself admits that faith has no need of being, let us write the theology without being that he never wrote. The response is attested, and skilful: it turns against Heidegger the most sincere concession he ever made.

    Marion has been challenged from two sides. The Thomists reproached him for making Thomas Aquinas an onto-theologian, whereas the Thomist esse, the act of being, is not a supreme being but the pure act that surpasses all essence; J.-D. Robert defended Thomas against Marion as early as 1983. Marion himself qualified his position in an article of 1995, “Saint Thomas d'Aquin et l'onto-théo-logie”, published in the Revue thomiste, often read as a partial retraction. On the other side, Heideggerian and unbelieving readers reproached him for remaining onto-theological in spite of himself: to think of God as love or as gift is still to give him a first name, a founding attribute, and therefore to place him at the summit of a hierarchy.

    Marion proves, by example, that the critique of onto-theology is not a critique of faith, and that it can even serve it. This is what Barth had done with Feuerbach, Bonhoeffer with modern autonomy, Weil with the Marxist critique of consolation. Twentieth-century Christianity systematically turned the critiques of religion into purifications of faith, and this reversal is, I believe, both a victory and a capitulation. A victory, because faith thus purified escapes the objections of Feuerbach, Marx, Nietzsche and Heidegger: it no longer claims to know anything of God, it no longer consoles, it no longer founds anything. A capitulation, because to escape them it has had to give up almost everything that made it a religion: a knowledge, a consolation, a foundation, an institution. What remains is a spirituality, rigorous, demanding, but all the more exposed to the opposite objection: of being no more than the pious name of an experience that atheists such as Bataille, Camus or, as we shall see, Comte-Sponville, also claim.

    In literature Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Idiot (1869) ; Nikolai Gogol, “The Portrait” (1835)

    At Rogozhin's house, Prince Myshkin stops before a copy of Holbein's Dead Christ, which he saw in Basel: “ce tableau ! Mais en considérant ce tableau un homme peut perdre la foi !”, that painting! Why, a man could lose his faith looking at that painting! (II, 4). Ippolit, the young consumptive, describes it in his confession: “ici on a réellement sous les yeux le cadavre d'un homme qui a infiniment souffert avant même d'être crucifié”, here one really has before one's eyes the corpse of a man who suffered infinitely even before being crucified, and he draws from it the image that haunts him, “cette force infinie, cet être sourd, aveugle et muet”, that infinite force, that deaf, blind and dumb being, an “énorme et repoussante tarentule”, an enormous and repulsive tarantula, that someone shows him, saying: “Cet être aveugle, sourd et tout-puissant, le voilà”, there it is, that blind, deaf and almighty being (III, 6).

    Why here: Dostoevsky wrote the difference between the idol and the icon before Marion, and from the most dangerous side. The Basel Holbein is, for Ippolit, an idol in the sense of God Without Being: an invisible mirror in which the gaze meets only nature, that is, its own terror, and the tarantula is the name of the causa sui seen by a dying man. Myshkin, for his part, looks at the same painting and loses nothing, or almost nothing; the essay would say that the line runs not between two images but between two gazes, and that is precisely Marion's thesis.

    Gogol, in “The Portrait”, has a young painter, Chartkov, buy the portrait of a moneylender with living eyes: “Chartkov went up to the portrait once more to examine those extraordinary eyes, and noticed, not without terror, that they were looking at him. This was no longer a copy of nature, but the strange life that might animate the face of a corpse risen from the grave”; the money found in the frame makes him rich and mediocre, and he dies mad after destroying every masterpiece he could buy; the second part reveals that the painter of the portrait, having understood what he had let into the world, ends as a monk and paints a Nativity [summary]. The portrait that looks back is exactly the idol: an image that captures the gaze instead of letting it pass, and from which one is freed only by painting something else. Marion theorized what Gogol had had painted.

    Sources: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Идиот (The Idiot), II, 4 and III, 6 (1869), trans. Victor Derély; Nikolai Gogol, “Портрет” (“The Portrait”), Arabesques (1835; revised version, 1842).

    Portrait: Aymeric De La Toune, CC BY-SA 4.0

    Assessment of Part Ten: the critique of religion changes sides

    Background: The thought of Bonhoeffer: The Cost of Discipleship, the Ethics, the prison letters · Levinas's philosophy: the other, the face, ethics as first philosophy, the Talmud · The philosophy of Jean-Luc Marion: the idol and the icon, givenness, the saturated phenomenon · Twentieth-century Christian theology: dialectical, existential, Catholic, death of God · The philosophy of Karl Jaspers: psychopathology, existence, philosophical faith, the Axial Age

    In the nineteenth century, the critique of religion was the work of unbelievers, and believers endured it. In the twentieth century, it is shared. Heidegger criticizes the God of the philosophers in the name of a divine god; Barth criticizes religion in the name of revelation; Bonhoeffer announces the end of religion in the name of Christ; Weil makes atheism a purification in the name of love; Levinas seeks the trace of God in the face of the other; Marion turns Heidegger around in the name of charity. Facing them, Wittgenstein keeps silent about what cannot be said, Bataille seeks ecstasy without God, Sartre takes atheism as his starting point, Camus refuses all divinity in the name of measure. And these two camps meet on one point: the refusal of the available God, the God who consoles, guarantees and founds. Heidegger writes that god-less thinking is perhaps closer to the divine god; Bonhoeffer, that the world become godless is perhaps closer to God; Weil, that the one who denies God is perhaps the closest to him. Three times the same “perhaps”, three times the same closeness of the godless and God, in three authors of whom it cannot be established that they read one another on this point. I do not claim that this convergence proves anything; I say that it redefines the question.

    The question can no longer be: can one leave religion? It becomes: what does one leave when one leaves religion? If one leaves the God-as-foundation, the God-as-consolation, the stopgap God, the most demanding believers of the century left them too, and are none the worse for it. What remains common to both, an attention, an orientation, a way of standing before what cannot be possessed, is perhaps what can be called, in the strong sense, a spirituality. And the question shifts once more: is this common spirituality the truth of religion, at last freed from its idols, or its last refuge, the form in which religion survives its own critique?

    It is also historical: what happened, in the real history of the West, when religion ceased to structure societies? The authors of the next part asked it as historians, jurists and sociologists, and they gave a name to what happened: secularization. But this name, far from closing the debate, reopened it. It is this trial of secularization that must now be conducted.

    Top of the part

    Part Elevensecularization on trial8 authors

    Background: Genesis 1 to 3: the creation, Adam and Eve, the fall · From Cain to Babel: the fratricide, the Flood, the tower · Marxism and religion: from Lenin to liberation theology · The philosophy of history: from Augustine to Löwith · French laïcité: from Jules Ferry's school to the law of 1905 · The Churches and the totalitarian regimes: Barmen, the concordats, state atheism · Vatican II, the secularization of Europe and the return of the religious · The Revelation of John: visions, the beast and the heavenly Jerusalem

    Marion left us before a paradox: a theologian, in order to free God from metaphysics, takes up the very gesture of the modern critique of religion and denounces the God of the philosophers as an idol. The critique of the idol thus crosses the border between believers and unbelievers, and that border is perhaps not where we thought it was. Until now, we have asked each author whether he had left religion or refounded one. Yet this question assumes that we know what it means, for a modern idea, to come from religion. To say that Comte refounds a cult, that Marx inherits eschatology, that Heidegger awaits a god, is to assert a filiation; and the filiation between Christianity and modernity is the subject of one of the great controversies of the twentieth century, the secularization debate. Between 1922 and 1976 it set against one another a Catholic jurist, a philosopher of Jewish origin, baptized a Protestant and returned to Stoic scepticism, and a philosopher who made modernity the opposite of a debt. This debate puts my thesis on trial: if Blumenberg is right, most of the “refoundations” this essay believed it saw are optical illusions.

    Carl Schmitt1888-1985political theology as the truth of modernity

    Background: Carl Schmitt's thought: decisionism, friend and enemy, political theology · The Churches and the totalitarian regimes: Barmen, the concordats, state atheism

    Politische Theologie. Vier Kapitel zur Lehre von der Souveränität (Political Theology: Four Chapters on the Concept of Sovereignty) appeared in 1922, then in a second edition in 1934. Its third chapter opens with a sentence that became the watchword of the whole discussion: “Alle prägnanten Begriffe der modernen Staatslehre sind säkularisierte theologische Begriffe”, all significant concepts of the modern theory of the state are secularized theological concepts.

    The sentence can be read at two levels, which Schmitt holds together. The first is historical: the concepts have migrated. The omnipotent God of theology became the omnipotent lawgiver of the modern state; sovereignty, a divine attribute, passed to the prince, then to the people. The second, the one that interests Schmitt, is systematic: political concepts do not merely have the same origin as theological concepts, they have the same structure, and one understands a political epoch only by understanding the metaphysical image of the world it gives itself. The definition that opens the book, according to which sovereign is he who decides on the state of exception, finds its foundation here. The exception, which suspends the legal order, occupies in jurisprudence the place that the miracle occupies in theology; I do not quote Schmitt's sentence, which I have not read on a reliable page, but the analogy is the heart of the chapter. Hence the parallel that, in his view, organizes all of modern history: deism, which excludes the miracle and makes God the clockmaker of a world governed by its own laws, corresponds to the liberal state under the rule of law, which excludes the exception and claims that the norm suffices for everything. The theology of the Counter-Revolution, that of Bonald, de Maistre and above all Donoso Cortés, saw what liberalism refused to see: that a decider is needed, and that the decision cannot be deduced from any norm.

    People often mistake Schmitt's tone. They read his formula as a denunciation in the manner of Feuerbach: modern politics would be nothing but disguised theology, and it would have to be unmasked. Hebekus has shown that the reverse is true. Schmitt does not reproach modernity for having stolen its concepts from theology, but for having forgotten it, and he wants the politics of decision to raise itself, of its own accord, to the theological height from which it descends. Secularization is not for him an illegitimacy to be corrected, it is a truth to be embraced, and decisionism is the politics that embraces it.

    Schmitt is thus, with Rousseau and Comte, one of the few authors in the corpus who claim refoundation; he is the only one to claim it as the truth of modernity as a whole. The others mostly undergo it without knowing it, and it is the next critic who reveals it to them: Stirner to Feuerbach, Marx to Stirner, Heidegger to Nietzsche. Schmitt, for his part, wants it. The sovereign who decides on the exception is a mortal god, and Schmitt, who wrote its genealogy, knows it. That this jurist put his talent at the service of the National Socialist regime in 1933, and that in 1934 he justified the murders of the “Night of the Long Knives” in an article whose title made the Führer the protector of the law, “Der Führer schützt das Recht”, is not a biographical accident unconnected with the thesis: it is what becomes of a political theology that sacralizes decision without saying in the name of which God. I write this without polemical pleasure: Schmitt is the limit case of refoundation, the one in which the sacred returns without even the mask of Humanity, in the sole form of authority.

    In literature Thomas Mann, Der Zauberberg (1924) ; Georg Büchner, Dantons Tod (1835) ; William Shakespeare, Richard II (1595)

    Naphta, the Jewish Jesuit of The Magic Mountain, answers Settembrini's Enlightenment with a political theology without God: “Nicht Befreiung und Entfaltung des Ich sind das Geheimnis und das Gebot der Zeit. Was sie braucht, wonach sie verlangt, was sie sich schaffen wird, das ist der Terror”, it is not the liberation and development of the self that are the secret and the command of the age; what it needs, what it demands, what it will create for itself, is terror; for “der Dualismus von Gut und Böse, von Jenseits und Diesseits, Geist und Macht muß, wenn das Reich kommen soll, vorübergehend aufgehoben werden in einem Prinzip, das Askese und Herrschaft vereinigt. Das ist es, was ich die Notwendigkeit des Terrors nenne”, if the Kingdom is to come, the dualism of good and evil, of the beyond and the here-below, of spirit and power, must be provisionally abolished in a principle that unites asceticism and domination: that is what I call the necessity of terror.

    Why here: Mann wrote Naphta in 1924, two years after Political Theology, and, drawing on Lukács, lent him Schmitt's thesis: the modern state holds together only through an avowed theological absolute, decision and terror, and liberalism is merely an impiety unaware of itself. Naphta ends by shooting himself in the head in a duel, for lack of an adversary; Schmitt had an adversary, and a master.

    Büchner, in 1835, had given the revolutionary version of the same absolute: his Robespierre proclaims from the tribune that “die Waffe der Republik ist der Schrecken, die Kraft der Republik ist die Tugend, die Tugend, weil ohne sie der Schrecken verderblich, der Schrecken, weil ohne ihn die Tugend ohnmächtig ist”, the weapon of the Republic is terror, its strength is virtue; virtue, because without it terror is ruinous; terror, because without it virtue is powerless. Shakespeare, finally, had written the theology of the sovereign before its secularization. Richard II, who is about to be deposed, maintains: “Not all the water in the rough rude sea / Can wash the balm off from an anointed king; / The breath of worldly men cannot depose / The deputy elected by the Lord”; the play shows that it can, and that the deposed king is no more than a man asking for a mirror. From the Lord's anointed to the sovereign who decides on the exception, the place is the same; Schmitt said it as a jurist, the poets had made three dramas of it.

    Sources: Thomas Mann, Der Zauberberg, VI, “Vom Gottesstaat und von übler Erlösung” (1924); Georg Büchner, Dantons Tod, I, 3 (1835); William Shakespeare, Richard II, III, 2 (c. 1595).

    Portrait: Auteur inconnu, Public domain

    KLKarl Löwith1897-1973the philosophy of history as disguised eschatology

    Background: The philosophy of Hegel: dialectic, the Phenomenology, Absolute Spirit, religion and concept · The thought of Marx: historical materialism, alienation, ideology, fetishism · The thought of Comte: law of three stages, sociology, religion of Humanity · The philosophy of history: from Augustine to Löwith · Karl Löwith's thought: from Hegel to Nietzsche, history as secularized eschatology · The Revelation of John: visions, the beast and the heavenly Jerusalem

    Karl Löwith, a student of Heidegger before becoming one of his harshest critics, driven out of Germany by the racial laws, taught in Japan and then in the United States. It was there that he published Meaning in History. The Theological Implications of the Philosophy of History (Chicago, 1949), translated and reworked in German under the title Weltgeschichte und Heilsgeschehen (World History and Salvation History, 1953). The book goes back in time: it starts from Burckhardt and moves backwards through Marx, Hegel, Proudhon, Comte, Condorcet and Turgot, Voltaire, Vico, Bossuet, Joachim of Fiore, Augustine and Orosius, as far as the Bible.

    The thesis is simple. The idea that universal history has a knowable meaning, directed towards a fulfilment, is neither Greek nor natural. The Greeks thought of time as a cycle; they did not seek the meaning of history, but the logos of the cosmos. Oriented history comes from Hebrew and Christian faith, from the expectation of a final fulfilment, the eschaton, which gives meaning to everything that precedes it. The modern philosophies of history, of progress as of revolution, were born when this schema was transposed into immanence: fulfilment is no longer expected from God at the end of time, it is produced by man within time. The philosophy of history is Christian eschatology minus God: it keeps the form, it changes the subject.

    The chapter on Marx is the most famous. Löwith reads the Manifesto there as a prophetic document disguised as science: the proletariat is the chosen people, the revolution is the judgement, the classless society is the kingdom, and the whole of history is a history of salvation transposed into economics. The formula is plain: “It is the old Jewish messianism and prophetism”, Löwith continues, speaking of Marx. This is the objection I addressed to Marx in Part Six: a revolution that promises the end of suffering and the meaning of history takes the form of salvation. Löwith formulated it as early as 1949, with an erudition I do not claim to equal.

    The chapter on Comte, less often cited, also sheds light on Part Six. Löwith sees in it the same transposition, in a more naive and more explicit form. The law of the three stages, which moves humanity from the theological age to the metaphysical age and then to the positive age, is a history of salvation in three ages, and Löwith recalls that it has a precise medieval ancestor: the division of history into three reigns, that of the Father, of the Son and of the Spirit, in Joachim of Fiore, the twelfth-century Calabrian abbot whom the Franciscan Spirituals had made the prophet of a new age. Positivism, which believed it had dismissed theology, reproduced its most daring schema, the advent of a third age on earth. And Comte, unlike Marx, drew the consequence himself by founding the Religion of Humanity, with its Great Being, its sacraments and its calendar. Comte's refoundation was therefore not an eccentricity of old age, as his scientistic disciples claimed, but the logical outcome of the law of the three stages: whoever believes that history is heading towards a fulfilment must sooner or later celebrate its cult. The link between Comte and Löwith's thesis is attested by the very structure of the book; the remark on religious foundation as a necessary consequence is mine.

    But Löwith's conclusion is not the one we expect. He asks neither that we return to the Christian faith, the original of which modernity would be the degraded copy, nor that we complete secularization by purifying progress of its theological remnants. The Christian faith, according to him, was never a historical expectation: the Christian awaits the kingdom, he does not await it from history. And critical reason, for its part, finds no meaning in history: “To the critical mind, neither a providential design nor a natural law of progressive development is discernible in the tragic human comedy of all times.” What Löwith proposes, at the end of the book, is a withdrawal: the Greek view of nature, the Stoic wisdom that accepts the world without asking it for meaning. Habermas, as early as 1963, gave this gesture its critical name in an article in Merkur: “Karl Löwiths stoischer Rückzug vom historischen Bewusstsein”, Karl Löwith's Stoic withdrawal from historical consciousness.

    Löwith is thus an ambiguous ally. He gives my thesis its best historical support: the philosophies of history refound a religion of salvation without God, and that is why they were able to demand sacrifices that only a religion obtains. But his conclusion joins, by another path, the exceptions we have identified. His Stoicism is an exit without refoundation: it promises nothing, sacralizes nothing, demands of the individual no sacrifice to the future. It may be compared with Spinoza, and with the amor fati of Nietzsche, whom he knew closely, since in 1935 he had devoted a book to the Nietzschean philosophy of eternal recurrence, Nietzsches Philosophie der ewigen Wiederkunft des Gleichen. It remains to be seen whether one can live in this withdrawal. Blumenberg, Taylor and Habermas will answer, each in his own way, that modernity does not live there.

    In literature Leo Tolstoy, War and Peace (1869) ; Gustave Flaubert, Sentimental Education (1869)

    The second epilogue of War and Peace is no longer a novel: it is a treatise on history, which denies great men and Providence the power to explain it, and which ends with an analogy with Copernicus. Just as we had to renounce the immobility of the earth that we feel in order to admit a movement that we do not feel, “in the present case it is similarly necessary to renounce a freedom that does not exist, and to recognize a dependence of which we are not conscious”.

    Why here: Tolstoy arrives, through the novel, at the conclusion of Meaning in History: neither a providential design nor a law of progress is discernible in history, and those who see one, Napoleon or the historians, mistake their consciousness for a cause. But Tolstoy draws from it a dependence that Löwith called Stoic and that the essay judges to be without a way of life; both have dismissed eschatology, and both remain before a necessity that must, after all, be inhabited.

    Flaubert, the same year, wrote the other version of the disenchantment of history. Sentimental Education passes through 1848 with Frédéric Moreau, who watches the sack of the Tuileries, the shooting and the coup d'état as he watches his life, without entering into it; the novel ends with two friends agreeing that the best thing they ever had was a botched visit to a brothel, twenty years earlier. This is 1848 as farce, the essay says with Marx; it is above all the end of all historical expectation, and Flaubert's novel does what Löwith's treatise observes: history no longer has a meaning, and neither do the characters.

    Sources: Leo Tolstoy, Война и мир (War and Peace), second epilogue, XII (1869), English trans. Louise and Aylmer Maude; Gustave Flaubert, L'Éducation sentimentale, III, 1 and III, 7 (1869).

    HBHans Blumenberg1920-1996the legitimacy of the modern age

    Background: Greek myths: sources, gods and divine generations · Scholasticism and the condemnations: faith and reason in the medieval university · Prometheus and Pandora: the sharing of the sacrifice, fire, evil · Carl Schmitt's thought: decisionism, friend and enemy, political theology · Karl Löwith's thought: from Hegel to Nietzsche, history as secularized eschatology · The thought of Hans Blumenberg: the legitimacy of the modern age, metaphorology, work on myth · The Revelation of John: visions, the beast and the heavenly Jerusalem

    One of the two serious objections announced in the prologue did not come from a believer. It came from Hans Blumenberg, in Die Legitimität der Neuzeit (The Legitimacy of the Modern Age, 1966), a book he reworked in depth between 1973 and 1976 in response to his critics, and whose first part, devoted to secularization, is a methodical refutation of Löwith and Schmitt. I owe this objection its best form, for it forces me to make the thesis more precise.

    Blumenberg starts from a semantic observation. The word “secularization” comes from law: it first designates the passing of Church property into lay hands, in particular during the confiscations of the Napoleonic era. To say that progress is secularized eschatology is therefore to use a concept that implies an expropriation: a property that legitimately belonged to someone has been taken from them. Blumenberg shows that secularization, so understood, functions as a “Kategorie des geschichtlichen Unrechts”, a category of historical injustice; in the 1962 lecture that prepared the book, he already spoke of a “Kategorie historischer Illegitimität”, a category of historical illegitimacy, a formula that gives the lecture its subtitle. Whoever says “secularized” insinuates that modernity lives on stolen property and is not legitimate in its own right.

    For this reproach to hold, Blumenberg continues, three conditions would have to be met: the transferred property would have to be identifiable as the same property before and after; the first owner would have to have been its legitimate possessor; the transfer would have to have been unilateral. Yet none is met in Löwith's case. Christian eschatology awaits an end that breaks into history from outside, that judges it and interrupts it; modern progress is an immanent principle, realized in history through the accumulation of human knowledge and power. These two contents are not the same thing in two garbs: they are heterogeneous. What creates the illusion of their identity, Blumenberg states in a sentence I give in full, for it contains his whole thesis: “die historische Identität und methodische Identifizierbarkeit der als säkularisiert vermeinten Vorstellungen ist ein Schein, der entsteht durch die Identität der Funktion, die ganz heterogene Gehalte an bestimmten Stellen des Systems der Welt- und Selbstdeutung annehmen können”, the historical identity and methodological identifiability of the ideas supposed to be secularized are an appearance, which arises from the identity of the function that quite heterogeneous contents can assume at certain places in the system of interpretation of the world and of the self.

    Here is the decisive concept: Umbesetzung, reoccupation. Christianity opened certain questions, it hollowed out certain places in the interpretation man gives himself of himself and of the world: the question of the meaning of history as a whole, that of the totality of the real, that of an end. When Christianity ceased to answer them credibly, the questions remained, and modernity was summoned to answer them in its turn, with contents that had nothing Christian about them. Progress is not disguised eschatology; it is the modern answer to a question that eschatology had posed, and which it had to take up, so to speak, in spite of itself. The identity of the place has been mistaken for the identity of the occupant. Blumenberg even sees here the origin of the excesses of the philosophies of history: they overloaded the concept of progress because they believed themselves bound to answer an immoderate question, that of the totality of history, which modernity had not posed itself.

    As for the legitimacy of modernity, it does not come from an inheritance, but from a Selbstbehauptung, a self-assertion. Blumenberg dates it precisely: it is man's response to the theological absolutism of the late Middle Ages, that of nominalism, which had made God an arbitrary and all-powerful will, before which the world no longer offered any guarantee of order. Against a hidden and unpredictable God, man had to take charge of himself, to know and master nature in order to find his bearings in it. Modernity is not a Christianity that has lost its faith; it is a response to an internal crisis of Christian theology, a response that owes it nothing other than its provocation.

    The exchanges are attested. Blumenberg built his criteria on the example of Löwith. Löwith answered him with a review, dated 1968 in his Sämtliche Schriften (vol. II, pp. 452-459); in it, according to Weidner, he reproaches Blumenberg for demanding a substantial identity as proof of secularization while denying that such an identity could ever exist, that is, for imposing on his adversary an impossible burden of proof. Schmitt, for his part, replied in 1970 in the last chapter of Politische Theologie II, reproaching Blumenberg for already presupposing, in his demonstration, the standpoint of the modernity he claims to legitimize. Blumenberg replied in the revised edition: Schmitt's formula is in his eyes “die stärkste Form des Säkularisierungstheorems”, the strongest form of the secularization theorem, but he proposes to reverse it. Modern political concepts are not secularized theological concepts; they are theologized concepts, to which an absoluteness they do not have is attributed, because one expects from politics what one expected from God. The two men then corresponded, from 1971 to 1978, at Blumenberg's initiative; the correspondence was published in 2007.

    This last inversion is, I believe, the key: it makes it possible to answer Blumenberg without proving him wrong. What does he say, in sum? That modernity does not inherit Christian contents, but finds itself before empty places that it is tempted to occupy, and that, when it occupies them, it overloads its own concepts with an absoluteness that does not belong to them: it theologizes. This is what I call a refoundation. I must, however, concede an important point. If one takes the essay's thesis in its extensive version, the one which says that every modern structure resembling a Christian structure is a disguised religion, then Blumenberg is right against it: that thesis proves too much. It makes religion unfalsifiable, since it will be found wherever one finds a hope, a community, an ideal or a history. It belongs to what Blumenberg calls a metaphysics of substance, which assumes that contents persist beneath metamorphoses: it is the laziness of the historian who sees shadows everywhere.

    The criterion set out in the prologue finds its justification here; it owes more to Stirner than to Löwith. A thought refounds a religion not when it occupies a place left empty by Christianity, which is inevitable, but when it installs in that place an absolute in the name of which the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded, and whose critique becomes a sacrilege. Progress as a hypothesis about the accumulation of knowledge is not a religion; Progress as the end of history, in the name of which the death of entire generations can be demanded, is one. Society as an object of study is not a religion; Comte's Great Being, before which one kneels, is one. The sovereign as an organ of decision is not a religion; the sovereign whose decision makes the law and whom no one judges is one. The criterion is not resemblance of structure, which Blumenberg is right to reject, but the sacrifice demanded: Stirner's question, that of the fear of Man which is only a modified form of the fear of God. Thus armed, the thesis becomes falsifiable. It can be false for a given author: it is, I believe, for Blumenberg himself, whose Selbstbehauptung demands no sacrifice and promises no salvation, which makes him an unexpected ally of the thesis. It remains true for the others, Comte, state Marxism, Schmitt, and perhaps Heidegger, whom Blumenberg no longer forbids me to accuse, since his own concept of theologization says what I reproach them with.

    In literature Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, “Prometheus” (1774) ; Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818) ; Franz Kafka, “Prometheus” (1918)

    Goethe's Prometheus speaks to Zeus like a proprietor: “Ich kenne nichts Aermeres / Unter der Sonn', als euch, Götter! / Ihr nähret kümmerlich / Von Opfersteuern / Und Gebetshauch / Eure Majestät”, I know nothing poorer under the sun than you, gods: you meagrely nourish your majesty on sacrificial tributes and the breath of prayer; and he ends: “Hier sitz' ich, forme Menschen / Nach meinem Bilde, / Ein Geschlecht, das mir gleich sey, / Zu leiden, zu weinen, / Zu genießen und zu freuen sich, / Und dein nicht zu achten, / Wie ich!”, here I sit, forming men in my own image, a race that shall be like me, to suffer, to weep, to enjoy and to rejoice, and to pay no heed to you, as I do.

    Why here: the poem is Blumenberg's Selbstbehauptung, self-assertion against theological absolutism, and Blumenberg himself devoted the last part of Arbeit am Mythos to this Prometheus. The gods are poor in it because they live on sacrifices: this is the essay's criterion read backwards, a divinity that has being only through what is immolated to it, and the man who stops immolating starves it to death. The poem does not occupy the place of God, it leaves it empty and works beside it.

    Mary Shelley subtitled Frankenstein “the Modern Prometheus”, and her Victor warns: “Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge”; the creature answers him: “I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed.” The novel shows what reoccupation costs: the man who takes the creator's place also inherits the creature's questions, and he has no answer. Kafka, finally, summed up in four contradictory legends what is known of Prometheus, the last saying that everyone grew weary, the gods, the eagles, the wound; “Blieb das unerklärliche Felsgebirge. Die Sage versucht das Unerklärliche zu erklären. Da sie aus einem Wahrheitsgrund kommt, muß sie wieder im Unerklärlichen enden”, there remained the inexplicable mass of rock; the legend tries to explain the inexplicable; since it comes out of a ground of truth, it must end again in the inexplicable. This is the last page of Arbeit am Mythos, and Blumenberg chose it.

    Sources: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, “Prometheus” (written c. 1774, published in 1785 and then 1789); Mary Shelley, Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, ch. 4 and 10 (1818); Franz Kafka, “Prometheus” (1918, posthumous).

    Voegelin and Aron1901-1985; 1905-1983secular religions

    Background: From Cain to Babel: the fratricide, the Flood, the tower · Gnosis and Gnosticism: from Valentinus to Hans Jonas and Voegelin · The philosophy of history: from Augustine to Löwith · The thought of Eric Voegelin: political religions, gnosticism, order and history · The thought of Raymond Aron: critical philosophy of history, secular religions, the opium of the intellectuals · The Churches and the totalitarian regimes: Barmen, the concordats, state atheism · The Revelation of John: visions, the beast and the heavenly Jerusalem

    Schmitt and Löwith speak of concepts and of philosophies of history. Two authors, at almost the same moment and without having consulted each other, carried the question onto harsher ground: that of the regimes which, in the twentieth century, actually demanded of millions of people that they sacrifice themselves, or sacrifice others, to an earthly absolute. Eric Voegelin called them political religions, Raymond Aron secular religions. Both expressions name what this essay has been describing from the start, and that is why I place them at the heart of the secularization quarrel rather than in the chapter on totalitarianisms where they are usually filed.

    Voegelin, born in Cologne and trained in Vienna under Hans Kelsen, was teaching political science at the University of Vienna when, in the spring of 1938, he had a short and dense essay printed, Die politischen Religionen (The Political Religions). The first edition, ready in April 1938, was suppressed by the National Socialist management imposed on the publisher Bermann-Fischer after the Anschluss; Voegelin, stripped of his licence to teach, left Vienna on 13 July, and the second edition appeared in Stockholm, with a preface dated Christmas 1938. The book's thesis is summed up by the Neue Deutsche Biographie: Voegelin interprets National Socialism as a form of innerworldly religiosity, “innerweltlicher Religiosität, die das rassisch determinierte Volk vergöttliche und mit einem eigenen Mythus der Erlösung verknüpfe”, a religiosity that deifies the racially determined people and joins to it a myth of redemption of its own. The central concept is that of innerweltlich, innerworldly, religion: a religion whose realissimum, its supreme object, is no longer beyond the world but within it, race, class, the State, and which nonetheless receives from it everything that religions received from their god, faith, worship, obedience, promise.

    Fourteen years later, in the United States, Voegelin gave this intuition a genealogy in The New Science of Politics (Chicago, 1952), where it joins the quarrel between Löwith and Blumenberg. We must, he writes, “recognize the essence of modernity as the growth of gnosticism”. By Gnosticism Voegelin does not mean first of all the ancient sect, which he knows through Hans Jonas, but an attitude: the certainty of possessing a knowledge that makes it possible to transform the world and deliver it from its imperfection. Its point of origin is Joachim of Fiore, whom Löwith was encountering at the same moment at the bottom of his own genealogy, and its mechanism is immanentization: “The attempt at constructing an eidos of history will lead into the fallacious immanentization of the Christian eschaton”. The formula, which American conservatism later reduced to a slogan, says what Löwith said of Marx and of Comte: the salvation that Christianity awaited from the end of time is promised by human action within time. But Voegelin pushes the analysis as far as the political regime. Totalitarianism is not for him an accident of modernity, it is its outcome: “Totalitarianism, defined as the existential rule of Gnostic activists, is the end form of progressive civilization”. He gives the reason in terms this essay could adopt: modern Gnosticism sought to supply society with the civil theology that Christianity denied it, and the totalitarianism of our time must be understood, he writes, as “journey's end of the Gnostic search for a civil theology”.

    One passage of the book bears closely on our first part. Voegelin there takes up, in connection with the Puritans, the old thesis of the falāsifa according to which the multitude must not touch philosophical questions, and he concludes, after evoking the murder of God that Nietzsche had announced, that one must admit that “Averroës had a point”. The connection is attested, and it throws light on Voegelin's leaning: his diagnosis of modernity is also a nostalgia for the medieval reserve, which kept speculation on the meaning of history out of “vulgar” hands. This is Averroes' hierarchical division, and, give or take a few nuances, the gesture of Leo Strauss.

    Raymond Aron reached the same notion by another path, that of sociology and of war. Editor-in-chief of La France libre in London, he published there during the war two articles on secular religions, the better known of which, “L'avenir des religions séculières”, dates from 1944. The definition he proposes there has become classic; I give it in paraphrase, not having been able to verify its wording: Aron calls secular religions those doctrines which take, in the souls of his contemporaries, the place left by vanished faith, and which locate the salvation of humanity here below, in the distant future, in the form of a social order to be created. The definition contains three elements: a place left empty, that of faith, a vocabulary Blumenberg would rediscover more than twenty years later; a salvation, that of humanity; a displacement of this salvation here below, into a social order to be built. Aron does not say that communism is a religion because it resembles Christianity; he says that it is a religion because it fixes a last end and judges good and evil in relation to it. A commentator quotes in this connection a sentence of Aron's in English translation: such doctrines “set up an ultimate and quasisacred goal and define good and evil in relation to this ideal”.

    Eleven years later, Aron drew from this analysis a polemical book, The Opium of the Intellectuals (1955), whose title turns Marx's formula against the Marxists: it is no longer religion that is the opium of the people, it is Marxism that has become the opium of those who think. This is the gesture this essay has seen recur from author to author, from Stirner to Camus. Aron formulates it as a sociologist, without Stirner's violence or Camus's lyricism, and that is his strength. He does not reproach intellectuals for hoping; he reproaches them for having turned a political hypothesis into a truth of salvation, and for having drawn from it the right to justify, in the name of the future, what they would have condemned in the present. The connection with Camus is constructed: The Rebel (1951) and The Opium of the Intellectuals are, four years apart, the two great French books against the deification of history, one written by a moralist, the other by a sociologist, and they earned their authors the same hostility from the intellectual left.

    This civil theology also has ancestors we read much earlier. The expression comes from Varro, by way of Augustine, and Voegelin handles it as a connoisseur of The City of God; but the thing has antecedents closer to our purpose. Plato, in Book X of the Laws, had wanted a theology of the city armed with a penal law, and Rousseau, in the penultimate chapter of The Social Contract (IV, 8), a civil religion whose dogmas were guarded by banishment and death. Voegelin does not make this connection in the pages I have read; it is my own, and it throws light on the difference between the two epochs. Rousseau wanted a civil religion limited to a few dogmas, which left each person the rest of their conscience; Plato already went further, as far as forbidding private worship. The political religions of the twentieth century no longer leave anything over: they occupy the whole soul, because they lay claim at once to knowledge, to salvation and to government. What Voegelin calls Gnosticism is perhaps first of all this, the fusion of what Plato and Rousseau still kept apart, the opinion useful to the city and the truth that sets free.

    The connection with Marcel Gauchet is of another order. Gauchet took up the notion of secular religion on his own account to describe the totalitarianisms, and his reading is closer to Aron's than to Voegelin's: he sees in them not a return of heretical Christianity, but an attempt to reconstitute, in a society that has left religion, the unity and hierarchy that religion once ensured. If this reading is right, secular religions do not prove that the exit from religion is impossible, but that it is dangerous, because it leaves behind it a nostalgia for the One that regimes can exploit: a conclusion much closer to the criterion than to Voegelin's genealogical thesis.

    These two notions confirm this criterion, and they test it. They confirm it, because the feature that Voegelin and Aron each retain in their own way is that of the criterion: secular religion is a belief that authorizes sacrifice. The deified Volk of 1938 demands that one die for it and kill for it; the social order to come of 1944 justifies sacrificing present generations to those who will enjoy it. The sacrifice criterion, set out in the prologue and refined in connection with Feuerbach, finds here its most massive and bloodiest cases: after Voegelin and Aron, one can no longer say that refoundation is a matter for philosophers and positivist sacristies. It has had its police, its camps and its trials.

    But they also test it, for the notion of secular religion runs the risk already recognized in the lazy form of the secularization thesis: seeing gods everywhere. The objection was formulated as early as the 1950s by Voegelin's own teacher. Hans Kelsen devoted to the notion a manuscript, Secular Religion, which he withdrew from the University of California Press in 1964 and which was not published until 2012; in it he attacks Voegelin and all those who see a theological structure in modern doctrines that postulate no belief in God, on the grounds that a theory capable of proving everything, even the religious character of irreligious theories, ends up proving nothing, and turns the concept of religion into an empty shell. This attested response is aimed at a former pupil. Blumenberg, for his part, never debated with Voegelin: the colloquium Jacob Taubes wanted to organize between them in Berlin in 1967 did not take place, and no direct exchange is known; but Die Legitimität der Neuzeit takes the word Gnosticism from Voegelin in order to reverse its meaning, since it makes modernity not a triumphant Gnosticism but a “second overcoming of Gnosticism”. The confrontation is therefore half attested: Blumenberg answers Voegelin's thesis in a book, he does not answer Voegelin.

    I believe that Kelsen and Blumenberg are right against Voegelin's genealogical thesis, and wrong against Aron's functional thesis. Voegelin asserts a filiation: modernity comes from Gnosticism, through Joachim and the medieval sects, as from a heresy that ended up winning. This filiation is unverifiable in its generality, and it has the drawback of making the whole of modernity, liberalism and science included, one and the same evil, which Voegelin himself moreover toned down in his later work, according to his entry in the Neue Deutsche Biographie. Aron, for his part, asserts an analogy of function: a political doctrine becomes religious when it occupies the place of faith in souls and receives from it the power to demand. This analogy presupposes no inheritance; it is a matter of observation. It is therefore compatible with Blumenberg, for whom the empty places of theology call for reoccupations, and it makes precise what he leaves in the shadow: not all reoccupations are of equal worth. Some answer an inherited question with a modest hypothesis, others with a sacrificial absolute. Secular religion, in Aron's sense, is the name of the second kind, and it is indispensable to me. The notion of political religion, understood in Voegelin's genealogical sense, is in its turn a philosophy of history, one of decline, and it falls under the reproach it addresses to the others.

    In literature Arthur Koestler, Darkness at Noon (1940) ; George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) ; Ignazio Silone, Pane e vino (1936)

    Rubashov, an old Bolshevik arrested in Darkness at Noon, reasons in his cell with the logic he has served: the Party cannot be mistaken, since History is right and the Party is its organ; therefore, if he has doubted, he is guilty; his second interrogator, Gletkin, no longer even needs to convince him, and Rubashov confesses to imaginary crimes in order to render History one last service, before the bullet in the back of the neck. In Orwell, O'Brien explains to Winston, under torture, that the Party seeks power for its own sake, that God is power, and that reality exists only in the mind of the Party, which is immortal; the torture ends when Winston loves Big Brother.

    Why here: the two novels are Aron's secular religion described from within, in its liturgy, confession, and in its dogma, the infallibility of an authority that occupies the place of God and demands the lives of its faithful. Koestler shows the believer who sacrifices himself, Orwell the priest who demands; Rubashov and O'Brien are the two faces of the criterion. And Orwell has O'Brien say what Voegelin said of Gnosticism: the Party no longer promises a paradise, it is itself the immanent eschaton.

    Silone, lastly, a former communist leader, brings back in Bread and Wine a hunted revolutionary, Pietro Spina, in the cassock of a false priest, to the villages of the Abruzzi; the peasants take him for a saint, and he discovers that his socialism was a faith that had merely changed Churches. The disguise says it all: secular religion recognizes itself only by putting back on the habit of the religion it has left.

    Sources: Arthur Koestler, Darkness at Noon (1940) ; George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four, III (1949) ; Ignazio Silone, Pane e vino (1936).

    Portrait: Studio Harcourt, Public domain

    LSLeo Strauss1899-1973Athens and Jerusalem

    Background: The Bible: books, canons and languages · The philosophy of Averroes: the Commentator, the intellect, the reply to al-Ghazali, Latin Averroism · The thought of Maimonides: the Guide for the Perplexed, the Mishneh Torah, prophecy · Spinoza's philosophy: substance, attributes, modes, conatus, kinds of knowledge, the Theological-Political Treatise · Plato's myths: Er, Gyges, the noble lie, the androgyne · From the Judges to the Kings: Samuel, Saul, David and Goliath, Solomon and the Temple · The thought of Leo Strauss: natural right, esotericism, Athens and Jerusalem

    All the authors of this part argue about the way in which we left religion. Leo Strauss disputes that we left it at all. He disputes it not as a believer, which he never claimed to be, but as a philosopher, and that is why he is, I believe, the most serious adversary of the very thesis of the exit.

    Strauss was born in 1899 in Kirchhain, a small rural town near Marburg, into an Orthodox Jewish family; he studied at Marburg, defended in 1921, under the supervision of Ernst Cassirer, a dissertation on Jacobi, and spent 1922 in Freiburg, where he attended Husserl's lectures and fell, like Levinas, Gadamer, Arendt and Karl Löwith, whose friend and correspondent he would remain, under the sway of Heidegger. His first book, written between 1925 and 1928 and published in 1930, is devoted to Spinoza's critique of religion, that is, to the very book that our third part made one of the founding acts of modern critique. In the preface to the English edition of 1965 he would present it as the work of a young Jew in Germany caught “in the grip of the theologico-political predicament”. This theologico-political problem, the question whether a society can be founded on reason alone or whether it rests on a revealed law, would be, he says elsewhere, “the theme of my studies”.

    The book's thesis, as the 1965 preface restates it, reverses the story this essay has followed. Spinoza, and with him the whole Enlightenment critique, did not refute revelation. He could not, for belief in an omnipotent God who reveals himself when he wills and hides himself when he wills rests on a premise that, according to Strauss, can be refuted neither by experience nor by the principle of contradiction. And the indirect proof of this is the very means the critics used: “Spinoza and his like owed such success as they had in their fight against orthodoxy to laughter and mockery”; they tried to drive orthodoxy out by laughing at a position from which no proof drawn from Scripture or from reason could dislodge it. The modern critique of religion would thus not have won its case; it would have won a battle of opinion. And a genuine refutation would demand more than any philosopher has ever supplied: “The genuine refutation of orthodoxy would require the proof that the world and human life are perfectly intelligible without the assumption of a mysterious God”; it would require at the very least the completion of the philosophical system.

    This sentence says that the exit from religion, in the strong sense in which the Enlightenment understood it, would have presupposed that reason become a total knowledge, master of the world and of life. Now that is what I have called a refoundation. The only possible refutation of revelation would be the installation of another absolute, completed reason, man the master of everything; and we know what secular religions made of that ambition. Strauss thus closes the door on both sides: one does not refute revelation without making oneself god, and if one gives up making oneself god, one does not refute it.

    Conversely, and Strauss insists on this with the same rigour, revelation does not refute philosophy either. In Natural Right and History (1953), he formulates this impasse in the harshest terms for philosophy itself: “Philosophy has to grant that revelation is possible”, which amounts to granting that the philosophic life is not necessarily the right life; and further on, “the mere fact that philosophy and revelation cannot refute each other would constitute the refutation of philosophy by revelation”. For philosophy claims to be a life grounded on evidence; if it itself rests on a choice that no evidence grounds, it confirms what faith said of it. It is this conflict without an arbiter that Strauss calls Athens and Jerusalem, a title he gave to several lectures, in 1946, in 1950 and in 1967, the last published the same year in Commentary.

    One recognizes here, displaced by eight centuries, the question of Averroes and of Maimonides, and it is no accident: it was by reading them that Strauss formed his thesis. Persecution and the Art of Writing (1952) maintains that the philosophers before modernity, under the threat of persecution, wrote in such a way as to convey one teaching to the majority of their readers and another to a few; Maimonides, Judah Halevi and Spinoza himself are said to be among these writers. Strauss took seriously the warning Maimonides places at the head of the Guide, not to explain his secret teaching, to the point of writing that no historian possessed of a sense of decency could lightly disregard the entreaty of a superior man such as Maimonides. We find again Averroes' division between those who demonstrate and those who are persuaded, which the first part set out; Strauss makes of it, rather than a prudence of circumstance, a permanent truth about the relation between philosophy and the city: the city lives on opinions, and in particular on opinions about the gods, which philosophy can neither share nor destroy without danger.

    This thesis, hotly debated, seems to me partly fragile: it is unverifiable by construction, since the absence of signs of a hidden teaching can always be read as proof of its skill, and it has fostered among some disciples a way of reading texts in which suspicion takes the place of philology. One must also recall a letter Strauss wrote from Paris to Löwith in 1933: in it he asserted that one could protest against what he called the “shabby abomination” of the Hitler regime only on the basis of the principles of the right, “from fascist, authoritarian, and imperial principles”. The correspondence with Löwith, partly published under the title “Correspondence Concerning Modernity” (Independent Journal of Philosophy, 4, 1983, and 5/6, 1988, trans. G. E. Tucker), is one of the places where his position takes shape: the two former pupils of Heidegger, so close in their critique of historicism, diverge there over the possibility of a return to the Ancients.

    His relations to the other protagonists complete his placing. As early as 1932, he wrote a review of Carl Schmitt's The Concept of the Political, in which he argued that Schmitt, despite all his efforts, remained a prisoner of the liberal horizon he was fighting, for want of being able to give reasons for his commitment to the political. The critique joins ours by another path: Strauss sees in a sovereign decision that cannot say in the name of what it decides the very symptom of the modernity Schmitt claimed to overcome. With Löwith he shares the rejection of progress and the gaze turned towards the Greeks; but where Löwith withdraws into the Stoic contemplation of nature, Strauss reopens the political question, that of the best regime, which classical philosophy posed and which modernity is said to have abandoned. With Blumenberg, finally, no dialogue is attested, but the disagreement is total: Blumenberg defends the legitimacy of the modern age as self-assertion, Strauss sees in it a break with ancient wisdom, of which Machiavelli is said to be the author and which the critique of religion is said to have made possible.

    Strauss also strikes at our reading of Spinoza. The third part presented the Theological-Political Treatise as one of the acts by which modern philosophy emancipated itself from Scripture, and Spinoza as one of the rare exceptions in the series, the one who keeps the name of God without refounding a cult. Strauss does not dispute that Spinoza wanted to free philosophy; he disputes that he refuted what he was freeing it from.
