    Leopardi's shepherd speaks to the moon: “Che fai tu, luna, in ciel? dimmi, che fai, / silenziosa luna?”, what are you doing, moon, in the sky? tell me, what are you doing, silent moon? He does not ask why there is something, he asks what it is all for; and the moon, which perhaps knows “questo viver terreno”, this earthly life, does not answer. “Questo io conosco e sento, / che degli eterni giri, / che dell'esser mio frale, / qualche bene o contento / avrà fors'altri; a me la vita è male”, this I know and feel: from the eternal rounds, from my frail being, some other perhaps will draw some good or contentment; for me life is an evil; and the ending: “è funesto a chi nasce il dì natale”, the day of birth is baleful to whoever is born.

    Whitman, in “Miracles”, takes the question from the other end: “Why, who makes much of a miracle? / As to me I know of nothing else but miracles[…] To me every hour of the light and dark is a miracle, / Every cubic inch of space is a miracle”. No God in the poem, and no debt: wonder before what there is, spoken without asking to whom it is owed.

    Why here: the two poems are the two treatments of the question that the essay retains last, the shepherd on the side of Schopenhauer and lament, Whitman on the side of Wittgenstein and wonder without an answer. Beckett, finally, dissolved the question on stage: Waiting for Godot begins with “Rien à faire”, nothing to be done, spoken by a tramp who cannot get his boot off, and Godot, of whom we shall never know whether he is someone, does not come; Beckett always refused to let God be read into his name. Carnap would have said that the play shows the pseudo-problem; Wittgenstein, that it shows what cannot be said. The essay holds for both at once, and so does the play.

    Sources: Giacomo Leopardi, “Canto notturno di un pastore errante dell'Asia”, Canti XXIII (1830) ; Walt Whitman, “Miracles”, Leaves of Grass (1856) ; Samuel Beckett, En attendant Godot (1952).

    IMIris Murdoch1919-1999the Good without God

    Background: Plato's philosophy: Forms, soul, city, the Good · The thought of Simone Weil: attention, affliction, decreation, rootedness · Sartre's philosophy: being-in-itself, being-for-itself, freedom, bad faith, commitment · The thought of Iris Murdoch: the novels, the Good, attention · Eros and Psyche: the primordial god, the ladder of the Symposium, Apuleius's tale

    Wonder asks nothing and founds nothing. Iris Murdoch asks more: she maintains that there is, at the heart of moral life, an absolute that is not God, and that we must keep from religion what was most demanding in it while abandoning what was most consoling. That is why she puts the criterion to a fine test: her Good is an absolute, but an absolute that calls for no sacrifice, only the dispossession of the self.

    She is known above all as a novelist, an injustice that English philosophy took a long time to repair. She taught at Oxford from 1948 to 1963, in a milieu dominated by the analysis of moral language, and she brought there readings that her colleagues considered exotic: Sartre, to whom she devoted her first book, Sartre: Romantic Rationalist (1953), Simone Weil, Plato read as a living author, and Buddhist thought. In 1968 she called herself, according to a phrase reported by the entry devoted to her, “a kind of Platonist”. Her philosophy is essentially contained in a small book, The Sovereignty of Good (1970), which gathers three lectures: “The Idea of Perfection”, delivered in 1962 and published in 1964, “On ‘God’ and ‘Good’”, given in 1966 and published in 1969, and “The Sovereignty of Good over Other Concepts”, the Leslie Stephen Lecture at Cambridge, in 1967. She would take all this up again, complicating it, in Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals (1992), her last major book of philosophy, after The Fire and the Sun (1977), devoted to Plato and the arts.

    The adversary of the first lecture is not a theologian; it is the modern subject as drawn both by existentialism and by the analytic philosophy of her day: a pure will, choosing freely among neutral facts, whose morality consists in its public acts. Murdoch had read Sartre closely, and she sees in this figure the secular descendant of the voluntarist God: a being who brings values into existence by choosing them. Murdoch sets against it another picture of moral life, in which the essential is played out before the choice, in the way we see. Our gaze is spontaneously distorted by the ego, by its fantasies, its resentments and its consolations; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry quotes her phrase about “the fat, relentless ego”. The moral task is therefore first of all one of perception: to see the other as he or she is, as real as oneself, distinct from oneself. It has a name: attention.

    The word comes from Simone Weil, and the debt is attested. In 1976 Murdoch cited Waiting for God among the only three philosophical works that had marked her deeply, together with the Symposium and Fear and Trembling. In Weil, attention is a religious category, and she says so plainly: “L'attention, à son plus haut degré, est la même chose que la prière. Elle suppose la foi et l'amour”, attention, at its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer; it presupposes faith and love. And further on: “L'attention absolument sans mélange est prière”, absolutely unmixed attention is prayer. Murdoch takes up the word and withdraws faith from it: the supreme object of attention is no longer God, but reality, other people, beauty, the Good. She also takes from Weil the idea of “decreation”, but transposes it into a soberer vocabulary: the ego must fall silent, and she calls this silence “unselfing”. Her sharpest formula: “We cease to be in order to attend to the existence of something else”.

    Her example is one of the most famous in the century's moral philosophy, because it is tiny. She is looking out of the window, absorbed in a wound to her pride: “I am looking out of my window in an anxious and resentful state of mind, oblivious to my surroundings… Then suddenly I observe a hovering kestrel”. And everything changes: “The brooding self with its hurt vanity has disappeared. There is nothing now but kestrel”. When she returns to her worry, it seems less important to her. The experience has nothing mystical about it in the sense James or Otto meant. Without revelation, without content, without consolation, it merely removes the ego from the centre of the picture, and that is why Murdoch holds it to be moral: natural beauty, art, the study of a foreign language or of a difficult science all do the same thing, they oblige us to submit to something that is not ourselves.

    Towards what is this attention directed? On this point Murdoch meets our question. In “On ‘God’ and ‘Good’”, she proposes a definition of God that is at the same time a leave-taking: “I shall suggest that God was (or is) a single perfect transcendent non-representable and necessarily real object of attention”. And she adds that moral philosophy must try to keep a concept that has all these characteristics without being God: that concept is the Good. Murdoch's Good is the Good of the Republic, the principle that is beyond essence and that makes all things visible as the sun makes objects visible; the Stanford entry reports that she herself compares the Good to a light that enables us to see the good in particular things. Part One of this essay quoted Plato's Greek text on the Good “beyond essence”; Murdoch is a faithful and free reader of it, since she keeps the sun without keeping the world of Forms. The Good is not a person; it neither commands nor rewards. It is what orients, and it retains, she says, something irreducibly mysterious: “A genuine mysteriousness attaches to the idea of goodness and the Good”.

    Prayer, then, does not disappear; it changes its nature. The Wikipedia article on the book reports the formula according to which prayer, properly understood, is not petition but an attention to God which is a form of love; I give it in paraphrase, not having read it in the text. What Murdoch proposes is a prayer without an addressee, or rather a prayer whose addressee is no longer someone: patient and loving attention to what is. The kinship with Hadot's spiritual exercises is real: for both, philosophy is a conversion of the gaze. But the difference is real too. Hadot describes ancient exercises that he does not claim have a transcendent object; Murdoch maintains that there is an object, the Good, and that it is real. She is more of a metaphysician than he is, and closer to Simone Weil.

    She is also opposed, without having known it, to Comte-Sponville's spirituality of immanence, for which the universe suffices and which makes mystical experience a yes to everything that happens. Murdoch would not accept this identification of the Whole and the Good. Reality, for her, is not good because it is; it is the place where one can learn to see the good, which is not the same thing. Her Good judges the world, it does not bless it. The confrontation is constructed, since Murdoch died in 1999 and L'Esprit de l'athéisme dates from 2006; it sets against each other two ways of keeping the absolute without God, one that dissolves it in the totality, the other that maintains it above it.

    Measured against the criterion, Murdoch is a limiting case, and that is what makes her precious. She unambiguously installs an absolute: the Good is sovereign, transcendent, necessary. One could therefore rank her among the refounders, alongside those who put Man, Society or History in the place of God. But this absolute demands no sacrifice: it does not ask that individuals be immolated to it, but that we cease to immolate ourselves to our own fantasies. The dispossession it requires is not submission to an authority that would speak in its name, since the Good does not speak and has neither Church nor priests; it is an unburdening of the gaze. Murdoch therefore belongs, I believe, to the family of exceptions, where she occupies a place that was missing: between Spinoza and Hadot, who think immanence and exercise, and Simone Weil, who keeps the faith, she proposes a transcendent absolute without God, which demands nothing but attention. Her weakness is the one Marx would have pointed out: a morality of vision risks leaving the world as it is, provided one sees it clearly. Murdoch was not unaware of this, and her novels are full of characters who see rightly and do not act. But she replied that we act badly because we see badly, and that most of the crimes committed in the name of an absolute were committed by men who no longer looked at anyone.

    In literature Marcel Proust, The Captive (1923) ; George Eliot, Middlemarch (1872) ; Iris Murdoch, The Sea, the Sea (1978)

    The death of Bergotte, in The Captive, before the little patch of yellow wall in the View of Delft, leads Proust to the only page of In Search of Lost Time that resembles a metaphysics: “tout se passe dans notre vie comme si nous y entrions avec le faix d'obligations contractées dans une vie antérieure ; il n'y a aucune raison dans nos conditions de vie sur cette terre pour que nous nous croyions obligés à faire le bien, à être délicats, même à être polis[…]. Toutes ces obligations qui n'ont pas leur sanction dans la vie présente semblent appartenir à un monde différent, fondé sur la bonté, le scrupule, le sacrifice, un monde entièrement différent de celui-ci[…], ces lois dont tout travail profond de l'intelligence nous rapproche et qui sont invisibles seulement, et encore !, pour les sots”, everything in our life happens as if we entered it with the burden of obligations contracted in a former life; there is no reason in the conditions of our life on this earth why we should consider ourselves obliged to do good, to be considerate, even to be polite; all these obligations, which have no sanction in present life, seem to belong to a different world, founded on kindness, scruple, sacrifice, a world entirely different from this one; those laws to which every profound work of the intellect draws us nearer and which are invisible only, and even then!, to fools.

    Why here: this is Murdoch's Good, almost word for word, in an unbelieving novelist writing thirty years before her: a transcendent, unrepresentable, necessarily real object of attention, which obliges without promising and which one reaches through a work of the intellect and not through prayer. Proust does not say “God”, he says “those laws”; Murdoch will say “the Good”, and the substitution is the same, except that Proust draws no morality from it and Murdoch draws her whole morality from it.

    The finale of Middlemarch gives this morality of attention its most modest form. Dorothea has founded nothing; “the effect of her being on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs”. This is unselfing before the word: a good that asks for neither worship nor sacrifice, only that we look at others. Murdoch, finally, wrote against herself: Charles Arrowby, the narrator of The Sea, the Sea, a man of the theatre retired to the seashore, believes he is stripping himself bare and merely sequesters, in his house, the woman he loved as an adolescent; his cousin James, a Buddhist, dies in silence after saving him: the sovereignty of Good told from the point of view of the fat, relentless ego that does not see it.

    Sources: Marcel Proust, La Prisonnière (1923) ; George Eliot, Middlemarch, Finale (1872) ; Iris Murdoch, The Sea, the Sea (1978).

    The Buddhism of the philosophers: a spirituality without God?

    Background: Schopenhauer's philosophy: the Will, suffering, compassion, the denial of the will · Buddhism: landmarks for a religion without a creator God · Contemporary spiritualities: New Age, meditation, spiritual but not religious

    If one looks in the history of religions for a spirituality without a creator God, Buddhism is the obvious candidate; it has haunted this essay since Schopenhauer without ever being looked at squarely. This must be done with a precaution that is the very subject of this section: the Buddhism the European philosophers of the nineteenth century speak of is not, first of all, the Buddhism of Buddhist countries; it is a figure that Europe constructed, largely out of its own anxieties, and that it successively admired, feared and then adopted. Our question therefore arises twice: is Buddhism an exit from religion without refoundation? And did Europe, in taking it as a model, find an exit, or did it invent for itself a replacement religion?

    Schopenhauer is one of the first great European philosophers to claim Buddhism as his own, and he does so in the name of atheism. In the critique of the Kantian philosophy that closes the first volume of The World, he rails against the habit of translating the Brahman of the Hindus or the Tien of the Chinese as “God”, and he lays down as an established fact that Buddhism knows nothing of the God of the monotheisms: “Daß namentlich der Buddhaismus, diese auf Erden am zahlreichsten vertretene Religion, durchaus keinen Theismus enthält, ja, ihn perhorrescirt, ist eine ganz ausgemachte Sache”, that Buddhism in particular, this religion with the greatest number of adherents on earth, contains absolutely no theism, and even abhors it, is a thoroughly settled matter. Just before, he had asked whether theism properly so called is not found only in the Jewish religion and in the two religions that came out of it. Buddhism is thus for him the historical proof that a religion can do without God, and that it is all the truer for doing without him.

    What he finds there above all is the confirmation of his own doctrine of salvation. The fourth book of The World, whose final sentence on nothingness we read in Part Six, makes nirvana the mythical expression of the denial of the will to live. In § 63, Schopenhauer quotes the Buddhist promise in the form in which he had read it: “Du sollst Nirwana erlangen, d.i. einen Zustand, in welchem es vier Dinge nicht giebt: Geburt, Alter, Krankheit und Tod”, you shall attain nirvana, that is, a state in which there are not these four things: birth, old age, sickness and death. And he says of the Indian doctrine of transmigration, of which this promise is the end point, that no myth has ever come, or ever will come, closer to the philosophical truth accessible to so few. But at the end of the book, in § 71, he distances himself from the word itself. Before the nothingness that awaits at the end of all virtue and all holiness, he refuses to do as the Indians do, who evade it “durch Mythen und bedeutungsleere Worte, wie Resorbtion in das Brahm, oder Nirwana der Buddhaisten”, through myths and words empty of meaning, such as reabsorption into Brahman or the nirvana of the Buddhists. He prefers to admit that what remains after the abolition of the will is, for those who still will, nothingness. Schopenhauer admires Buddhism because he finds his pessimism in it, and he corrects it as soon as he finds a consolation in it. In 1856 he had a bronze statuette of the Buddha bought for him in Paris, had it gilded and installed it in his drawing room in Frankfurt.

    Nietzsche inherits this reading and turns it around. In The Antichrist (1888), he takes care not to confuse the two religions, which he nonetheless ranks together among the nihilist religions, the religions of decadence. Buddhism comes out of the comparison enhanced: “Der Buddhismus ist hundertmal realistischer als das Christentum”, Buddhism is a hundred times more realistic than Christianity; it is heir to a long philosophical tradition, and when it appears, “der Begriff »Gott« ist bereits abgetan”, the concept “God” has already been disposed of. Nietzsche goes further: Buddhism is “die einzige eigentlich positivistische Religion, die uns die Geschichte zeigt”, the only properly positivist religion that history shows us, because it no longer says “Kampf gegen die Sünde”, struggle against sin, but “Kampf gegen das Leiden”, struggle against suffering. The Buddha, in this portrait, is a physician rather than a prophet: he treats a fatigue of civilization with a hygiene, life in the open air, temperance, wariness of the passions that heat the blood, and he excludes prayer as well as asceticism; Nietzsche even notes that there is no compulsion in the monastic community, “man kann wieder hinaus”, one can leave it again. The conclusion is aimed at Christianity: Buddhism is “eine Religion für späte Menschen”, a religion for late human beings, and “Europa ist noch lange nicht reif für ihn”, Europe is still far from ripe for it. And the difference, Nietzsche formulates a little further on: Buddhism does not promise, it delivers, whereas Christianity promises everything and delivers nothing.

    Beyond their opposition, these two readings make Buddhism a religion without God and the mirror of their own philosophy: the Buddhism of renunciation for Schopenhauer, the Buddhism of hygiene for Nietzsche. Roger-Pol Droit's inquiry changes the perspective here. In Le Culte du néant. Les philosophes et le Bouddha (Seuil, 1997), one of the two books submitted for his doctorate, La Découverte du bouddhisme et la philosophie européenne (1820-1890), defended in 1998 at Paris IV, Droit shows that nineteenth-century Europe long saw in Buddhism a cult of nothingness, a paradoxical and frightening religion that supposedly worshipped annihilation, and that this fear receded as the scholarly study of the texts developed. The scholar who founded this study in France, Eugène Burnouf, in his Introduction à l'histoire du buddhisme indien (1844), put the question in the very terms that would feed the fear. He recalls that the etymology of the word designates extinction, and he lists the possible interpretations up to the most radical: “en deux mots, le Nirvâna est-il le néant ?”, in a word, is Nirvana nothingness? Burnouf did not decide, and answered at once that the etymology settled nothing and that the usage of the different schools had to be examined; but the question had been asked, and the philosophers, from Hegel to the French spiritualists, turned it into an answer. Buddhism became, for Europe, the name of what it feared in itself: the nothingness it saw coming after God.

    This detour sheds light on our question. When Nietzsche announces that Europe is not ripe for Buddhism, or when he wonders, as early as the preface to On the Genealogy of Morality, whether the morality of pity is not European culture's detour “zu einem neuen Buddhismus? zu einem Europäer-Buddhismus?”, towards a new Buddhism, towards a Buddhism of Europeans, he is not speaking first of Asia: he is speaking of the death of God and of what follows it. The Buddhism of the philosophers is the projection, in the sense Feuerbach gave the word, of the question Europe was asking itself: what remains when heaven is empty? Neither Schopenhauer nor Nietzsche describes real Buddhism.

    For real Buddhism is not a spirituality without religion. It knows nothing of the creator and personal God of the monotheisms, and Schopenhauer was right on this point; but it is not without gods, who people its cosmology and are themselves caught in the cycle of rebirths, nor without the law of karma, nor rites, nor relics. Above all, it has an institution, the community of monks and nuns, the saṅgha, governed by a detailed discipline, the vinaya, with its rules, its expulsions and its ordinations. The refuge the faithful pronounce is threefold: the Buddha, the doctrine, the community. This is the point that matters for the criterion: a religion without God, Buddhism is not a religion without Law or without Church, and it shows that the absence of God is not enough to define an exit from religion, since everything else religion comprises, dogma, community, observance, can subsist without him. Conversely, it shows that the absolute of a religion is not necessarily a person: nirvana, the extinction of thirst, can hold the place that God holds elsewhere. Without deciding debates among Indologists that I am in no position to judge, I retain what all of them accept: that historical Buddhism is a complete religious tradition, and not a secular wisdom.

    Does it demand a sacrifice? The answer must be nuanced. Monastic renunciation is voluntary, and Nietzsche was right to observe that one can leave the community. Buddhism has, in principle, no political theology, and non-violence is at the heart of its ethics. But history has known state Buddhisms, warrior monks and Buddhist nationalisms, and the fact that the doctrine demands no sacrifice has not prevented the institutions from demanding one. It thus confirms a lesson met with in Girard and in Gauchet: it is not doctrine alone that decides whether a religion sacrifices, it is the meeting of doctrine and power.

    The Buddhism the West practises today is, for its part, a religious invention, perhaps the most durable since the religion of Humanity. It extracts from historical Buddhism a technique, meditation, and an ethics of compassion, leaving aside the cosmology, the rebirths, the gods and often monasticism. Comte-Sponville, whose spirituality of immanence gives a large place to the Eastern wisdoms, offers a philosophical version of it; the secular meditation of hospitals and companies is its technical version. This Buddhism is indeed a spirituality without God; but it is also a reinvention, which repeats the gesture of the nineteenth-century philosophers taking from Buddhism what they needed. It refounds no religion, since it demands nothing and installs no absolute. But it runs the opposite risk, the one Murdoch would have pointed out: an attention that no longer aims at anything real, an inner peace that is sufficient unto itself and can accommodate itself to any world whatever. Meditation taught to make employees more efficient is the opposite of what Nietzsche called a hygiene against the fatigue of civilization: it is its palliative care.

    Historical Buddhism, I believe, is not the proof that one can leave religion by leaving God; it is the proof that religion is not defined by God. The Buddhism of the philosophers is not a description but a symptom: that of a Europe seeking, after the death of God, a form of salvation without a saviour. And contemporary Western Buddhism illustrates the thesis in its own way: one can keep spirituality while leaving religion, provided one knows what one is keeping and where one has it from. Those who meditate knowing that they are borrowing a technique from a tradition they do not share are in the position of Spinoza keeping the name of God; those who think they have found in meditation a wisdom without history and without presuppositions are in the position of the atheists of the marketplace, who do not see the shadows they carry.

    In literature Hermann Hesse, Siddhartha (1922) ; Rudyard Kipling, Kim (1901) ; Jack Kerouac, The Dharma Bums (1958)

    Hesse's Siddhartha is not the Buddha: he is a Brahmin's son who meets Gotama, recognizes in him the Awakened One, and refuses to follow him, because a doctrine, even a true one, cannot pass on what the master found alone; he goes through wealth, love and disgust, and ends as a ferryman, listening to the river in which all voices merge into one “Om”, until his friend Govinda, kissing his forehead, sees all faces in his face. Why here: this is the Buddhism of the philosophers in its purest form, experience without doctrine, the river without the saṅgha, and the essay says why it is a projection: in 1922 Hesse writes a novel of the individual, where the real tradition begins with the threefold refuge, the second of which is the community.

    Kipling, who had seen India, gives the lama of Kim a more accurate voice: “I go to free myself from the Wheel of Things”, he says, seeking “The River of the Arrow”, whose water washes away sin. The lama has a monastery, a rule, relics, merit to acquire and a chart of the Wheel that he draws for the boy; he is religious in the full sense, and it is this Buddhism that the philosophers do not want. Kerouac, finally, told in The Dharma Bums how a handful of California poets reinvented a Buddhism of mountain peaks, wine and poems, without a monastery, with a Buddha who blesses everything one does: meditation without tradition, which, the essay says, became half a century later a form of palliative care for executives.

    Sources: Hermann Hesse, Siddhartha (1922) ; Rudyard Kipling, Kim, ch. 1 (1901) ; Jack Kerouac, The Dharma Bums (1958).

    The spiritualities of the Universe: a dictated Christ, an enchanted physics

    Background: Contemporary spiritualities: New Age, meditation, spiritual but not religious · Received revelations: spiritism, channeling, the Christ Letters · Quantum mysticism, synchronicity and the law of attraction

    The wisdoms this part examines have authors, books and a history that can be argued over. What most of our contemporaries meet under the name of spirituality, outside the Churches, rarely has any of these: texts received from a higher plane, a Universe that answers our desires, a quantum physics invoked to guarantee that consciousness creates reality. They must nevertheless be looked at, for two reasons. It is in this form, far more than in that of Hadot or Murdoch, that spirituality without a Church exists today in bookshops and on screens; and these spiritualities put the criterion to a test that is the reverse of the one Buddhism set. Buddhism was a religion without God; these present themselves as spiritualities without religion, and we shall see that they keep what is most questionable in religion without keeping what is strongest in it. I take two cases, chosen because they are typical, not because they are important, and I warn that they are not, in the sense I give the phrase in the rest of this essay, spiritualities without God: the first keeps Christ, the second replaces God with the Universe, which is not the same thing as doing without him.

    The Christ Letters (in French, Les Lettres du Christ) are nine letters presented as dictated by Christ himself to an anonymous South African woman who calls herself his “Recorder” (in the French edition, his “Porte-parole”), circulated online and then published as a book; in French under the title Le Christ revient, révèle sa surprenante vérité (Interkeltia, 2010), then as Les Lettres du Christ (Atlantes, 2012, then Pocket). In them Christ returns to correct the misinterpretations of the teaching he had given in Palestine under the name of Jesus. There is no sin against God; there is no Trinity; above all, there is no salvation through the cross. In the third letter, addressed to Good Friday, he asks that the drama attached to that day be abandoned: “I died[…] and that was, for me, a wondrous release”; and he demands that one turn away “from the old dogmas of ‘salvation by the blood of the lamb’, the Trinity, and other beliefs”. What replaces dogma is a metaphysics of universal Consciousness, of the ego as the source of all suffering, and of a creative energy that the letters describe in the vocabulary of electricity, magnetism and particles.

    The tools of this essay are enough to place this text, and there is no need to invent others. Schweitzer had shown that every age makes itself the Jesus it needs: the Jesus of the Letters is a master of consciousness, without apocalypse, without the Jewish Law, without a redeeming cross, that is, the exact opposite of the prophet the historians reconstruct, and the exact portrait of the spirituality of personal development. Renan had his fifth gospel, which was a landscape; this is a sixth, which presents itself as a dictation, and that is the decisive point. Kierkegaard, Barth and Weil criticized religion in the name of faith by renouncing any possession of God; the Letters criticize religion by making him speak. They contest the authority of the Churches in the name of an authority higher than that of all the Churches, and they submit it to no control: the notice placed at the head of each letter asks the reader first to make silence within, because it is only in this “completely receptive” state that the letters will penetrate their thought with their reality. One recognizes the gesture of Otto asking the reader without experience not to read on; but Otto described an experience, he did not claim to transcribe it at the dictation of its object. The objection I addressed to Schleiermacher applies here without softening: the Recorder's experience proves that she felt something, it does not prove that this something was Christ. There remains James's criterion, judging by the fruits and not by the roots; it is the most charitable, and it is on this ground that the text must be judged.

    On one point, and it is no small one, the fruits are good. The Letters refuse the sacrificial reading of the cross, the one Paul had installed by spiritualizing sacrifice instead of abolishing it, and which Girard, by an entirely different route, turned against the religion of sacrifice. A Christ who declares that he did not die to redeem anyone, and who asks that people stop mortifying themselves in his memory, stands on the side of the criterion. But the sacrifice driven out of the cross comes back by another door. God, say the Letters, cannot save man, because humanity, in ignorance of the laws of existence, will go on making the same mistakes, “thus creating his own sickness and misery”; the law of cause and effect is “imponderable”, and one can no more escape the law by which one reaps what one has sown in one's thoughts and feelings than the laws of electromagnetism, “for electromagnetism is the IMPULSE producing the Law of sowing and reaping”. The sixth letter specifies that the forms created by the ego's thoughts disturb the functioning of the body and are “the origin of physical discomforts or viruses or disease”. It is no longer a God who demands, it is a law; but the law makes the sick person the author of their sickness. The mechanism Girard described at the scale of the crowd is found here at the scale of the individual, in its gentlest and most insidious form: the victim is declared guilty of their own misfortune, and by no one, by the sole logic of a doctrine that leaves no room for chance. Paul's old sentence, whatever a man sows, that he will also reap, receives the guarantee of physics.

    That guarantee is the second case. Quantum mysticism has a genealogy, which I summarize from the historians of the New Age without entering into the physics, which is beyond my competence. In 1952 Jung published with the physicist Wolfgang Pauli Naturerklärung und Psyche, in which he set out synchronicity, the coincidence of a psychic state and an external event linked not by a cause but by a meaning, with the example of the golden scarab that taps at the window while a patient is recounting her dream. In 1975 Fritjof Capra, a physicist by training, published The Tao of Physics, which brings quantum mechanics close to the Eastern mystics; in 1980 David Bohm, also a physicist, proposed in Wholeness and the Implicate Order an undivided totality that he would discuss with Krishnamurti; in 1989 Deepak Chopra made Quantum Healing a medicine of consciousness; the film What the Bleep Do We Know!? (2004) and then Rhonda Byrne's The Secret (2006) popularized the “law of attraction”, according to which our thoughts attract the events that resemble them. The physicists have answered, from Murray Gell-Mann, who spoke of “quantum flapdoodle”, to Victor Stenger (The Unconscious Quantum, 1995): the observer of quantum mechanics is a measuring apparatus, not a consciousness that creates the world, and the entanglement of particles does not bind souls together. I have nothing to add to their answer, except that it does not reach what interests this essay.

    For the phenomenon is not new, and James had described it a century earlier. In lectures IV and V of the Varieties, he devotes long pages to what he calls the “Mind‐cure movement”, which its followers also call “New Thought” and of which the law of attraction is the direct heir. He takes it seriously, as “a genuine religious power”, and notes with irony that it has reached the stage where demand is strong enough for publishers to supply “insincere stuff, mechanically produced for the market”, which happens, he says, only to a religion well past its insecure beginnings. He also sees its limit. For Mrs. Eddy's Christian Science, the most radical branch of the movement, “evil is simply a lie, and any one who mentions it is a liar”; James sees in this “a bad speculative omission”. These are the once-born of his typology, and the sky-blue gospel he asked his hearers to turn their backs on in order to listen to the sick souls. Quantum mysticism changes nothing in this structure; it merely gives it a vocabulary more prestigious than that of Mesmer's magnetic fluid, which was its eighteenth-century version.

    This vocabulary is nonetheless instructive. This essay has met science turned into an absolute several times: Freud's god Logos, the Reason of the new atheists, and Wittgenstein's remark that the moderns stop before the laws of nature as the ancients did before God and fate. Quantum mysticism makes the reverse and complementary movement: it does not sacralize science, it asks it to testify for the sacred. It is the regime of error turned inside out. Lucretius and d'Holbach set physics against the gods; here physics is called on to restore them, under the name of Consciousness, Energy or the Universe. It is also § 344 of The Gay Science in reverse: Nietzsche confessed that science's will to truth still rested on a faith, and drew from it a demand for lucidity; quantum mysticism borrows from science its prestige without its will to truth, that is, without the one thing that made it an ascesis. As for synchronicity, Boyer gives the most economical explanation of it: a human mind equipped to detect agents and intentions everywhere, and Hume before him, who saw faces in the moon. The meaningful coincidence is a world that beckons to me; and a world that beckons to me is a world that addresses me, that is, under another name, Providence.

    It is here that wonder changes its nature. Wittgenstein said that the mystical is not how the world is, but that it is; synchronicity and the law of attraction look for the mystical, on the contrary, in the how, in the messages that events send me and in the answers the Universe gives my thoughts. One passes from wonder that there is a world to the conviction that the world answers me, and from there to the idea that it answers me according to what I deserve. I have maintained that to think being is not to owe it something; the law of attraction turns the fact into a gift, the gift into an answer and the answer into a debt, and the manuals that teach it prescribe, logically enough, daily exercises of gratitude towards the Universe.

    Measured by the criterion, the verdict must be exact. Neither the Christ Letters nor quantum mysticism refounds a religion in the strict sense: they install no absolute in whose name the sacrifice of others could be demanded, they have no clergy, and criticizing them is not a sacrilege, only a mark of ego or of low vibration. They have merchants rather than priests, as James had seen, and a public of pilgrims without a lineage, in Hervieu-Léger's sense. I place them among the other transfers of the sacred: the sacred passes from God to the Universe, or to a Consciousness that has all his attributes except the name. Their fault is not sacrifice, it is consolation, and the indicator I drew from Weil applies to them to the letter. A spirituality in which every misfortune has its cause in the thoughts of the one who suffers it consoles for injustice by making it understandable; but it does worse than console, it suppresses the Protestation Marx heard in the sigh of the oppressed creature. Leibniz asked the individual to sacrifice their complaint for the sake of the harmony of the whole; the law of attraction makes the complaint itself a negative thought, which aggravates the evil it deplores. It is a theodicy without God, and it has the defect of all the theodicies Ivan refused: it is right in advance against the suffering child. And on the day when the belief that one creates one's own illness leads someone to give up treatment, or to have it refused to a child, the sacrifice ceases to be metaphorical; it is there, and not in the vocabulary, that the border runs between a harmless spirituality and a hold over people.

    These spiritualities therefore confirm the thesis by a path I did not expect. They do not leave religion: they keep its revelation, its providence and its retribution, and give up only the Church, avowed dogma and the cross, that is, with the cross, the one place where Christianity looked the misfortune of the innocent in the face. They are atheists of the marketplace turned inside out: the men of § 125 did not know that God was dead; these do not know that their Universe is the old Providence in a lab coat. The answer this essay seeks is not to set science against them, since they already invoke it; it is to set against them what science, philosophy and the most demanding believers have in common, and what they have lost: lucidity about what one keeps and where one has it from, and the refusal to make the one who suffers evil bear the blame for it. Wonder that there is a world demands nothing of anyone; the Universe that answers me already demands that I think as I should.

    In literature Gustave Flaubert, Bouvard et Pécuchet (1881) ; Paulo Coelho, O Alquimista (1988)

    In chapter VIII of Bouvard et Pécuchet, the two copy clerks discover table-turning, which “par toute l'Europe, en Amérique, en Australie et dans les Indes, des millions de mortels passaient leur vie à faire tourner”, throughout Europe, in America, in Australia and in the Indies, millions of mortals spent their lives making turn, and then magnetism, whose fluid they pour onto their servant, who suffers from ringing in the ears, and onto a bloated cow. During an evening at their house, everyone brings their own coincidence, and the justice of the peace throws out his like a challenge: “Je suis né un 14, mon mariage eut lieu un 14[…] et le jour de ma fête tombe un 14! Expliquez-moi ça.”, I was born on a 14th, my wedding took place on a 14th, and my saint's day falls on a 14th! Explain that to me; the priest suggests demons. Flaubert lists the explanations like a catalogue of the science of the day: “Le vulgaire l'attribue à des Esprits, Faraday au prolongement de l'action nerveuse, Chevreul à l'inconscience des efforts, ou peut-être, comme admet Ségouin, se dégage-t-il de l'assemblage des personnes une impulsion, un courant magnétique?”, the common people attribute it to Spirits, Faraday to an extension of nervous action, Chevreul to the unconsciousness of effort, or perhaps, as Ségouin admits, an impulse, a magnetic current, is released from the gathering of persons? And when Bouvard admits that he believes in a fluid, the doctor challenges him: “Mais prouvez-le! montrez-le! votre fluide! D'ailleurs les fluides sont démodés”, but prove it! show it! your fluid! Besides, fluids are out of fashion.

    Why here: synchronicity found its name in 1952, but Flaubert's justice of the peace already had the thing, and quantum mysticism is the fluid of our century. Flaubert saw the essential, which is not credulity but fashion. The learned word changes every fifty years, electricity, magnetism, energy, the quantum; the structure remains, which asks the physics of the moment to guarantee that the mind acts on things. Bouvard and Pécuchet move on, moreover, in the next chapter, to religion: the novel knows that the one leads to the other.

    Coelho's novel is its happy version, sold by the million. Santiago, an Andalusian shepherd, sets off to look for a treasure at the foot of the pyramids on the strength of a dream; an old king teaches him that the whole Universe conspires to fulfil the desire of whoever pursues their “Personal Legend”, and an alchemist teaches him to read the signs the world sends him. Why here: it is the law of attraction turned into a tale, with what the essay holds against it. The world beckons on every page, and the one who fails is the one who did not want enough: the book knows no Ivan.

    Sources: Gustave Flaubert, Bouvard et Pécuchet, ch. VIII (1881) ; Paulo Coelho, O Alquimista (1988).

    André Comte-Sponvilleb. 1952a spirituality of immanence

    Background: Spinoza's philosophy: substance, attributes, modes, conatus, kinds of knowledge, the Theological-Political Treatise · The thought of William James: pragmatism, psychology, religious experience · The thought of Comte-Sponville: materialism, wisdom, spirituality without God · The thought of Michel Onfray: hedonism, Traité d'athéologie, Décadence, Théorie de Jésus · Contemporary spiritualities: New Age, meditation, spiritual but not religious

    In 2006 André Comte-Sponville published L'Esprit de l'athéisme. Introduction à une spiritualité sans Dieu. The book is built around three questions: can we do without religion? Does God exist? What spirituality for atheists? To the first two he answers as an atheist; to the third, as a mystic, and therein lies his originality.

    His first answer is measured. One can do without religion, in the sense that one can live without a Church, without dogma, without worship; one cannot do without communion, fidelity or love. The paraphrase comes from a review, and it renders the movement of the book well: the best of what religion provided, the bond between human beings, attachment to transmitted values, the capacity to love, can survive faith. Comte-Sponville calls himself a faithful atheist: he has lost faith, not fidelity to what the Christian tradition taught him of justice, compassion and love. The second is no less measured: atheism is for him a belief, not a knowledge; he does not claim to prove that God does not exist, he says as a philosopher why he does not believe, without contempt for believers.

    It is the third that interests us. Comte-Sponville maintains there that spirituality does not belong to the religions. It is the life of the mind insofar as it relates to the infinite, to eternity, to the absolute; and this absolute the atheist does not deny, he denies only its transcendence. The atheist's spirituality is a mysticism of immanence. He gives a formula for it that condenses the whole book: “Un Dieu ? Pour quoi faire ? L'univers suffit. Une Eglise ? Inutile. Le monde suffit. Une foi ? A quoi bon ? L'expérience suffit”, a God? What for? The universe is enough. A Church? Useless. The world is enough. A faith? What good is it? Experience is enough. And elsewhere: “A quoi bon rêver d'un paradis ? Le Royaume, c'est ici et maintenant”, what good is dreaming of a paradise? The Kingdom is here and now. And the last sentence of the book says it again: “Nous sommes déjà dans le Royaume : l'éternité, c'est maintenant”, we are already in the Kingdom: eternity is now. The philosophical formula that grounds this mysticism is Spinozist: “Tout est immanent au Tout”, everything is immanent to the All.

    The heart of this spirituality is an experience, and Comte-Sponville calls it by the very name Romain Rolland had proposed to Freud: the oceanic feeling. He defines it as “l'expérience d'une intériorité (mais qui me contient, et que je ne contiens pas), d'une immanence, d'une unité, d'une immersion, d'un dedans”, the experience of an interiority (but one that contains me, and that I do not contain), of an immanence, a unity, an immersion, an inside. He adds that this experience, which he says he has known himself, culminates in acceptance: “dire oui à tout ce qui est, à tout ce qui arrive”, saying yes to everything that is, to everything that happens. He sees in it the common ground of the mystics of every tradition, Christian, Buddhist, Taoist, an experience that is sufficient unto itself and does not need God in order to be lived. And he does not want to leave it to the fanatics: “la spiritualité est une chose trop importante pour qu'on l'abandonne aux fondamentalistes”, spirituality is too important a thing to be abandoned to the fundamentalists.

    The confrontation with Part Eight is constructed. In 1930, Freud could not discover in himself Rolland's oceanic feeling; he made it the survival of a primitive state of the ego, prior to its separation from the external world, and refused to see in it the source of religion, born in his view of infantile helplessness and the need for a father. In 2006, an atheist philosopher makes this feeling the heart of a spirituality without God. Rolland was therefore right against Freud on one point: the experience exists and does not need the personal God in order to be expressed. Freud was right against Rolland on another: nothing obliges us to see a revelation in it. Comte-Sponville holds both ends, Rolland's experience and Freud's atheism.

    The objections came from two sides, and one of them is attested. On the atheist side, Michel Onfray places Comte-Sponville in what he calls Christian atheism, and is said to have called him a “chrétien athée”, an atheist Christian. In Onfray's mouth this is an accusation: the faithful atheist keeps Christian morality, compassion, humility, love of neighbour, abandoning only God; he is still one of those pious atheists Stirner denounced. I have found no reply by Comte-Sponville to this formula. On the philosophical side, Hausemer made a graver objection, carried by the very title of his review, “André Comte-Sponville ou La disparition du mal”, André Comte-Sponville or the disappearance of evil: the Spinozist acceptance of everything that happens makes evil disappear. If I say yes to everything that is, I also say yes to the suffering of the child.

    This objection strikes home, and it brings us back to Ivan Karamazov. Ivan refused the harmony that would justify a child's tear; he returned his ticket. Comte-Sponville, like Spinoza and like the Nietzsche of amor fati, accepts the whole of reality. But Spinoza asked that evil be understood, not approved, and the Ethics is also a treatise on the power of acting, which in no way commands passivity before injustice. Comte-Sponville's spirituality is not, by the criterion, a refoundation: it demands no sacrifice, promises no collective salvation, asks no one to kneel before a Great Being. But it is exposed to another weakness: by saying that the universe is enough, it risks forgetting what is not enough, and what religion, at least, named. What this spirituality lacks is Marx's Protestation. The oceanic experience consoles; it does not protest.

    In literature Arthur Rimbaud, “L'Éternité” (1872) ; Albert Camus, Noces (1939) ; Jean Giono, Que ma joie demeure (1935)

    “Elle est retrouvée. / Quoi ? L'Éternité. / C'est la mer allée / Avec le soleil.”, it is found again. / What? Eternity. / It is the sea gone off / With the sun. The poem of May 1872 says what Comte-Sponville will put into prose: eternity is not another world, it is now, in the sea and the sun, and there one frees oneself “Des humains suffrages, / Des communs élans”, from human approval, from common impulses; then, without transition: “Là pas d'espérance, / Nul orietur. / Science avec patience, / Le supplice est sûr”, there, no hope, / no orietur. / Knowledge with patience, / the torment is certain.

    Why here: “Le Royaume, c'est ici et maintenant” is a line of Rimbaud before it is a thesis; but the poem also contains the objection the essay addresses to Comte-Sponville. No hope, no orietur, no “he shall rise”: eternity found again is without promise and without consolation, but “le supplice est sûr”, the torment is certain, and Rimbaud does not say yes to everything that is. The oceanic experience consoles, the essay writes, it does not protest; the poem feels eternity and keeps the torment, and in this it is more complete than the wisdom that claims it.

    Camus, in “Noces à Tipasa”, wrote the page Comte-Sponville readily quotes: the Roman ruins overgrown with wormwood, the sea, the sun, and a young man who says that there is nothing to hide and nothing to hope for, that the world is beautiful and that this is enough, that the gods speak in the sun and the scent of wormwood. It is the same immanence, in a man who, twelve years later, would write The Rebel: the kingdom of Tipasa was not enough, revolt was needed, and this is precisely the path the conclusion of the essay proposes to Comte-Sponville. Giono, finally, in Que ma joie demeure, brings down onto the Grémone plateau an acrobat, Bobi, who teaches the peasants to sow flowers, to listen to the stag and to keep joy without possessing it; joy does not remain, and Bobi dies struck by lightning. The title is a prayer from Bach turned into a question: immanent joy, here and now, and the storm that awaits it.

    Sources: Arthur Rimbaud, “L'Éternité”, Fêtes de la patience (May 1872) ; Albert Camus, “Noces à Tipasa”, Noces (1939) ; Jean Giono, Que ma joie demeure (1935).

    Portrait: Wikinade, CC BY-SA 3.0

    Luc Ferryb. 1951the man-God and horizontal transcendence

    Background: The thought of Luc Ferry: transcendental humanism, the Man-God, the revolution of love · The thought of Abdennour Bidar: self islam, leaving religion, man as khalîf

    Luc Ferry published L'Homme-Dieu ou le Sens de la vie in 1996, then, with André Comte-Sponville, La Sagesse des Modernes (1998), and, with Marcel Gauchet, Le Religieux après la religion (2004). Of all the authors in this part, he is the one who has engaged most directly in dialogue with the others. His thesis describes a double movement, which he calls on one side the humanization of the divine and on the other the divinization of the human.

    The humanization of the divine is secularization in Gauchet's sense: Christian contents become secular, love of neighbour becomes solidarity, charity becomes humanitarian action, salvation becomes happiness. The divinization of the human is the inverse and complementary movement: the values that modern man places above his life, the true, the just, the beautiful, love, impose themselves on his conscience as if they came from elsewhere. He does not invent them at will; he discovers them in himself as a demand that exceeds him. He no longer believes in God, but lives by values that bear all the marks of the sacred: one can die for them, and sometimes one does. Ferry calls this structure a transcendence within immanence, or a horizontal transcendence. The sacred is no longer above, in heaven; it is ahead, in other human beings and in the horizon of meaning they open.

    Ferry describes this shift from the standpoint of tradition. The bond that unites human beings, he writes, “n'est plus situé dans une tradition, dans un héritage imposé de l'extérieur, dans un amont de leur conscience, mais c'est en aval qu'il nous faut désormais penser ce qui pourrait être l'analogue moderne des traditions perdues: une identité post-traditionnelle”, is no longer located in a tradition, in a heritage imposed from outside, upstream of their consciousness, but it is downstream that we must henceforth think what could be the modern analogue of the lost traditions: a post-traditional identity. Transcendence no longer comes from upstream, from what has been received; it comes from downstream, from what is to be done. Later, Ferry would propose defining philosophy itself as “une doctrine du salut sans Dieu, une spiritualité laïque”, a doctrine of salvation without God, a secular spirituality.

    Ferry thus poses a problem for our essay, with a frankness that does him credit. He does not claim that modern man has left religion without remainder; he says that the sacred has shifted from heaven to man, and that this shift is the truth of modern humanism. Now this is what Stirner reproached Feuerbach with: Man has become the supreme being, and one has freed oneself from God only by worshipping humanity. The very title L'Homme-Dieu would have made Stirner smile. Ferry takes on the divinization of the human knowingly, which distinguishes him from Feuerbach but does not answer the objection.

    The objections are attested. Agnès Antoine, in Esprit in December 1996, wrote: “Il y a[…] quelque naïveté ou perversité à choisir comme titre du livre l'"homme-Dieu"”, there is[…] some naivety or perversity in choosing “man-God” as the title of the book. Cantin himself, following Fernand Dumont, wonders whether a transcendence lodged in the immanence of consciousness still deserves to be called transcendence. The objection is just, but it opens an alternative. Either horizontal transcendence is only a metaphor for the moderns' attachment to values they judge superior to their lives: there is then neither refoundation nor spirituality, only a morality. Or it is a true transcendence, and Ferry consecrates, after Feuerbach and Comte, a religion of Humanity, more discreet and more liberal.

    I believe that Ferry oscillates between the two, and that this oscillation is instructive. He makes the disposition to die for a value, liberty, justice or those one loves, the sign of its sacredness. This disposition is not enough to place him among the refounders in the strict sense: the criterion concerns the absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded, not freely consented self-offering, and nothing in Ferry demands of anyone that he die. But Ferry does not confine himself to noting these devotions; he calls them sacred, and that is the need to consecrate that Engels reproached Feuerbach with. He therefore belongs to soft refoundation: a religion of the human that has renounced clergy, dogma and constraint, and contents itself with consecrating that for which some human beings agree to die. It is the most liberal form of refoundation, and perhaps the only one compatible with a democratic society. It nonetheless remains a consecration, and one can apply to it the question Stirner put to Feuerbach: in the name of what does this ideal command me?

    In literature Victor Hugo, “Le Satyre” (1859) ; Émile Zola, Travail (1901)

    “Le Satyre”, at the centre of La Légende des siècles, brings up onto Olympus a shaggy faun whom the gods want to humiliate; he sings, and his song grows with him: the earth, man, the future, until, having become greater than heaven, he summons the gods: “Place à Tout ! Je suis Pan ; Jupiter ! à genoux”, make way for the All! I am Pan; Jupiter, on your knees!

    Why here: this is the divinization of the human and the humanization of the divine in a single line, eighteen years after The Essence of Christianity and more than a century before L'Homme-Dieu. The satyr does not deny the gods; he makes them kneel before the All of which man is the voice; and Hugo, who believed in God, writes here the horizontal transcendence of L'Homme-Dieu in its Romantic version, that is to say without Ferry's liberal restraint. The poem shows where soft consecration leads when it raises its voice: it demands that one kneel.

    Zola, in Travail, has an engineer, Luc Froment, found a workers' city on Fourier's model, the Crêcherie, which gradually absorbs the factory, the town and the Church; Abbé Marle says his last Mass in an empty church that collapses on him, and the novel ends, sixty years later, with a festival of humanity reconciled by work and love. It is Ferry's religion of humanity written by a novelist who wanted it and who, without knowing it, made a liturgy of it: the happy city has its festivals, its founders and its old Church that must be seen to fall. The essay's soft refoundation finds in Zola its closing chapter.

    Sources: Victor Hugo, “Le Satyre”, La Légende des siècles, first series, VIII (1859) ; Émile Zola, Travail, book III (1901).

    Portrait: Thesupermat, CC BY-SA 4.0

    Comte-Sponville and Ferrythe quarrel of the two wisdoms

    Background: The thought of Comte-Sponville: materialism, wisdom, spirituality without God · The thought of Luc Ferry: transcendental humanism, the Man-God, the revolution of love

    La Sagesse des Modernes, their book of dialogue on the great questions of ethics, attests that their disagreement was public. I have not read its text and I quote nothing from it; all that is known is that Ferry there judges Comte-Sponville's wisdom to be close to Buddhism. This disagreement bears directly on our question, and it can be reconstructed from their other books without attributing to them sentences they did not write.

    Comte-Sponville is a materialist. His avowed genealogy runs from Epicurus and Lucretius to Spinoza, with borrowings from the Eastern wisdoms: there is nothing other than nature, of which man is a part, and freedom is only necessity understood and accepted. Wisdom consists in ceasing to hope, in inhabiting the present, in loving what is; transcendence, in all its forms, is an illusion of a mind that believes itself greater than the world. Ferry is a Kantian: man is distinguished from nature by his freedom, his capacity to tear himself away from every natural or historical code, which grounds his dignity. Values are not deduced from reality, they impose themselves on it as an ought, and horizontal transcendence is the truth of human freedom: man is the being who never coincides with what he is.

    By the criterion, the two positions are not of equal worth. Comte-Sponville's wisdom refounds no sacrificial absolute, but it risks accepting too much and disarming revolt. Ferry's humanism keeps the capacity to protest, but pays for it with a consecration. Here we meet again the alternative between Spinoza and Kant, which Parts Three and Four brought out without settling it: acceptance without transcendence, or transcendence without God. Perhaps neither is a complete exit; but the first is closer to an exit without refoundation, and the second more capable of hearing Marx's Protestation. The conclusion will have to say whether one can have both.

    In literature Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, “Grenzen der Menschheit” (1781)

    The poem is Goethe's answer to his own “Prometheus”, seven years later. “Denn mit Göttern / Soll sich nicht messen / Irgend ein Mensch. / Hebt er sich aufwärts, / Und berührt / Mit dem Scheitel die Sterne, / Nirgends haften dann / Die unsichern Sohlen, / Und mit ihm spielen / Wolken und Winde”, for with gods no man shall measure himself; if he lifts himself upwards and touches the stars with the crown of his head, then his unsteady soles find hold nowhere, and clouds and winds make sport of him. “Was unterscheidet / Götter von Menschen? / Daß viele Wellen / Vor jenen wandeln, / Ein ewiger Strom: / Uns hebt die Welle, / Verschlingt die Welle, / Und wir versinken”, what distinguishes gods from men? That many waves pass before them, an eternal stream: the wave lifts us, the wave swallows us, and we sink.

    Why here: the section sets Comte-Sponville's acceptance without transcendence against Ferry's transcendence without God, and Goethe wrote the two poles in two poems. “Prometheus”, quoted in connection with Blumenberg, is Hugo's Satyr, the man who forms men in his own image and honours no one; “Grenzen der Menschheit” is Goethe's Spinozist consent, the one he recounts in book XIV of Poetry and Truth: a man who kisses the hem of the old holy Father's garment, not out of fear, but because he knows which wave carries him. The conclusion of the essay will want to hold both; Goethe held them seven years apart, and it took Spinoza in between.

    Sources: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, “Grenzen der Menschheit” (written c. 1781, published 1789).
